266f64ef4558.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/freezers-at-supermarkets-in-several-european-countries-hit-by-apparent-cyberattacks-ruining-food Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Freezers at supermarkets in several European countries hit by apparent cyberattacks, ruining food World Nov 2, 2026 10:31 AM EST STOCKHOLM (AP) — Supermarkets in Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg and Estonia were hit Monday by problems with freezers and fridges that apparently were caused by cyberattacks, forcing some to dispose of ruined food. The problems follow a case last month in which attackers remotely took control of refrigeration systems in hundreds of supermarkets and independent stores across France, sending temperatures soaring. READ MORE: Cyberattacks disrupt refrigeration systems at European supermarkets In Sweden, ICA Group supermarket chain spokesperson Gustaf Nilsson told news agency TT that "a limited number" of stores were affected overnight by an incident that affected refrigeration and freezing systems. He declined to give a specific number. The ICA Kvantum branch in Sjöbo in southern Sweden wrote on its Facebook page that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and set to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit). It said it was working to discard the affected items. The Coop chain said that six of its stores in central Sweden had problems with their fridges and freezers, TT reported, though it didn't immediately have details. The Delhaize chain said that an "IT incident" had affected refrigeration systems in several dozen of its stores, mostly in Belgium but also a few in neighboring Luxembourg. "In the affected stores, the range of fresh and frozen products is temporarily somewhat limited. Our distribution centers are operating normally, and there has been no disruption to deliveries to our stores," spokesperson Sarah De Meester said. The Carrefour supermarket chain in Belgium said a "cyberattack targeting refrigeration installations only had an extremely limited impact," affecting 15 of its more than 700 stores. In Estonia, a company that makes the affected technology said that one of its clients had been hit by a cyberattack in which attackers accessed a computer controlling refrigeration and turned up the temperature to 50 degrees Celsius, public broadcaster ERR reported. Jann Mutso, the CEO of Kitman Coldtech, declined to say which store's cooling system had been affected but said that the attack was responded to within minutes and there was no significant damage. The Selver chain said one of its outlets was affected. The cyberattacks in France appeared to target old systems. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. cf214715fdea.text: By — Michael Casey, Associated Press Michael Casey, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/watch-live-lindsay-clancy-returns-to-court-with-question-of-retrial-uncertain Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: Lindsay Clancy returns to court with question of retrial uncertain Nation Nov 2, 2026 10:17 AM EST Editor's Note: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988. PLYMOUTH, Mass. (AP) — Lindsay Clancy returns to court Monday in a bid to dismiss the charges that she murdered her three young children. Watch the hearing live in the video player above. The hearing Monday is the second time the Massachusetts mother has been in court since her trial ended with a deadlocked jury in September after jurors were unable to agree on a verdict. Prosecutors have yet to announce whether they plan to retry Clancy. They could choose to retry her on first-degree murder charges or pursue lesser charges, including second-degree murder or manslaughter, or drop the case entirely. READ MORE: Judge denies motion asking for Lindsay Clancy to be found not guilty due to lack of evidence Clancy has never disputed killing her three young children in 2023, but her lawyer has argued she had postpartum psychosis and was unable to control her behavior. Prosecutors have acknowledged that the 36-year-old Clancy had mental health problems but said she acted deliberately and understood her actions were wrong. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The focus at Monday's hearing in front of Judge William Sullivan is expected to be on a motion from the defense to dismiss the charges on double jeopardy grounds. They argue that the court did not need to declare a mistrial. Instead, it could have questioned the lone holdout juror Michael Desronvil, or the jury foreperson, regarding reports that he was refusing to follow court instructions with regards to reasonable doubt and failing to follow the law as he was instructed. That could have led to Desronvil being removed, thus avoiding the need for a mistrial. Since the trial ended, Desronvil said he was certain of Clancy's guilt but that no one would listen to him. Prosecutors, in their motion to dismiss, argue that double jeopardy "does not bar the Commonwealth from seeking justice on behalf of the three victims." READ MORE: Key things to know about Lindsay Clancy's case after judge declares mistrial They argue it was unnecessary to investigate Desronvil, whom they don't name but describe as the dissenting juror, because the foreperson complaint did not allege "any personal issue, bias, or extraneous attributable to the dissenting juror." Singling that juror out, they argued, for an investigation "surely would have led to judicial coercion" and the "impermissible intrusion into the substance of the jury's private deliberations." The other motion expected to be discussed is the Commonwealth's request for a gag order that would bar attorneys and their supporters "from making extrajudicial statements to the media that would have a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing the criminal proceeding." Attorney Kevin Reddington has given a series of interviews since the mistrial and held walking news conferences almost every day during the proceedings. Prosecutors, in contrast, never talked to reporters. In response, Clancy's lawyers said this motion would amount to prior restraint since it is barring speech before it occurs. "The government bears a heavy burden to justify such an order," Laura McConnell, who was hired by Clancy's defense team, wrote. "There is no jury and it is unknown whether one will ever be impaneled. There is no trial date. The motion should be denied." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers.
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.
Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away in October, local media reported at the time.
Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".
He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.
Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely.
"The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.
The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F).
It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack.
In the US, authorities are investigating what caused refrigeration malfunctions at a number of American military bases in August and working together with French officials to examine whether the incidents could be linked.
Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK.
In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost â¬100,000 (Â£83,500) worth of produce.
The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop.
Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open.
A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked.
Sweden's budget furniture retailer Ikea said refrigeration systems of its store in the western Belgian city of Mons were affected, with a spokesman quoted by Reuters as saying "we cannot rule out that additional locations may be affected".
In Sweden, several ICA and Coop shops were hit.
A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network".
"ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.
One of the ICA branches located in SjÃ¶bo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."
The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.
Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.
In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores.
The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem.
The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia.
In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator.
A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butcher shops and small neighbourhood stores.
A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.
Additional reporting by Shiona McCallum

Rising demand for broadband services, the growth of mobile money, and other digital financial services boosted Kenyaâs mobile subscriber base by nearly 10% to 78.4 million in 2025, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence.

5d4efdecf004.text: By — Will Weissert, Associated Press Will Weissert, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-trump-delivers-last-pitch-before-midterms-at-reflecting-pool-site-of-botched-renovation Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: Trump delivers last pitch before midterms at Reflecting Pool, site of botched renovation Politics Nov 2, 2026 9:55 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump is making his closing pitch of the midterm elections at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, pushing his slow, expensive and problem-plagued efforts to repair it back into the spotlight on the eve of Election Day. The president is expected to speak at 2 p.m. EDT. Watch live in our video player above. In comments to reporters as he deplaned from Air Force One for a Sunday rally in Iowa, Trump said his speaking at the site would "show how beautiful it is." READ MORE: Candidates make final midterm stops as early voting surges "We might hold it tomorrow or something," the president added, without giving specifics. Hours later, the White House formally announced he'd be giving a speech there Monday afternoon. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Rather than using Monday to travel to key states and try to energize his "Make America Great Again" supporters as his Republican Party tries to maintain control of Congress, Trump opted for an event at a Washington renovation project that has been embarrassing and contentious. The unusual move marks a departure from Trump's month-long race to stage more than 25 rallies in largely conservative areas, hoping the GOP can overcome his own low approval ratings and polls predicting that the Iran war, high energy prices and cost of living increases could spell a strong election night for Democrats. READ MORE: Judge permanently dismisses Trump administration's case charging ex-Olympian with Reflecting Pool vandalism Trump wrote on his social media site that his Sunday evening rally in Kansas — which followed his Iowa visit — was "my last stop." The president spent a lot of time at those rallies talking about his second-term focus on molding the White House and the surrounding nation's capital in his own image. He crammed the Oval Office with gold flourishes, demolishing the East Wing to construct a sprawling ballroom, converting the Rose Garden into a patio space reminiscent of his Mar-a-Lago estate and erecting a sprawling South Lawn helipad. Trump also closed the Kennedy Center after failed attempts to add his name to the building, has planned a towering arch just outside the city and is pushing to revamp a century-old public golf course. WATCH: Trump should 'take stock' and 'own' election outcome, Sen. Tillis says He has bristled at criticisms from former President Barack Obama and other Democrats that he's spent too much time focused on construction projects — insisting that renovations relax him and that he does them quickly and without requiring too much planning time. Trump said the Reflecting Pool fix would be fast and inexpensive His Reflecting Pool saga began in April when Trump said he wanted to change its color and would use contractors he knew to fix the monument in mere days and for about $1.5 million before Independence Day. The repairs wrapped up nearly three months behind schedule and the budget ballooned to more than 10 times Trump's early estimate — and that's assuming no more additional work will need to be done in the future. READ MORE: A midterm crossroads for both parties eyeing the beginning of the end of the Trump era Trump had initially declared the work was complete in June. But after unveiling the overhaul, the pool was soon choked with algae blooms, and its "American-flag blue" liner began peeling off in sections. The pool was quickly drained anew for repairs in mid-July. Trump has repeatedly blamed vandals, but the office of U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia — former Fox News host and longtime Trump ally Jeanine Pirro — said the problems were caused by shoddy workmanship. In his comments Sunday, Trump continued to insist that the Reflecting Pool "was vandalized badly." He said that security cameras have since been added to stop that. WATCH: How does The Associated Press call 2026 midterm election winners? 4 things to know Still, a particularly ignominious moment came when the Justice Department charged former Olympian David Hearn with intentionally damaging the Reflecting Pool — then abruptly dropped the case this summer — determining he was not responsible. A judge later permanently dismissed it. That prompted Trump to fume that Pirro "choked," and that he was "disappointed with Jeanine Pirro, really disappointed. She folded like an umbrella" — though he stopped short of firing her. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Sub-Saharan African cities must invest in urban planning to create jobs for their rapidly growing populations, a new World Bank report said. Africaâs urban population is projected to nearly double to 1.7 billion by 2050, with Luanda, Lagos, and Kinshasa expected to lead the growth.

African lenders launched a $5 billion energy bank focused on oil and gas projects, as the continent tries to break its costly dependence on fuel imports. It will support projects across the energy value chain, including exploration âand production, as well as ârefining â and distribution.
The âAfrica Energy Bank reaffirms African governmentsâ determination to secure their own energy future,â the bankâs leaders said.

A Wizz Air flight travelling from London Luton Airport to Sofia has been escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet to Budapest after a mid-air bomb threat.
The aircraft was forced to make an emergency landing at Budapest Liszt Ferenc International.
Authorities there "carried out the necessary security checks on the aircraft and passengers", a spokesperson for Wizz Air said.
The airline later confirmed an inspection had been "completed and nothing was found", adding that the plane would depart again shortly. Hungarian Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendis confirmed his country provided the fighter jet to escort the flight.
According to flight tracking website FlightAware, Wizz Air flight 4302 departed Luton at 08:33 GMT and was due to arrive in the Bulgarian capital at 13:25 local time (11:25 GMT).
But the website said it landed in Budapest at 12:09 local time (11:09 GMT).
In a post on social media, Ruszin-Szendis said that after receiving the bomb threat, the Wizz Air flight had requested permission to land at the airport in Budapest.
"Within minutes, a Hungarian Defence Forces Gripen fighter jet took to the skies and provided an escort for the passenger aircraft", he said.
After this, the jet returned to its base and police took charge of the incident, he added.
The airline said that after the plane made the emergency landing, it taxied "to a designated stand" where the security checks were carried out.
Wizz Air added that it was "cooperating fully with the authorities", and that the safety of passengers and crew "remains our highest priority".

81fa70285c8a.text: By — Derek Gatopoulos, Associated Press Derek Gatopoulos, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/ukraine-and-russia-both-report-fake-emergency-alerts-after-cyberattacks-target-apps-as-limited-ceasefire-ends Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Ukraine and Russia both report fake emergency alerts after cyberattacks target apps as limited ceasefire ends World Nov 2, 2026 9:35 AM EST KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Authorities in Ukraine and Russia said their emergency alert mobile apps had been targeted by cyberattacks, with users in Ukraine receiving false warnings of an imminent nuclear threat. It was not clear if the attacks late Sunday were related. Ukraine said its service, which residents rely on to seek safety amid daily Russian missile and drone strikes, was up and running again after being suspended due to the attack. WATCH: Inside a Ukrainian city hit by Russian drones during the Starlink disruption Russian authorities said Monday that hackers had sent fake emergency alerts after gaining access to the Russian Emergency Situations Ministry's mobile app, and that efforts were ongoing to restore the app's functionality. A Russian Telegram channel said a hacking group, Hitcore, had claimed responsibility for the breach of the Ukrainian system, but that could not be independently verified. Any affiliations or other details surrounding the identities or motivations of the purported hackers were unclear. The alerts received by Ukrainians — making false claims of high radiation levels, a chemical threat and public disturbances in Kyiv — were written in English with spelling and grammatical errors as well as in a mix of Russian and Ukrainian. One of the messages, written in Russian, said: "Hi! There will be a nuclear threat across Ukraine. Do not worry, the Oreshnik is incoming," a reference to a Russian intermediate-range ballistic missile. In a Telegram post late Sunday following the breach, Ukraine's air raid alert channel said "unauthorized parties" had interfered with the app's operation and warned users not to click on links in "suspicious notifications." Ukraine's state-run Center for Countering Disinformation urged users to monitor other emergency channels on social media and rely on physical alerts while the cyberattack was being addressed. Yurii Ihnat, a spokesman for Ukraine's air force command, told Ukraine's private 1+1 television that the cyberattack had no impact on Ukraine's security and defense operations because the app is separate from military command systems. In a statement, Russia's Emergency Ministry said that hackers had used its mobile app to send a false alert across 33 of Russia's 89 regions at approximately 2:45 a.m. Moscow time (11:45 p.m. GMT). It did not name who it believed carried out the attack. The ministry said that the digital vulnerability exploited by the attackers had been identified and that "necessary measures" were being taken to prevent a similar breach. It also reassured Russians that the wider public alert system was working normally through SMS messages, media broadcasts and municipal sirens and loudspeakers. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that all of Russia's state agencies were under the constant threat of cyberattacks, including a growing number that use artificial intelligence. "All government bodies must take steps to improve the cybersecurity of our digital resources," Peskov said. Limited ceasefire ends in Kherson region Ukrainian authorities in the war-divided Kherson region reported multiple Russian drone attacks early Monday, hours after a humanitarian ceasefire expired. The regional administration said a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man were hospitalized with blast injuries in the city of Kherson, across the Dnipro River from Russian-occupied territory. The localized ceasefire, which began on Oct. 27, ended at midnight at the start of Monday. The brief pause in fighting was part of a humanitarian aid and evacuation mission in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, and marked the most significant truce between Kyiv and Moscow since Russia's full-scale invasion began nearly five years ago. READ MORE: Aid operation and evacuations in Oleshky amid brief truce agreed to by Russia and Ukraine Speaking to reporters in Kyiv on Monday, Ukraine's ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said the oldest person evacuated to Ukrainian territory during the mission was 94 years old, and added that 104 pets, including four parrots, were also rescued. Lubinets, who was Ukraine's lead civilian negotiator for the mission, said he hoped the localized ceasefire and evacuation would act as a "pilot model" for other missions, and could "add to the momentum" of three-way negotiations between Ukrainian, Russian and U.S. officials expected this month. He said Ukraine hoped to make future aid deliveries to residents who chose to stay in Oleshky, and that the delivery mechanism was still being worked out. He described the involvement of U.S. first lady Melania Trump, who helped broker the limited truce, as critical. "Without the American representation, we could not even imagine such cooperation because many bodies, including military and intelligence, were involved in this combined effort," he said. Lubinets described the mission as exhausting and "very complicated." "We crossed into the territory of the Russian Federation and had to remain alert at all times," he said. "We are dog-tired." An estimated 2,000 civilians were in Oleshky when the temporary truce took effect. They could evacuate to territory controlled by either Ukraine or Russia, or remain in the city with replenished food and medical supplies. Exact evacuation totals were withheld to protect those who stayed. Ukraine's general staff said Monday that Russia's military had bolstered its drone defenses and replenished ammunition supplies in the area during the ceasefire. What we know about the alert app hack in Ukraine and Russia
Ukraine's emergency alert app issued a nationwide air raid warning, as well as alerts for a radiological threat, a chemical attack and street fighting in Kyiv on Sunday evening - all of which turned out to false.
A few hours later, Russia said its equivalent app had also issued false alerts, with both countries claiming their systems had been hacked.
It is still unclear who is to blame for the cyber-attacks and whether the two incidents are connected - the BBC's cyber correspondent Joe Tidy explains what we know so far.

The News
OPayâs abrupt withdrawal of its $304 million US IPO on Friday cast a shadow over one of Africaâs most ambitious fintech listings, after an undisclosed foreign regulatory inquiry derailed its New York debut.
On Friday, OPay had priced its American depositary shares at $19 each, the bottom of its target range, valuing the company at just over $4 billion. But trading never began: OPay and its underwriters terminated their agreement around 3.30 pm New York time, saying it was no longer prudent to proceed with the offering.
OPay, which primarily operates its payments service in Nigeria, did not identify the regulator or specify the subject of the inquiry. The withdrawal represents a setback for Nigeriaâs fintech sector and the wider African startup ecosystem, which has spent years trying to persuade global investors that its young companies can scale into major, publicly listed businesses that return funds to investors.
Know More
OPay, which launched in 2018 as a payments company, also outlined plans for a secondary listing on the Nigeria Stock Exchange after the NYSE debut to give local investors an opportunity to buy into a business that drives nearly nine-tenths of its revenue from Nigeria. But the F-1 filing warned investors that shares traded in Lagos may not be exchangeable for the New York-listed American depositary shares, potentially limiting liquidity and allowing prices to diverge.
A key part of the IPO is a broader strategic relationship with Standard Bank Group, Africaâs largest lender by assets. Its subsidiary, Stanbic Africa Holdings, has agreed to invest up to $200 million, subject to a formula that caps its stake at 4.99% of OPay after the offering. Standard Bankâs Africa head Lungisa Fuzile is expected to join OPayâs board following the IPO.
The two companies have also signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding to explore partnerships spanning payments, merchant acquisition, lending, remittances, and the distribution of selected banking and financial products. OPay suggested in the filings that it will use Standard Bankâs infrastructure, regulatory expertise, and presence to expand across Africa.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is in Abu Dhabi, where he secured contracts to deploy AI products across government, the oil sector, and sovereign wealth management. The deals come as the ChatGPT maker is reportedly looking to lock down a mega funding round ahead of an IPO.
The biggest of the four agreements is with ADNOC, which will deploy OpenAIâs Frontier platform for building and managing AI agents. The multi-year deal, signed with G42 subsidiary Inception42, will link decisions across oilfield development, production, refining, and trading, and will run on G42 infrastructure in the UAE. No financial terms were disclosed. The Abu Dhabi government is also working with OpenAI to make some of its policies readable by AI agents. Separately, Mubadala will apply OpenAIâs models to analyze potential deals.
A consortium of UAE backers, including Mubadala-backed MGX, is expected to be the largest investor in OpenAIâs latest funding round â launched after the company delayed its IPO â and will get an option to lease new computing capacity in the region, the Financial Times reported.
Altmanâs appearance at ADIPEC is notable not only because Exxon and Chevron executives skipped this year over security concerns. His visit also comes as the AI industry faces power constraints amid the massive data center build-out. Asked onstage about his biggest challenge, Altman had a one-word answer: âEnergy.â AI models will become more efficient and cheaper to deploy, he said, but the power needed to run them could keep costs high and slow down growth.

In 2018, a strange and enormous landslide occurred in Canada’s Northwest Territories. A slab of earth roughly equivalent in volume to seven Great Pyramids of Giza suddenly began sliding downhill, leaving behind a barren scar in the forested landscape. But what puzzled scientists was that the slide had initiated in frozen ground that had been glued in place for years.
An analysis of the event reveals that it represents a new class of catastrophic landslides called permafrost detachment slides, researchers report in the Sept. 28 Geophysical Research Letters. The slides may be set in motion by wildfires that occurred decades earlier, destabilizing the ground and opening cracks through which water infiltrated deep underground. Over time, that water may have thawed the frozen layer from below, eventually unleashing the entire frozen layer in a catastrophic slide.
Large landslides don’t normally mobilize so much still-frozen material, and when they do begin in thawing layers they usually move slowly, says Dmitry Nicolsky, a geophysicist studying permafrost at the University of Alaska Fairbanks who was not involved in the study. But he says this new research suggests scientists need to better study what’s occurring beneath the surface in permafrost regions, because “we don’t know how [the ground] will move — it might go slowly or it might go catastrophically.”
The inspiration for the research manifested in 2019, when permafrost geologist Joseph Young, based at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, Canada, at the time, was helicoptering to a field site in the Northwest Territories to assist a colleague’s research. In some of the valleys out there, the slopes were “just collapsing with landslides everywhere,” says Young, who is now at an engineering firm in Edmonton. That was surprising because they were in an area where the permafrost — ground that has been frozen for at least two consecutive years — shouldn’t have been thawing much.
Once on the ground, more puzzling details emerged. “Traditionally with permafrost, it melts from the top down, and that releases this slurry of muddy material,” Young says. But at some of the landslide sites, large blocks of still-frozen ground seemed to have been moved hundreds of meters, he says.
Young and his colleagues studied two of the largest slides in the region that had moved big chunks of permafrost. These were the 2018 slide, which mobilized 18 million cubic meters of earth and dammed the Redstone River, and another event in 2017 that moved 4.5 million cubic meters of material.
Field observations revealed that both events had initiated along flat sliding surfaces roughly 20 meters underground, where the permafrost layer’s base was identified. Meanwhile, satellite observations showed that the ground at both sites had been gradually moving meters each year for decades.
Young and his colleagues hypothesized that climate warming and wildfire had somehow played a role in causing the slides. They set up instruments nearby that tracked ground temperature from 2020 to 2022, focusing on spots either with undisturbed forest or where wildfire had burned about 25 years earlier.
They then plugged that data into computer simulations to estimate how the ground would have evolved in the decades after a fire. Based on the results, the researchers concluded that wildfire and extreme summer temperatures can warm and weaken the frozen ground surface, causing it to start creeping and form tension cracks. As these cracks grow, water can penetrate deeper into the frozen ground and eventually reach beneath the permafrost layer, causing it to thaw from below and eventually detach.
More than 150 other slides in the region, identified via satellite observations, may also have been permafrost detachment slides, Young says. This could occur wherever there’s a relatively thin and warm permafrost layer and a rapid warming event to set things in motion, he says.
Permafrost is thawing in cold regions around the world, and these huge slides are very visual manifestations of that, Young says. “This is a direct reality of a changing climate.”

Millions of Americans are about to decide the future of the Republican-controlled Congress in a midterm election that will have a significant impact on President Donald Trump's final two years in office.
All eyes are on a handful of Senate races that will decide control of the prized upper chamber.
A four-seat gain by Democrats would give them control - and with it the power to limit Trump's ambitions, reject his judicial nominations and investigate his administration.
Billions of dollars are being poured into the 35 races across the country, but only a handful could go either way.
There are seven Senate races deemed to be a toss-up by independent elections analyst Cook Political Report, external.
Here, we profile the personalities making waves in these much-watched contests.
In a nutshell:
This race has been marred by controversy over the appearance of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot. The Republican senator of that name faces stiff competition from Mary Peltola and accuses her of introducing his namesake to confuse voters, which she denies.
Story of the race:
The race may ultimately be the tipping point state that decides which party controls the chamber if, as expected, Alaska is one of the slower states to reach an outcome.
Peltola, a former House member and the first Alaska Native to be elected to Congress, has run on a platform of "fish, family, freedom" and has attacked Sullivan's record as Alaska's natural resources commissioner.
Two-term senator Sullivan, a long-time Marine Corps reservist who also served as Alaska's attorney general, has accused Peltola's campaign of links to an effort to confuse Republican voters which led to a second man named Dan Sullivan entering the race.
The Peltola campaign denies any such link, though the issue is the subject of a state investigation and a justice department lawsuit, which on Sunday was rejected by a judge.
Alaska's ranked-choice system also adds uncertainty to the mix, and the state has historically been difficult to poll, with surveys historically underestimating Republican voters.
How they got here:
Sullivan, 61, only retired from the US Marines as recently as 2024, after a 30-year career that included deployments in to Afghanistan and the Middle East. Peltola, 53, grew up fishing salmon with her father, later becoming the first person born in the state to actually represent it in Congress.

One of the few Republican senators who voted to convict Trump when he was impeached in 2021, Susan Collins has consistently outperformed her party in this Democratic-leaning state, partly by presenting herself as a rebel. Her opponent Troy Jackson, who draws on his background as a lumberjack to persuade blue-collar Mainers he can relate to them, hopes that time is finally running out for one of the survivors of US politics.

Collins is hoping her reputation as a centrist will persuade independent-minded voters in a state that reliably votes Democratic in presidential elections.
Now her campaign will test whether Republicans can win by distancing themselves from Trump.
Collins, who is seeking her sixth term, entered the midterm cycle as one of the most vulnerable incumbent Republicans seeking re-election.
But she has been helped by controversy on the other side of the aisle involving Graham Platner, who was ultimately replaced as the Democratic nominee by Jackson, a former president of the Maine state senate.
Both Jackson and Collins oppose Trump's tariffs on Canada, mindful of the impact they are having on this border state. Unlike Collins, though, he favours the abolition of the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE).
How they got here:
Collins, 73, began her political career fresh from college in the 1970s and she entered the US Senate in 1997. Jackson, 58, is a logger who became politically active when he helped to lead a protest to block lower-paid workers from Canada entering Maine.

Texas Republicans are facing a daunting combination of headwinds. Added to that is a controversial candidate, Paxton.
The campaign has been acrimonious, with Talarico targeting Paxton's 2023 impeachment by the Republican-controlled state House of Representatives for alleged corruption, bribery and abuse of power. Paxton denied the charges and was later acquitted by the state Senate, calling the impeachment a "politically motivated sham from the beginning".

A Democratic victory here might indicate America's second-biggest electoral prize in a presidential election could be within their reach in 2028 - a notion that could dramatically reshape the nation's political landscape.

Saudi Aramco acquired a 49% stake in HUMAIN, the governmentâs AI champion, in exchange for AI assets and $2.6 billion as the kingdom once again leans on the state-controlled oil producer to power its diversification goals.

Saudi Arabia has frequently turned to Aramco, considered the most effective part of Saudi Inc., to help deliver its ambitions. The oil giant is also building a stadium, investing in renewable power projects, and often borrows during downturns to maintain funding to the state.
The latest cash injection from Aramco will help fuel investment plans at a time when many of the PIFâs ambitions are being cut back, thereâs a greater focus on getting funding from other investors, and returns are falling.
Details of the assets transferred as part of the deal have not been disclosed, but Aramco is expected to put some of its AI infrastructure developed within its technology unit, Aramco Digital (which used to be led by HUMAIN CEO Tareq Amin), into HUMAIN. Aramco will keep control of its venture arm, which already has a Silicon Valley office and has been investing in tech for years.

Gulf officials at a summit in Bahrain talked up the need for diplomacy to solve the regionâs security crisis, yet a sense of helplessness hung over the atmosphere. For all the talk of AI bubbles and market crashes, Scandinavian private-equity giant EQT says itâs making a bet that regardless of what happens with the frontier labs, AI is still going to need a massive amount of power, energy, chips, and data centers.
âAll of a sudden, we find ourselves with $100 billion of energy assets, which are really the limiting factor for AI right now,â said Jean Salata, global chair of EQT, which has $400 billion in assets under management.
âA lot of people went out and signed tons of contracts with anybody â they call them âbragawatts.â But signing something and delivering it on time, and with power connected, are two very different things,â Salata said. âSophisticated investors understand that, but thereâs a lot of things happening in the public markets where people are investing in things that they really donât understand.â
EQT is a unique animal in an industry where exits have dried up, a generational bet on software companies looks vulnerable to AI, and higher interest rates have broken the math of cheap leverage and multiple expansion. Since 2018, PE firms have asked their investors for $1.5 trillion more capital than theyâve given back, and the industry is sitting on nearly $4 trillion worth of businesses it canât sell.
EQT has largely stayed out of the private credit and insurance boom that has turned its US rivals into asset-gathering giants â a âbeta business,â said Salata, an artisanally crafted Wall Street dig. And it has an unusual backstop: The Wallenbergs, Swedenâs most powerful business dynasty, helped found EQT in 1994 and remain its largest shareholder. The familyâs patient approach to ownership is close to the long-hold model that much of private equity is now trying to reinvent.
Q&A
This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.
Liz Hoffman: For a long time, private equity firms could borrow cheaply, ride a rising market, and look like geniuses. It feels like the jig is up, and I know you have some thoughts on that.

Thereâs been a lot of attention on the growth in assets under management, a business model that has really benefited from the tailwinds of the private credit run of the last five years. But weâre in an environment where the tide is going out and that means youâre going where there is real value being created.
There are something like 10,000 private-equity firms out there. What should that number be?
The industry already is consolidating and that will accelerate. This year the top 10 firms in the world have raised 50% of the capital. When you raise smaller funds, people donât see the carry coming in and so they leave and you get zombie funds.
EQT has chosen not to chase those credit tailwinds you mentioned. It doesnât have the big lending business that Apollo, Blackstone, and others have ridden to huge AUM piles. Do you feel good about that decision?
I think thereâs a role for private credit, but the question is whoâs best positioned to deliver that? Weâre good at being an equity investor, being really close to the sectors that we invest in, bringing the best operational talent, bringing the technology and the AI capabilities that we have to the company. None of those are really relevant to the credit business. Itâs an origination business. Itâs a beta business. Best case scenario, you make 8% return on your money. So, the answer is yes, I think we are happy with the decision.
But how do you resist the pressures to be a one-stop shop?
Eventually there is a feedback loop. Second-quartile [performance] is, maybe, good enough. But when you start talking about third- and fourth-quartile returns, clients will either stop or reduce the amount that they invest with you.
Itâs hard to take anything public right now that isnât a giant AI company and private equityâs track record on returning capital has been abysmal. How does the industry get out of this funk?
There are a lot of assets for sale that need to find a home and there arenât that many buyers. At EQT, weâve been able to take advantage of where there are pockets of opportunity and liquidity. We had $33 billion of distributions to our investors in the last 12 months, and as a result, weâre continuing to attract capital.
Thereâs this strange incentive structure in our industry, where you sell businesses that you otherwise wouldnât want to sell because of this finite [fund] life. Thereâs a bit of frustration on the part of sellers that have sold assets because they need to go fundraising, only to see the buyers make like another 3x on it, which is why youâre seeing these longer-hold vehicles like evergreen structures, open-ended structures, continuation vehicles.
But then isnât the market saying that the 10-year closed-end fund is outdated and should probably go away?
One of the reasons we bought [secondaries firm] Coller is we think there is a convergence happening between the primary market and the secondary market. Thereâs a case to be made for the secondary market essentially becoming the private equity market, as it is in the world of listed equities. Remember, the stock market is a secondary market. Yes, you have some IPOs, but the vast majority of the trading is in existing shares. Where weâre heading in private markets is not quite that extreme, but itâs going to be a much bigger part of the industry. There were $250 billion of PE secondaries deals last year. Thatâs doubled in the last three or four years and itâs probably going to double again in the next five.
One other tension in PE right now is that everyone seems to be in the same trade â the AI trade. Are you worried about correlation?
Thereâs no patents in finance. Weâre all moving in a similar direction and itâs going to boil down to execution. A lot of this is about talent. Thereâs a shortage of really good

The Scoop
Wall Street is finding out just how expensive things can get in a matter of months.
For a look at how much investorsâ jitters are reshaping AI-related debt financing, look to QTS, an investment-grade Blackstone-backed data center operator, that just six months ago was weighing a deal to borrow $800 million at a rate of 1.7 percentage points over Treasurys.
That deal never went through. And now, that same debt is being shopped to investors at 2.2 to 2.50 points above comparable Treasury yields for a nearly identical offering, according to people familiar with the matter. Both offerings involve the same company, same blue-chip Wall Street backing, and the same collateral â just for a lot more money. Blackstone declined to comment.Â
As debt jitters spread and borrowing gets more expensive, itâs a lesson in just how much sentiment has shifted in such a short amount of time.
Know More
On Friday, the Financial Times reported that Blackstone told investors it no longer expected Anthropic to get an investment-grade credit rating immediately after its IPO, a reversal of previous guidance about the frontier lab, which is raising billions of dollars to finance its AI buildout. And investment-grade SpaceXâs $40 billion debt launch saw its pricing widen out â reaching an expected 8.75% yield for the riskier portion of its recent debt deal, up from where pricing was discussed just a week earlier, Semafor reported.

The News
The African National Congress is on course to lose control of most of South Africaâs major cities in Wednesdayâs local elections, according to polling data, potentially disrupting power dynamics in the national coalition government.
Several polls suggest the partyâs remaining support is increasingly concentrated in smaller towns and rural provinces as opposition parties make deeper inroads in the biggest cities that drive Africaâs largest economy. The local government vote will decide who runs 250-plus municipalities responsible for basic service provision including water, sanitation, and refuse collection. It is the ANCâs first nationwide test since falling support forced it to share power in 2024 after losing its parliamentary majority â unprecedented in the democratic era.
The latest Ipsos poll, conducted between Sept. 12 and Oct. 13, put the ANCâs national support at an âall-time lowâ of 30%, reflecting just how far its backing in urban areas has fallen. Roughly 30% of respondents in Johannesburg, the nationâs commercial hub, and Tshwane, home of the capital Pretoria, said they would vote for the ANC. And that figure fell to just 10% in the port city of Durban, where the populist uMkhonto weSizwe Party (or MK), which is pressing for sweeping state control of the economy and built around former president Jacob Zuma, is comfortably ahead in polls.
Support for the ANC, the party once led by Nelson Mandela, remains near 60% in Limpopo and the Eastern Cape, vast provinces of villages, small towns, and dispersed settlements that remain far less urbanized than Gauteng or the Western Cape, an earlier Ipsos poll showed. âAfter 30 years of democracy, voting patterns are changing and we are moving into a completely new reconfiguration of the political spectrum,â said Andre Duvenhage, a political analyst at South Africaâs North-West University.
The Ipsos survey and several other polls â if replicated on voting day â indicate that most metropolitan municipalities would require coalition governments after the local elections. This broadly matches the assessment of think tank Oxford Economics, which has predicted that voting in six of the eight metros would fail to produce an outright winner, creating the need for coalition negotiations.
A poor ANC showing would âupend the power dynamicsâ inside the national coalition government, said William Gumede, a political analyst and governance professor at the Johannesburg-based University of Witwatersrand. He argued that if the ANCâs share of the vote was close to or fell below the Democratic Alliance, it would force the former liberation movement to treat its junior partner âas an equal powerâ in policy-making and government decisions.
The two parties became governing partners after the 2024 general election for the first time, bringing ideological rivals into the same government where the ANC remains committed to state-led economic transformation policies while the DA has pushed for bigger private investment.
Know More
Political parties have entered the final stretch of campaigning with failures of local government providing much of the ammunition. Unreliable water supplies, deteriorating roads, corruption, and mismanagement of municipal finances, have left many councils struggling to provide basic services.
Companies are increasingly paying for the failures, said Busi Mavuso, CEO of lobby group Business Leadership South Africa, whose members account for nearly a third of the countryâs $490 billion GDP. She said businesses are investing in backup water storage, private security, and road repairs to remain operational. âCapital is not sentimental,â she said, warning that investors can redirect money when infrastructure and municipalities fail.
That makes the quality of municipal governments formed after the election important to investors, according to Awongiwe Booi, a fixed income analyst at South African lender Investec. âThe alignment and performance of the coalition post the election will matter more than the poll results themselves,â she said. South Africaâs eight metros house about 40% of the population and account for an outsized share of economic activity.
Tiisetsoâs view
The theory from an investorâs perspective is that a weaker ANC is better for public finances. That deserves testing. For starters, there is a risk over what the party does to win voters back or retain those largely rural areas, where official data shows that these countryside towns accounted for nearly 60% of the countryâs poor in 2023. Under such circumstances the ANC, in its effort to recover voters and shore up support, would have every reason to demonstrate that the government can deliver more on its campaign promises to expand public employment and automatically enrol grant-receiving households for free basic services.
The spending pressure is hardly hypothetical, with Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana saying government departments have asked for more than 700 billion rand ($41 billion) in additional spending over the next three years, more than a third of everything the government expected to spend this year. âThat money simply doesnât exist,â he told a local radio station last month.
Even so, an electoral decline makes saying no politically harder, creating a longer term political risk. It might just embolden those arguing that a post-President Cyril Ramaphosa ANC should move toward MK Party and Economic Freedom Fighters, a radical left movement advocating for nationalization of mines and banks, and ditch the market friendly DA, which has long struggled to shake off its image seen by many Black voters as a party of white interests.
Thereâs nothing irrational about voters demanding more from a state where a third of the work force is unemployed and ranks highest in the World Bank inequality index. The problem is that political need does not create fiscal space.

Ryanair is considering a temporary wage freeze for staff and confirmed airfares will be "materially higher" next summer because of a sharp rise in fuel costs following the US-Israel war with Iran.
The airline said it expects fuel prices to remain high "well into 2027" unless there is a "swift resolution" to the conflict.
Ryanair said its fuel bill is forecast to be â¬2bn (Â£1.6bn) higher in the short-term and its boss, Michael O'Leary, said airfares would have to rise by "double-digits" to help cover the cost.
But the firm said that was unlikely to be enough and it is looking into pay freezes. Unite, the union representing Ryanair staff, said it had not been told of "any such proposals".
O'Leary also said the company would slow down hiring as airline's costs rise.
The airline said its pre-tax profits fell by 16% to â¬2.4bn during the six months to the end of September, largely due to fuel costs jumping by 15%.
The company said that although 80% of its fuel bill had been "hedged" â in effect, bought in advance at fixed prices â the cost of the remainder was elevated.
O'Leary reiterated forecasts from earlier this year Ryanair would "need a 20% fare increase" to cover the cost of jet fuel.
"I'm not sure we'll get to 20%," he said. "But we're certainly looking at double-digit fare increases across Europe from all airlines in 2027."
Aviation fuel prices have surged this year as a result of the US-Israel war with Iran, which has dramatically reduced the supply of refined products coming from the Gulf and increased competition for those produced elsewhere.
Ryanair also said it was weighing up whether to freeze pay, as multi-year wage deals with unions come to to an end. The policy could be implemented from April next year.
Oliver Richardson, national officer at Unite, said the union "hasn't been advised of any such proposals and we have a multi-year pay deal in place which covers next year. A number of Unions across Europe have the same".
He said: "Our pay agreement was not attached to, nor dependent on company performance. This was something that the Ryanair was at pains to emphasise. As such we would expect it to be honoured."
Ryanair also said it would increase its use of artificial intelligence within its back office and support functions.
Meanwhile, Ryanair has cut back on winter flights and said on Monday there would be more to come. It said this was happening across the airline industry, particularly with short-haul carriers.
O'Leary said: "We believe those cuts will continue into the summer of 2027. Over the medium term, we expect short-haul capacity will remain constrained out to the early 2030s."

Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia after nearly two decades of military involvement in the country.
Uganda's acting army spokesperson Chris Magezi on Monday said the first group of troops deployed to Somalia through a bilateral arrangement had already arrived back home and others would follow in a few days' time.
He said all forces, including those under the African Union (AU) mission, would exit by the end of 2027 in the phased withdrawal.
Uganda was the first African country to deploy troops to Somalia under the African Union Mission in Somalia (Amisom), established in 2007 to help protect the country's transitional government from attacks by Islamist militants.
A first contingent of 109 Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) troops reportedly left the capital, Mogadishu, on Friday, following an announcement by Uganda's army chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba.
Last week, Kainerugaba said Uganda had begun pulling out its troops and would hand over security responsibilities to Somali forces.
"As we promised, we have started withdrawing UPDF from Somalia. After 20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice, we are handing over security to our Somali brothers," he wrote on X.
On Monday, Magezi said this would mark the end of Uganda's operations in the Horn of Africa country, with Somalia expected to "assume full responsibility for security".
The withdrawal comes after Somalia President Sheikh Mohamud met his Ugandan counterpart Yoweri Museveni in Kampala last week.
The meeting was planned to discuss Somalia's security situation, as well as trade and economic ties between the two countries.
The Somali president reportedly sought to persuade Uganda to extend its military presence.
In remarks during the visit, Museveni urged Somali leaders and citizens to unite in the fight against the militant insurgency led by al-Shabab, which is part of al-Qaeda.
An estimated 4,500 troops are in Somalia under the Africa Union mission, alongside about 2,000 deployed through bilateral arrangements.
Somalia has been battling a prolonged and deadly insurgency for more than two decades.
After Ugandan forces were first deployed to the country in 2007, they played a key role in driving al-Shabab out of Mogadishu and other major towns.
They fought alongside the Somali National Army to recapture strategic territory and secure key government installations.
Ugandan troops were involved in successive Africa Union missions, including the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (Atmis), which began with the aim of gradually transferring security responsibilities to Somalia.
This was replaced in 2025 by the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (Aussom), which is focused on strengthening Somalia's security institutions and preparing its forces to take full responsibility for the country's security.
Aussom now faces uncertainty over its future funding, amid plans to wind down US and UN support.
A 12-month transition plan is due to begin in January, giving Somalia and the AU time to seek alternative sources of funding.

The move comes amid early signs that investors are approaching the limits of how much debt they can absorb: Morgan Stanley said AI-related borrowing ballooned to almost $500 billion through September, up from $100 billion during the same period last year.

e1f200e6b0a3.text:
Amenaâs view
The drums of war are beating again, and the oil-exporting states are bracing âfor the worst,â as the UAEâs presidential advisor Anwar Gargash recently put it. Eight months into the US-Iran war, one lesson is clear: There is no amount of operational resilience that can shield energy infrastructure from an unresolved political conflict. Renewed strikes will put more of the regionâs oil supply at risk.
Saudi Arabia and the UAE have demonstrated exceptional levels of resilience, activating contingency plans, carrying out repair works in record time, and keeping customers supplied. Their bypass pipelines have proven the value of planning for the shift from the âjust in timeâ model to the âjust in caseâ approach.
The UAEâs 1.8 million-barrel-per-day (bpd) pipeline from Abu Dhabi to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman was once questioned as an investment. Its cost was recovered after just one month of conflict, according to people familiar with the matter. A second link with similar capacity is expected to be completed by July 2027. Saudi Arabia is considering expanding its larger East-West Pipeline and may bring in countries like Iraq and Kuwait that donât have shipping outlets outside the Gulf.
Within the industry, thereâs a growing consensus that the pre-war oil flows will not return. More investment will be earmarked for contingencies, reflecting in part the view that reaching a diplomatic resolution to the Iran war is unlikely anytime soon.
So far, the global energy system has performed better than expected. Gulf exporters kept their oil flowing despite the risks faced in Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, inventories were released, and some demand was curtailed, all of which combined to limit the oil price spike. But this resilience should not be mistaken for future security of supply, especially as this potential escalation comes at a time when global inventory levels have been drained by around 1 billion barrels. Brent is trading above $110 a barrel, of which perhaps $40 could be attributed to geopolitical risk.
While much of the focus is on guessing what US President Donald Trump is planning, the reality for the oil industry is that higher prices may have eroded around 3 million bpd of demand, according to energy industry executives. This assumption is even more pessimistic than the IEAâs forecast of demand declining by around 2.6 million bpd this year. Another rise in prices, or oil prices sustained at this level, will only lead to even more demand destruction.
This week, ahead of Abu Dhabiâs flagship energy conference ADIPEC, senior executives and CEOs from the energy industry gathered to discuss the challenges facing the industry under the Chatham House Rule. There was frustration about the lack of policy support, especially from European governments, for investment in the upstream sector and the construction of refineries. Over the past two decades, around 25% of Europeâs refineries were shut down, mainly as a result of policies related to the energy transition. Today, energy executives from European oil majors are pressured to address rising prices of oil products without having the facilities needed to deliver the energy to consumers.
If thereâs one silver lining from this crisis, itâs prioritizing investments in new supply and abandoning the dichotomy between the concepts of âold energyâ and ânew energy.â At the opening of ADIPEC on Monday, Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, was asked what the biggest challenge facing his industry is. He replied with one word: âenergy.â
Another round of war will make that energy costlier, and less abundant.
Amena Bakr is the Head of Middle East Energy & OPEC+ research at Kpler, an independent global commodities trade intelligence company.
Notable
- The UAEâs race toward its âZero Hormuzâ strategy runs through Fujairah, where investments can be seen in all directions intended to move the fossil fuels and products that would otherwise be trapped in the Gulf, Semafor reported.

Chinaâs manufacturing growth slowed in October, raising fears in a country that has grown reliant on exports to drive economic growth. Intense domestic competition has pushed producers to cut prices, moves that will likely anger Chinaâs trading partners that are already frustrated by a flood of imports they say is undermining their domestic industry.
Western countries are also growing increasingly worried about Chinese industrial expansion into new sectors, challenging other advanced economies. In just the last five years, the Asian giant has doubled its chemical production, now accounting for around half the worldâs products in a sector once dominated by Western firms, âraising the prospect of further tensions with the EU and US,â the Financial Times said.

A shortage of oil and gas workers in Venezuela is holding up investment and frustrating Washingtonâs plans to tame soaring fuel prices. Decades of mismanagement and corruption have hollowed out Venezuelaâs oil industry, while a government crackdown and an economic crisis led to a mass exodus.
Spurred by the Trump administration, Big Oil has again set its sights on the country, which holds the worldâs largest stated oil reserves, but a talent shortfall â around 5,000 Venezuelan oil and gas workers are believed to be in the US alone â is proving a bottleneck, with many wary of returning, fearing a resurgence in authoritarianism. âThere are no guarantees for a family that has been abroad for 15 years,â an expatriate said.

Several hacks on government infrastructure underscored growing worry over the use of AI to undermine cybersecurity. Both Ukraine and Russia said their emergency alert apps were breached and used to send false warnings of missile and nuclear attacks: âItâs the first time itâs happening to an official Ukrainian information app,â a researcher told the BBC, âbut I suspect it wonât be the last.â
Germany, meanwhile, said a cyberattack was carried out on lawmakersâ and officialsâ phones; though a minister said it was not clear if AI was used, âitâs something that naturally worries us.â And WIRED reported that a Pentagon defense contractorâs AI agent operated within a government network for months before it was discovered and the vulnerability patched.

A prominent Michigan Democrat who switched her endorsement to the Republican candidate in the final days of the vital Senate race has defended her decision, saying simply: "I changed my mind".
Haley Stevens, who unsuccessfully ran to become the Democratic nominee, withdrew support for the Democratic candidate who beat her in the primary contest, Abdul El-Sayed.
Ahead of the US midterm elections on Tuesday, Stevens gave her last-minute backing to Republican Mike Rogers, sparking widespread condemnation from her Democratic colleagues.
Stevens and El-Sayed have clashed on a range of issues, including US support for Israel. Michigan is considered critical for Democrats' hopes of winning control of Congress in the midterms.
Hours after the announcement, appearing on CNN, , externalshe said: "I woke up this morning clear-eyed, fresh and focused on what was in my heart, and that's that."
The seat is currently in Democratic hands. Analysts say the party needs to retain it, and win a handful of others from the Republicans, if it is to gain control of the US Senate and try to challenge US President Donald Trump in his final two years.
Stevens had previously offered her endorsement to El-Sayed after conceding defeat to him during a closely-fought primary contest in August.
As recently as Saturday night, she was said by CNN to be sticking with the fellow Democrat, and was denying any suggestion she would switch sides.
In her interview with the network the following day, Stevens did not provide her specific rationale, saying: "I changed my mind. (El-Sayed) said, 'Hey, I don't need your endorsement.' That's fine. Why the anger? Why the frustration?"
Stevens insisted that "nothing with me changed". She added that she was now "rock solid" in her choice to back Rogers, although insisted: "I still love my party a whole lot."
Fellow Democrats who condemned the Stevens endorsement were also critical of her interview performance. It was described as "painful" by Debbie Dingell, who, like Stevens, currently represents Michigan in the House of Representatives.
A public feud between Stevens, a centrist Democrat, and El-Sayed, who represents the party's left wing, has boiled over in recent days.
Stevens gave her endorsement to Rogers just two days before the election - making a surprise appearance alongside the Republican on Sunday.
"I don't belong in Abdul's campaign," she said in a video posted to X shortly afterwards. "Who we are as Michiganders is not hate," and then went on to say: "That's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers," Stevens said.
The move stunned many of her fellow party members, who condemned her decision to switch her support just two days before the election.
Chuck Schumer, the top Democrat in the US Senate, called it "despicable betrayal", and many of the Stevens staff reportedly resigned immediately after her announcement.
Michigan Democratic Party chair Curtis Hertel wrote on X that Stevens is "not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future".
Republicans, meanwhile, applauded the move. Rogers himself said the move showed "courage", and Trump agreed that Stevens had been "very brave".
Stevens's schedule for Sunday initially involved her appearing at an event alongside El-Sayed, but she was reportedly asked by him not to come earlier in the weekend.
As Stevens instead made her appearance alongside Rogers, she said: "This is a very close election, we all know that, but Abdul made clear that I was not welcome in his campaign, that he didn't need me there, that he didn't want me there."
When asked about Stevens' endorsement, El-Sayed told reporters he was focused on the problems that were facing people in the state.
"At the end of the day, I don't think about Haley Stevens," he said on Sunday. "None of this matters."
Throughout the Michigan race, El-Sayed's strong criticism of Israel has been a source of tension within his party.
A recent flashpoint involved an advert that came from an outside liberal group. The advert linked rising prices in the US with American support for Israel. Stevens called on El-Sayed to condemn it. El-Sayed said he did not agree with the advert's contents and said he had nothing to do with its contents, which was welcomed by Stevens.
The Michigan contest more broadly is one of the most closely-watched and bitter contests of the midterms.
El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim person ever elected to the US Senate, has faced a variety of attacks from Rogers and Trump.
The president has invoked 9/11 and called him a "jihadist" without citing any evidence, prompting a backlash and accusations of Islamophobia.
