The haze billowing out from wildfires in the Indonesian regions of Kalimantan, Papua and Sumatra knows no borders.
Carried by winds to nearby Singapore and Malaysia, the toxic smog has in recent weeks impacted populations across maritime South East Asia, triggering respiratory illnesses and headaches.
It's also giving the region's governments a different kind of headache - split between the mounting frustrations of their citizens and the risk of souring diplomatic ties with Indonesia.
"People are fed up, angry and anxious," Eugene Tan, associate professor of law at the Singapore Management University, tells the BBC. "The governments have to respond to them, or else what is more an external issue has become an internal one with ample headroom for politicisation."
Indonesia's wildfires are a yearly occurrence, widely associated with industrial-scale land clearing to make way for crops like oil palm.
But the blazes this year have been particularly difficult to tame due to a strong El NiÃ±o, which has exacerbated drought conditions in the country's forests and peatlands.
Whereas previous haze episodes in Singapore and Malaysia have typically lasted for a few days, this time it stretched into weeks.
In Malaysia, locals started a boycott of Indonesian products in protest against the haze, after lawmaker Syed Saddiq called for sanctions on companies linked to the wildfires and said Malaysians should "treat them as an outcast in the region".
There have also been complaints in Singapore, a country that has come to expect seamless efficiency from its leaders.
"There appears to be the view that the government dropped the ball in dealing with the haze, given that it was known that the El NiÃ±o weather phenomenon would be severe and that early warning was given," says Tan.
"Clearly, Singaporeans expect the government to decisively deal with the polluters."
A diplomatic dilemma
Singapore's government, for its part, has made it clear that the haze problem is a priority.
Hundreds of haze shelters have been set up across the island, and masks are being distributed to children, the elderly and other vulnerable residents.
Authorities have also said they're looking to strengthen existing haze legislation and are investigating 10 Singapore-registered companies for potential links to the wildfires in Indonesia.
Last week, Singapore's foreign minister Vivian Balakrishnan met Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto in Jakarta for what the former described as "honest" and "sincere" conversations that produced "constructive approaches".
The meeting came as both countries announced they would set up a joint task force to deal with the haze - an apparent dÃ©tente after weeks of simmering bilateral tensions.
As the haze spiralled into yet another crisis for Prabowo's beleaguered administration, some officials pushed back against criticism.
One senior official ruffled feathers when he said the wildfires were out of human control and that oxygen in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia "also comes from our forests".
That remark was "disappointing" and "not right", according to Singaporean senior minister K Shanmugam - a rare rebuke from the city state, which prides itself on its diplomatic prowess.
"The haze is affecting our health seriously, and it's really unacceptable," Shanmugam told reporters. Since the haze impacts citizens on both sides of the border, there should not be "any bilateral issues" in addressing it, he added.
"The Indonesian public is suffering as well, and it is in Indonesia's interest as much as ours to deal with the companies that are causing these problems."
Days later, Indonesia announced it would reduce gas exports to Singapore, citing domestic energy needs - a move that many saw as retaliation to Singapore's rhetoric.
To be sure, Indonesia has faced recent electricity shortages in parts of the country. Singapore also says the reduction, which amounts to less than 2% of its total daily demand, will have little impact on its gas supply.
But the abrupt announcement came just days after Indonesia's energy minister warned that they could halt gas exports to countries that don't "respect Indonesia". That same day, Prabowo made reference to "countries that like to insult Indonesia" when talking about the wildfires.
"It's a tired playbook of using Singapore as the bogeyman, driven by the 'abang-adik' [big brother-little brother] syndrome," Tan says, referring to a historical dynamic that Singapore's leaders have long tried to shrug off: the expectation that it should defer to its larger neighbours.
"Singapore leaders expressing concerns about the haze and how it affects the people of both countries have been taken to mean that Singapore has been disrespectful to its neighbour."
Waiting for winds to change
In contrast, Malaysia's official rhetoric on the haze has been relatively muted.
Its foreign minister Mohamad Hasan has ruled out lodging a formal diplomatic protest with Indonesia or taking legal action, saying such actions "would mean we were prepared to sever relations".
For now, Malaysia has agreed to explore a memorandum of understanding with Indonesia to strengthen wildfire prevention efforts.
It would also rely on diplomatic mechanisms, Mohamad said - like the Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.
The agreement, which came into effect in 2003, commits members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) to collaborate on tackling the recurring haze.
But many see it as toothless, as it is unable to punish agricultural companies linked to wildfires or to force individual governments to do so.
The agreement has turned out to be "just not worth the paper it was signed on", says James Chin, professor of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania.
"The moment the haze disappears, the moment the political pressure's off, it's back to business as usual."

Calls are being made for the defence of the Shetland Isles to be strengthened after increased sightings of Russian trawlers off the coast of Scotland.
Recent analysis by the Daily Telegraph, external also revealed that there have been more than 500 incidents where Russian boats have been stationed above undersea cables linking Britain with Europe and the US.
These cables carry the majority of telecoms data abroad.
The growing importance of undersea infrastructure prompted a parliamentary report, external last year to warn of security vulnerabilities in areas including transport and supply chains, financial services and payment systems.
There are also concerns that the Â£30m SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland could be a Russian target.
But do the Shetland Isles really need better protection by the military?
Why are there concerns now?
In recent years there have been a number of incidents in the Baltic Sea where underwater cables have been damaged or completely cut.
In December last year, Finnish police detained a vessel sailing from Russia, which was suspected of damaging an undersea telecoms cable running from Helsinki to Estonia, across the Gulf of Finland.
In 2022, Shetland was cut off from the mainland after a nearby subsea cable was damaged.
And last year there were two cable breaks in Shetland, which disrupted internet services and, in one case, took weeks to repair.
There has been no suggestion that there was any Russian involvement in the Shetland incidents but they demonstrate how fragile the cables are and show the devastating effect on the islanders when they are damaged.
In July, Royal Navy warships and helicopters spent 21 days monitoring Russian activity in UK waters and the North Atlantic - this was a 25% increase on previous time spent monitoring.
The recent Telegraph revelation of more than 500 incidents where Russian boats have been stationed above undersea cables has also caused concern.
What is the history of Shetland's defences?
Jon Sandison, a high school history teacher and Shetland tour guide, said there were real concerns that Shetland could be attacked after Germany invaded Norway in 1940, during World War Two.
"Shetland could have been a stepping stone towards Orkney and mainland Scotland," he said.
There were many army, naval and RAF personnel stationed across the isles and coastal defences were built to defend Lerwick and the rest of the archipelago.
The SaxaVord Spaceport sits on a former RAF base and RAF Skaw played an important role in efforts to detect enemy aircraft from 1941.
RAF Saxa Vord was later involved in Nato's radar network to monitor Soviet activity during the Cold War.
The radar station closed in 2006 but it was revived in 2018 for Arctic surveillance as an automated remote radar head.
Sandison said that while military presence reduced in the second half of the 20th Century, Shetland's geographical position would never change.
"Where we are in the UK is always going to be a pivotal geographical location in relation to the North Sea, the Arctic Circle and wider scope of Britain," he said.
He added that coastal infrastructure was built very quickly during the Second World War.
"Air raid shelters, anti-aircraft defences - it's remarkable how much was built in a short space of time," he added.
"Not much of the infrastructure remains. It's part of our history, and part of our past."
What are the politicians saying?
First Minister John Swinney has accused the UK government of leaving "Scotland's vast coastline dangerously exposed".
He pointed to waters off Shetland as an area of significant Russian activity.
"I don't think we've got nearly the presence in those areas that we require today," he told BBC Scotland News.
Liberal Democrat MP Alistair Carmichael, whose constituency covers Shetland, has urged the UK government to step up efforts to protect critical infrastructure.
He told the BBC's Radio Scotland Breakfast programme: "This is something we do need to be taking seriously.
"We're not expecting an imminent problem here but this is a time where the government is already telling us that we should all be keeping baked beans and a wind-up torch in a cupboard."
Carmichael added that if the world had changed so much, some of the decisions made by the UK government to remove military presence from the northern isles may now need to be looked at again.
He said that over the last 20 years, there had been just one local full-time soldier running a reserved unit in Shetland but they were now managed from the Scottish mainland.
Carmichael said there should be restoration of a full-time presence to support the unit and more reserves should be recruited in the northern isles as numbers were low.
But he added: "If the signal that the government is sending the community is that we don't even think its important enough to send one full-time solider to run these units then you can't expect the community themselves to be particularly enthusiastic about it."
What is the significance of the spaceport?
SaxaVord in Unst is the UK's first fully-licensed spaceport with several companies interested in using the site to launch small satellites into orbit.
In September, the UK government announced investment of Â£30m in the project, as part of a new Â£7.8bn space strategy.
Alistair Carmichael said the spaceport would draw more attention to Shetland as a significant asset.
The German and UK governments plan to use SaxaVord to deepen their co-operation on space.
In October, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor Friedrich Merz met in Berlin and announced plans to work more closely on economic growth, defence and technology.
SaxaVord Spaceport was identified as a focus for immediate work on European launches.
Two German companies are currently in a race to be the first to test a rocket in Shetland.
Chief executive Scott Hammond said: "The space strategy is absolutely critical.
"We're at the heart of the UK government's plans for assured access to space.

f4fd0a24d661.text: A federal judge on the eve of Election Day barred the Trump administration from demanding California officials set aside ballots from registered voters it suspects are noncitizens, finding the effort likely violates the Constitution. Why it matters: Courts had already rejected the Justice Department's attempts to force California to separate the ballots. Monday's ruling goes a step further, directly barring federal officials from making those demands even as DOJ turns to the Supreme Court to compel the state to comply. Driving the news: Chief U.S. District Judge James Boasberg ruled Monday that the Trump administration likely violated the Constitution by pressuring California officials to change how they count ballots. His order prohibits the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security from demanding officials set aside ballots or depart from existing state election procedures based on federal lists of suspected noncitizens. Boasberg found that the Constitution gives states and Congress, but not the executive branch, authority over election rules. The federal ban on noncitizen voting does not mean the administration can rewrite those rules. By the numbers: The DOJ claims it identified more than 20,000 suspected noncitizens on California's voter rolls. After Boasberg ordered DOJ to turn over its list, an expert found that at least 22 members of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights — all known U.S. citizens — were wrongly included. The expert found another 66 members were almost certainly on the list. Boasberg found the expert credible and concluded the list's errors posed a real threat to eligible voters. What he's saying: "The President evidently believes that it would be good public policy for more stringent procedures to be put in place," Boasberg wrote. "No matter how strong that policy case may be, however, it does not justify overstepping the bounds of the Executive Branch's limited constitutional authority in this domain." The White House referred Axios to the Department of Homeland Security for comment. DHS and the Justice Department did not immediately respond to Axios' requests for comment. Catch up quick: In a separate lawsuit , DOJ sought to force California and Los Angeles County to segregate ballots from suspected noncitizens. A federal judge rejected that request Wednesday, as did an appeals court on Friday. Monday's ruling is different in that it restricts the federal government from making its demands rather than simply refusing to order California to comply. It also follows a broader nationwide temporary restraining order Friday that prohibits similar demands and threats of prosecution against election workers. Yes, but: Boasberg did not prohibit federal officials from investigating illegal voting or compiling lists of suspected noncitizens. Federal law makes it a crime for noncitizens to vote in federal elections, and DOJ can prosecute people who knowingly break that law. But that doesn't give DOJ the authority to order states to change how they verify voter eligibility or count ballots, Boasberg wrote. California can continue following its election procedures while federal prosecutors pursue illegal voting, Boasberg said. What's next: The Supreme Court could still order California to set aside the disputed ballots.

Republican Gov. Greg Abbott has scrambled to revise his earlier pro-data center policies, while his Democratic opponent has pledged a stringent moratorium, which could affect about 29% of the net capacity additions planned nationally for 2028.
While roughly 300-plus state and local moratoriums are threatening the US buildout, governmentsâ ambitions to harness the AI boom elsewhere are also facing hurdles: The developer of a massive data center in the Australian outback scrapped its construction timeline after the regulator extended its review period, and Singapore-linked projects in Indonesia have run into stiff opposition from environmentally concerned locals.

27e64d66ae0f.text: By — Maria Briceño, PolitiFact Maria Briceño, PolitiFact Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/palm-beach-plane-crash-footage-isnt-ai-generated-despite-social-media-claims Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Palm Beach plane crash footage isn't AI-generated, despite social media claims Nation Nov 2, 2026 5:24 PM EST This article originally appeared on PolitiFact. Footage from Palm Beach County, Florida, shows a plane nosediving into the ground at full speed, cratering the pavement, and dissolving into fire and smoke. It looks unreal. So unreal that some social media users say it's fake. "The Video You're All Seeing From The 'Plane' Crash Was 100% Ai Generated SOMEONE IS LYING TO US !!!!!! That Was Not An Airplane," read a Nov. 1 X post sharing video of what looks like an AI detection video analysis. "Notice How The Ai Detector Only Detects Ai Generated Content From The 'Plane.'" Other X posts also questioned the footage's veracity. But the crash happened and the video has been corroborated by legitimate news outlets. A business jet, a Learjet 60, was headed to the Bahamas from Austin, Texas, when it crashed into a neighborhood near Cresthaven, Florida, at approximately 12:51 p.m. ET, on Nov. 1. Everyone on board died, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Nov. 1. The authorities have not said what caused the crash, but Tom Chapman, a member of the National Transportation Safety Board, said Nov. 2 that the aircraft experienced turbulence and encountered ice. The incident is under investigation, he said at a press conference that day. Timothy Monville, who's leading the investigation into the crash for the safety board, said the federal agency has "just begun" documenting the incident. "We have a lot of work to do on scene," he said. "This will be a several-day process, and the biggest obstacle that we're going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway." The crash footage has been shared by The Associated Press, CNN, CBS News and BBC. We also found its original source, Aki Kuusisto, a digital creator from West Palm Beach, who first shared the clip on Facebook. "This was not quite what I had in mind when I installed the dash cam," Kuusisto said in the post's comments. The X posts show screen recordings of the clip being submitted to Hive Moderation, an AI-detection tool. The recordings show the tool's analysis reporting that it detected AI-generated content in the clip. Hive Moderation is an imperfect tool and PolitiFact has used it before. However, when we introduced Kuusisto's footage to the tool, it didn't flag it as AI-generated or manipulated. Flames rise following an aircraft incident in Palm Beach County, Florida, on Nov. 1, 2026, in this still image obtained from video. Photo by Eduin Cruz via Reuters Darren Linvill, co-director of the Media Forensics Hub at Clemson University, told PolitiFact people are right to be skeptical of viral videos as AI improves. But some people have grown so distrustful of AI they're disbelieving the truth, a phenomenon known as the "liar's dividend." "This is when people are so accustomed to being lied to, they don't know the truth when it is presented to them," Linvill said. "That is what is occurring with the video of the Palm Beach crash." It's not surprising the crash was captured on camera considering how abundant personal recording devices are today. But Linvill added that people should get their news from reliable sources. One of the X accounts that questioned the veracity of the plane crash footage, for example, has been amplified by bot accounts that promote narratives by Russian Storm-1516, a campaign that uses Russian and non-Russian influencers to promote false claims in the U.S. and other countries. Our ruling An X post said footage of Nov. 1 plane crash in Palm Beach County, Florida, "was 100%" generated with artificial intelligence News outlets have shared the dash cam footage confirming the video's veracity. An AI expert told PolitiFact that although the video is dramatic and frightening, it is authentic. We rate this claim Pants on Fire! A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. f04a20fcb362.text: By — Hannah Grabenstein Hannah Grabenstein Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/why-health-insurance-premiums-are-rising-according-to-experts Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Why health insurance premiums are rising, according to experts Nation Nov 2, 2026 5:09 PM EST Like groceries, gas and other everyday necessities, annual premiums for employer-provided healthcare coverage are expected to rise sharply next year, with workers shouldering more of the costs. Analysts predict that premiums will jump as much as 9.5% in 2027, though experts say the resulting costs may not be as high as projected. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. This year, the average cost of an employer-based family healthcare plan was $28,303. That amounted to a 5% increase from 2025, a KFF analysis found. And workers contributed on average 9% more than last year, or around $7,470 annually. "Many people with job-based coverage have real affordability issues," said Matthew Rae, associate director of the KFF's healthcare marketplace program. WATCH: Health care costs a major concern for voters ahead of midterms Americans pay high prices for healthcare in general, said Meredith Rosenthal, professor of health economics and policy at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. That's both relative to actual costs for delivering care, like drugs and medical tests, as well as to what other developed nations pay. Over the last five years, while inflation, wages and healthcare premiums have all increased at roughly the same rate, workers still contributed around a quarter of the premiums for their employer-provided family health insurance. KFF also found that 44% of large firms that offer health benefits said they increased employee contributions as the cost of insurance rose. Here are three reasons why the cost of healthcare is rising for the 157 million Americans who get their insurance through work. Providers are charging patients more for care Fifteen years ago, average premiums for family coverage were lower — totaling $15,220, with workers contributing about $4,190. While experts told PBS News that the rise in premiums is due to both long-term and more recent factors, one cause that can be largely ruled out is insurer markups, said Zack Cooper, associate professor of public health and economics at Yale University. In 2011, insurers imposed an average markup of about 19%. By 2024, that was down to nearly 15%. In reality, prices are the main reason for the high cost of health insurance in the U.S., Rosenthal said. Health spending accounted for 91% of the growth in average premiums between 2011 and 2024, Cooper's work has found. Tariffs and high energy prices affect healthcare providers, he said. Providers, like hospitals and pharmaceutical companies, also set their own prices without much regulation, Rosenthal said. That means competition in the market is the primary mechanism for keeping prices down, which "mostly does not work very well," she added. Because Medicare is able to negotiate some costs, the price of an MRI in the private market is about double what Medicare pays, she said. A related issue is the relative lack of antitrust regulation, Cooper said, adding that more hospitals and physician practices are consolidating each year. More than 1,000 hospitals merged between 2002 and 2020, but the Federal Trade Commission took enforcement in only 13 instances, according to a 2024 study Cooper co-authored. "Those mergers generally benefit the parties merging, but don't really bring much benefit to the public," who often see prices go up, particularly when the companies used to be competitors, Cooper said. "Fundamentally, if you want to get premiums under control, you've got to get healthcare spending under control," he added. People are getting more care Hospital costs are negotiated over long periods of time, Rae said, so spikes in spending can be more accurately attributed to people using more healthcare. Why are people getting more care? It's not totally clear, Cooper said. One possible explanation is that insurance companies are reacting to public pushback over prior authorizations by relying on them less, he said. "When you dial back prior authorizations, utilization goes up," he said. More people also used prescription drugs in 2025 than in 2019, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The population is also aging, which is accompanied by more chronic conditions and more sickness. That's more of a longer-term driver for increased healthcare spending, Rae said. The GLP-1 factor GLP-1 agonists, which can manage or treat conditions like diabetes and obesity, are still relatively new, under patent and in high demand — a perfect storm for sky-high prices, experts said. READ MORE: In the gray world of GLP-1 supplements online, health experts urge caution These breakthrough drugs aren't the only emerging medical technology to break the bank. Specialty pharmaceuticals, like promising new cancer treatments, are also often expensive, Rosenthal said. "Specialty pharmaceuticals in the last decade have been a really important driver of overall healthcare spending. It's a small share of total spending, but it's growing more rapidly," she said. A Gallup poll in July found 15% of Americans have ever used a GLP-1 medication for weight loss, while 11% were currently using one of the meds in 2026 — up from 3% in 2024. The nation's obesity rate reflects the growing uptake, Gallup found. While almost 40% of Americans had obesity in 2022, the rate ticked down to 36.8% this year. The rate of people who have been diagnosed with diabetes remained steady at 12.8%. Employers often don't cover GLP-1 drugs, KFF found. Fewer than 1 in 5 companies with 200 or more employees

7f246d0cc989.text: By — Mike Stobbe, Associated Press Mike Stobbe, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/washington-state-resident-dies-from-bird-flu-following-exposure-to-infected-cattle Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Washington state resident dies from bird flu following exposure to infected cattle Health Nov 2, 2026 5:04 PM EST NEW YORK (AP) — A person in Washington state has died from complications of the bird flu, the first such U.S. death in a year. The Yakima County resident, who had previous health conditions, was exposed to avian influenza at a dairy with infected cattle and had been hospitalized. The person died Sunday, county health officials said. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Two other U.S. deaths have been tied to bird flu since it became a national public health concern in 2024. The first, announced in January 2025, was an elderly person in Louisiana who had a version of bird flu known as H5N1. The other, in Washington state, died in November 2025 from a rarer version called H5N5. Yakima County officials did not release any additional details about the person who recently died. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said the person was infected with H5N1. County officials have reported that 33 dairy herds recently have tested positive for H5N1. They say three human infections have been linked to exposure at a dairy, and that the Yakima Health District is working with the state health department to find people who were in close contact with those people and monitor them for symptoms. The H5N1 bird flu has been spreading widely among wild birds, poultry, cows and other animals for several years. Health concerns escalated in early 2024 when infections spread among U.S. livestock. Its presence in the environment increases the chances that people will be exposed, and potentially catch it, officials have said. More than 70 human infections have been reported in the U.S. since the beginning of 2024, according to the CDC. But there is no known person-to-person spread and the risk to the general public is low, the agency says. The agency analyzed the genetic sequence of the virus from the person who died in Washington and found no changes that would make the virus spread more easily or cause more severe illness, a CDC spokesperson said Monday. Officials continue to urge people who have contact with sick or dead birds to take precautions, including wearing respiratory and eye protection and gloves when handling poultry. People who work on farms are considered to be at higher risk. The Associated Press' health and science coverage receives financial support from the AP Fund for Journalism and private foundations. The News
US President Donald Trump plans to remove South Africa and Rwanda from African Growth and Opportunity Act eligibility next year, stripping both countries of duty-free access to the US market under Washingtonâs flagship Africa trade program.
Trump formally notified Congress and both governments of his decision, the Office of the US Trade Representative said Monday, after an annual review determined Pretoria and Kigali have been engaging in âconcerning and pervasiveâ practices inconsistent with AGOAâs eligibility criteria. These include âbarriers that undermine American trade and investmentâ and practices that âpose a threat to US national security and foreign policy interests in the region,â US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said.
The statement also cited corruption in South Africa, while its concerns about Rwanda extended to the rule of law, political pluralism, and human rights. The decision follows months of US tension with both governments. Washington has clashed with Pretoria over Trumpâs claims of a âgenocideâ against white South Africans, which experts have dismissed, and is ending PEPFAR aid to the country. South Africa hoped to use its critical mineral resources as leverage in trade talks.
South African Trade Minister Parks Tau said the âdecision does not define the broader relationshipâ between the countries and that South Africa would continue pursuing trade, investment and shared economic opportunities with the US. The trade ministry said it had offered additional concessions and called it âunfortunate that the US is now raising new issues that have not been the basis for discussions.â
With Rwanda, the dispute centers on the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo: The US sanctioned Rwandaâs military in March and its defense ministry last week, accusing them of backing M23 rebels and using minerals from rebel-held territory in their supply chains.
Know More
South Africa has the most to lose as AGOAâs largest beneficiary, exporting about $1.7 billion worth of goods under the program in 2025, including vehicles and agricultural products. Rwandaâs exposure is far smaller, with US imports from the country totaling about $44 million last year. Standard trade will continue, but affected exports could become more expensive, and the damage may spread across southern Africa and impact thousands of jobs.
âThe loss of AGOA will reverberate through the SADC region as several countries, including Lesotho and Botswana, are part of the South African supply chain that provides goods and products for the US under AGOA,â said Witney Schneidman, a former US deputy assistant secretary of state for African affairs.
AGOA, established in 2000, is authorized only through the end of 2028, and Schneidman said this episode highlights the need to modernize it. âChina, the EU and South Africaâs other partners donât turn their trade relations âon and offâ as the US does,â he said.

6d2674c85c76.text: By — Philip Marcelo, Associated Press Philip Marcelo, Associated Press By — Michael Casey, Associated Press Michael Casey, Associated Press By — Christopher Weber, Associated Press Christopher Weber, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/flash-flooding-triggers-evacuations-in-southwest-and-a-dire-warning-for-a-colorado-spa-town Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Flash flooding triggers evacuations in Southwest and a dire warning for a Colorado spa town Nation Nov 2, 2026 4:32 PM EST Heavy rainfall produced flash flooding and mandatory evacuations in a swath of the Southwest on Sunday, including in a Colorado tourist town bracing for its main river to rise to historic levels, as weary residents in the normally arid region deal with another massive drenching. Officials in Pagosa Springs, a town of more than 2,000 in the Rockies located near ski resorts and known for its hot springs, warned of potentially "catastrophic flooding" as the San Juan River was forecast to crest at more than 20 feet (6.1 meters) late Sunday night. "To put the forecast into perspective, during the devastating 1911 flood that wiped out most of what existed as the town of Pagosa at that time, the San Juan River crested at approximately 17.8 feet (5.4 meters)," the Archuleta County Sheriff's Office said in a Facebook post. "This is a potentially catastrophic flood event." Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. By sundown Sunday, the river's crest had reached about 14 feet (4.2 meters), according to Vicky Schaffer, a spokesperson for the county. Roads in and out of the town were closed and residents who weren't under evacuation orders were urged to stay home. Communities in northern New Mexico and central Arizona, meanwhile, also issued mandatory evacuations while the rains forced the closure of several highways. READ MORE: Is El Niño making storms and flash floods in the Southwest worse? In the picturesque town of Sedona, Arizona, officials ordered residents near Oak Creek to leave immediately as floodwaters trapped multiple people in their homes. Arizona expects months' worth of rain in a couple of days This aerial photo provided by Sky Yazzie shows flooding in Flagstaff, Arizona, on Sunday. Photo by Sky Yazzie via AP Nearby Yavapai County and the community of Camp Verde issued similar evacuation orders for residents living near swollen rivers and creeks. More than 100 miles (160 kilometers) southeast of Sedona, officials in Gila County ordered the total evacuation of Gisela, a community of several hundred residents along Tonto Creek. The wet conditions even produced flash floods, river flooding and swift boat rescues in Tucson, some 230 miles (370 kilometers) south of Sedona. "We are getting two or three months of rain in a span of a couple of days," said Aaron Hardin, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Tucson. Rain fell nearly nonstop Sunday in Flagstaff, Arizona, flooding local roads and overwhelming storm drains. Authorities were searching for a man who slipped and fell into fast-moving floodwaters "and was not seen resurfacing," according to a police statement Sunday evening. Outside Our Lady of Guadalupe Church, people filled plastic bags with sand to try to prevent further flooding inside. Luke Willson said water got into the garage, the basement and underneath the church building, as well as in an office where the computers are. "The pumps are pumping, but they're not pumping fast enough," he said. To the southeast, in the Pinetop-Lakeside area of central Arizona, "manhole covers are popping up all over" and residents reported sewage backing up into homes because of flooding, the region's sanitary district said in a statement. The latest round of soaking rains started Saturday evening and was expected to saturate the region through Monday. The weather service estimates as much as 4 inches (10 centimeters) of rain could fall across the region, fueled by a series of Pacific storm systems. The weather service issued flood warnings and watches for nearly all of Arizona and parts of southern Utah, southwestern Colorado and western New Mexico, in addition to part of southern Nevada. That includes the sparsely populated Four Corners region where the states meet. The weather service office for Salt Lake City said previous storms already soaked places like Zion and Capitol Reef National Parks, warning that could worsen flooding and "backcountry roads will likely become impassable from this excessive runoff." Roads into Colorado tourist town closed Officials in Pagosa Springs said anyone in low-lying areas along the San Juan, Rio Blanco, Navajo and Piedra rivers should head to a designated shelter at a local church. They advised residents not to wait to leave their homes as emergency crews may be extremely limited during the worst of the storm. The highway entering town also was closed to inbound traffic, and residents were advised to avoid contact with the San Juan River after sewage was discharged into it. Katie German, owner and chef of Bruin Coffee in Pagosa Springs, said downtown had been evacuated and that there was street flooding. German said she was most worried about the one bridge into town washing out and trucks carrying everything from food to fuel not having a way in. Town officials had just lifted an evacuation order from flooding last week only to reimpose it Saturday with the San Juan forecast to crest Sunday night at 21.9 feet (6.7 meters). "I'm worried about my business, worried about my employees, definitely worried for everybody in this town," German said. Officials in La Plata County, west of Pagosa Springs, said all public roads were closed due to the flooding. Evacuations were also ordered in nearby Durango, Colorado,

9dbbd0a81065.text: By — Adithi Ramakrishnan, Associated Press Adithi Ramakrishnan, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/is-el-nino-making-storms-and-flash-floods-in-the-southwest-worse Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Is El Niño making storms and flash floods in the Southwest worse? Science Nov 2, 2026 4:19 PM EST NEW YORK (AP) — A chaotic climate phenomenon is intensifying heavy rains and floods in the Southwest, experts say. A natural warming cycle called El Niño is sizzling Pacific Ocean waters, leaking moisture into the air that can fuel passing storms. Such El Niño events can happen irregularly every couple of years, but scientists say the latest iteration is particularly extreme. "We've had super El Niños in the past, but this is a super duper El Niño," said meteorologist Jeff Masters of Yale Climate Connections. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The phenomenon wasn't the only cause of the severe storms, but scientists say it's making heavy rains more likely and intense across the Southern U.S. Flash floods on Sunday prompted evacuations across northern New Mexico and central Arizona, and a Colorado ski town braced for its main river to rise to catastrophic levels. And just last week, another wet storm subjected southwestern states to days of flooding. Over 20 trillion gallons of water have fallen on the Four Corners states and Nevada in the past two weeks, according to calculations by former National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration chief scientist Ryan Maue. Experts say this year's extreme El Niño is adding more moisture to the air and shifting atmospheric winds toward the Southwest, creating more ideal conditions for storms. "The likelihood of big precipitation in the Southwest interior does go up this time of year, but we're seeing it to a degree we actually haven't seen before," said climate scientist Daniel Swain with the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources. READ MORE: El Nino is here. It'll be big, bad and costly, scientists fear The world's oceans have already warmed over time because of human-caused climate change, and the El Niño heats things up even more. "The fact that the ocean temperatures are already warmer than they were, say, 100 years ago, makes these El Niño situations even more intense," said meteorologist Randy Cerveny with Arizona State University. The phenomenon is changing weather patterns around the world: regions including Peru and Ecuador are also seeing record-breaking flooding, Swain said. The El Niño event is expected to peak in December, and experts say its onslaught could continue for months afterward. To stay safe, experts recommended watching the forecast, planning ahead and heeding evacuation warnings from local authorities. "We're not at the peak of the heating in the Pacific Ocean. So yes, we will see more of these particular events," Cerveny said. The AP's climate and environmental coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. 213499a4b103.text: By — Brian Melley, Associated Press Brian Melley, Associated Press By — Jon Super, Associated Press Jon Super, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/karl-bushby-embraces-his-mother-as-he-completes-his-28-year-walk-around-world Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Karl Bushby embraces his mother as he completes his 28-year walk around world World Nov 2, 2026 4:12 PM EST HULL, England (AP) — Karl Bushby embraced his weeping mother in his arms Monday as he returned to his northern England home to complete a 28-year odyssey to walk around the world. "Where have you been?" his mother, Angela, asked as he arrived outside the home he left in 1998 that was now decked with a banner saying "Welcome Home Son." He didn't need to tell her. Bushby set out from Punta Arenas, Chile, on Nov. 1, 1998, and walked 31,000 miles (50,000 kilometers) across four continents and 30 countries to get home. He navigated shifting ice over the Bering Strait and swam across the Caspian Sea and English Channel to avoid taking a boat or plane — or any transport — to propel him forward. He vowed not to return until he could complete the journey on foot. It was an eye-opening adventure full of danger and drudgery that was interrupted for years at a time by the unexpected: the 2008 financial crash that sapped funding from sponsors, the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic and mountains of bureaucratic red tape to get across international borders. A trek made possible by kind strangers British adventurer Karl Bushby walks through Hull, England, on Monday, on his way to the city center before making his way back to his mother's home after 28 years of his journey walking across the world. Photo by Jon Super/AP On the final day of the journey, Bushby pushed his cart toward a hero's welcome at City Hall before setting off for the last stretch to see his mother. "Sorry to keep you waiting," he joked to the crowd of hundreds who cheered his arrival. "Is that it, is it done?" The ex-paratrooper said he looked like he was 10 years old when he left his mother's row house at the age of 29. He returned at 57 — softer, grayer and weathered, but far more worldly. "They say it takes a village but literally it took a world to get me here," Bushby said. "The kindness of strangers, so many, from individuals to nation states to get me back here today. I didn't do this alone. There was a big team. The biggest team. Earth." The idea started with a birthday card from his dad Bushby had a thirst for adventure, but his mission only came into focus when his father, Keith, sent him a birthday card in the mid-90s. His dad, an army veteran himself, mentioned an argument two special forces troops had about the possibility of walking from London to New York over the Bering land bridge, believed by some scientists to have been used by early humans to migrate from Asia to the Americas at a time of lower sea levels. Perilous jungles, scorching deserts and frozen tundra slowed him down, but bureaucratic holdups brought his adventure to a halt for long periods. Bushby originally calculated the distance could be covered in about five years, but he knew that was unrealistic. "You just dump a whole bucket full of reality on that," he said. "We suspected that it was 12 years plus. And the plus was a big plus. But never in our wildest dreams would we ever have imagined 28 years." Danger on land and sea followed by border problems He dodged Colombia's armed conflict in the dangerous Darién Gap, the roadless and rugged jungle, rainforest and mountains between South and Central America in 2001, and was then jailed for 18 days after crossing a restricted border zone in Panama. After being airlifted to safety during the 56-mile (90-kilometer) Bering Strait crossing in 2006 with American adventurer Dimitry Kieffer, they started again and faced a standoff with a polar bear, survived near-death plunges into freezing waters and almost lost all their supplies when their sleds plunged in the sea. After managing the rare crossing, the pair were jailed and faced deportation for entering Russia illegally. It took Bushby almost 10 years to make his way through Russia in fits and starts because of visa struggles and weather that only allowed travel a few months a year. When Russia denied him a visa in 2012, Bushby walked in protest from Los Angeles to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C., which eventually led to him getting the proper paperwork. Family firsts and a long-awaited reunion Bushby has met several times over the decades with family members who have met up with him on his journey. He was greeted on the beach in Dover by his father and brothers after crossing the channel last month. He reunited with Adam, his 36-year-old son from an early marriage whom he had rarely seen, and he met his 12-year-old granddaughter for the first time, which he said was amazing. Bushby hadn't seen his mother in a decade, setting the stage for an emotional and somewhat awkward reunion captured amid a throng of cameras and a documentary film crew. "Behave yourself, mother," he joked, as his mother wrapped her arms around him and wept. "Get yourself together." He said he had long tried to imagine that moment he would return to find his mother at the gate where he left her so long ago. He said it was an emotional reunion that was "one great, big, blurry mess" he was trying to process. "It was kind of almost shocking to see my mother after so long," he said at a news conference later. "She's changed a lot. We've all changed a lot in that time." Next steps for a man who walked millions In the final days of his trip, Bushby spoke of his anxiety over the trip ending, not knowing what he would do next and coming to terms with having to live in his mom's basement. "It's like stepping across the event horizon into a black hole," he told The Associated Press. "I have no idea what's about to happen in my life." There will be plenty to keep

At least 26 people were killed after Russian bombs hit an aid distribution centre, in an attack that Ukraine's leader has called "utterly horrific".
Five people were injured and 27 initially reported missing after at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit the village of Komyshuvakha in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, regional head Mykhailo Semikin said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that after the first strike on the local school "used for humanitarian needs", there was a second attack on the place where people were sheltering.
He posted a video showing a huge crater left after Monday's attack, and rescuer teams searching through the rubble.
The Russian military has not publicly commented.
Zelensky initially put the death toll at 18, but Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS later said 24 people, including two rescuers and four police officers, were confirmed to have been killed.
In his video address late on Monday, Zelensky said 26 people were now known to have died.
He earlier said that "the Russians could not have been unaware that the local residents who remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid there every week" on Monday.
"This is yet another proof that Russia does not want any de-escalation."
He said that after a recent successful joint Russian-Ukrainian operation to evacuate civilians from the Russia-occupied southern city of Oleshky during a temporary ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, "there was a moment when the next steps could show that peace is possible".
"With such killings, Russia is sending the exact opposite signal - Russia is counting on further killings," Zelensky said.
Meanwhile, Semikin described the Russian attack as a "terrible tragedy" for the village, confirming that "people are still under the rubble".
He said rescue teams were working at the scene, but they had been forced to halt their operation a number of times because of Russian drone attacks in the area.
A day of mourning has been declared for Tuesday across the entire Zaporizhzhia region.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Teams from Ukraine, Russia and the US are due to resume peace talks in the next few days after negotiations were suspended in February, with Moscow stepping up attacks as Kyiv virtually ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.
However, no major breakthrough is expected at the talks that are likely to be held in Abu Dhabi, the United Arab Emirates.

5b69a49952c9.text: President Trump told Axios in a phone interview Monday he's "in no rush" to decide whether to resume fighting in Iran . Why it matters: The midterm elections have been seen as an inflection point for Trump on whether to unleash a massive bombing campaign to try to bring the war to an end. But it appears the president, at least for now, will continue on dual tracks — letting negotiations play out while preparing to go back to war if he concludes a deal isn't reachable. What he is saying: "One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially. They have no money, no gasoline and their people are getting very tired of it," Trump said in the interview. Driving the news: Qatari mediators have written a draft agreement outlining a three-day sequence of confidence-building measures aimed at resuming direct U.S.-Iran negotiations, according to regional sources. A diplomat with knowledge of the situation said the Qatari mediators are waiting for feedback from the U.S. and Iran. Qatari mediator Ali al-Thawadi traveled to Tehran on Monday to continue talks on the draft agreement and the diplomat said progress is building. Trump is giving diplomacy a chance but is clear-eyed about the chances of reaching a deal. "We are talking to them. It's going fine. The problem with them is ... they try and tap tap tap [us along]. There's less urgency [on the Iranian side] than you think there would be, but they want to make a deal more than they ever wanted," Trump said. Between the lines: Trump is weighing three courses of action, backed by three different camps: 1. Make a deal: Vice President JD Vance and White House envoy Steve Witkoff are urging him to move toward a deal because a renewed war might not change the situation for the better. Most Gulf countries support this position and have communicated that to Trump, sources say. 2. Go back to battle: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu wants to resume combat, as does Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. They argue that Iran can't be trusted to make a deal let alone abide by one, and that Trump should finish the job militarily. 3. Maximum economic pain: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are advising Trump to maintain the "no war, no deal" status quo and allow the economic pressure campaign to continue, sources said. Ratcliffe told Trump that prolonged economic pain will induce Iran to make more concessions — or create enough instability inside the country that citizens revolt, a source with direct knowledge said. The CIA declined to comment. The other side: Iran's civilian leadership sounded hopeful on Monday about the prospects of reaching a deal. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei "granted the government certain authorities" to try to reach an agreement through diplomacy. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Monday that the diplomatic exchanges "have become very intensive." "Qatar and Pakistan are playing very active roles as mediators. We have presented our conditions and our proposal, and everything depends on Washington's political rationality. If they choose genuine diplomacy, we are ready to engage. But if they intend to engage in deception and military operations, they will face a response more painful and severe than in the past," he said. Araghchi said that if the U.S. accepts Tehran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, then "negotiations will resume." "Otherwise, the current situation will continue, and Iran will not bow down," he said. The big picture: Russia and China are taking an active role in the effort to reach a deal. Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke by phone Monday with Iran's Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Gen. Mohsen Rezaei. The two discussed the efforts to reach a diplomatic agreement. Rezaei, who is very close to Khamenei, was also the recipient of a letter Vance sent recently proposing to resume negotiations. Russia has also offered to be part of any nuclear agreement, including by receiving Iran's enriched uranium stockpile. At the same time, Rezaei's deputy visited Beijing on Monday and met with the Chinese foreign minister. China is also urging the U.S. and Iran to resume direct negotiations to end the war. What they're saying: Vance told reporters on Monday that he and Trump "feel pretty good about the prospect of reaching a settlement" with Iran. "We made some progress and we will see if we can make some more," Vance said. He added: "We haven't set deadlines (for resuming strikes). We want to make sure the Iranians don't rebuild or try to rebuild their nuclear program. We do think there is a pathway there but it requires a firm and verifiable commitment that they don't rebuild their nuclear program."

The US midterms campaign is set to be the most expensive on record - with the total cost projected to reach nearly $12bn (Â£9bn), according to Open Secrets, an independent organisation that tracks campaign finance.
Most of the spending is driven by outside political groups - known as Super Political Action Committees (Super Pacs) - pouring large sums of money into some key races ahead of election day on 3 November.
The top individual donor is billionaire businessman Elon Musk, who has spent almost half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates, particularly in Texas where many of his companies are based.
BBC Verify has looked into the figures and where the money was spent.
How much has been spent?
There are rules on how much people, parties and political action committees (Pacs) can give directly to candidates.
But Super Pacs can accept unlimited contributions from individuals, corporations, labour unions, and other political committees. They can't give that money directly to candidates but they can spend it supporting them indirectly.
According to the latest Federal Election Commission, external (FEC) filings which run to mid-October, more than $9.5bn had been spent in this midterms cycle.
Pacs and Super Pacs make up more than half of that - at about $5.5bn - with their spending in the last couple of months almost doubling.
Candidates, parties and outside groups have to report their spending to the FEC, but the full totals won't be available until after the midterm elections.
However, Open Secrets has projected the total will be $11.9bn based on trends in past cycles.
This would be about 30% more than what was spent during the last midterm elections in 2022.
Which donors have spent the most?
The top 40 donors gave $2.4bn up until 14 October, according to the liberal-leaning think tank Brennan Center for Justice, external, which is a record high for that point in a midterms cycle.
"Spending in the 2026 midterms is shattering records, with more of the money coming from the wealthiest donors and groups this election," says Michael Beckel, a US campaign finance expert.
As well as individuals, organisations can also give to Pacs. For example, Geosor Corp and Fund for Policy Reform, both founded by the billionaire financier George Soros, have given a combined $102m to liberal groups.
Aside from Soros, former New York City mayor and businessman Michael Bloomberg has been the biggest Democratic donor, giving more than $60m.
Several billionaires including Jeff Yass, who runs one of the world's largest trading firms, and Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein, the owners of a US business supply company, have given over $100m this campaign to Republican causes, according to FEC filings.
But Musk has given by far the most of any individual, donating almost half a billion dollars as of October.
Musk has given most of this to a Super Pac he set up in 2024 called America PAC, as well as to the Republican-aligned Senate Leadership Fund.
Most of his money has been spent on the Texas Senate race, supporting Republican candidate Ken Paxton, who is running against Democratic candidate James Talarico.
America PAC's investments in the Texas race total more than $45m. It has also invested around $10m into both of the Senate races in Michigan and Ohio.
"Crypto companies have also been very active this cycle, with Ripple and Coinbase combining to give $63 million to fund Super Pacs promoting the crypto industry's interests," says Brendan J Glavin of Open Secrets.
What has the money been spent on?
Campaigns and political groups spend money trying to reach voters in a variety of ways - including hiring staff to do on-the-ground voter outreach and hosting campaign events like rallies. They also spend money to conduct internal polling.
However, the majority of funds are spent on advertising - especially on TV.
In this cycle, $11.15bn has been spent on advertising up until the end of October, according to ad tracking firm AdImpact, external.
"Traditional broadcast television remains the top beneficiary of advertising expenditures, though expenditures on digital ads continue to increase," says Beckel.
Similarly to Musk's spending, AdImpact tracked that most of the money has been spent on advertising in the Senate races in Michigan, Texas and Ohio, followed by Iowa and Maine.
Graphics by Tom Shiel.

9dca86bd4667.text: President Trump extolled his administration's Reflecting Pool project , dug up debunked claims of vandalism and applauded the new White House helipad in a Monday pre-Election Day speech. The big picture: Trump's deep focus on remaking the nation's capital has taken center stage as the clock ticks down to midterm elections. Driving the news: "The pool is now better and more beautiful than it's ever been before, and we're very proud of it," Trump said in Monday's speech, adding, "We went through a lot with vandalism." But Trump's own Justice Department dropped vandalism charges against former Olympian David Hearn , whose case was later killed by a judge after prosecutors acknowledged that faulty installation caused the damage to the Pool. Trump added the administration was "giving serious thought" to renaming the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to the "Trump Reflecting Pool," before later saying he was kidding. Throughout the speech, he held up printed images he identified as pipes, joints and other Pool materials. He also showed an image that appeared to show "8647" sprayed onto the base of the emptied pool, claiming "that was a Comey phrase" — a reference to his former FBI director and top foe. Zoom out: He also discussed his White House renovation projects, including the recently installed helipad and Scotts Miracle-Gro's lawn restoration after the UFC fight on White House grounds. Friction point: Trump's projects, including his D.C.-area arch and White House ballroom, have been broadly panned by Americans in polling. "This project should be a project that unites all Americans," Trump said Monday of the newly reopened Reflecting Pool, which stood empty for an extended period earlier this year. Zoom in: His pre-election pitch at times sounded more like a typical rally speech, where he touted his immigration policies and war with Iran while slamming Democrats as "a party that hates America." This is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime," he said. "The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history." He also reiterated his pitch to distribute $5,000 checks should Republicans win in the midterms. What's next: After inviting Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to speak, Trump then touted his planned " triumphal arch ," detailed plans for a "promenade" from the Lincoln Memorial to the Potomac River and teased his golf course renovation . "We have a lot of great things planned for Washington, and I could get into the nation, but for that you don't have enough time," Trump said. He ended his closing argument by lauding a "golden age," saying, "We were laughed at like we were stupid people. We were laughed at by every ruler, every president, every prime minister, every king, every queen. But they don't laugh anymore." Axios' Josephine Walker contributed to this report. Go deeper: Trump to make midterm closing argument at Lincoln Reflecting Pool

8da482b9b1d3.text: By — Veselin Toshkov, Associated Press Veselin Toshkov, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/initial-results-suggest-iliana-yotova-wins-runoff-to-become-bulgarias-1st-elected-female-president Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Initial results suggest Iliana Yotova wins runoff to become Bulgaria's 1st elected female president World Nov 2, 2026 3:44 PM EST SOFIA, Bulgaria (AP) — Acting President Iliana Yotova is the apparent winner of Bulgaria's presidential runoff, initial results of the vote count on Sunday showed, as former interim Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov conceded defeat. According to the count by several polling agencies, Yotova received 58% of the vote. If confirmed by official results, she would become Bulgaria's first elected female head of state. Gyurov, backed by reformist pro-Western opposition parties, is said to be trailing at around 38%. Gyurov conceded defeat saying that "this is how the Bulgarian citizens have voted," and added that the results had to be accepted as they stood. Official results were not expected before Monday. The vote was the first major test for Prime Minister Rumen Radev's Moscow-friendly Progressive Bulgaria party, which endorsed Yotova. In April's parliamentary vote, the party won 131 of the 240 seats in Parliament, securing an outright majority. Observers note that a victory for Yotova will keep the presidency in the hands of the governing majority. Such a concentration of power could prevent the effective maintenance of checks and balances on policy decisions by institutions, they say. Yotova, 62, took over the presidency in January, when Radev stepped down to run for parliament, and was seeking her own elected mandate. She's expected to continue Radev's policy of keeping Bulgaria on its European path, while also supporting better relations with Russia and the lifting of sanctions. After casting her vote on Sunday, Yotova said she voted for a Bulgaria that makes its own decisions and maintains a strong voice on the international stage. "I voted for national consensus through dialogue, for institutions that work for citizens, for a strong state with its own foreign policy in a strong Europe," she told reporters. The Balkan country joined NATO in 2004 and the European Union in 2007. While there is a broad consensus among the parties in parliament on the country's pro-Western path, widespread pro-Russia sentiment based on traditional historical and cultural ties with Russia has divided society, particularly since the start of Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Both Yotova and Radev have called for a diplomatic solution to end the war in Ukraine but remain evasive about possible Russian involvement in drone attacks in the Black Sea region. During a television debate between the two presidential contenders, Yotova advocated for a settlement involving both Ukraine and Russia, saying that "peace could come only through negotiations." She also proposed a security meeting involving all six Black Sea countries to sign a moratorium on hostilities. Bulgaria's presidency is primarily ceremonial. Although the head of state has no executive powers, and all major policies must be approved by parliament, direct election gives the president greater political authority. The president leads the armed forces and can veto legislation, signs international treaties and appoints ambassadors. Presidents in Bulgaria are elected for a five-year term and can serve no more than two terms. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Sullivan for weeks. His rustic home stood dark a day after FBI agents visited friends who donated to his quixotic campaign to unseat the Republican senator with the same first and last name — Dan S. Sullivan. The only display of politics at his home was a yard sign from the League of Women Voters: "Stand Up for Democracy: Vote 2026." What may have begun as a ploy to harm the reelection prospects of Sen. Sullivan has taken a serious turn as President Donald Trump's administration weighs criminal charges over a campaign tactic known as ballot stacking. Sullivan, a former elementary school teacher. FBI agents knocked on her door Saturday during a round of interviews with the campaign's dozen contributors. "I'm a bit incredulous about their whole angle," Hunter said, "because they're targeting a person who's been a real contributor in this community." Recruiting candidates to draw votes away from an opponent has been a part of Alaska's quirky politics for years. This time around, the state's open primary and ranked choice voting systems add another wrinkle, making it easier for lesser-known candidates to play spoilers when no contender secures a majority. The tactic has drawn fresh scrutiny as the incumbent Sullivan fights off a serious challenge from Democrat Mary Peltola, a former U.S. representative, in a race that could determine control of the Senate. 2 Sullivans vie for 1 Senate seat A building sits along the ocean Saturday in Petersburg, Alaska. Photo by Joshua Goodman/AP Peltola has denied any role in the alleged chicanery as she has sought to distance herself from a New York Times article published last week that linked a group backing the former congresswoman to a Democratic operative trying to recruit decoy candidates. "This is Alaska. We're not in the business of tricking each other up here," Peltola told supporters at a rally in Anchorage last week. Dan J. Sullivan's entry into the race has drawn scrutiny since June, when the Alaska Division of Elections tried to remove him from the primary ballot, determining he had not filed his candidacy as a Republican in "good faith." That decision was overturned by state courts. To avoid any confusion, state officials identify Dan S. Sullivan on the ballot as a Republican and the incumbent. Dan J. Sullivan repeatedly said he entered the race on his own accord and had no contact with Peltola's campaign — "zero, none, zilch," he told The Associated Press in June. He answered "no" when asked if any Democratic operatives had contacted him to run. "This is my choice," he said at the time. A federal lawsuit brought by the Republican Trump administration to revive efforts to undermine the former teacher's candidacy — and challenge a potential Peltola win by blocking certification of the election results — was dismissed on Sunday by a federal judge. The Justice Department quickly appealed. The AP's efforts to reach Dan J. Sullivan since the Times article have been unsuccessful. Several of the donors the AP interviewed said they have not spoken to him in quite some time. The senator, meanwhile, is seeking to ride the controversy to a third term. "My costume is the real Dan Sullivan – not the fake guy," he quipped to trick-or-treaters on Saturday night. The FBI comes to Little Norway The controversy has thrust Petersburg, a fishing community of 3,000 residents known as Little Norway for its late 19th-century settlers, into the center of a federal investigation and a crush of media attention. It's the type of small town where everyone seems to know everyone else's business, and more than a dozen residents said they liked and admired Dan J. Sullivan, calling him a creative teacher who ran an after-school program, Little Kids Rock, to teach guitar. At a lively Halloween party at Kito's Kave, a local dive, a patron poked fun at the surge of interest by dressing up as an FBI agent. Another wore a "Petersburg Election Scandal" prison placard around her neck. The charge: "Being a Registered Voter in Alaska." Retired fisherman Ed Wood said he wrote a $1,000 check to Dan J. Sullivan's campaign to repay the support Sullivan and his wife gave to a costly, decade-long battle to block the state from logging a forested hillside that sits above Petersburg. Retired businessman Charles Flint looks at his phone during an interview on Saturday in Petersburg, Alaska. Photo taken with smartphone. Photo by Joshua Goodman/AP Another donor, retired boat seller Charles Flint, described Dan J. Sullivan as a "liberal thinker" who sometimes voted for Republicans. Flint said that Dan J. Sullivan never told him why he entered the race. "He probably viewed himself more as a spoiler than a legitimate long shot," said Flint, who has a "Mary for U.S. Senate" yard sign supporting the Democrat outside his coastal home. "I'm sure he's probably thinking now, 'Maybe I shouldn't have done this.'" Friends said they are certain that Dan J. a67930aa21e4.text: The top Senate GOP super PAC has nearly tripled its spending on streaming and social media platforms this election cycle to more than $200 million, Axios has learned. Why it matters : In a record cycle for ad spending, more political money is shifting to streaming, where super PACs have greater freedom to target voters, bargain and experiment — but platforms have more power to set the rules. In some states, streaming and social media have swallowed half of the Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) budget, according to a source familiar with the group's spending. SLF's $200M+ total for the 2026 cycle (up from $71M in 2024) includes tens of millions of dollars funneled through the SLF-linked Texas PAC and its affiliated nonprofit One Nation. The other side: The top Senate Democratic super PAC declined to provide a dollar figure for their spending on streaming. "Senate Majority PAC invested more this cycle in digital communications than any previous cycle, running digital campaigns in 12 states," SMP communications director Lauren French told Axios. Zoom in : Streaming and social platforms offer campaigns the power to target more specific audiences compared to traditional broadcast, and make it easier to measure the impact. "Its way more surgical than a linear broadcast buy," Zack Roday, managing director at Think Big, told Axios. But platforms can also set their own rules around which types of ads they want to accept. Some, like Netflix and TikTok, don't allow any candidate or issue ads . Republicans have complained about restrictions on ads that include transgender issues on Disney-owned platforms. Between the lines: Super PACs often pay multiple times what a campaign pays for ads on broadcast TV and radio because of laws ensuring candidates get the lowest rates. Online, super PACs can negotiate directly — and use their fat budgets and sprawling election maps as leverage. SLF works with platforms like SiriusXM, Paramount, Hulu, YouTube and others to lock in discounts based on their overall spending plans, according to the source. Groups can also experiment with different lengths and formats for ads online, breaking the 30-second broadcast mold. What to watch: Streaming ads can also be trickier for outside tracking. While Meta and Google provide public data on political ad buys, not every platform provides that kind of visibility, Streaming buys aren't covered by the same FCC filing requirements as political ad reservations on broadcast TV and radio. Broadcast filings can offer a preview of a group's targets months in advance, but streaming reservations are much harder to see. Although AI is changing the game, and there is a growing industry of companies offering better tracking tools. Super PACs still have to report independent expenditures to the FEC through 24- and 48- hour reports. Zoom out: Strong grassroots fundraising has helped Democratic candidates crush Republicans in dollars brought in directly to candidates. The GOP is hitting back with cash-flush committees and super PACs fueled by ultra-wealthy donors. In addition to super PACs moving more money to streaming, the National Republican Senatorial Committee jumped on a court decisions to coordinate ad buys with campaigns — giving them access to the candidate rate. It also allowed NRSC to negotiate with streaming platforms on behalf of multiple campaigns. The bottom line: It's just the beginning on maneuvering on streaming and coordinated buys. "That is definitely going to be the story of 2028," Kenny Day, senior vice president at IQM corporation, told Axios. He said the Supreme Court decision on coordinated spending "was too late for either party to really take advantage of the allowance of coordinated spending" in the 2026 cycle. Editor's note: This story has been corrected to show that the more than $200 million total included money spent through Texas PAC (not that it excluded that spending).

A court in South Africa has found a man guilty of stealing more than $500,000 (Â£372,822) in cash from a farm owned by South African president Cyril Ramaphosa, in a case that mired the head of state in an impeachment saga.
Imanuwela David was found guilty of theft on Monday, as well as conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal at Phala Phala farm in the Limpopo province in 2020.
Froliana Joseph, a cleaner at the property, was also found guilty of conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal.
Her brother, Ndilinasho Joseph, was acquitted on all charges.
David was accused of breaking into the cattle farm in February 2020 and taking $580,000 (Â£432,000) in cash from a sofa on the property. David then went on a spending spree, buying a range of cars including three Mercedes - among them one for his girlfriend - a Porsche, two Volkswagens as well as diamond-encrusted Rolex watches and a house.
David told the court he had made the money through businesses including diamonds and Bitcoin, claims the court rejected. The court also found that David was the only one of the two convicted who had any of the stolen cash in his bank account.
Pre-sentencing will take place on 13 November.
There have been many twists and turns in what is known as the Farmgate scandal.
The theft was largely unknown until 2022 when it was brought to light by Arthur Fraser, South Africa's former intelligence chief and an ally for the former president Jacob Zuma, when he claimed that Ramaphosa hid the theft from the police and tax authorities.
Ramaphosa admitted the theft took place but denied any wrongdoing.
An independent panel that same year found Ramaphosa could have questions to answer over the burglary. MPs voted against establishing an impeachment inquiry.
In May this year, the constitutional court ruled that parliament had acted unlawfully by shelving the panel's report, and in July Ramaphosa blocked the parliamentary inquiry through a provincial court.
