Climate negotiators head to Turkey next month for the United Nations annual climate summit, just two months after an alarming U.N. report said the world has a vanishing chance of limiting global warming to safe levels.
The report’s projections will likely ripple through discussions at the event, known as the Conference of the Parties or COP, including one of its more urgent messages: In order to bring planet-warming gases under control, countries have to slash methane pollution, fast.
Because methane is more powerful over a shorter period of time than carbon dioxide—about 80 times more over 20 years—cutting methane emissions represents an expedient way to claw the world back from its current trajectory. But measuring methane, especially from livestock, its primary human-caused source, continues to stir controversy. Two new reports on methane say measurements of the gas are being manipulated and underestimated.
In a new analysis published Oct. 29 and commissioned by Greenpeace International, researchers dive into a method for measuring methane known as “global warming potential*,” or GWP*. Their findings underscore the concerns of many scientists who have said that if rich, livestock-heavy countries use GWP* to measure their livestock emissions, they can continue emitting vast quantities of methane and misrepresent the total emissions in reporting their progress toward global climate goals.
“Proponents of GWP* will tell you methane is part of the natural carbon cycle, we just need to keep it stable,” said Sophie Nodzenski, a campaigner with Greenpeace. “We argue that methane levels are already too high. Methane is the climate emergency brake. It disappears so quickly from the atmosphere and is so warming—if we acted on methane right now, we could see results within the next 15 years.”
Under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, greenhouse gas measurements have been standardized as carbon dioxide equivalents, based on their GWP, typically over 20- and 100-year time frames (GWP20 and GWP100, respectively). This has helped make different greenhouse gases more comparable.
Carbon dioxide, the most abundant greenhouse gas, persists and accumulates in the atmosphere over centuries. But because methane’s impact is speedy and brief, causing an initial burst of warming and then degrading after about 12 years, scientists have argued that GWP100 doesn’t accurately reflect its warming power.
About 10 years ago, scientists at the University of Oxford developed GWP*, in which emission rates of methane and other short-lived climate pollutants are equated to single pulses of carbon dioxide. This measurement reflects that methane doesn’t have the same cumulative effect as carbon dioxide and also that the methane emitted from cow belches originates from vegetation that originally removed carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. It assumes a steady climb in emissions won’t cause additional warming because methane degrades relatively quickly while methane sinks—mostly involving molecular processes that naturally break down the gas —mean emissions can remain stable.
Climate scientists say the science underpinning GWP* is legitimate and represents another tool to more accurately understand planet-warming emissions and how they behave. They worry, however, that the method is being used to justify weakening efforts to cut emissions from livestock and have warned against using it to measure emissions, especially as the livestock industry, including in the United States, has embraced it.
The industry has called for a “split gas approach,” underpinned by GWP*, to “better reflect the distinct warming behaviours of long- and short-lived GHGs.”
Industry groups did not respond to requests for comment from Inside Climate News.
But earlier this year, 42 prominent climate scientists warned that using GWP* threatens to undercut essential methane reductions because its calculation allows industries or countries to set “no additional warming” targets. That effort followed an open letter to New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, also signed by top climate scientists and bearing the same warning.
Last year, New Zealand, where the economically critical livestock industry accounts for nearly half the country’s greenhouse gas emissions, became the first country to set a “no additional warming” target based on GWP* accounting principles.
But critics and the new Greenpeace report say that applying GWP* to reflect progress toward the global climate goals enshrined in the Paris Agreement is potentially deceptive. They maintain it allows countries with historically high methane emissions to claim major reductions even for minor cuts, and in some cases report “negative emissions,” “climate neutrality” or “no additional warming.”

The report, based on modeling by the consultancy group Cerulogy, finds that these countries, which include two beef powerhouses, Brazil and the U.S., could cut actual methane by just 0.6 percent in 2030 compared to their 2020 emissions, yet report a 30 percent reduction under GWP*.
“As long as you are not causing more warming than your very recent baseline, you’re essentially fine,” Nodzenski said. “This is why it benefits high livestock producers. If they take a recent baseline, all they need to do is keep their emission level sort of stable.”

Davidâs view
Before there was the other Dan Sullivan, there was the other Mike Doyle.
Four years ago, when longtime Pittsburgh Democrat Mike Doyle retired from Congress, a left-wing legislator named Summer Lee won the primary to replace him. Republicans nominated a local politician from the suburbs to face her who had a fortuitous name: Mike Doyle.
Some voters were perplexed. The new Doyleâs lawn signs called him âthe right Mikeâ without explicitly identifying him as a Republican â a moniker that would be a non-starter in the safely Democratic seat. Local Democrats got worried calls, asking why Lee was running against their beloved liberal congressman. The Democrat Doyle called an emergency press conference to clarify that he was not the Republican Doyle: âMy name is on the ballot, but itâs not me.â
Lee won, albeit by a smaller margin than other Democrats in her district had in the past. Nothing else came of the story. There was no federal investigation of the Doyle scheme; no demands not to seat Doyle if he won; no statement from the governor saying that he might not certify the election.
All of that has unfolded in Alaska this cycle. The clandestine Democratic effort to recruit a candidate who shares the name of the stateâs incumbent Republican senator could have major implications for what happens after Tuesday.
The plotâs exposure damaged Democrat Mary Peltola, knocking her off-message, and now threatens her partyâs chances of winning control of the Senate. President Donald Trumpâs administration is investigating, and also sued to block the certification of the results should Sullivan lose â though a federal judge tossed out the suit over the weekend. Those efforts, along with the announcement of investigations into candidates within 60 days of the vote, show how the Trump administration is jettisoning unwritten norms at the Justice Department.
The Alaska mess is weighing heavily on Democrats who hope to win control of Congress tomorrow. Victory in either chamber would mean a two-year license on oversight powers, empowering Democrats to subpoena the Trump administration and its allies in the private sector. There is a thirst for vengeance among some Democrats that is testing their public stance that they must restore standards blown up by Trump.
Thereâs also a shared sense, among most Democrats, that following those standards has gotten them nothing, while Republicans have benefitted from bending the rules.Â
âDonald Trump and [House Oversight Committee Chairman] James Comer have basically written a playbook on how to politicize investigations and attack political enemies and weaponize government,â said Robert Garcia, the California Democrat who is in line to lead the House Oversight Committee in a Democratic majority. â[Attorney General] Todd Blanche? His whole job is just to grift for the president.â
The argument over which party first used âlawfareâ to get what it wanted is an old one. Democrats have long celebrated the Watergate investigation as an example of the Constitution and US legal system working as designed. Republicans are more likely to call the episode a coup against a president whoâd just won a landslide.
But the current debate begins, like so many irritating conversations, with the 2016 election. For all of Hillary Clintonâs errors, like telling coal miners that their jobs would vanish if she won, Democrats largely believe that she would have won the election against Trump had the FBI not abandoned its â60 day ruleâ and announced an 11th hour investigation into emails found on Huma Abedinâs laptop. Some believe that Barack Obama acted too timidly when Republicans refused to co-sign a letter warning of Russian interference in that campaign.
Nobody has ever accused Trump of acting timidly. Ten years on, his Justice Department is still probing the origins of the Russia investigation into his first campaign. When Joe Biden replaced Trump, he kept on the US attorney who was investigating his son. When Trump replaced Biden, he sacked the prosecutors whoâd worked on post-Jan. 6 investigations.
Democrats felt like suckers. Biden publicly promised that his Justice Department would act independently. Privately, he was resentful of Attorney General Merrick Garlandâs choices to hold off on investigating Trump until November 2022, after Republicans were more or less united in denouncing any Trump probe as âlawfare.â
This is on many Democratic minds as they watch the Justice Department in Alaska â even though itâs not the only race where one party meddled in a way that might confuse voters. In Maine, a conservative PAC is sending out mail for a left-wing spoiler candidate for governor. In Ohio, a conservative PAC is doing the same for a socialist Senate candidate who could threaten Democrat Sherrod Brownâs chances. In Nevada, a conservative PACâ¦ okay, you get the point.
âTheyâre obsessed with meddling in elections,â Garcia said. âWe have to put in place new rules and a new standard to get things back to a place where we donât have the president trying to rig elections constantly.â In Pennsylvania, when I asked Gov. Josh Shapiro how Democrats should respond to Trumpâs Justice Department, he was hopeful they would be the âparty of law and orderâ â by showing that this was not the way to use the governmentâs bottomless resources.
âI said every single day to our team and to the public that I enforce the law without fear or favor,â said Shapiro, referring to his six years as state attorney general. âThat is not the case in the Trump administration.â
Despite the ongoing debate of how far to go, Republicans are portraying a party intent on going after the president in order to rev up their base. âTheyâve already filed articles of impeachment in this Congress,â House Speaker Mike Johnson alleged. Mario Alberto Morales made his first court appearance on a felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon for striking Miguel Parra Hernandez with an unmarked SUV on Oct. 10, as Morales chased the 48-year-old construction worker through a parking lot. A grand jury indicted Morales, 33, on Friday. During Monday's hearing, Judge Matthew Peneguy set bond at $30,000. Prosecutors had asked that bond be set at $75,000, according to the Harris County District Attorney's Office. Morales is one of just a few federal officers who have faced criminal charges over their actions on the job during President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown. Other encounters have come under investigation. READ MORE: An ICE officer is charged with assault for striking a man with a car in Houston ICE has asserted that Parra Hernandez ran in front of Morales' vehicle, an account that prosecutors say is contradicted by video. Surveillance camera video shows Morales' vehicle drive over a median and strike Parra Hernandez as he runs away. David Lindenmuth, Morales' attorney, has said his client was "truly a good man" and did not commit a crime. Parra Hernandez broke his leg and is recovering at a rehabilitation facility while in federal custody, according to Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare. Morales had worked as an ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations officer for a little more than a year, Lindenmuth said. He unsuccessfully ran for Congress this year and previously served in the Army. US President Donald Trump has notified Congress of his intention to remove South Africa and Rwanda from a preferential trade programme, from 1 January 2027.
The African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa) allows eligible African countries to export thousands of products to the US duty-free.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement that an annual review had found that both countries were engaging in practices inconsistent with the programme's eligibility requirements.
He added that the Trump administration had additionally notified the two countries of the decision.
The Trump administration cited barriers to US trade and investment, as well as concerns over national security and foreign policy interests in the region.
In Rwanda's case, Washington also raised concerns about human rights, political pluralism, the rule of law and workers' rights.
The move comes barely a week after Rwanda's defence ministry was hit with sanctions by US Treasury for its alleged role in the armed rebellion in eastern DR Congo.
The US Treasury said Rwanda's defence ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 rebels in eastern DR Congo, providing weapons, equipment, logistics and training.
For South Africa, the US additionally pointed to corruption.
"The Trump administration is working to ensure our African partners take the necessary steps to meet the eligibility criteria," Greer said.
The announcement comes amid strained relations between Washington and both countries, with the proposed termination threatening their access to preferential trade arrangements with the US.
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners.
US Ambassador to South Africa Leo Brent Bozell III said it was regrettable that South African policies led to its termination from Agoa.
"This was a predictable and preventable outcome resulting from the rejection by South Africa's government of real concerns raised by the US," he wrote on X.

273290382ee2.text: By — David Fischer, Associated Press David Fischer, Associated Press By — John Funk, Associated Press John Funk, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/evidence-suggests-parts-of-jet-broke-off-before-florida-crash-ntsb-investigator-says Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Parts of a Learjet may have broken off midair before Florida crash that killed 9, investigators say Nation Updated on Nov 2, 2026 5:35 PM EST — Published on Nov 2, 2026 2:31 PM EST WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — Parts of a business jet likely started to break off even before it slammed into the ground and erupted in a ball of flames in South Florida, killing all nine people on board, a federal investigator said Monday. Video recorded by passersby captured the Bahamas-bound Learjet's rapid nosedive Sunday afternoon before it exploded in Greenacres, about 7 miles (11 kilometers) southwest of West Palm Beach. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining the crater as shocked residents looked on in horror. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site and little remained of the plane. READ MORE: Palm Beach plane crash footage isn't AI-generated, despite social media claims "Debris was everywhere. Debris hit my house. Everything was on fire. The road was on fire," Anthony Blackmon, who lives near the crash site, told NBC affiliate WTVJ. "I've always seen it on the news, never thought it would happen so close to somebody like how it happened today." Federal investigators outline the probe but decline to speculate Watch Monday's National Transportation Safety Board briefing on the plane crash in the player above. National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman said during a news conference Monday that investigators found evidence the aircraft started breaking up before it hit the ground and that debris from the aircraft could be spread far and wide. "We do have some indication that the aircraft was breaking up before impact," Chapman said. "We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site." Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti said key components of the jet's tail may have been lost during the turbulence or as it nose-dived. "If that happens you cannot control an airplane at that point. And that very well could explain the missile-like profile just before it hit the ground," said Guzzetti, a former NTSB and the Federal Aviation Administration investigator. Weather conditions will be a major focus of the investigation, Chapman said. Rain pounded the region on Sunday, and one of the pilots reported icing conditions at a high altitude in communications with air traffic control. Weather radar maps from the time of the crash that FlightRadar24 combined with the plane's flight path seem to show it flying directly into a storm cell that was rapidly expanding upward. But Chapman said investigators still have to determine what the weather conditions were at 35,000 feet. Chapman said the plane was originally equipped with a cockpit voice recorder that investigators hope to recover. "We have a lot of work to do on scene," NTSB investigator Timothy Monville said at the news conference. "This will be a several-day process, and the biggest obstacle that we're going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway." Mother identifies one of the pilots The jet began its journey at the Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas with two crew and seven passengers, Chapman said. Authorities have not released the names of the people who died and the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office declined to discuss the death investigation, which is ongoing. Camila Corteleti told the New York Post and New York Times that her daughter, 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, was one of the pilots. She earned her pilot's license in 2023 while a 17-year-old senior at West Boca Raton Community High School in Florida, local news reports said at the time. Her pilot's license showed she had the rating to fly that model of Learjet but not to be in command of the flight. Her father, Allan Filgueiras, told The Associated Press he wasn't prepared to speak about the crash. A man who was driving close to the scene as the plane crashed suffered leg wounds, Monville said, but he didn't know the extent of the injury. Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter asked for sympathy for the crash victims. "Please keep them in your thoughts and prayers," Baxter said. Pilot reported turbulence and ice, then the jet fell rapidly Police work near the scene of a plane crash in Greenacres, Florida, on Monday. Photo by Rebecca Blackwell/AP The plane was heading east at 35,000 feet (11,000 meters) when the pilot started to report problems. The pilot said ice was accumulating on the jet and that turbulence was jolting it by as much as 700 feet (210 meters), according to air traffic control recordings captured by LiveATC.net. "We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence," the pilot told controllers. The situation rapidly deteriorated. The pilot requested permission to climb another 2,000 feet (610 meters) and then quickly declared an emergency as the jet lost altitude at an alarming rate. "We're descending 8,000 — mayday, mayday — we're descending 10,000 feet per minute," the pilot radioed. "We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute," the pilot radioed. Moments later, the pilot said: "We're going to crash into the ground." Video shows the plane banking sharply to the right before crashing and exploding. Some area residents are still not allowed to return home Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel G. Flores said at the news conference that the county "doesn't have a clue" when residents who live near the crash site will be able to return to their homes as investigators continue to comb the area. Massachusetts prosecutors have given their clearest indication yet that they plan to retry Lindsay Clancy for the murder of her three children in 2023.
At a hearing on Monday, Judge William Sullivan scheduled a 16 November hearing where he plans to rule on a handful of motions that could determine how a retrial would proceed, including a request to dismiss the first-degree murder charges.
Clancy faced a weekslong trial on those charges over the summer. It fell apart in early September after a 12-person jury failed to reach a verdict.
If there is a retrial, Judge Sullivan said, it could happen as soon as March 2027.
The prosecution did not say on Monday whether Clancy would face the same charges or amended charges in the event of a retrial.
When the parties meet again later this month, they will hear the judge's rulings on the motions argued in court on Monday, and potentially will discuss dates for a retrial, Judge Sullivan said.
Kevin Reddington, Clancy's attorney, pushed the judge for a spring trial.
"I am not going to have this woman sit incarcerated for the next year or two or three," he said. "I want a date and I want it this spring."
But prosecutor Jennifer Sprague said she wants to hear Judge Sullivan's rulings on Monday's arguments before the prosecution commits to a new date or specifics for a potential retrial.
When the judge asked for more details on how prosecutors planned to proceed with a potential retrial, Sprague responded: "This would be a retrial - as to what that looks like will depend".
But that appeared to frustrate Reddington.
"Why do we not know if the next trial is going to be murder in the first degree or a lesser charge, why do they need to wait for the motions? I need to know logistically."
Clancy was charged with three counts of first-degree-murder, which is the intentional and premeditated killing of another person.
Prosecutors could decide to bring lesser charges against Clancy in a retrial. For example, second-degree-murder charges, apply to unlawful killings committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning.
Despite Sprague's statement in court, District Attorney Timothy Cruz has not yet confirmed that Clancy will face a retrial and has not announced future plans for the case.
Much of Monday's conversations in court focused on the one holdout juror, also known as Juror Doe, and the defence's investigation into him. Juror Doe disagreed with the other jurors, who appeared to want to find Clancy not guilty by way of insanity. The lack of agreement led to a hung jury and mistrial.
In some of the most fiery moments of the three-hour hearing on Monday, Reddington requested a plethora of evidence including the holdout juror's phone and phone records.
Heather O'Connor, the attorney who represents Juror Doe, said she was in court because Clancy's defence team has "combined several allegations" to try to argue that a mistrial should not have been declared, she said.
That is among the motions Sullivan said he will rule on in a few weeks.
Clancy does not deny killing her children, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors claim the killings were intentional.

58fac3d53604.text: By — Marc Levy, Associated Press Marc Levy, Associated Press By — Mike Catalini, Associated Press Mike Catalini, Associated Press By — John Hanna, Associated Press John Hanna, Associated Press By — Calvin Woodward, Associated Press Calvin Woodward, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/voters-on-the-left-and-right-fear-the-america-theyve-known-is-slipping-away Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Voters on the left and right fear the America they've known is slipping away Politics Nov 2, 2026 2:14 PM EST The stakes in Tuesday's elections are so high that Shane Dunn voted for the first time in his life, at age 65. After a career as a cook up and down the East Coast, Dunn moved to the Philadelphia suburbs and voted last week in Levittown. "I was always a busy man," he said. But now, "I'm learning what's going on within our country and this is actually what brought me out." Democrats got his vote. "It feels great, to put my word in," he said, patting his "I Voted" sticker. Voters across the United States are getting their word in as they determine control of Congress, governors' offices and more in the final two years of Republican Donald Trump's presidency. What many see is that the America they've known is slipping away. They see lawlessness from those who create laws, politicians stirring hate among neighbors, billionaires ruling the roost and a culture that doesn't speak to how they live. Not to mention those crazy gas prices. Voter angst is evident on both sides In dozens of Associated Press interviews with people casting advance ballots, the angst was palpable, most sharply from Trump's opponents but also from many supporters. "I saw my vote today as trying to put the brakes on just the madness," said Arthur Horner, 59, who runs a tariff-slammed food importing and marketing company. He voted Democratic in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. In Sioux City, Iowa, cattle rancher Elizabeth Marlett, 61, left the courthouse stewing about processed food, her son's struggles to get veterans' benefits and what she sees as society's leftward lurch. "Family values are going by the wayside, and they need to be brought back," she said. "Our liberties have been stomped all over. Religion has been stomped all over." She voted Republican. The anger stirred by a cursing president who abides no slights is too much for some. "He's just destroying us," Democrat Linda Markle, 72, said outside a library in Bucks County, Pennsylvania. "I am so afraid for this country." "All people do now is just hate each other," she said, and Trump "seems to have given them the courage to go ahead and be like that." 'He's kind of going a bit crazy,' a Trump supporter says Republican Chris Smith, 27, a Harrisburg software engineer who voted for Trump in 2024, sympathizes to a point. But Smith likes Trump's manufacturing push and voted Republican because he considers the party more fiscally responsible. In Ohio, independents Lori and David Wilkinson have voted for Republican George W. Bush for president in the past, and David recently praised Republican Gov. Mike DeWine in a letter. WATCH: Poll gauges voter enthusiasm for both parties a week before election Trump? "He's the worst president in United States history," David said at the Wayne County election center. "You get up every day, and you're like, 'What's he going to do now?'" Also voting there was Trump supporter Therese Mennell, who understands the distaste. "There's that kind of arrogant vibe about him that people don't like, and sometimes I shut him off because of the way he talks," the retiree said. "But, I mean, he's doing the right thing. He is saving our country." Despite his unpopularity in polls, Trump repeatedly asked supporters to pretend he's on the ballot, hoping to motivate otherwise reluctant voters. That cuts both ways. A family voting tradition is handed down Brothers Samontae Mwangi, 20, and Gathenya Mwangi, 19, voted for the first time in Topeka, Kansas, with their grandfather, Lynn Henderson, 68, a retired tire worker and former Marine. Henderson's mother died recently, and he wanted his grandsons to have an event to remember him by. All three hoped for Democratic victories. "It really could change, make a difference, I feel, if a lot of people vote," Gathenya said. Denise Wunder, a retired sandwich shop manager whose top issue is illegal immigration, saw the stakes differently. "I think Trump is kind of our last hope, because otherwise this world's going to go to hell in a handbasket," she said outside the Topeka center. "Yeah, he says stupid stuff, but, you know, so do we." In Nanuet, New York, independent Primrose D. Sullivan, a nurse who voted Democratic, singled out the billionaires allied with Trump. "I don't begrudge any of our wealthy people, Jeff Bezos or, you know, Elon Musk," she said. In Scottsdale, Arizona, David Lee, 63, described his conservative upbringing and past Republican votes before explaining his turn toward Democrats. He considers Trump's immigration enforcement lawless. "Nobody wants open borders, but you're treating these people without due process, sending people to countries they don't even belong to," he said. "There's no more rules." Trump supporters interviewed by the AP signaled tolerance for surging gas prices from the Iran war. "Iran has been killing Americans for 50 freaking years," said David Stouffer, 59, a mortgage bank branch manager and three-time Trump voter in Harrisburg. "Yeah, I'll suffer with some higher gas prices in the interim until they get that nonsense figured out." "He's made the tax cuts real," he added. "He has secured the borders." Two days of hearings on a challenge to Australia's landmark social media ban for children will begin at the country's highest court on Tuesday.
In a major test of the world-leading policy, a digital rights group will argue that the ban for under-16s robs children of their right to free communication. A separate challenge launched by platform Reddit will be jointly heard.
Introduced last December, the ban is a key part of sweeping changes the Australian government has spearheaded in recent years on online safety.
Supporters say the ban protects children from harmful content but critics say it is too blunt an instrument and efforts should focus on improving online safety.
The constitutional challenge in Australia's High Court was filed by the Digital Freedom Project a few weeks before the ban started on 10 December last year. The group is lead by New South Wales parliamentarian John Ruddick.
Two teens who originally spearheaded the case, Noah Jones and Macy Neyland, have since withdrawn as plaintiffs though Jones is still expected to attend Tuesday's hearing.
Speaking about the legal challenge last November, Jones told the BBC that there were bad things online but a blanket ban for under-16s was not the right answer.
"We shouldn't be using the resources and money of these social media platforms to try to avoid fines from our government," he said.
"They should be using this money and resources to try to get rid of the predators and harmful content out there."
Reddit also launched a High Court challenge to the ban, arguing the policy has serious implications for privacy and political rights.
Communications Minister Anika Wells last year said the government would not be "intimidated by legal threats."
"We will not be intimidated by big tech. On behalf of Australian parents, we will stand firm," she said last November.
Under the ban, ten platforms - Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, Snapchat, X, Kick, Threads and Twitch - must take "reasonable steps" to ensure no one under 16 years old can access its site.
Platforms risk fines of up to A$99m (US$70m, Â£52m) for serious or repeated breaches, but since the ban started, no company has been fined.
The eSafety Commissioner - the body tasked with enforcing the ban - has launched several investigations into alleged non-compliance by Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube.
WhatsApp and online gaming sites like Roblox and Discord were not included in the ban, nor were educational platforms like YouTube Kids and Google Classroom.
In the first few days of the ban, Meta - which owns three of the banned platforms - said it had closed about half a million accounts.
Some children said they were booted off their accounts in the days before and when the ban started - but many have said they were able to easily circumvent the age checks which included uploading credit card details, photo IDs or a selfie.

8855caef2d80.text: By — Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/what-to-know-about-the-affordable-care-acts-open-enrollment-period Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What to know about the Affordable Care Act's open enrollment period Health Nov 2, 2026 1:53 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — People heading into the Affordable Care Act open enrollment period with plans to sign up for insurance should expect a variety of changes in 2027, including higher premiums and fewer coverage options. The sign-up window for the marketplace, also known as Obamacare, starts Sunday in most states and runs through Jan. 15. Big changes to the exchange include expiring financial assistance, rising rates, potential delays in working with a broker, new restrictions on immigrants, and stricter enrollment checks. Financial help, including premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions, is now restricted for many groups of people who were previously eligible. Across the board, healthcare experts predict less coverage and higher prices, with the average price of health insurance purchased through the marketplaces expected to rise by 13% in 2027, according to analysis of new CMS data by the healthcare research nonprofit KFF. Increases are driven by multiple factors Cynthia Cox, a vice president and director of the ACA program at KFF, said the increase is primarily driven by rising healthcare costs, hospital market concentration, and potential factors such as the No Surprises Act, which took effect in 2022 and bans surprise billing, or the rising availability of GLP-1 drugs. The people who will be most affected by the new increases are those who do not qualify for a subsidy. "They may or may not be able to afford to continue to keep their coverage into next year," Cox said, adding that "a lot of them have already moved into bronze plans, which are the cheapest plans." READ MORE: Affordable Care Act enrollment shrank dramatically in many states over the past year, new federal data shows A CMS fact sheet about open enrollment that was distributed Friday says "Americans using HealthCare.gov will have robust access to low-cost plans." The price of ACA insurance has skyrocketed for many people during Trump's second term after Republicans opposed extending COVID-era subsidies that had helped offset the costs of health insurance for most enrollees during Democratic President Joe Biden's administration. That resulted in 1.2 million fewer people signing up for coverage in the exchanges. Nearly 20 million people in US are actively enrolled in ACA plans As of February, roughly 19.2 million people in the United States were actively enrolled in ACA marketplace health plans, according to the Department of Health and Human Services website. The number of enrollees grew during the COVID-19 pandemic when enhanced subsidies became available through the American Rescue Plan Act and Inflation Reduction Act, both signed into law by Biden. New regulations starting in 2027 will also limit tax credits for certain lawfully present immigrants, which could result in an additional 1 million uninsured individuals over time. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has been removing ACA enrollees from the program as part of the ongoing campaign against what it characterizes as waste, fraud and abuse. In September, Vice President JD Vance and other officials in the Republican administration announced plans to remove 760,000 ACA enrollees from public healthcare exchanges, alleging the individuals were fraudulently enrolled in the program or simply did not exist. Vance said the discovery and canceled subsidy payments for hundreds of thousands of people from the exchanges, part of an administration-wide crackdown on fraud, would result in $2.2 billion in cost savings. It's unclear how many more people will drop off of ACA coverage in 2027, Cox said. But with higher premiums, immigration eligibility changes and the anti-fraud efforts, "I think there's going to be fewer people enrolled in this market, but it's going to be harder to understand why." Ukrainians have grown weary of the relentless alerts blaring from their phones and echoing through their streets, day and night, warning of Russian drones and missiles.
On Sunday night, the system delivered something to make them sit up and take note â a succession of more extreme threats that quickly escalated to impending nuclear strikes, chemical attacks and combat on the streets.
But many in the country did not take them seriously and doubted the veracity of the messages.
Sofia Kochmar, 34, a mother-of-one living in the western city of Lviv, said she was initially concerned but quickly questioned the authenticity of the alerts.
"The first thing I saw was the word 'nuclear' and that made me pretty nervous and scared. So my first thought was that something nuclear was actually flying toward us."
"But then the notification mentioned 'street fighting in Kyiv', and I thought, wait, no, that's impossible."
The alerts included some messages written in Russian, and one included a link to a Telegram channel apparently owned by a hacker group.
Within 15 minutes, Ukraine's Air Force issued a statement saying the alert app had been compromised and clarifying there was no radiation threat. But it took more than an hour to issue "all clear" messages.
Anastasiia Romanytska, a 29-year-old ballerina living in Kyiv, said she does not have the alert app installed but friends forwarded her the warnings.
"My first reaction was, 'Is this some kind of joke?' But then my body reacted as if I was under stress. My heart started racing, and my stomach tightened up."
"Still, somehow I immediately realised that it wasn't something serious. Or maybe I just really wanted to believe that."
There are a number of apps delivering phone notifications of air raid warnings, with maps showing areas under threat, all using the same data as the official government-backed app.
Yevhen Baliutov, a cybersecurity expert at Kyiv School of Economics, told the BBC it was clear to him the Ukrainian alert system was hacked by Russians, saying many Ukrainians had clicked a link included with the alerts leading to a Russian Telegram channel, potentially exposing them to further disinformation, phishing attempts or data breaches.
"This is a war, so it's no surprise that Russia will try to hack, will try to send us fake news, will try to manipulate, and will use that for their propaganda."
While both Russia and Ukraine are widely believed to carry out cyberattacks against one another, the informal language used in the hoax alerts on Sunday pointed to so-called hacktivist groups, which could be aligned to Moscow or Kyiv but are not formally directed by either government.
Baliutov said it was also logical that Ukraine would have responded by launching a cyber-attack on the Russian emergency alert system. Both sides have similar capabilities in cyber warfare, he added.
Kochmar said after the initial concern, Ukrainians quickly turned to joking about the incident.
"All our work group chats immediately blew up. Everyone started messaging each other, discussing what was happening. And what I found fascinating was how quickly we turned the whole thing into a joke."
Although the impact of this incident had been limited, it illustrated the weakness of a crucial system, Baliutov said.
"It's very dangerous for Ukraine and for our people. When developing such applications, we need to consider security from the very beginning, without skipping essential security measures. When millions of people rely on a service, we cannot afford to take shortcuts with security."
The authorities already faced the challenge of maintaining public alertness after four and a half years of war with ceaseless attack warnings sounding sometimes hourly. Now they must reassure people the systems in place to protect them are robust, trustworthy and should be followed.

8334e0a464ae.text: The world seems convinced the end is near — and social media is amplifying that belief, convincing people to stock up on food, water, generators and other items. Why it matters: Online chatter is fueling viral predictions of societal collapse amid growing unease about the future. But you're probably not going to die tomorrow. What they're saying: Michael Mills, a researcher at the University of Kent who has studied doomsday prepping for more than a decade, told Axios that modern doomsday fears aren't necessarily about a specific apocalyptic scenario. "It's an overall reaction to uncertainty in most cases," Mills said. He noted that whereas Cold War-era survivalists were often focused on nuclear conflict, modern preppers worry about terrorism, climate disasters, geopolitical threats and emerging technologies. He described the modern mindset as a "multifaceted concern with uncertainty." State of play: Viral posts have repeatedly urged people around the world to stock up on food and water, following similar recommendations from various governments and warnings from former FBI Deputy Director Dan Bongino. The situation has gotten so buzzy that President Trump was asked about it in an interview Monday. He said Americans don't need to stock up because the U.S. is "in good shape. We're strong. We have a great military and we will not have those kind of problems." Separately, conservative commentator Tucker Carlson — a man with 17.9 million followers on X alone — published a lengthy post Sunday evening alleging that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pressuring Trump to launch renewed attacks on Iran after the midterms, potentially with a nuclear weapon. For what it's worth, Carlson has been predicting similar doomsday scenarios for a while, and he's been wrong before. And the Pentagon's newly reported plan calls for U.S. military bases to prepare to operate without outside support for at least 90 days, terrifying some people into asking , "What's the government know that they're not telling us?" The big picture: Worries about financial insecurity , skyrocketing health care costs , a lack of rainy-day savings and younger generations' perceived inability to buy a house all contribute to the feeling that life is not okay. Then you've got AI , which could cut thousands of jobs, enable a cyberattack or help engineer a dangerous, and potentially deadly, biological disease. And then there's the geopolitical situation: wars, genocide and the possibility of global warfare as China continues to threaten Taiwan and rumors abound that the U.S. and Israel will reignite the Iran war with a fresh round of attacks. Zoom in: Political uncertainty can also fuel doomsday prediction culture, particularly around major elections . Mills described the prepper movement as historically right-leaning, with fears increasing during the Obama and Biden administrations and subsiding among some preppers after Trump's 2016 victory. During elections, "where it can often seem that everything is at stake... we don't know which way those contests are going to go and so naturally that uncertainty kind of flares up," Mills said. Reality check: Preparing for a catastrophe doesn't make you a conspiracy theorist. Governments commonly warn people about potential disasters, like advising them to evacuate before a hurricane. Mills distinguishes ordinary emergency readiness from prepping, which typically involves preparing for disasters lasting weeks or months, sometimes longer. The bottom line: Nobody knows what catastrophe, if any, might come next. But feeling prepared and stocking up for a couple of days without power can make sitting in the dark a little less scary. Go deeper: Here's how AI could kill us all (if the worst fears come true)

8af800fbd3c8.text: By — Sarah Raza, Associated Press Sarah Raza, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-administration-promised-farmers-15-billion-in-weeks-before-midterms Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump administration promised farmers $15 billion in weeks before midterms Politics Nov 2, 2026 1:25 PM EST SIOUX FALLS, S.D. (AP) — President Donald Trump's administration has made $15 billion worth of promises to agriculture producers in the last few weeks before the midterm elections, initiatives intended to help offset higher costs for diesel and fertilizer that farmers have endured largely due to his tariffs and the war in Iran. Whether that will motivate more voters to turn out in agricultural states where traditionally Republican seats are now seen as competitive is unclear. It may explain his increased attention on rural areas, including visits Sunday to Iowa and Kansas, two days before the election. A look at the Republican administration's pledges to farmers: Whom these efforts will help Besides the more than $15 billion worth of payments and initiatives announced by Trump's Department of Agriculture, the agency plans $13.8 billion in safety net program payments for eligible producers for the 2025 crop year, offsetting shortfalls for farmers who grow key crops such as corn, soybeans, wheat and rice. Of the $15 billion, more than half will go toward an $8 billion one-time payment plan for farmers buffeted by soaring diesel prices. The USDA said it will release more details about the payments this month. It is not clear when the payments will go to farmers, who rely on diesel for trucks, tractors and combines. Gregg Ibendahl, a farm management specialist at Kansas State University, said he estimates the payments to "more than cover the increase in fuel costs," and that the money could help with high fertilizer prices. At least $5 billion was announced in guaranteed loans for ranchers and fishermen. An additional $1.8 billion in payments is for producers and landowners who participated in conservation programs, $573 million will go toward fertilizer manufacturing projects and $57 million is for expanding meat processors. For specialty crop producers, $86.6 million in grants will be awarded to innovative projects. On Thursday, the agency said it would purchase up to $472.5 million in agricultural commodities to support producers and give to charitable programs. The money will primarily come from the USDA and doesn't need immediate congressional approval. The USDA also announced other efforts, such as expanding sales of a diesel normally used only for off-road use, helping ranchers by making cattle sale data more transparent and strengthening wolf management policies to protect livestock. Why farmers are struggling It has been a frustrating year for farmers. Increased costs for fertilizer and fuel have made it difficult to turn a profit. Last year, tariffs drove up expenses for other equipment that farmers use, and the trade war with China resulted in a near boycott of U.S. agricultural goods. On Friday, diesel was averaging $6.32 per gallon, down slightly from its peak in September but 70% higher than the price a year ago, according to motor club AAA. Filling up a 100-gallon tank now costs $260 more than it did one year ago. WATCH: Farmers struggle with crops as climate change makes weather less predictable "That input side risk, I think, is the thing that really has hurt farmers this year, as well as the fact that there has been a lot more uncertainty about what's going to happen in the world," Ibendahl said. He said he expects these ad hoc payments to be a big help for farmers who otherwise would not make a profit this year, but they do not address the broader issues driving up prices. "It's hard to go to your lender in the next spring and say, 'OK, well, we're looking pretty good this year, but it's all because of these extra temporary government payments, so how much can you make me a loan (for) next year for my crop?'" he said. Alexandra Middlewood, an associate professor of political science at Wichita State University, said she has heard mixed reactions from farmers, who are happy their business will survive this year but see these programs as one-time bailouts rather than a long-term solution. What farmers may vote on Rural voters, including farmers and those who rely on the agricultural economy, have been an instrumental voting group for Trump. Michael Smith, a political science professor at Emporia State University, said many rural voters like the president, but some of his policies have hurt the agriculture industry. Immigrant deportations have threatened the agricultural labor force, and cuts to foreign aid and SNAP food stamps hurt the market for agricultural products. "Some people who admire Trump really just admire the person, the man," he said. "But it doesn't mean they necessarily like his policies. Well, Trump himself isn't on the ballot this year. His policies are." Cost of living and access to health care are top issues for rural voters, Middlewood said. She added that there is a perception the administration has not done enough to address these issues, even as Trump boasts at campaign rallies about a booming economy. Middlewood, who is based in Kansas, does not expect frustrated rural voters to shift to the Democratic Party, given how long the state has been a Republican stronghold. But some voters may decide to sit out of this election or vote independent, which would hurt Republican candidates. "Independent voters make or break elections," she said. "And so that's really what it's going to come down to this year is those independent voters and who they're breaking for." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their fridges and freezers, and raising concern about the vulnerabilities of internet-connected hardware from industrial machinery to humble domestic appliances.
Smart devices which are connected to the internet can include fridges, central heating, and even washing machines.
And while that makes them easier to control remotely, in theory, any device which goes online can potentially be exploited by malicious actors.
However, that doesn't mean hackers can easily take control of it, and big brands generally go to great lengths to make sure their tech is secure.
Exploits have been found before in some devices. In 2015, researchers demonstrated how a vulnerability in a Samsung smart fridge could allow them to intercept internet traffic.
But there's no evidence domestic appliances are being targeted in the cyber-attacks which targeted supermarkets in November.
Ciaran Martin, former chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says manufacturers needed to do more to make connected devices secure.
"There's a lot more that we need to demand of big tech to give us safer devices and products in the first place," he said.
He advised consumers to keep devices updated and enable multi-factor authentication wherever possible.
"I know it's a pain, but it only takes a few seconds," he said.
Since April 2024, UK law has required manufacturers of certain consumer smart devices to meet minimum cyber security standards, including requirements around passwords and security updates.
The NCSC said it was working with international partners and industry to understand the supermarket incidents, but it was unaware of any impact on the UK.
However, researchers from UK Cyber Defence have identified more than 800 refrigeration and building-control interfaces associated with British retailers that can be accessed over the public internet.
That doesn't necessarily mean they can be hacked, but it could leave them exposed to attackers exploiting weak passwords or software vulnerabilities.
The government has already held talks with senior food retailers about cyber resilience, following earlier attacks on supermarkets.
Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, has said cyber incidents are a major concern for retailers, with businesses working alongside the NCSC to share intelligence and strengthen their defences.
It would not be the first time that hacks have raised concern about impact on food supply.
When UK supermarkets M&S and the Co-op were targeted by ransomware hackers in May 2025, the retailers struggled to stock some shop shelves with fresh deliveries.
Customers across the UK complained of empty shelves in the days following the attack.
Tom Hegel, a researcher at cyber-security firm SentinelOne, said retailers must be clearer about responsibility.
"The question retailers need to answer is who owns the security of that equipment, not just who repairs it," he said.
He said internet connectivity can make everyday technology more convenient, but security needed to keep pace.
"Once an attacker can operate those controls, legitimate functions such as defrosting become tools for disruption," he said.
"Changing a setting can destroy physical stock, not just interrupt a computer system."
Could cars, power plants and water supplies be vulnerable?
Outside of the home, connected tech is used to remotely manage industrial machinery and vehicles.
Cyber security expert Ken Munro pointed to a 2015 demonstration in which researchers remotely hacked a Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, prompting improvements in vehicle security.
"Fortunately, the vehicle industry woke up to this and fixed the problem," he said.
Mobile connections are also widely used to monitor equipment in power plants and water networks, allowing engineers to manage systems remotely.
Munro said UK utilities were generally good at securing these connections, but standards varied around the world.
His biggest concern was smaller, poorly funded utility companies which may still be relying on older, vulnerable equipment.
Without proper protections, "any factory or equipment" connected to the internet - ranging from carmakers to electricity or transport infrastructure - could face similar risks, said Olivier Daloy, a cybersecurity expert at Zscaler.

cf5ec3840d74.text: The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to mandate that California separate ballots of more than 20,000 voters the government suspects are "likely" non-citizens. The big picture: A federal appeals court rejected the administration's bid to set aside mail ballots last week, erecting another roadblock in the DOJ's pre-election quest to demand the state root out claims of voter fraud in the final days of the midterm elections. Driving the news: "Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back," the DOJ wrote in an application filed to the high court. "The only way to preserve the district court's ability to grant relief to the United States after a full merits proceeding, therefore, is to segregate the challenged ballots now," the application, signed by Solicitor General D. John Sauer, continued. The DOJ's initial lawsuit came after the administration threatened California officials with emergency court action unless it probed potential ineligible voters over 48 hours and set aside ballots. Catch up quick: A federal appeals court and a federal judge stymied the administration's bid. U.S. District Judge David Carter cast doubt on the government's voter lists in a late October order denying the administration's request for a temporary restraining order, citing the "vagueness" of the government's "descriptions of its procedures and the unreliability of its similar claims in other states." And in last week's 2–1 ruling, a federal appeals court found that granting the request "would provoke catastrophic change, upending the administration of the election." What they're saying: "We will continue pursuing every available legal avenue to protect the integrity of our elections and ensure federal law is enforced," Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said in a statement shared to X. The California Secretary of State's office did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

13c8a9a936b9.text: By — Steven Sloan, Associated Press Steven Sloan, Associated Press By — Hillel Italie, Associated Press Hillel Italie, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/kennedy-center-names-2026-honorees-as-trump-renovation-battle-moves-show-offsite Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Kennedy Center names 2026 honorees as Trump renovation battle moves show offsite Arts Nov 2, 2026 1:11 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — The Kennedy Center said Monday that Paul Anka, David Foster, Andy Garcia, David Mamet and Barbara Mandrell would be recognized at this year's Kennedy Center Honors, which will be held away from the iconic performing arts venue for the first time as President Donald Trump battles with a federal court over his plans to renovate the building and add his name to it. All of the nominees have had substantial careers in their respective fields. Mamet is among the most acclaimed playwrights of his time, known for his hard-boiled dialogue in "Glengarry Glen Ross" and "American Buffalo" and other works. Mandrell is a member of the Country Music Hall of Fame whose many hits include "Years" and "Sleeping Single in a Double Bed" and Foster is among the most successful producers of the past 50 years, working with everyone from Chicago to Natalie Cole. Anka has written or co-written such iconic songs as "My Way" and the theme to the "Tonight" show when Johnny Carson was host. Garcia's acting credits include "The Untouchables," "The Godfather Part III" and the HBO film "For Love or Country." Several are either friendly with Trump or have been outspoken in support of conservative politics. Mamet told Fox News last year that he was once a "brain-dead liberal" who "discovered my conservative beliefs." Anka is a longtime friend of Trump who once rewrote "My Way," originally written for Frank Sinatra, with MAGA-themed lyrics. Foster has performed for Trump in the past. READ MORE: Kennedy Center Honors to be held at Capital One Arena amid fight over adding Trump's name The Kennedy Center Honors were established in 1978 and have been given to a broad range of artists. Until Trump's first term, presidents of both major political parties traditionally attended the annual ceremony, even when they disagreed politically with a given recipient. Prominent liberals such as Barbra Streisand and Warren Beatty were honored during the administration of Republican George W. Bush, and a leading conservative, Charlton Heston, was feted during the administration of Democrat Bill Clinton. Trump skipped the awards during his first term but has been far more involved with the Kennedy Center since returning to the White House. He fired the institution's board of directors and replaced them with loyalists who named him chairman. He personally announced last year's honorees and hosted the show that honored them. His administration has spent much of this year locked in a legal battle over whether and how to honor Trump, with the president insisting his name be added to the building in some form. As that plays out, the Kennedy Center has closed with its stages absent of performances for months. This year's honors program will be held on Dec. 7 at Washington's Capital One Arena. "We are proud to honor this year's class and to continue a tradition that has defined the Center for nearly 50 years," Trump said in a statement. Italie reported from New York. a539e2237f16.text: By — Amna Nawaz Amna Nawaz By — Maria Ramirez Uribe Maria Ramirez Uribe Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/watch-zelenskyy-confirms-ukraine-hacked-back-after-russias-cyberattack-of-its-emergency-alert-system Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Zelenskyy confirms Ukraine hacked back after Russia's cyberattack of its emergency alert system World Updated on Nov 2, 2026 4:47 PM EST — Published on Nov 2, 2026 1:06 PM EST Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that his country retaliated against Russia by hacking its emergency alert system. "We only respond on their attacks," Zelenskyy said in an interview with PBS News' Amna Nawaz. The cyberattack, the Ukrainian leader said, was a response to Russia seemingly hacking Ukraine's emergency alert system, which notifies residents of imminent threats. "They attacked our system," he said. "It was a cyberattack." READ MORE: Ukraine and Russia both report fake emergency alerts after cyberattacks target apps as limited ceasefire ends Ukrainian authorities said on Sunday that users received false warnings of an imminent nuclear threat on their emergency alert mobile app. The alert system was suspended but is now back up and running. SUPPORT PBS NEWS: Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass "When it was very clear … that it's their personal attack against our people, civilians," Zelenskyy said. "Of course, we responded." Russian authorities on Monday said hackers gained access to their emergency mobile app and sent fake emergency alerts. Here are other key takeaways from his interview with PBS News. Zelenskyy describes his relationship with Trump as 'emotional' When Nawaz asked Zelenskyy to describe his relationship with President Donald Trump in one word, Zelenskyy paused. "Emotional," he said. Trump has previously described Zelenskyy as "not a good guy," and has said he shouldn't be the Ukrainian president and doesn't want an end to the war. WATCH: Ukraine less reliant on U.S. as Trump-Zelenskyy rift deepens, former ambassador says Following the release of an American imprisoned in Russia, U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff described Putin as a "humanitarian." Putin has been indicted for war crimes by the International Criminal Court. WATCH: American imprisoned by Russia released as Witkoff meets and praises Putin "Sometimes we need to be pragmatic in this war," Zelenskyy said. "Who is an enemy? Who began this war? Putin. Don't find good words to describe him. I'm not sure that it will be helpful." Zelenskyy also criticized Trump's deal with Russia to import tons of Russian diesel to the U.S. "If you are really about money, business and pragmatism, so don't speak that it will have influence on the price in the United States," Zelenskyy said. "No, it's not true, it doesn't work." WATCH: Ukraine disputes Trump's claim of energy ceasefire as Russian diesel deal draws fire Experts say it's unlikely the deal will reduce global diesel prices in the near future. The Ukrainian president told Nawaz the pragmatic thing to do is to support Ukraine. "We have to support Ukraine," he said. "Because it has to be strong, because otherwise Putin will go further to Europe and to the different parts of NATO countries." Zelenskyy has asked Trump to reduce limits to Ukraine's use of Starshield Zelenskyy said he has asked Trump several times to reduce limits to Ukraine's use of Starshield, a military-grade version of Starlink satellite internet service. The system is funded by the Pentagon and operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX. Starshield, which is a key component of Ukraine's military communications network, has geographic restrictions. It can't be used to carry out attacks inside Russia. It can act defensively and in the Russian occupied territories of Ukraine. Zelenskyy said if given the opportunity, Ukraine would use the system to identify and attack missile launch sites inside Russia. He said Ukraine would not use Starshield to carry out massive attacks on Russia or energy sites due to the likelihood of civilian casualties. Lifting Starshield limits would mean Russia wouldn't "have opportunity to use each day ballistic missiles against us," Zelenskyy said. "Because we will block their launches." The Ukrainian president said Trump seemed open to the reduction of limits. "He said that he will try. It doesn't depend on him," Zelenskyy said. "He said that it depends mostly on SpaceX. He said that he's supportive, and I was very thankful." In mid-October, Starshield was partially disabled. The details of what happened are unclear. WATCH: How Starlink disruptions affected Ukraine's battlefield operations Musk said limits to Starshield's speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and Trump. Trump has said he didn't order the restrictions and doubted that Musk was to blame for the disruption. Asked who he thought was to blame for the disruption, Zelenskyy said he's unsure whether Musk can act alone. "I'm not sure that he can do it with Starshield because it's military. It's government version," Zelenskyy said. "I'm not sure that he could do it personally alone without any representatives from American government." Asked whether he believes Musk supports Ukraine and wants it to win the war, Zelenskyy said "I don't know." He said he wanted to speak with Musk following the Starshield disruptions but "they didn't connect with us." See more of our interview with Zelenskyy on Monday's PBS News Hour. 2c2923437d0a.text: By — Lindsay Whitehurst, Associated Press Lindsay Whitehurst, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-administration-asks-supreme-court-to-sideline-20000-disputed-california-mail-ballots Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump administration appeals to Supreme Court to sideline 20,000 disputed California mail ballots Politics Updated on Nov 2, 2026 4:37 PM EST — Published on Nov 2, 2026 12:53 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's administration appealed to the Supreme Court on Monday in its push to sideline thousands of disputed California mail ballots the day before the pivotal midterm elections. The emergency appeal came after a divided appeals court rejected the request to set aside ballots from some 20,000 people the federal government suspects may not be citizens. It also came just hours before another federal judge ruled against the administration's efforts to make last-minute changes in California's election. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The federal government says those ballots should not be counted until the voters' status can be verified. California officials say the list is highly unreliable and likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens. The Republican Trump administration has prioritized identifying noncitizen voters this year, despite them being rare. READ MORE: Analysis: More than 40% of names on DOJ list of alleged noncitizens not on California's voter rolls A district court judge had previously denied the Justice Department's request and warned that the demand could disenfranchise citizens in Tuesday's midterm elections to determine control of Congress. Also on Monday in Washington, Chief Judge James Boasberg ordered the Trump administration to stop making its demands, finding they violated the U.S. Constitution. "The Executive Branch has likely violated the Constitution's Elections Clause, which commits authority over election rules to the states and Congress alone," wrote Boasberg. At the high court, the Justice Department asked for a "limited injunction" that would direct California to set aside the ballots while the case plays out. "Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back," Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote. Voting has been underway in California, a largely Democratic state, since early October. All of the state's roughly 23 million registered voters are mailed a ballot. Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed. California election officials have said that finding and setting aside the challenged ballots now would be logistically impossible. California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said the appeal "reeks of desperation and is another attempt to undermine our elections and trample on the rule of law." Lower courts have sided with the state, with a district judge warning that segregating ballots would "wreak havoc" on the midterm elections and erode trust in the democratic process. "If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger," wrote U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, who was nominated by President Bill Clinton, a Democrat. A 2-1 appeals court panel upheld his order, with one judge appointed by Trump and another appointed by President Joe Biden, a Democrat, voting in favor. The third judge on the panel, also appointed by Trump, argued in a dissent that California's unwillingness to separate the ballots encourages the "violation of federal law." The Justice Department has sought to move the case along quickly, unsuccessfully asking an appeals court to intervene early. Trump's administration has racked up a series of wins in emergency appeals before the Supreme Court in his second term, but the justices previously rejected the president's push to restrict mail ballots ahead of the midterms. Associated Press writer Sophie Austin in Sacramento contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 03cfeb7d032b.text: Cyberattacks are wreaking havoc on an unlikely target across Europe: supermarket refrigerators. Why it matters: Hackers are turning everyday, internet-connected equipment into physical hazards, spoiling food and causing costly damage. U.S. supermarkets use similar technology, and the Pentagon is already investigating suspected cyberattacks involving refrigeration systems at six military commissaries. Driving the news: Suspected cyberattacks sent refrigerator and freezer temperatures soaring at dozens of European supermarkets overnight, spoiling food and threatening costly losses. Grocery chains Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt reported incidents affecting stores in Belgium and Luxembourg, while Swedish chains ICA and Coop reported similar disruptions, per Reuters . A Belgian company that operates Delhaize's refrigeration systems said hackers switched the units into defrost mode. Here's what to know. Supermarkets hacked in Europe Supermarkets in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported cyberattacks or IT disruptions, forcing some stores to discard spoiled food. Dozens of stores were affected, including an ICA supermarket in Sweden that said hackers set its refrigerator and freezer temperatures to 122°F, per ABC News . Authorities haven't shared who specifically is behind the attacks, per NBC News . Empty refrigerated shelves at a Proxy Delhaize supermarket in Maleizen, Belgium, following a refrigeration outage. Photo: Wiktor Dabkowski/Bloomberg via Getty Images Flashback: The incidents follow similar attacks in France last month, when hackers seized control of hundreds of refrigeration units, causing fires and spoiling food. It's unclear whether the attacks are connected. What they're saying: France's finance minister Roland Lescure said at the time that the attack "touches the heart of our food security." "It was a wake-up call for everyone," he said. How fridges get hacked How it works: Hackers aren't opening up each individual fridge and setting new temperatures. Instead, they target computer systems that control the temperatures of multiple refrigerated units remotely. Many stores use internet-connected controllers — small computer-like devices, sometimes with touchscreens — that allow maintenance workers to remotely monitor temperatures without having to visit every store. Hackers can exploit software flaws or stolen login credentials to change temperatures or activate defrost functions. Case in point: Danish manufacturer Danfoss said it identified security flaws last year and had long recommended customers install updates, according to The Guardian . In the Netherlands, some affected refrigeration systems used default passwords and were connected to unsecured networks. A supermarket manager discards spoiled food following a refrigeration outage linked to suspected cyberattacks across Europe on Nov. 2 in Belgium. Photo: Wiktor Dabkowski/Bloomberg via Getty Images The cost of hacked refrigerators Spoiled food: If temperatures rise overnight, the stores end up finding ruined meat, dairy and frozen products the next morning. In some French supermarkets, the soaring hot temperatures lasted for six hours, per Reuters. Spoiled food becomes unsafe to sell. Overheating and fires: Refrigerators can also overheat and cause fires. French prosecutors confirmed that the October attacks caused fires and food losses. Supermarkets lose money: Some stores lost more than €130,000. Two markets in the French region of Alsace reported combined losses of €270,000, per The Guardian . Intermarché's parent company estimated its nationwide losses in the tens of millions of euros. Yes, but: Not every attack causes extensive damage. In Estonia, a refrigeration company said technicians responded to the breach within minutes and halted any massive losses, per AP . Fridge attacks in the U.S. Zoom out: Many U.S. supermarkets use refrigeration technology similar to that found in Europe. Danfoss markets refrigeration monitoring and management systems in the U.S. Copeland, a U.S.-based refrigeration technology company, sells controllers that manage the grocery store display cases and walk-in refrigerators. What we're watching: The Pentagon is investigating whether cyberattacks caused freezer malfunctions at at least six U.S. military commissaries in August.

57b88ed6349c.text: By — Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press By — Volodymyr Yurchuk, Associated Press Volodymyr Yurchuk, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/a-brief-ceasefire-between-russia-and-ukraine-opens-a-perilous-escape-window-from-khersons-riverside-kill-zone Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter A brief ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine opens a perilous escape window from Kherson's riverside kill zone World Nov 2, 2026 12:38 PM EST KOZATSKE, Ukraine (AP) — A white towel on her gate and a white rag in her hand were Ukrainian Nataliia Diadiuk's only ways to tell Russian drone operators she is a civilian. When a brief ceasefire kicked in on Oct. 27, she had a moment of respite. The 53-year-old is one of a handful of residents left in Kozatske, a riverside village located in the kill zone of Ukraine's Kherson region less than 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from a Russian-controlled area. READ MORE: Ukraine and Russia both report fake emergency alerts after cyberattacks target apps as limited ceasefire ends "I really want silence," Diadiuk said, fighting back tears as she stood on an empty street lined with abandoned houses. "And I want to see the people who left, all of them. People left for both sides." Diadiuk's life has been reduced to basic survival: rainwater to drink, firewood gathered around town for heat, a radio she tries to tune in to for news, and the remnants of humanitarian aid that had not reached her in two years until the brief ceasefire that ended Sunday night just days after it began. Going out means dodging every kind of weapon, including mines scattered everywhere. The neighbors she mentions are more often the dead than the few still living nearby. A team from The Associated Press gained rare access to a so-called red zone to see firsthand what life in the kill zone looks like, a visit made possible only because of a brief, localized ceasefire tied to the humanitarian aid mission in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky. People walk next to damaged buildings, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in the frontline city of Kherson, Ukraine, Oct. 28, 2026. Photo by Reuters stringer Oleshky has drawn the world's attention, but civilians are trapped in many more places on both sides of the front line. During the mission, Ukrainian regional officials, police, the Ukrainian Red Cross Society and volunteers, with the facilitation of civil-military cooperation specialists, used the rare window of time to reach people on their side of the river, some of them cut off for nearly two years. In all, 180 people were evacuated from riverside communities and the city of Kherson, including 23 children, the regional administration said. About 140,000 people remain in the Ukrainian-held part of the Kherson region. Before the war, the whole region, now nearly 70% under Russian control, had about 1 million residents. The riverside is designated a red zone, the highest level of military danger. With the ceasefire over, residents will again face drones, artillery, glide bombs and airdropped mines. Still, many refuse to leave. Some cannot afford to start over, and others will not abandon the places where they grew up. Life is grim in the kill zone On the road to Diadiuk's village, burned-out cars sit abandoned where they were hit, alongside wrecked ground robots that Ukrainians try sending down roads too dangerous for people. A relic of peacetime still stands on that road: "Thank you for keeping the roadside clean." In the village, many houses are reduced to burned walls. Glide bombs have left craters, and the tail fins of shells stick out of the asphalt like flowers. Mines dropped from drones lie everywhere, some petal-shaped, others improvised and wrapped in foil or plastic, so every step must be taken with care. Thick vegetation swallows the ruins of empty houses. What Diadiuk finds hardest to bear is the howling of the dogs left behind in the houses, surviving much as she is. "Even for the sake of these, I can't leave them," she says, pointing to two thin dogs that never stray far from her. But she shares what little food she has with other dogs as well. A woman walks on a street covered with an anti-drone net, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in the frontline city of Kherson, Ukraine Oct. 30, 2026. Photo by Nina Liashonok/ Reuters Isolated and forced to fight for survival every day, she has lost track of time. "I turn on my phone only to see what day it is," she says. She charges it with solar panels. Diadiuk collects rainwater, strains it through gauze, treats it with chlorine and boils it. "The water here is more or less all right," she says. "There are a lot of dead lying in the houses, so it's good water only in a manner of speaking." Why people stay The village's ordeal began in the first days of Russia's full-scale invasion, when it was occupied. After Ukrainian forces liberated it, Kozatske gradually came under siege by drones as the war turned increasingly technological. "Before, I'd just open the door and walk out," said Oleksii Shavokin, 54, who lives a little farther down the street. "Now I open it a crack, stick my ear out and listen to the sky." His house burned down in early 2023 after a mortar attack, he said, but he patched it up and stays on there. He lives off old humanitarian aid and eggs from the hens he still keeps. "I ration my food so it lasts. I'm used to it," he said. "Now I eat once a day, in the evening, and that's quite enough." He has lost 30 kilograms (66 pounds) from a weight of close to 100 kilograms (220 pounds).
