President Trump delivered his closing message in Washington at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool after days of campaigning in mostly red states. Lisa Desjardins reports. Geoff Bennett: On this Election Day eve, candidates spent the day making their final pitches to voters following a weekend of last-minute rallies and a high-profile Democratic defection in Michigan. Amna Nawaz: President Trump delivered his closing message here in Washington, D.C., today at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool after days of campaigning in mostly red states. Lisa Desjardins has our report. (APPLAUSE) Lisa Desjardins: Today, President Trump's closing message from a place off the trail, but close to the White House. President Donald Trump: The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history. Lisa Desjardins: The president chose the location to tout the newly reopened Lincoln Reflecting Pool. President Donald Trump: Despite all that we went through, the Reflecting Pool right now looks better than it ever looked, and it is better. Lisa Desjardins: But Trump's effort there has mostly made headlines for problems, peeling paint and algae blooms after spending millions on repairs, a symbol of a polarizing president who is off the ballot, but heavily on voters' minds this election, as in New Hampshire this morning. Rob Fremeau, New Hampshire Voter: I will stick with our Republican governor, Kelly Ayotte, and every other office I'm going to vote Democratic to counter Trump. Lisa Desjardins: And Kansas, which has become an unexpected Senate battleground. Julie Bees, Kansas Voter: I'm a registered Republican, but I voted Democrat in the Senate race because I wasn't happy with the way our Republican senators have just been bowing to the wishes of President Donald Trump. Lisa Desjardins: Across the country, early voting is surging. This center in Wichita saw long lines today. Some in other states waited hours over the weekend. Time is running out for candidates making their final pitches, including in Texas. Ken Paxton (R): I'm not exaggerating when I say, if we lose Texas, we lose America. State Rep. James Talarico (D-TX): This election is about whether you want a senator who puts money in your pocket or who puts money in their own. Lisa Desjardins: And Maine... Troy Jackson (D): And you're a unicorn? Lisa Desjardins: ... where Democratic Senate candidate and former logger Troy Jackson dressed as a cord of wood for Halloween. Troy Jackson: People are coming out in droves because they know this government is broke and it has to change. Lisa Desjardins: The costume served as a rebuttal to an attack ad from his opponent Republican Susan Collins' campaign. Bill Green, Former Maine Sportscaster: But we're not talking about buying a cord of wood here. We're sending someone to the U.S. Senate, and Troy doesn't have the tools he needs to be effective. Lisa Desjardins: Meanwhile, in Michigan, a striking reversal that ignited a political firestorm. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-MI): I'm a proud Democrat. And I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States. Lisa Desjardins: Democratic Representative Haley Stevens announced Sunday she's backing the Republican in her state's Senate race. For weeks, Stevens has supported her progressive primary opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, after narrowly losing to him. But tensions rose, including over his outspoken criticism of Israel. She demanded specific statements from him and then was disinvited from an event with him. Rep. Haley Stevens: I'm a really proud Democrat. Lisa Desjardins: Something she referenced in an interview last night. Anderson Cooper, CNN Host: People change their mind. I'm just wondering, what changed? Rep. Haley Stevens: Nothing with me changed, Anderson. This is -- look, this is about Abdul getting angry and angrier and saying, I don't want these people in my campaign. Lisa Desjardins: Stevens has been a fierce critic of President Trump, but yesterday he praised her decision alongside House Speaker Mike Johnson. President Donald Trump: It's a smart thing to do because El-Sayed would destroy our country. So I thought that was fantastic. Rep. Mike Johnson (R-LA): I have spoken to her, encouraged her to stay safe and keep speaking the truth. And I think she's doing that very well. Lisa Desjardins: For his part, El-Sayed said he's more focused on the issues. Abdul El-Sayed (D): At the end of the day, I actually don't think about Haley Stevens. I'm just less interested in the politics of it all than I am in the policy of it all. Lisa Desjardins: A final New York Times/Siena poll taken before Stevens' announcement shows El-Sayed leading Rogers by a whopping 11 points. That poll has Democrats in the lead or virtually tied in all seven of the battleground states that will determine control of the Senate, including Texas, Maine, Ohio, Kansas, Iowa, and Alaska. And regarding Alaska, a federal judge over the weekend rejected a Trump administration lawsuit aiming to block the results if Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan loses. Also today, the DOJ announced charges for 63 individuals in connection with election-related crimes. It's part of the administration's monthslong effort to crack down on voter fraud, which multiple studies and audits have shown to be extremely rare. A major election with high turnout and high drama to the end. Amna Nawaz: And in another legal development, late today, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to block California from counting 20,000 ballots that the Trump administration alleges were cast by potential noncitizens. Geoff Bennett: More than 57 million Americans have already cast their ballots ahead of Election Day. Our Lisa Desjardins is back with more on what those early votes can and cannot tell us. So, Lisa, how does this year's early vote stand as comp

321992dfdaab.text: In our news wrap Monday, investigators believe parts of a private jet may have broken off before it crashed in Florida, a federal judge dismissed the Trump administration's lawsuit against Harvard University over whether it uses race as a factor in its admissions and supermarkets across Europe reported a new wave of cyberattacks targeting their refrigeration systems. Geoff Bennett: And we start the day's other headlines in South Florida. Federal investigators say parts of a private jet appear to have broken off before it crashed yesterday, killing all nine people on board. This image from a driver dashcam captured the moment of impact, which caused a massive explosion and left behind a crater near West Palm Beach. National safety officials say they're looking far beyond the crash site for evidence of what went wrong. Thomas Chapman, National Transportation Safety Board: We do have some indication that the aircraft was breaking up before impact. And so some of this is yet to be determined. We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site. Geoff Bennett: The pilot of the Bahamas-bound Learjet 60 reported ice and turbulence to air traffic control before it rapidly descended. Officials have not released the names of the victims. In Washington, D.C., a federal judge dismissed the charges today against two former FBI officials, saying the case against them can only be described as weaponization. Nikki Flores and Bradley Benavides had been accused of lying to Congress in 2023 about their knowledge of efforts to investigate Hunter Biden's laptop. Last week, the same judge criticized prosecutors for trying to add additional charges without going through the proper procedures. Those two were dropped. The Justice Department could still pursue a grand jury indictment against the two former officials. In Massachusetts, a federal judge dismissed the Trump administration's lawsuit against Harvard University today over whether it uses race as a factor in its admissions. The DOJ had sued the Ivy League school earlier this year for access to years of admissions data. The administration alleged that Harvard was not complying with the 2023 Supreme Court decision that prohibits race-based admissions programs. But the judge sided with Harvard, whose lawyers said the case was intended to punish the school for refusing other administration demands. Turning overseas now, supermarkets across Europe reported a new wave of cyber attacks targeting their refrigeration systems today. At least one store said hackers remotely raise temperatures in refrigerators and freezers to as high as 122 degrees Fahrenheit, forcing employees to throw out spoiled food. Incidents were reported in several countries, including Belgium, Ireland, the Netherlands, and Sweden. Richard Nilsson, Store Manager (through interpreter): Some organization hacked into the temperature monitoring system. It's insane. I don't see what they stand to gain from it. It's a form of terrorism really. Geoff Bennett: It follows a similar cybersecurity incident in France last month. Authorities have not identified who was behind the attacks, and no one has claimed responsibility. The FDA has approved a generic version of the world's only twice-yearly injection to prevent HIV. The medication is called lenacapavir, and it's expected to cost around $40 per person each year. That makes it comparable in price to daily medications, but experts point out the convenience of only needing two doses a year. It's a major step toward making the drug more available in around 120 low- and middle-income countries. The Kennedy Center has announced its latest group of honorees as the ceremony prepares for the first time ever to be held off-site. This year's honors will recognize Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright David Mamet, 16-time Grammy winning producer and composer David Foster, legendary singer-songwriter Paul Anka, Country Music Hall of Fame artist Barbara Mandrell, and Oscar nominated actor Andy Garcia. The Kennedy Center itself has been closed for months amid a legal battle over President Trump's plans to renovate the building and add his name to it, forcing the December 7 ceremony to move to Washington's Capital One Arena. Today, a 57-year-old British man completed an extraordinary journey, walking 31,000 miles across the world over nearly three decades. Woman: Where have you been? Karl Bushby, British Adventurer: Where have I been? Well, we're back now. Geoff Bennett: Karl Bushby embraced his mother as he returned home to Hull -- that's in Northern England -- after his extraordinary journey. The former paratrooper set out from the southern tip of Chile in November 1998 at just 29 years old, inspired by an idea from his father, who was an Army veteran. Bushby's journey took him through some 30 countries across four continents. Along the way, he reflected on what kept him going. Karl Bushby: It's a mix of the mission, the challenge. Behind the scenes there, there was the wanderlust, a guy who had an affinity for horizons. Geoff Bennett: Bushby was determined to make the entire journey on foot, never hitchhiking or relying on transportation, but his trek was delayed for long stretches by the COVID pandemic, border restrictions, and other obstacles. On Wall Street today's stocks ended mixed amid ongoing concerns in the AI sector. The Dow Jones industrial average managed a gain of about 200 points, but the Nasdaq dropped more than 1 percent. The S&P 500 also started the week in negative territory. And Milton Coleman, a pioneering editor at The Washington Post who broke racial barriers and helped shape generations of journalists, has died. Coleman was the first Black journalist named to the paper's masthead and rose to become its highest-ranking Black editor. He oversaw The Post's local news coverage, mentored generations of journalists, and championed efforts to make newsrooms more representative of the communities they cover. Milton Coleman

8d7bd70727e4.text: A Russian strike on an aid station and shelter killed at least 26 people in southern Ukraine on Monday. It was the latest in an unceasing series of Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities and the civilians living there. Before the bombing, Amna Nawaz spoke with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as the war remains at a stalemate both on the battlefield and at the negotiating table. Amna Nawaz: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced this evening that a Russian strike on an aid station and shelter killed at least 26 people in Southern Ukraine today. It was the latest in an unceasing series of Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities and the civilians living there. Before that bombing, I spoke with President Zelenskyy from Kyiv for a wide-ranging interview as the war remains in a stalemate, both on the battlefield and at the negotiating table. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, welcome back to the "News Hour." Thank you for joining us. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukrainian President: Thank you very much for an invitation, Amna. Amna Nawaz: So I want to begin with some news just from last night. The air raid alert app that most of Ukraine relies on to alert them to incoming attacks, that was seemingly hacked. It was sending out false alerts about chemical and nuclear threats in Ukraine. Russian authorities then said today that their emergency mobile app was also hacked and sending out fake alerts. Do you know what happened? Did Russia hack your system and did Ukraine hack them back? Volodymyr Zelenskyy: Yes, it's true. You are absolutely right, Amna. They attacked our system. It was cyberattack, one of the hundreds and thousands of those been made by Russians before on banking system, on pensions, social support, a lot of different support for civilians. And also, of course, they want each day to make chaos in Ukraine in all our cities, one of such steps by Russia. And, of course, we -- as always, we said, and I underline it several times, that we only respond on their attacks. So, of course, after the attack, when we -- it was very clear for all our people and for all our personal and the intelligence that it's their personal attack against our people, civilians, of course, we responded. Amna Nawaz: So you're confirming you did hack them back? And was that hack limited to this emergency mobile app? Volodymyr Zelenskyy: Yes, absolutely. We just responded on the attack. Amna Nawaz: I see. OK. I do want to ask about news over the last few days as well, because Ukraine has now resumed strikes on Russian energy strikes -- sites rather. As you know, President Trump and his envoys have long been pushing for some kind of energy cease-fire. He's also repeatedly blamed you for the rise in global fuel prices because of those attacks. Tell us why Ukraine resumed those strikes in Russia. Volodymyr Zelenskyy: We always respond, as I said, the same, like on this cyberattack, the same with the energy. But also, with energy, we have been very clear and open to President Trump when he said that he asked us not to attack refineries. I said, OK, we will not if Russia will not attack our energy system. And Russia did it several times. And it was awful attacks, massive attacks, very tough against our people. We had huge problems with electricity. And that's why we responded. What is painful for them? First of all, it's refineries, oil, energy, gas, and et cetera, and diesel, yes. So that's why we did it. And we asked the president to give phone call to Putin and ask him to support energy cease-fire because Trump proposed it. But, as we understood, the Russians delayed. I said it publicly. We will not attack their refineries. I hope that they will -- at the end, they will at least support not to attack our energy system. But they attacked. All these days, they attacked us. And, at the end of these four days, we responded. Amna Nawaz: I want to ask you about your ongoing war effort and the degree to which it depends on this Starlink and Starshield system, satellite communication system that Elon Musk owns. You have said that that system is back to a normal speed after there was a slowdown late last month. I'm sure you saw reports that Elon Musk, who owns the system, ordered the slowdown. He had said President Trump was responsible. President Trump denies that. It's very unclear to many people what happened here. I'm asking, what is your understanding of who was behind the slowdown? What do you believe happened? Volodymyr Zelenskyy: Between us, I think that it can't work without one of the sides. Technically, Elon and SpaceX can slow down, can stop it, and then tactically bringing back, yes. And now it works. So, it means that -- I mean, this -- both sides decided to block or to unblock. I don't know... (CROSSTALK) Amna Nawaz: When you say both sides, just to clarify, you say it would take both the president and Elon Musk to slow it down, or do you believe Musk acted alone? Volodymyr Zelenskyy: No, no, he could act alone. I don't know -- I don't know the rules. Amna Nawaz: Do you believe he did? Volodymyr Zelenskyy: I'm not sure that he can do it with Starshield, because it's military. It's government version. I'm not sure that he could do it personally alone, without any representatives from American government. But I don't know who from American side from the government did it, who allowed him. I think it was a dialogue between some people, and in -- during this dialogue, the decision was negative for us. Amna Nawaz: Do you believe that Elon Musk supports Ukraine, that he wants Ukraine to win the war? How worried are you, if he was behind the slowdown, that it could happen again? Volodymyr Zelenskyy: I don't know really, between us. I wanted very much to speak with him about different issues. We had conversation at the beginning of the war. We spoke about different things. And then, after, I gave so many positive messages about him. I was very thankful for Starlink. And we are really very thankful for this. We have b

3961206e1c6f.text: The Trump administration is preparing to deport at least 150 Afghans over the next 48 hours, first to Pakistan and then to Taliban-controlled Afghanistan. Many of those facing deportation are relatives of those who worked alongside the United States. They could face severe retaliation from the Taliban upon their return. Nick Schifrin discussed more with Shawn VanDiver of Afghan Evac. Geoff Bennett: The Trump administration is preparing to deport at least 150 Afghans over the next 48 hours, first to Pakistan and then to Taliban-controlled Afghanistan. Many of those facing deportation are relatives of those who worked alongside the U.S., and they could face severe retaliation from the Taliban upon their return. Here's Nick Schifrin. Nick Schifrin: Geoff, attorneys and advocates for Afghans here in the U.S. and those stuck in limbo overseas say the U.S. has not done enough for years for those who fought alongside or are family members of those Afghans who helped the U.S. during its 20-year campaign in Afghanistan. Tonight, a group of more than 60 members of Congress are calling on the Departments of Homeland Security and State to cancel the deportation. And now they say the 150 Afghan deportees fear for their lives if forced to return to their country of birth. We now turn to Shawn Vandiver, president of AfghanEvac, an organization which aids in resettlement efforts. Shawn Vandiver, thanks very much. Welcome back to the "News Hour." Tell us about these Afghans who are being deported today, tomorrow. What are their stories? Shawn Vandiver: The simple fact is that these are family of people who served alongside our military. These are women. We know of reportedly three women who are supposed to be on this flight. These are -- there's a police officer, a former police officer. And it doesn't even matter what their job was. The fact is that these folks have been here in the United States for a long period of time and now they're in grave danger, being sent back to certain death at the hands of the Taliban. Nick Schifrin: Talk about that certain death. There are some judges who have ruled, no, the risk isn't that high. What do you believe the risk is to these Afghans if they are forced to return to their country? Shawn Vandiver: Well, the horrifying pictures in my phone of Afghans who were killed because of their service alongside us since the fall of Kabul would tell otherwise. We know that people are being taken. People are being harmed by rogue members of the Taliban maybe, but certainly people are being harmed,. And that -- those judges, frankly, don't know what they're talking about. They should read the country conditions reports that exist out there and are surely attached to those cases. Nick Schifrin: And, in fact, the State Department says that there is a risk to everyone going back to Afghanistan, as they call it, level four. I talked to the State Department, the White House. They referred me to the Department of Homeland Security. DHS declined to provide any details for the deportations, but the administration has argued that they are deporting criminals from the country, including those who arrived here illegally, and that some of the deportees do have felonies. What's your response to that overall argument? Shawn Vandiver: Even if the deportees have felonies, which most of these folks don't have crimes -- we know that -- but even for those who do, whatever their crimes were, the sentence is not supposed to be death. And that's why AfghanEvac is working alongside Congress and others to lead our campaign to stop the flight. And your viewers can go to AfghanEvac.org to learn more and help us out. Nick Schifrin: And, finally, you and I have been talking about this for years. How do you think today's deportation reflects a broader policy approach by this administration, U.S. in the past? Part of a trend or not? Shawn Vandiver: Well, when this administration took over, we had some hopes that they would continue the safest, most secure legal immigration pathway that we had built during the Biden administration called Enduring Welcome. They shut it down on day one, and every day since, AfghanEvac and our partners have been working against a hostile administration, an administration hostile to Afghans. It's been horrific. These folks do not deserve to live in this limbo. It is quite literally killing them. And I just can't imagine, as a parent, for example, not having held my baby for six years, almost six years, because whoever sits behind the Resolute Desk doesn't think we're good enough to be reunified with our family. Nick Schifrin: Shawn Vandiver is president of AfghanEvac. Thank you very much. Shawn Vandiver: Thank you.

e02860db8bd3.text: Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens’ decision to back Republican Mike Rogers in the U.S. Senate race has sent shockwaves through the Democratic Party. To discuss the shifting dynamics in the Senate race, Amna Nawaz spoke with Michigan Democratic Congresswoman Debbie Dingell. Amna Nawaz: Michigan Congresswoman Haley Stevens' decision to back Republican Mike Rogers in the U.S. Senate race has sent shockwaves through the Democratic Party. For more on the shifting dynamics in the Senate race, Michigan Democratic Congresswoman Debbie Dingell joins me now. Congresswoman, it's good to see you. Thanks for joining us. Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-MI): Thank you. It's good to be with you. Twenty-four hours. We're going to be done in another day. Amna Nawaz: Another day, but, in the meantime, there's some big headlines today, as we just noted. You have said that you spoke with Haley Stevens multiple times over the last week. She told you she would not endorse Mike Rogers, and then she did. I'm sure you have seen in some of her latest interviews. She said she did it because she believes Rogers loves this country. From your conversations with her, does this explanation make sense to you? Rep. Debbie Dingell: I was stunned when it happened on Sunday. Haley is a human being. She's gone through a very difficult race in the primary. I don't know what changed or why she did do this. And I think this has become a -- has been and continues to be a huge distraction from what the issues are when people go to the polls tomorrow. Amna Nawaz: Congresswoman, no doubt the economy cost of living remains the number one issue, but this is a key state that Democrats need to win. And, as you mentioned, it was a very tight primary race, a very heated and divisive primary race there. We know this issue of the U.S. approach and policy towards Israel deeply divided these two candidates in Haley Stevens and Abdul El-Sayed. Stevens is a stalwart supporter of the state. El-Sayed has sharply criticized the state. I mean, it's fair to say your party has not dealt with this issue. How do you reckon with that? Rep. Debbie Dingell: The hate that we have seen in this state for the last few months, the ads on all sides are despicable. They are full of hate. They have contributed to pitting people in Michigan against each other, and they're unacceptable, and I condemn every last one of these negative ads. The Jewish community has always been important that I hear them, that I talk to them, that I understand what they're saying, because I lived in Dearborn for 30 years. And Arab American and Muslims were my next-door neighbors. They were my friends. And yet I had lunch with a group of Arab American leaders on Saturday. You should have heard the fear in their voice of what -- they want Abdul to win, but they're afraid of the violence that could be directed at them. Everybody deserves, no matter what their faith is, no matter what their cultural background is, to live in this country feeling safe and to be treated with respect and with dignity. Amna Nawaz: Congresswoman, as it relates to this Senate race, though, which is Democrats' fight for control of the Senate, is critical for your party, are you worried that Haley Stevens endorsing the Republican means voters who were unsure about El-Sayed feel they have permission to vote for the Republican too? Rep. Debbie Dingell: You know, I was trying to figure this out when it just happened. I did feel on Saturday that this is leaning towards Abdul. It's going to be a tight race. But as I was out yesterday, NAACP, the UAW disability dinner, canvasses, this put a lot of energy into people. You saw several members of our congressional delegation put out strong statements of support for Abdul. Amna Nawaz: You think this has tipped the race in El-Sayed's favor? Rep. Debbie Dingell: I do. I think it's backfiring. Amna Nawaz: Well, let me ask you then before I let you go. Democrats say that it is a big tent party. Is there room for someone like Haley Stevens in the Democratic Party? Rep. Debbie Dingell: Haley has hurt herself with many Democrats. And I think there are people that can -- that have strong feelings and need to be part of the Democratic Party. But I think the way that this was handled has left many people upset, not thinking that they can trust her. It's just been a very difficult weekend. Amna Nawaz: That's Michigan Democratic Congresswoman Debbie Dingell joining us today. Congresswoman, we know it's a busy day for you. Thank you for making the time. Rep. Debbie Dingell: Thank you.

2b86d3130bb8.text: In the run-up to the midterm elections, experts have documented a surge of Islamophobia in political ads and speeches. Special correspondent Fred de Sam Lazaro reports on some of the targets of that rhetoric and the impact it’s making. It's part of our series, Race Matters. Amna Nawaz: In the run-up to tomorrow's midterm elections, experts have documented a surge of anti-Muslim rhetoric and xenophobia in political ads and speeches. Special correspondent Fred de Sam Lazaro brings us a report on some of the targets of that language and the impact it's having. It's part of our series Race Matters. Imam Abdulahi Farah, Dar Al-Farooq Mosque Islamic Center: People are choosing tribalism over humanity. Immigrants are blamed. Muslims are blamed. Black and brown communities are blamed. Fred de Sam Lazaro: During a recent prayer service at the Dar Al-Farooq Mosque Islamic Center outside Minneapolis, Imam Abdulahi Farah had a pointed message, both for politicians and his own community. Imam Abdulahi Farah: Whether it's oppression, whether it's hate, whether it's injustice, whether it's done by someone you know or someone from outside, you have to take action. Fred de Sam Lazaro: Minnesota's Somali population has been in the national spotlight since last year amid a series of massive fraud scandals. Man: Evacuated because of a shooting. Fred de Sam Lazaro: But the community is now again under intense scrutiny over a rash of gun violence that authorities blamed on gangs of young Somali men. Minnesota Republicans seized on the events. Rep. Tom Emmer (R-MN): These criminal gangsters, which I would argue are enemy combatants more than anything, they're not holding them accountable. Lisa Demuth (R), Minnesota Gubernatorial Candidate: This is not who we are. We need safe communities, not Somali gang shoot-outs like the one that happened here. Fred de Sam Lazaro: So did President Trump, who said Minnesota is being -- quote -- "taken over by Somali immigrants" and the state needed to fight back. The president has also singled out Minnesota Congresswoman Ilhan Omar. President Donald Trump: I think she's a sick, a very dishonest person, but -- who hates our country. And she comes from a country that is essentially not even a country, Somalia. It's real shithouse, OK? Fred de Sam Lazaro: Federal investigators raided Omar's home last month as part of an investigation into whether she or family members committed immigration fraud. Omar has denied any wrongdoing. President Donald Trump: We can't let radical left jihadists... Fred de Sam Lazaro: But this election cycle, the president and his allies have widened their attacks on Muslim candidates. Narrator: Abdul raises money from dangerous people who finance terrorist networks. And his family has been linked to the Muslim Brotherhood and al-Qaida. Fred de Sam Lazaro: In particular, Michigan's Democratic Senate nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, linking him without evidence to extremist groups. President Donald Trump: We don't want to have a jihadist. We're going to have to get a special medal detector for Abdul. Vice President J.D. Vance: We have to understand what happens when our nation gives in to these kinds of people, to young men with zero attachment to its land or to its history. Fred de Sam Lazaro: The rhetoric, though, has gone well beyond El-Sayed himself. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. spoke at a campaign event for El-Sayed's opponent, former Republican Congressman Mike Rogers. Robert F. Kennedy Jr.: There's 500 million Arabs in the world. And yet they don't produce science. They don't win the Nobel Prize. They don't win the Field Prize. They don't win the Wolf Prize. They don't produce literature. Fred de Sam Lazaro: In fact, Arabs have won all of those awards. Anti-Muslim sentiment was also widespread at the Republican Midterm Convention in September. Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX): Islamism, likewise, produces murder and oppression. Sharia law has no place in America. (CHEERING) Sara Tabor, Republican Voter: Islam doesn't have the same principles and values that we do as Christians. Lisa Holomshek, Republican Voter: All the mosques that are being built, it's out of control. Saher Selod: The rhetoric certainly is something that I haven't seen since 9/11. Fred de Sam Lazaro: Saher Selod is the director of research at the Institute for Social Policy and Understanding, a think tank focused on America's Muslim community. Selod has tracked Islamophobia in U.S. politics. Saher Selod: I have never seen the level of anti-Muslim political ads that we're seeing during this campaign cycle. The fact that it was already somehow acceptable to run on this type of racism and animus means that it's trending to a certain extent within the general population. If it was so unpopular, then they wouldn't -- they wouldn't feel like that this would be a successful strategy. Fred de Sam Lazaro: Back in Minnesota, officials are trying to navigate the political realities of the moment while searching for real solutions. Booker Hodges, Bloomington, Minnesota, Police Chief: A lot of this outside rhetoric, unfortunately, is political, and it's not helping. Fred de Sam Lazaro: Booker Hodges is police chief in the Minneapolis suburb of Bloomington. (GUNFIRE) Fred de Sam Lazaro: Last month, suspects fired over 100 rounds on a residential street in the city, a shooting Hodges linked to Somali gangs. Booker Hodges: I know that it's not the entire community that's doing this, but we do ourselves a disservice if we don't call it what it is. b6c30a586903.text: NPR’s Tamara Keith and Amy Walter of the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter join Geoff Bennett to discuss the latest political news, including President Trump's focus on the Reflecting Pool on the day before the election, the last-minute spectacle in the Michigan Senate race and the early signals to watch on Election Night. Geoff Bennett: Well, if it's the day before Election Day, that means it's Politics Monday. And here with us is our usual duo, Amy Walter of The Cook Political Report With Amy Walter and Tamara Keith of NPR. It's great to see you both. So, on the eve of these midterms, President Trump is relitigating the damage done to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, even though his own Justice Department, we should say, concluded that the botched construction, not vandalism, was responsible for the damage there. But, Amy, what does it tell us about the president's priorities that he's still focused on this, when voters are focused on the economy and the direction of the country? Amy Walter, The Cook Political Report: Yes, I mean, you really -- the split screen between voters' concerns and what the president wants to talk about is not just apparent today in this press conference, but has been apparent to voters for quite some time. And you can see that opinions about how the president is handling the economy, driven, of course, by inflation and the cost of gas, but also driven by this frustration that voters have that they don't think the president cares enough about it or is working hard enough on these issues. We hear it from voters all the time that they feel like, well, wait, why is the president talking about this and not talking about the things that he campaigned on, which is lowering my costs? I also think it's notable, when I'm listening to other Republicans, how they're closing out their campaign. Again, you said the election is going to be about the economy. We all know that that's a top issue. But when you listen, especially in these red states, Republicans are closing out their campaigns, not on talking about what they're going to do to improve the economy, but how terrible the Democrats are. It would be very problematic, say a number of them in places like Texas and Kansas, if you elected this Democrat, because then it means Democrats are in charge of the Senate, so hoping -- not really trying to sway swing voters, just trying to turn out their base, which, as we have talked about all year, still seems very, very uneager to vote. Geoff Bennett: And, Tam, when the president in his remarks was talking about tomorrow's election, he didn't sound entirely optimistic. I mean, you heard him use that same refrain about how the midterms are often tough on the sitting president's party. He was almost telegraphing defeat. Tamara Keith, National Public Radio: Yes, he was talking in the past tense, saying, like, we gave it a good try. And, certainly, the president and his allies did everything they could to tilt this playing field in favor of Republicans, redrawing congressional district lines, just huge amounts of money, like truckloads of money being spent on the air. But part of this is also decisions that President Trump made along the way, candidates he chose to support that are now creating major headaches for Republicans. Like, Republicans should not have to have spent something like $400 million on air in the state of Texas to hold on to a Senate seat there, and it's not clear they're going to be able to hold on to it. Geoff Bennett: Let's shift our focus to what's happening in Michigan, where the congresswoman there, Haley Stevens, who lost to Abdul El-Sayed in the Senate race, she -- Senate primary, rather -- she abruptly endorsed the Republican, Mike Rogers. Amy, is this last-minute spectacle surrounding Haley Stevens, is it likely to have any real impact on the outcome of the race, or is this more about the personalities involved? Amy Walter: Yes, I do really think it's much more about the personalities than the -- than any sort of ideological piece. To be fair, there is an ideological divide between the two of them and specifically on the issue of Israel. And this is a real issue and concern within the Democratic Party writ large, so not to minimize that. But the frustration I think that Stevens has and she's been communicating in the last 24 hours seems much more personal than it is about policy, that feeling as if El-Sayed and his campaign sort of rebuffed her, did not treat her well. I don't know if you know this, but politicians sometimes have egos. (LAUGHTER) Amy Walter: And they can get bruised rather much so. I think on both sides of this debate, that there are two egos. We actually, at The Cook Political Report, shifted this race, as a matter of fact, into leaning Democrat. We believe that ultimately, when you look at all the data that's out there, especially when you look at how El-Sayed has consolidated the Democratic base, we just don't think there are enough Democrats out there or Democratic-leaning voters who were thinking, hmm, should I vote for El-Sayed, should I vote for Rogers, that are going to be moved enough to tip this race. Geoff Bennett: And, Tam, Stevens' defection appears to have had the opposite of the intended effect, which is that it has galvanized Michigan Democrats largely around El-Sayed. And El-Sayed, and he's raised like 42.5 million in 24 hours. Tamara Keith: Yes, he has raised a lot of money. And this -- so many people have already voted, have already made up their minds. This is a really late move. Yes, it was absolutely a November surprise that maybe we weren't expecting yesterday. But in terms of actually moving votes, changing the outcome of the race, it feels too late. Geoff Bennett: Is there a particular race that you're paying close attention to tomorrow as a bellwether, let's say? Amy Walter: Oh, oh, so many, Geoff. I can't wait to talk to you about all of the races that I'm watching. But there's one in particular in Tex

ac20adcd6bba.text: Millions of votes have been cast in this midterm election. Traditional battlegrounds have expanded in the fight to control Congress. It all comes down to one question: who won? This year, PBS News is again relying on the Associated Press to call winners in critical races. For a closer look at how the AP makes those race calls, Deema Zein spoke with David Scott of the Associated Press. Amna Nawaz: The 2026 campaign has been the most expensive in U.S. history, and it's all leading to tomorrow night, when the votes are counted. Deema Zein has a look at what happens next. Deema Zein: Millions of votes have been cast in this midterm election. Traditional battlegrounds have expanded in the fight to control Congress. It all comes down to one question: Who won? This year, the "News Hour" is once again relying on the Associated Press to call winners in critical races. For a closer look at how the AP makes those race calls, I'm joined by David Scott, V.P. of election services at the Associated Press. David, thanks for joining us. David Scott: Happy to be here. Deema Zein: So I want to jump right in. People watching results on election night want to know the winner. So tell us, how do you know when the race is over and which candidate won? David Scott: So the thing that we're looking at primarily is the vote count. We are reflecting the choices that Americans have made at the ballot box as they make their choice about who they want to lead the country, who they want to represent them in Congress or in the statehouse. And so we start there. And, really, the question we're asking ourselves is, are the trailing candidates or a trailing candidate able to catch the leader? And when we have determined, based on all of the evidence, primarily the vote count, but other things that we take into account, what happened in the advance vote, what's the history of a state, what our poll shows about what took place and what voters were thinking about on election night, but really the vote count, when we see and we are certain that the trailing candidate can't catch up, that's when we declare a winner. Deema Zein: And who makes that ultimate decision? David Scott: We have got a big team at the Associated Press that makes up our decision team. And they're all journalists. They are people who cover politics. They are data analysts. They are experts in political science. They are folks who study this year-round full-time. We have folks who focused on turnout and what the expected vote it is. What's the denominator? How many votes are going to be cast in this election? And then, of course, the numerator, what are each candidate getting? And, again, we're trying to answer that question. When we look at all the votes that have been counted so far, what do we see about what's outstanding? And has a candidate reach the point where none of the others are able to catch them and they will be the winner? And that's when we declare a winner. Deema Zein: And not until that moment. David Scott: Not until that moment. Our certainty is our standard. We're not trying to be first. We're not trying to race to a decision. We are looking at what's coming in. But we also feel an obligation to let an the voters know, to let America know, this is who you have chosen to lead. And so we're being swift, but always focused on accuracy first. Our standard is certainty. We are certain when we declare a winner that the trailing candidates can't catch up. Deema Zein: Do bad calls actually happen? And, basically, why should Americans trust AP to get it right? David Scott: We have been doing this literally since the founding of the Associated Press; 1848 was the first time that we counted the vote and declared winners two years after the founding of a cooperative. It's part of who we are as a news organization. We think that the choices that Americans have made is a news story. It's really important. In this year's primaries, we declared winners in more than 11,000 races. And we made three mistakes. And one was because of bad information from election officials, for example. And another one was because of a technical problem. So they do happen, but they're very rare. Deema Zein: David Scott, vice president of election services at Associated Press, thank you so much. David Scott: Happy to be here.

Industry groups want cyber threat-sharing law renewed through defense authorization bill
Banks, utilities, and other industries are asking lawmakers to extend liability protections through 2035.
A coalition of 35 industry groups is urging Congress to use the annual defense policy bill to renew a law that gives companies legal protections when they share information about cyber threats with the federal government.
In a Nov. 1 letter to the leaders of the House and Senate Armed Services committees, the groups asked negotiators to keep a provision in the House bill that would extend the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 through 2035. The law lapsed during last year’s record government shutdown and has since stayed in place through a series of spending bills. Its current extension expires Dec. 11.
The signers include the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, Business Software Alliance, American Bankers Association, Airlines for America, the American Public Power Association and the National Rural Water Association.
“In this environment, the speed and breadth with which defenders share information determines whether they keep pace with adversaries,” the groups wrote. “That speed depends on the legal certainty CISA 2015 provides.”
The key liability protections in the law are designed to shield firms from lawsuits and regulatory penalties when sharing threat information with federal partners like the FBI or National Security Agency. That data often includes personal or proprietary information tied to individuals and companies affected in cyber intrusions.
Industry groups have consistently warned lawmakers that allowing the measure to lapse would create legal risks for companies sharing breach data, leading to a drop in private sector threat disclosures.
On the first day of the shutdown last year, cybersecurity attorneys were already fielding calls from clients about whether their existing agreements still protected them.
Congress restored the law through January 2026, when it reopened the government in November 2025. Lawmakers extended it again in February of this year, this time through Sept. 30, then moved the deadline to December in a stopgap funding bill.
A sticking point in the Senate reauthorization process has been what else to put in a longer renewal. Sens. Gary Peters, D-Mich., and Mike Rounds, R-S.D., pushed for a 10-year extension during last year’s shutdown.
But Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., told Roll Call last month that he wanted a provision barring federal officials from pressuring social media companies to restrict speech. Paul — who has routinely pushed back on clean extensions of the law — said he and Peters had discussed the amendment several times without reaching an agreement.

aa699d11d00c.text: By — Michelle Price, Associated Press Michelle Price, Associated Press By — Samy Magdy, Associated Press Samy Magdy, Associated Press By — Elena Becatoros, Associated Press Elena Becatoros, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/u-s-launches-new-attacks-on-iranian-targets-days-after-netanyahu-pressed-trump-for-more-strikes Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter U.S. launches new attacks on Iranian targets days after Netanyahu pressed Trump for more strikes World Nov 3, 2026 10:07 AM EST The United States launched strikes on Iranian targets, a U.S. official said, in what appeared to be a limited operation on the eve of Tuesday's crucial midterm elections. Iranian state media reported explosions being heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas. Unlike earlier in the war, the strikes were not publicly announced. President Donald Trump previously said the U.S. wouldn't launch strikes on Iran before the midterms. The unpopular war and the resulting impact on U.S. gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for his Republican Party as it tries to keep control of Congress. READ MORE: Trump says U.S. will stop giving $4 billion in aid to Israel next year A U.S. official, who wasn't authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said Monday that the strikes targeted Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against the U.S. in the strait. The move came as Iran said it had a two-day plan to reopen the critical waterway, through which about a fifth of the world's oil supply flowed during peacetime, and resume nuclear talks with the United States. Vice President Vance buoyed hopes for a negotiated settlement Back-channel negotiations have also been playing out as Israel and some Middle East allies lobby Trump on the way ahead in the more than 8-month-old war that's rattled the global economy and wreaked havoc on Iran. Speaking before the U.S. official confirmed strikes, U.S. Vice President JD Vance told reporters Monday that he and Trump "both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement." The Trump administration was last known to have carried out attacks in early September. But thousands of U.S. troops remain in the waters off Iran to maintain a naval blockade aimed at preventing tankers carrying Iranian oil from reaching the global market. Another aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are also on their way to the Middle East. The region is on edge about the prospects of the U.S. resuming full-scale operations against Iran, and the new strikes are likely to renew concerns. Netanyahu pushed Trump for strikes in a weekend call Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pushed for another wave of strikes on Iran after the U.S. elections, according to two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter. A return to full-scale war with Iran could help Netanyahu form an emergency government after he and his far-right allies lost their parliamentary majority in last week's elections. Trump has alternated between threatening major strikes and pushing for a deal with Iran. The two officials said diplomatic efforts have made progress and that mediators are trying to advance a framework for Iran to cease its attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in return for the U.S. lifting its blockade on Iran's ports. They said more talks are planned for this week. The two officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified briefings they had received from American and, in one case, Israeli officials. The third person, who was briefed on the call, was not authorized to comment publicly and also spoke on the condition of anonymity. Iranians keeping watch on U.S. elections Some people in Tehran were hopeful that the midterm elections would bring a shift in U.S. policies. "The American people need to make a fundamental decision and bring about real change. They need to put an end to the leadership of someone who is so extreme and who runs things through lies, someone who supports Israel, a country that is literally killing children," said 69-year-old Reza Rezaei. He said he hopes for changes that will "bring about peace and stability, not just for Americans, but for the whole world." One woman was less optimistic. "It doesn't really make much difference who comes into power," said Raheleh Movahhed, also of Tehran. "The American government and its policies have always had a problem with us. I'm not talking about the American people, mind you. I'm talking about their policies." Iran's chief negotiator says it's up to the US to prevent renewed war Iranian state television quoted the country's chief negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, as saying on Tuesday that Iran had "delivered a firm and rational response to the American side. The ball is now in America's court to prevent war." It was not immediately clear what response he was referring to. Qalibaf also warned that Iran's armed forces remained at the highest level of defensive readiness. "If Washington makes another strategic miscalculation, it should know that this time it will face a new battlefield and will find itself even more desperate than it is today," he said. Iranian authorities announce plans to train 1 million paramilitary volunteers Iran opened its third military training center in Tehran on Monday as authorities announced plans to train 1 million paramilitary volunteers nationwide, amid fears of renewed conflict. Members of the Basij, a paramilitary force affiliated with Iran's Revolutionary Guard, attended the inauguration, the semiofficial ISNA news agency reported. "Starting this week, across the country 1,500 training bases will start working in all cities and towns, and will aim for training 1 million sacrificial volunteers," said Ali Kows

7e7a9372225c.text: By — Lindsay Whitehurst, Associated Press Lindsay Whitehurst, Associated Press By — Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/listen-live-supreme-court-hears-case-on-catholic-preschools-and-lgbtq-families Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter LISTEN LIVE: Supreme Court hears case on Catholic preschools and LGBTQ families Politics Nov 3, 2026 10:00 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court will hear arguments Tuesday in a case brought by Catholic preschools that say it's unconstitutional to exclude them from a state-funded program over their admissions policy for LGBTQ+ families, the latest religious-rights case before the conservative-majority court. Arguments begin at 10 a.m. EST. Listen live in the video player above. Colorado says their refusal to admit kids from those families violates the state's anti-discrimination law. But St. Mary Catholic Parish and the Archdiocese of Denver argue that the policy is based on religious teachings about same-sex marriage and that excluding them violates their free-exercise rights. WATCH LIVE: Election night 2026 PBS News special coverage President Donald Trump's administration is supporting the Catholic institutions. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. A win for the preschools could further narrow a landmark 1990 Supreme Court decision that found religious practices don't create exemptions from laws that otherwise apply broadly. Written by conservative icon Justice Antonin Scalia in a case over the spiritual use of peyote, a cactus containing mescaline that's sacred to many Indigenous people, the decision has nevertheless long been a target of the conservative legal movement. In the Colorado case, the high court could be sympathetic to the schools. The justices have sided with religious schools in similar disputes before, ruling in recent years that they can't be excluded from programs in Maine and Montana that provide public aid to private schools. In 2025, though, the court deadlocked over a plan to establish a publicly funded Catholic charter school after Justice Amy Coney Barrett recused herself. The Colorado universal preschool program was created by a 2020 ballot measure. It provides public funding for preschool at schools chosen by parents. The plaintiffs, represented by the group Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, say the state has allowed other preschools to prioritize children with disabilities or those from low-income families, so admission based on religious beliefs about gender and same-sex marriage should be allowed, too. The Catholic preschools say their enrollment has dropped 20% since the program started. Colorado argues that the other admissions decisions are in line with the state's anti-discrimination rules. Libya's highest religious authority, the Dar al-Ifta, has issued a ruling banning Muslims from buying, selling or wearing clothing bearing the Nike logo.
The ruling, issued by the Tripoli-based institution, states that the US sportswear giant was named after the Greek goddess of victory and that its famous swoosh logo was inspired by her wings.
It argued that wearing clothing displaying the logo amounted to promoting symbols associated "with polytheism," or the worship of more than one god.
Libya is home to the ancient Greek city of Cyrene, where archaeological remains include a statue of the Greek goddess of the same name.
The religious committee also accused Nike of supporting Israel and called for a boycott of companies that back the country.
It referred to a statement issued by its Council for Research and Sharia Studies on 5 November 2023, urging Muslims to boycott Western companies it considers supportive of Israel during the war in Gaza.
The ruling, known as a fatwa, is a religious opinion on a matter of Islamic law. It was approved by Libya's Grand Mufti, Sadiq al-Gharyani.
The BBC has contacted Nike for comment.
The Dar al-Ifta is an influential religious institution based in Tripoli, in western Libya. The country is politically divided, with rival authorities and institutions operating in the east and west after years of conflict following the toppling of long-time leader Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.
Although its religious rulings can carry considerable social influence, they are not necessarily government orders or legally enforceable.
Last year it ruled against wearing jewellery and watches bearing the logo of French luxury jewellery house Van Cleef & Arpels, arguing that its four-leaf clover design was associated with Christian beliefs and the pursuit of good luck, which it said contradicted Islamic teachings.
The latest fatwa does not announce a state ban on Nike products or specify penalties for people who continue to buy or wear them.
Social media reactions were mixed, with some users welcoming the ruling, while others questioned its significance, describing it as ironic or a distraction from more pressing issues.
The ruling comes amid wider debates over the rise of religious conservatism in public life in Libya.
In 2025, authorities in eastern Libya announced restrictions on rap music, theatre and dance performances, citing concerns that some lyrics and performances violated public morals and Islamic values.
The measures were subsequently extended to western Libya.
The Dar al-Ifta has also previously issued religious rulings against music, although there is no clear evidence that it was directly involved in the restrictions on performances.
Nike does not operate an official store in Libya, however Nike-branded products are available through local sportswear retailers.
Sportswear brands such as Nike and Adidas are popular across North Africa.
In Libya, as in other countries in the region, counterfeit versions of popular sportswear brands are also sold in local markets.

Democrats used these messages four times as often as Republicans, the report says. The ads appeared in nearly every battleground state, as well as three toss-up governor races.
Ads cited by the report blame AI for price-gouging, harm to children, and even healthcare denial, while data center-focused ads press Republicans on water use and threats to farmland.

âIt would be a betrayal of their campaign promises, and not only would it squander our victory ââ it would create resentment in the base that will cost us in 2028,â it continues.

6d7d6558c6cf.text: By — Ali Swenson, Associated Press Ali Swenson, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/election-day-underway-after-a-surge-in-early-voting-as-trump-sows-on-results Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Election Day underway after a surge in early voting, as Trump sows doubt on results Politics Nov 3, 2026 9:48 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — The final day of voting in this year's midterm elections arrived Tuesday against a backdrop of uncertainty after a year in which President Donald Trump has tried to interfere in how states run their elections and sown doubts about the outcome should Republicans lose. Millions of Americans already have cast their ballots, with early voting turnout on pace to eclipse that of the last midterm elections. In contrast to the president's continued rhetoric about election cheating, voting so far has unfolded with relatively few problems. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Trump has spent months trying to use the power of the presidency to put his thumb on the scale of this year's elections, which will determine whether his party keeps control of Congress. His Justice and Homeland Security departments have been involved in a massive hunt for voters who are not U.S. citizens, at one point engaging in a made-for-the-cameras predawn operation that led to more than two dozen arrests in California. The Department of Justice was planning its largest-ever effort to monitor Election Day polling places, countered by an even larger effort among Democrats and allied groups, and at the president's urging had sued to block certification of Alaska's results if the outcome of the Senate race favored Democrats. At the same time, Trump's constant false claims about widespread voter fraud led election officials and Democratic groups across the country to plan for the possibility of immigration agents at voting sites or federal officers seizing voting machines. His administration has insisted that no armed federal officials would be guarding the polls on Election Day. Courts have blocked the Trump administration's efforts to influence elections In the run-up to Tuesday, none of the steps Democrats most feared had come to pass, and the Republican administration's legal maneuvers had been largely blocked by the courts. One of the Trump administration's most high-profile attempts to interfere in state elections was turned away Monday night by the U.S. Supreme Court, which rejected its push to force California to set aside thousands of ballots as part of its search for noncitizen voters. In another Monday night ruling, a federal judge said the Trump administration must stop sending voter lists of alleged noncitizens to election officials. Even the administration's own record of arrests and charges has demonstrated what research and state investigations have made clear for years — that instances of noncitizens casting ballots are extremely rare. Monday's rulings followed another defeat for the president at the Supreme Court less than two months ago, when it rejected his attempt to limit mail balloting through changes at the Postal Service. That directive was included in one of two executive orders Trump has signed during his second term that attempted to federalize certain aspects of elections, even though the Constitution gives the states, and sometimes Congress, the authority to set election rules. Voting begins smoothly with some weather disruptions in the Southwest The first polling sites were open Tuesday morning across much of the East Coast, with few disruptions so far. In New York's suburban Westchester County, where some voters are casting ballots in a competitive U.S. House race, election officials said an issue with voting machines accepting paper ballots was requiring ballots to be placed in emergency bags for later counting. But they stressed that the ballots would remain secure and monitored, that they would later be counted and that voters could continue casting ballots while they worked to resolve the issue. You can also follow the NewsHour's live coverage on YouTube, Twitter, Facebook, and TikTok, and see highlights on our Instagram. Heavy rains and flash flooding in a swath of the Southwest were expected to make it harder for some voters to reach polling places in parts of Colorado, Arizona, Utah and New Mexico. Election administrators in the Navajo Nation announced changes to several of its polling locations, and in Utah's rural San Juan County, voters were being allowed to vote electronically on Tuesday because some of them may not be able to reach polling places. Election administrators and voting rights advocates have been advising voters casting late absentee ballots to use drop boxes or deliver them to polling places in person rather than mail them. The advice came after concerns emerged that recent changes in U.S. Postal Service operations could result in postmarking delays that would mean mail ballots could not be counted. Late-arriving ballots or late postmarks disenfranchised tens of thousands of voters in California, Oregon and Washington, which mail ballots to all voters, during this year's primaries. Trump hasn't committed to accepting the election results The most significant disruptions ahead of Election Day were the Trump administration's attempts to interfere. Voting rights groups, Democrats and the Justice Department have been exchanging a flurry of legal filings over alleged noncitizen voters, federal election monitors, federal intimidation of election officials and other concerns. They reveal how Trump's attempts to expand federal control over state-run elections — combined with high-stakes races — are resulting in court battles that could extend past Election Day into ballot counting an

22c06f963c77.text: Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/live-results-florida-senate-midterm-election Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Live Results: Florida Senate midterm election Politics Nov 3, 2026 9:30 AM EST WATCH LIVE: Election night 2026 PBS News special coverage WASHINGTON (AP) — Florida Republicans will try to extend their dominance in statewide elections Tuesday as voters decide races for Senate, governor and other state and legislative offices. The election will mark the first under a new congressional map adopted by Republicans to boost the party's chances of keeping control of the closely divided House. Once the nation's most evenly divided swing state, Florida has shifted steadily to the right in the last quarter century. At the time of the 2000 presidential election, Democrats had held a voter registration advantage over Republicans for decades. That advantage would erode until 2021 when registered Republicans overtook registered Democrats. Today, there are 1.5 million more Republicans in Florida than Democrats. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News In the race for governor, Democrats have nominated a former Republican to lead them out of the electoral doldrums. Former Rep. David Jolly defeated five other candidates in the Aug. 18 primary with 61% of the vote. Jolly took an unlikely path to running for governor as a Democrat, joining the party in 2025 after leaving the GOP in 2018. He has tapped former Democratic Rep. Gwen Graham as his running mate. Graham is the daughter of the late Bob Graham, the longtime Democratic senator and governor. The Republican nominee is Rep. Byron Donalds, who won the 11-candidate primary with the help of an endorsement from President Donald Trump. Donalds received about 48% of the primary vote, almost double that of the runner-up, Lt. Gov. Jay Collins. Donalds backed Trump over Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis in the 2024 presidential primaries and was considered as a possible Trump running mate that year. Trump and Vice President JD Vance have each campaigned for Donalds in Florida since the president launched his midterm campaign push last month. READ MORE: Trump casts his midterm ballot early in Florida Six other independent or third-party candidates are also on the ballot. In this year's Senate race, Republican Sen. Ashley Moody defends her seat against Democratic state Rep. Angie Nixon as well as an independent candidate. Moody was state attorney general in January 2025 when DeSantis appointed her to fill the seat vacated by Marco Rubio, who was tapped by Trump to be secretary of state. She is now running to complete the final two years of Rubio's term. Nixon, a democratic socialist, received 56% of the August primary vote against retired Army Lt. Col. Alex Vindman, who received about 44%. Vindman, a former National Security Council staff member, was a key witness in Trump's first impeachment in 2019. Losing a Nebraska seat in the U.S. Senate or House could set up Republicans to lose control of Congress. Even if Republicans hold onto their seats, a near-loss could signal an erosion of Republican power in a state that has not voted for a Democratic presidential candidate since 1964. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Sen. Pete Ricketts, the Republican incumbent who took office in 2023, is running against Independent candidate Dan Osborn, a union organizer. Cindy Burbank, the Democratic nominee, dropped out of the race in July. Osborn has insisted he will not caucus with Democrats or Republicans, though he has received funds from Democratic donors, which Republicans contend is evidence that he will align with Democrats, if elected. Ricketts was appointed in 2023 to the Senate to fulfill the term of Sen. Ben Sasse, a Republican who left Congress to become president of the University of Florida. The next year, Ricketts won the same seat in a special election by a margin of more than 25 percentage points, even more than President Donald Trump's 20 percentage point margin of victory in the state. READ MORE: Here's when polls are closing in your state this midterm election But the optics of this midterm race have been challenging for Ricketts, as they have been for many Republicans on the ballot this year. The president's tariffs and rising fuel prices have hit the state's agricultural and manufacturing industries hard. Ranchers and beef producers in Nebraska have opposed Trump's attempts to address soaring beef prices by importing more beef, saying it would lower their profits. And Osborn has been able to use Ricketts' family history as son of the founder of TD Ameritrade to portray him as political insider who is out of touch with Nebraskans' concerns. The contrast works well for Osborn, who embarked on a political career after leading a 77-day strike at the Kellogg's plant in Omaha, where he worked as a mechanic in 2021. Osborn, who had been an employee of the company for nearly two decades, was fired following the strike and went on to run for U.S. Senate against the incumbent Republican, Sen. Deb Fischer, in 2024. Though Fischer won the race, Osborn came within 7 percentage points of his opponent, a surprising outcome. Ricketts has raised $14.5 million for his campaign as of mid-October, while Osborn had raised $11 million. Millions more in outside spending have poured into the race. READ MORE: When will we know 2026 midterm election results? It may take some time, but that's normal On the congressional map, Democrats are once again targeting Nebraska's 2nd Congressional District, where Democrat Denise Powell is up against Republican Omaha City Councilor Brinker Harding. They are running to fill the seat of retiring Republican Rep. Don Bacon, a moderate Republican who has criticized the Trump administration over Ukraine and tariffs. Democrats have zeroed in on the district, which includes the state's largest city, Omaha, and is sometimes called the "blue dot," as a possible opportunity to flip a seat. In June, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee announced it had added Powell to its "Red to Blue" program, which supports Democratic candidates running in competitive districts. The 2nd Congressional District was the only district in the state to vote for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. The gubernatorial race in Nebraska has also become competitive. Republican Gov. Jim Pillen, who took office in 2023, is being challenged by Democrat Lynne Walz, a former member of the state Senate. Nebraska's governorship has been held by Republicans since 1999, but the national political environment has prompted Trump to travel in and campaign. "When I'm on the ballot, people show up and you always win," Trump said at an early October rally in Grand Island, appearing on stage with Ricketts, Pillen and Flood. About 39% of all ballots cast in Nebraska's 2022 race for governor were cast early or by absentee ballot. The latest advance vote totals for Nebraska can be found in the AP's advance vote tracker. About half of counties are expected to release no or relatively few in-person Election Day results in their first report, including the most populous counties of Douglas and Lancaster. Cindy Hyde-Smith is being challenged by Democrat Scott Colom as she seeks a second full term. Voters on Tuesday will also decide contests for U.S. House and two state House special elections. Although no federal office has changed party hands in Mississippi since 2010, the Senate matchup been more competitive than expected, even drawing a campaign visit from President Donald Trump. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Here are some of the key facts about the election and data points the AP Decision Team will monitor as the votes are tallied. When do polls close? Polls close at 7 p.m. local time, which is 8 p.m. ET. What's on the ballot? The Associated Press will provide vote results and declare winners in contested races for U.S. Senate, U.S. House and two special elections for state House. How many people voted in the last midterm election? About 709,000 ballots were cast in the 2022 midterm elections in Mississippi. How much of the vote is cast early or by absentee ballot? About 7% of the ballots cast in the 2022 midterm election were absentee ballots. The latest advance vote totals for Mississippi can be found in the AP's advance vote tracker. When are early and absentee votes released? Mississippi voters tend to vote in-person on Election Day. The state offers limited in-person absentee and mail absentee voting. All counties are expected to release at least some in-person Election Day results in the first vote update of the night. The limited amount of mail and in-person absentee results are expected to be released throughout the night. How long does vote counting usually take? In the 2024 general election, the AP first reported results at 8:19 p.m. ET, or 19 minutes after polls closed. The vote count reached the halfway mark at 10:06 p.m. ET and 90% of total votes were reported by 9:49 a.m. ET on Nov. 8, 2024. When will the AP declare a winner? The AP does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it's determined there is no scenario that would allow a trailing candidate to close the gap. If a race has not been called, the AP will continue to cover any newsworthy developments, such as candidate concessions or declarations of victory. In doing so, the AP will make clear that it has not yet declared a winner and explain why. How do recounts work? Mississippi does not have automatic recounts or permit candidates to request a recount. Recounts in the state are held only in the event of a court order. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is subject to a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome. -- Camille Baker and Robert Yoon, Associated Press A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. e758e389587f.text: By — Camille Baker, Associated Press Camille Baker, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/live-results-texas-governor-midterm-election Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Live Results: Texas governor midterm election Politics Nov 3, 2026 9:30 AM EST WATCH LIVE: Election night 2026 PBS News special coverage WASHINGTON (AP) — The 2026 midterm election is one of the biggest tests of Republican dominance in Texas — and Democrats' best shot in decades at winning a key U.S. Senate seat in the state. Voters in the Lone Star state will cast ballots in a hotly contested U.S. Senate race and elect U.S. House representatives to districts newly redrawn to favor Republican candidates in contests that could be decisive in Democrats' bid to retake control of Congress. Voters will also elect a governor, state and local representatives and judges, and decide on ballot measures. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Facing off in the race for Senate are Democratic state Rep. James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton, the state's embattled attorney general and an ally of President Donald Trump. Paxton beat out the seat's incumbent of over two decades, Sen. John Cornyn, for the Republican nomination in a tight primary runoff race after Cornyn lost favor with the president and Paxton received Trump's last-minute endorsement. Trump's support for Paxton, who has promised to champion the president's priorities if he wins the election, has been both a crucial asset and a liability for the candidate. The candidate's website says he is "running to help President Trump finish the border wall" and states that he plans to help the president deport "criminal illegal aliens." But Texas shares over 1,200 miles of border with Mexico, and the rising number of arrests by Immigration and Customs Enforcement risks alienating Latino voters, who make up over 30 percent of the state's electorate. Talarico has stressed the need for border security but also called for legal immigration to be made easier, saying in campaign materials, "our border should be like a front porch — it should have a welcome mat out front and a lock on the door." Both candidates have made affordability central to their campaign messaging. Talarico has promised to cut taxes for the middle class, increase taxes on billionaires and repeal Trump's tariffs on imports. Paxton has said he plans to cut taxes, reduce federal spending and remove regulations on energy companies that harm the economy. Trump carried Texas in the last three presidential elections, defeating Democratic nominee and former Vice President Kamala Harris by over 10 percentage points in 2024. The state has not elected a Democratic senator since 1988. Yet recent polls suggest a tight race. The Texas race could become the most expensive Senate race in the country's history. As of mid-October, Talarico had raised more than $146.3 million, eclipsing Paxton's $22.3 million. But hundreds of millions more in independent expenditures have given Paxton the advantage in total spending. Elon Musk, the world's richest man and a Texas resident, gave $158 million to the Republican-supporting Senate Leadership PAC, which donated the same amount to Texas PAC, a group supporting Paxton. Musk also gave $10 million to the Lone Star Liberty PAC, which supports Paxton. Among the most competitive House races in the country is the one for Texas' 34th Congressional District on the state's southern Gulf Coast. Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez is running for reelection against Eric Flores, a Republican and Army veteran endorsed by Trump. In the 2024 election, Gonzalez won the district by a thin margin of less than 3 percentage points, and its boundaries were redrawn in 2025 to advantage Republicans. In a possible sign of growing wariness of associating with the president, Flores' campaign appeared to remove a reference to Trump from a section of his website. Democrats are hoping to reclaim Texas's 15th Congressional District, an inland strip in the southern part of the state and the only part of the Rio Grande Valley represented by a Republican in the U.S. House. Monica De La Cruz, the incumbent Republican, is facing Democrat Bobby Pulido, a Tejano musician and political newcomer, in a newly redrawn version of the district that favors Republicans. De La Cruz won her 2024 reelection by a margin of nearly 15 percentage points. Another race that has become increasingly competitive is the Texas governor's race between Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who has held office since 2015, and Democratic state House Rep. Gina Hinojosa. Texas has elected only Republican governors since 1994, and Trump endorsed Abbott. But the most recent polls show a tight race, making the current contest one of the most vulnerable in Abbott's career.
