AI technology can create realistic clones of people’s voices. The resulting proliferation of synthetic voices ushers in all sorts of new scenarios, good and bad. “Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type, and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, [of] anybody doing or saying anything,” says Hany Farid, a computer scientist at Dartmouth University.
Some of these voice clones are deeply meaningful to people, as in the cases of people who lost their ability to speak. But voice clones can also cause harm, as with scams and deepfakes. And some uses fall into murky gray zones, such as voice clones that “speak” after a person has passed away. What happens to a person’s digital voice after they’re gone?
In this episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me, hear more from Farid, as well as from a former hospital chaplain and AI researcher, and from Jules Rodriguez, a man who communicates with a voice clone. You’ll also hear about a choice Jules made about what will happen to his voice once he’s gone.
Episode 5 transcript
Laura Sanders: What’s a voice you like to listen to?
Kate Nilson: That is a great question. I hope my students don’t listen to this. I was having Snoop Dogg read their assignments to me the other day, just because I thought it was funny. But I don’t know if I would say that’s my favorite.
Sanders: That’s speech language pathologist and professor Kate Nilson. And if you’re wondering, this is a real, legitimate thing that anyone can do.
Snoop Dogg audio: Vector mathematics. Think about a car trip. Your displacement from your starting point is a vector.
Sanders: Snoop has partnered with a company called Speechify. If you subscribe, you can get famous voices like Snoop’s, Gwyneth Paltrow, MrBeast to read whatever you want. It turns out people are doing this in all sorts of ways. Here’s Snoop in a marketing video.
Snoop Dogg: I’m glad to be the voice of reason so you can focus better, understand more, and enjoy listening to the internet in the voice of Snoop Dogg.
Sanders: Welcome to The Deep End, Talk To Me. In this episode, we’re stepping out of the lab and into the new digital world we all live in. We’re going to get into some of the good, bad and strange scenarios that come up when voices can be cloned and let loose in the world. Let’s talk about it.
[voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? Hi. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi. Your voice is you.
Sanders: As we’ve heard in earlier episodes, ultra-realistic voice clones can be extremely meaningful to people who can no longer speak.
Jules Rodriguez: So when I first heard my cloned voice, it felt like I reappeared. When my wife first heard it, she cried because of how close it sounded like me before I lost my voice. I knew of the potential of this technology at that moment.
Sanders: These digital copies of voices have restored connections to their loved ones.
MA Fernandez: You know, the first thing he played for me, I was like chills all over.
Sanders: And even back to themselves.
Patrick Darling: The first time I performed with the AI voice, I was surprised how physically connected I felt with it.
Sanders: These voice clones have been transformative for people who have lost the ability to talk. But the existence of realistic digital copies of voices has effects that ripple farther out into society.
Hany Farid: So here’s where sort of state of the art is. Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, anybody doing or saying anything.
Sanders: That’s Hany Farid. He’s a computer scientist at Dartmouth College and cofounder of Get Real Security, a firm that sorts real from fake. I called him to ask how these voice clones have changed our world.
Farid: If you had asked me, I don’t know, five years ago, is this possible? I would say, yeah, maybe, but not anytime soon. And then all of a sudden, boom, it just came out of nowhere.
Sanders: This shift happened in a very, very short amount of time, and it has big implications, both good and bad.
Farid: And so we are living in, I think, in equal parts an exciting time and a terrifying time, and somehow those are coexisting.
Sanders: Farid tells me about some of his research, which asks people to decide whether something, like a voice or a video, is real.
Farid: My bread and butter is developing technologies to distinguish real from fake. And we work with media outlets and law enforcement and courts, et cetera. But one of the questions you always want to ask when you’re in my business is, well, do you need the mathematics and the computation? Just let somebody listen to it or look at it. And can they tell the difference?
Sanders: It turns out they cannot. In laboratory tests, people can’t reliably say whether a voice they hear was created by a machine or by a real living, breathing person.
Farid: It’s essentially like they’re flipping a coin.
Sanders: But there’s another, even higher bar for voice clones to pass. That’s whether they can mimic a specific person well enough to slip by undetected.
Farid: The other question too is what if I, for example, play a real voice sample of your voice, Laura, and then I clone your voice using my favorite AI cloning technology, and then I type something and I get you to say something, and I play those two samples to somebody, and I don’t ask them if it’s real/fake. I say, is this the same person? Is the AI not only able to make something that is natural, but is it identity preserving?
Sanders: Okay, give it a try yourself. Is this the same person?
[Sanders voice clone] And how about now? Is this the same person?
Farid: And when you ask them, is it the same person? They say yes, which means the AI has figured out with roughly 20 seconds or so of your voice how to make their AI sound like you, which is mind-blowing.
Sanders: In the earlier episodes of this season, you’ve heard ex

4f1f7a6f6fab.text: By — Ben Finley, Associated Press Ben Finley, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/trump-says-u-s-will-stop-giving-4-billion-in-aid-to-israel-next-year Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump says U.S. will stop giving $4 billion in aid to Israel next year World Nov 3, 2026 9:28 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump says the U.S. will stop providing $4 billion in aid each year to Israel in 2027 but will sell arms to its closest ally in the Middle East. The Republican president told Fox News Channel during a phone call on Tuesday that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had approached him about the idea and that they have been talking about it for a couple years. Trump says Israel doesn't need the aid and it's a lot of money for the U.S. to spend. But Trump also says that U.S. aid to Israel has become a Democratic talking point for candidates such as Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. "You can consider it barter. You can consider military aid or cash," Trump said. "Look, we give them $4 billion of things and money, and they don't need it. And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we've been talking about it for a couple of years because it's a lot of money." There was no immediate comment from Netanyahu's office. The United States has sent tens of billions of dollars in military aid to Israel over the last few years. An academic study published last year showed the U.S. under the administrations of President Joe Biden, a Democrat, and Trump provided at least $21.7 billion in military assistance to Israel after the start of the Gaza war in 2023. The study was published on the second anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks in Israel that provoked the conflict. Another study, also published last year by the Costs of War project at Brown University's Watson School of International and Public Affairs, said the U.S. had spent roughly $10 billion more on security aid and operations in the broader Middle East in the previous two years. While the reports relied on open source material for most of their findings, they offered some of the most comprehensive accountings of U.S. military aid to close ally Israel and estimated costs of direct American military involvement in the Middle East. c4a90b067f33.text: By — Jill Colvin, Associated Press Jill Colvin, Associated Press By — Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press By — Will Weissert, Associated Press Will Weissert, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/midterm-elections-come-to-a-close-in-referendum-on-trumps-presidency Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Midterm elections come to a close in referendum on Trump's presidency Politics Nov 3, 2026 9:20 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Voters struggling with high prices and angry over an unpopular war with Iran will decide Tuesday whether to drastically shift power in Washington in midterm elections that will serve as a referendum on President Donald Trump's second term. Democrats were cautiously optimistic as they watched Republicans spend the campaign's final stretch pumping tens of millions of dollars into states and districts that Trump won handily two years ago. They're betting that discontent over Trump's failure to deliver on his promise to tackle rising costs and perceptions that he has focused more on gilding the nation's capital than their pain at the pump will depress Republican turnout and drive their own voters to the polls. Republicans held out hope their money advantage would help stem the tide, but they were bracing to lose control of the U.S. House and fighting to hang onto the U.S. Senate — an outcome that seemed unlikely earlier this year, given a map widely seen as favoring their party. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Still, margins are tight in both chambers; one or two seats could tip the balance. Democrats need a net gain of four seats in the 100-member Senate to win the majority, an uphill climb because many of the most competitive races are in historically red states. In the 435-member House, they need only three. More than 57 million people had already cast ballots as of Monday, with turnout surpassing the early vote four years ago in many closely watched states. Trump, whose party has struggled when he's not running to turn out the low-propensity voters who've fueled his victories, has told voters to act as though he is running, even as many Republican candidates have tried to keep their distance. "I really want you to pretend I'm on the ballot," he told the crowd in Salina, Kansas, on Sunday at the final of several dozen rallies in the campaign's closing weeks. On Tuesday, Mark Barker, of Palm Beach Gardens, Florida, said Trump was very much top of mind as he voted. "I've just been following Trump the whole time. I really think he's doing an awesome job," said Barker, noting the president's promise of $5,000 for every U.S. adult if Republicans retain control of Congress, border policy and war in the Middle East. "Everything he's done has been outstanding." In Raleigh, North Carolina, 57-year-old librarian James Moore said he voted for Democrats to push back on Trump's big tax breaks and spending cuts bill. "I'm paying more taxes. I'm paying more for my healthcare. I'm paying more for everything," he said. "We need more representatives in Congress that are going to stand up to Trump." Trump's aggressive schedule had stops in the reddest states, including Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas, underscoring his party's challenges. He also has continued to make false claims about voting fraud, such as insisting noncitizens are casting ballots en masse. His administration has filed lawsuits in Alaska and California, and Democrats fear interference and voter intimidation as his Justice Department threatens to prosecute local election officials. The election could reshape the political landscape The results will shape the final two years of Trump's second term after the Republican-controlled Congress acted as a rubber stamp to much of his agenda. While Trump has proven adept at steamrolling efforts to rein him in, Democrats taking control of even one chamber of Congress would open the floodgates to investigations and possible impeachments. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and tech titan Elon Musk, a former top Trump adviser, are among possible targets. An especially strong showing for Democrats would also boost potential presidential candidates, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. It could also complicate the paths of Vice President JD Vance and other Republicans who may be looking to turn their loyalty to Trump into momentum. Republicans tried to buck historical precedent — a president's party almost always loses seats during the midterms — with an aggressive redistricting effort aimed at creating a more favorable congressional map. But the plan may fall short as new districts drawn in Florida and other states to be safely red may not vote that way. Other Trump choices could prove costly. In Texas, Trump worked to oust longtime incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in favor of scandal-plagued Attorney General Ken Paxton, setting the stage for an extraordinarily expensive race against Democratic nominee James Talarico, who Democrats hope may finally help them realize their dream of flipping the state. In North Carolina, Sen. Thom Tillis retired after clashing with Trump. The president's chosen replacement, former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley, has struggled to gain traction against the Democrats' candidate, former Gov. Roy Cooper. "Everything depends on turnout. If we turn out our voters, we win, and that's what we've been planning for," said Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters, expressing optimism on the eve of the election. The money crunch that has hit AI in recent weeks is coming for the space industry, which shares DNA, investors, and market vibes with artificial intelligence.
âIf youâre a high-quality, well-run company with a good balance sheet and a good business model, you are very well positioned because everyoneâs paying attention,â Dylan Taylor, CEO of Voyager Technologies, said on this weekâs episode of Compound Interest. Everyone else is âbeing cast aside.â
Voyager builds space infrastructure for the Pentagon and defense contractors, and is working on a commercial space station, Starlab, to replace the International Space Station when it is retired in 2030. The company is publicly traded, which last month allowed it to raise $400 million on terms roughly in line with a hot convertible-debt market.
âLow cost of capital [is] a secret weapon,â Taylor said, âbecause the first question is, âhow do you compete with SpaceX?ââ
Even Elon Muskâs behemoth is feeling the squeeze: It throttled usage of its Grok AI bot this week because, as Musk said in an X post Sunday, it was getting too expensive. Taylor, like most space executives today, counts Musk as both a competitor (for contracts and capital) and collaborator (Voyagerâs hardware hitches a ride on SpaceXâs rockets).
The space and AI trades are increasingly twinned, tapping into similar pools of capital, riding similar national-security vibes, and carrying similar potential of catastrophic escalation. âItâs the same thing,â Taylor said of the two, but for a different reason: their potential to reshape every corner of the economy. âEveryone is in the space industry,â he said. âThey just donât know it yet.â
We also talked to Taylor about building data centers in space, which would sidestep the energy needs and political backlash back on Earth. And if they break? Just âbuild more,â is Taylorâs quintessentially American answer.

c86c5ee9d33e.text:
A wireless implant that clears excess sugar from the blood could someday offer a drug-free way to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.
In mice with both conditions, the under-the-skin device brought high blood sugar back to normal within 60 to 90 minutes of being switched on, researchers report October 22 in Science. After six weeks, the treated mice lost up to 10 percent of their body weight and had lower triglycerides, a type of fat in the blood.
Diabetes affects about 830 million people worldwide. Conventional type 2 diabetes treatments like insulin and GLP-1 drugs require careful dosing. Even experimental diabetes-controlling implants still rely on the hormone insulin, which clears sugar from the bloodstream but doesn’t rid the body of it, says Martin Fussenegger, a bioengineer at ETH Zurich. The new implant instead removes glucose from the body without added drugs, genes or living cells.
The 3-centimeter-long device contains a catalyst made of gold flakes and platinum particles on spongelike graphite. When electricity powers it, the catalyst converts glucose into gluconate, a compound that is easier for the kidneys to flush out in urine. With less glucose available for energy, the body may turn to its fat stores instead, Fussenegger and colleagues suspect. In mice, that shift showed up as higher blood levels of chemicals released when fat breaks down, such as ketones. “This system kind of targets the root cause, which is the energy surplus by glucose in the body,” Fussenegger says.
The implant works like an automatic sugar-removal system: A wearable glucose monitor detects high blood sugar levels and sends readings through a smartphone that switches the implant on. When levels return to a safer range, it switches off. The automated system ran for two weeks in eight mice. The catalyst itself remained able to convert glucose after up to three months under their skin, though the study didn’t establish how long the entire device would last.
And it’s still unknown how well the device would work in people. “This is a potentially promising method,” says David Klonoff, an endocrinologist at Sutter Mills-Peninsula Medical Center in Burlingame, Calif., who was not involved in the study. “But the risks are significant and must be carefully ruled out before it can be safely tested on humans.”
Researchers need to determine how much gluconate the kidneys can clear, Klonoff says. If it builds up, it could disrupt the body’s acid-base balance, causing symptoms such as nausea or confusion; excreting it could also deplete electrolytes such as sodium and potassium, he notes.
Scaling up the device is another challenge. Humans consume about 250 grams of carbohydrates daily, compared with two grams for mice, Klonoff estimates. Meeting that demand could require a much larger implant or multiple devices, he says. In a lab test, a larger device cleared nearly all glucose from about 5 liters of solution, roughly an adult’s blood volume, though not a full day’s glucose intake.
Fussenegger’s team plans to test the device in pigs and sheep before considering human trials. If proven safe and effective, it could offer an alternative to existing diabetes treatments and a new weight-loss option for people regardless of whether they have diabetes, he says.

BP isnât likely to reverse its pivot away from renewable power generation anytime soon, CEO Meg OâNeill told Semafor. Since she took the helm in April, OâNeill has been focused on salvaging the companyâs finances. She got a big helping hand in the third quarter as its profits nearly quadrupled thanks to high oil and gas prices and a busy trading desk, which OâNeill channeled into cutting debt by nearly 40%.
She is also carrying forward the spinoff of BPâs renewable energy businesses that started under her predecessor, although it hasnât always been easy: Lightsource BP, the companyâs utility-scale solar arm, has been on the market for months. Lightsource âis a very big and complex business, but weâre making headway on that,â she said on the sidelines of ADIPEC. âIn terms of investing in low-carbon [energy], we need to do that only when we can generate shareholder returns,â she said, citing green hydrogen projects in Europe as an example.
But renewable power isnât a good match for BPâs skill set, she cautioned: âThere are people who can do utility-scale solar and make money at it. Weâre happy to let people who are experts in that do their thing, and we will stay focused on oil and gas.â

3ee27fae139c.text:
Timâs view
Todayâs US election is a test of how much voters will want to punish the president for soaring gasoline and power prices.
Energy costs are always an important factor in elections; gas prices are the only economic indicator displayed in big bold numbers at major intersections. But between the war in Iran and the data center power rush, thereâs rarely been an election in which energy prices â and the policy decisions pushing them up, from the White House to local zoning boards â are so much in the headlines.
The average gas price during US President Donald Trumpâs two years back in office is the highest itâs ever been halfway through a presidency, according to a Financial Times analysis. Since the oil embargoes of the 1970s, US presidents have been keenly aware that Americans have a very limited willingness to tolerate pain at the pump in the service of foreign policy objectives. And in many of the key congressional battlegrounds, AI-linked increases in household power bills are a central point of tension, making the votes a kind of referendum on how hard to hit the brakes on data center development, too.
If Democrats succeed in regaining a majority in one or both houses of Congress, the US energy story is in for big changes over the next two years. The partyâs leaders will face an immediate challenge, needing to decide how much hardball theyâre willing to play with Republicans and the White House over permitting reform. Federal budget fights will likely resurface arguments about tax incentives for EVs and other clean tech. Investigative committees will demand answers from the administration about everything from offshore wind lease pullbacks to the diesel deal with Moscow. Meanwhile, a new cohort of state and local leaders will grapple with what kind of pressure to apply on the power demands of Big Tech.
These are the storylines Iâll be focused on here until 2028. Happy voting!

A spate of cyber-attacks that hit supermarket chains across at least 10 European countries on Monday has prompted European Union officials to warn of a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain.
Supermarkets have reported problems in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Germany and Sweden, and the significant increase in freezer temperatures has forced retailers to discard food.
Temperatures in chains across Europe reportedly rose as high as 50C (122F).
No-one has yet admitted carrying out the cyber-attacks.
The European Union has raised concerns about the attacks, which come three weeks after a cyber-attack disrupted as many as 700 French grocery stores, causing food losses estimated at tens of millions of euros.
The security of refrigeration systems as well as other devices that can be monitored remotely has heightened concerns about government-backed hybrid attacks.
The EU's food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the bloc was taking the incidents very seriously and warned of further disruption in the future.
Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier was careful not to attribute blame, but said: "These incidents of course show once again how cyber-attacks can disrupt essential services and affect citizens' daily lives."
"These are not isolated incidents and of course we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents."
In Italy, Giorgia Meloni's government called a meeting with intelligence chiefs, but said the impact was "currently very limited" and most of the food distribution chain had up-to-date security systems able to fend off such attacks.
At least four Co-op supermarkets in Sicily and one business in Tuscany were affected, according to the national cybersecurity agency.
Meloni's office said those businesses affected were "mostly still equipped with obsolete security systems, with interfaces directly exposed to the internet and inadequate authentication mechanisms".
Belgian supermarkets were among those hardest-hit, with dozens of stores reporting refrigeration failures. Federal prosecutors have opened an investigation.
Mathieu Tilman, a manager at a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, said he was shocked by this kind of attack: "I don't even understand how anyone could do this... How can we end up throwing away so much food? I find it truly distressing. In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."
In Ireland, 13 SuperValu stores were impacted by what the chain's owner, Musgrave Group, called a cyber-incident. "Replenishment of chilled and frozen ranges in the affected stores is well under way," a spokesman said on Monday.
A small number of corner shops in the Netherlands also suffered disruption. Last month, supermarket chain Albert Heijn had to take several services offline because of a separate cyber-attack.
There was disruption to refrigeration systems at the Rewe BÃ¼sken supermarket in western Germany after a cyber-attack on system provider Danfoss, the company told the BBC. Its systems have been back in operation since Monday afternoon.
In Portugal, the Mosqueteiros group said that incidents at seven IntermarchÃ© stores had been linked to a cyberattack, which "appears to have targeted an external service provider responsible for managing the refrigeration systems".
Swedish chain ICA also said "a limited number" of its stores had experienced refrigeration problems, without confirming a cyber-attack, and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
In Finland, irregular temperatures were detected in a few smaller grocery stores belonging to the Kesko group, which said it was investigating the issue.
In Estonia, at least one supermarket was attacked by hackers who raised the temperature in the refrigeration units to 50C, public broadcaster ERR reported.
In the UK, the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned British retailers to update the software on fridge temperature controls.
The agency said the country was likely to suffer an AI-powered cyber-attack on critical national infrastructure within two years.
Richard Horne, the head of the National Cyber Security Centre, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme there were a couple of instances in the UK where "vulnerable technology has been exploited" after the cyber-attacks.
"We don't know the full impact, but we do know there are a couple of instances where vulnerable technology has been exploited and we're working with those organisations."
Asked if there was any evidence that supermarkets in Britain or freezers of the same make or model had been targeted, Horne said: "It's not just supermarkets, it's through the whole food supply chain, and we've been working through the night alerting organisations where we can see they've got exposed technology that's vulnerable in this way."

d3bbfb8b554c.text: There's a lot at stake for energy in the midterms, from the fate of the bipartisan permitting deal to the growing backlash against data centers and electricity prices. Why it matters: The results could spotlight which energy topics resonate with voters — and which have become political liabilities. Gasoline and diesel prices have been big on the campaign trail, offering a chance to see how much voter frustration over energy costs matters at the ballot box. Data center politics: There are sharp differences between the parties, even though data centers aren't especially popular with either party's slate of candidates. Why it matters: The pace of the AI buildout affects power demand and emissions. State of play: 32.4% of Democratic candidates support moratoriums at the federal, state, or local level, compared to just 3.4% of Republicans, per Data Center Watch, which tracked hundreds of races. Zoom in: Meanwhile, Ballotpedia is tracking dozens of ballot measures on data centers, many of which would impose new restrictions. Ohio is a hot spot. Control and permitting: The outcome will affect the politics of the lame-duck session — and that means the politics of the bipartisan permitting deal. What they're saying: If Democrats take both chambers, "leaders might opt to wait until they hold the gavels next year to renegotiate compromises," the research firm ClearView Energy Partners said in a note. Yes, but: A reminder that backers of the current bill think it's folly to expect political space to write a more liberal bill that President Trump would sign, or that could even pass the Senate. Threat level: What if the results are very close? ClearView notes that if Trump and allies contest the results, "weeks of post-election skirmishing could complicate passage of any bill." Political lessons: The results could offer clues about where energy and climate policy are headed. State of play: Exit polling is not famously precise, but it could provide a barometer of how much voters truly care — or not — about data centers. It's also worth watching how candidates who made high gas and diesel prices central to their campaigns fare tonight. My thought bubble: Keep an eye on the performance of progressive vs. centrist Democrats. If the latter overperform, it could be another sign that aggressive climate policies won't return to vogue with Dems. Zoom in: Let's say, for instance, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro's (D) victory is even more of a blowout than expected. That could bolster more centrist, oil and gas-accepting candidates in the 2028 cycle (when he might run for president). The next Congress: Regardless of chamber control, don't look for many opportunities for big new energy laws if permitting goes kaput. Yes, but: There will be no shortage of messaging bills and positioning for the 2028 White House race. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) has pledged to bring back clean energy tax credits killed in the 2025 GOP budget law. What we're watching: Limited chances for common ground around nuclear power and geothermal. For instance, the wide-ranging Senate permitting bill contains several bipartisan geothermal bills that already cleared the House. Oversight power: If Democrats take control of either chamber, expect aggressive investigations of White House energy policies and investments, a topic we recently explored. State utility bosses: A number of states have elections for electricity regulators, who often exert powerful control over power prices and planning. Zoom in: One place to watch is Georgia, where two Democratic victories would flip party control of the state's Public Service Commission for the first time in decades. The Atlanta Journal-Constitution has more. Governors: The winners of governors' races will have a big say in everything from oil and gas development to electricity prices. Zoom out: S&P Global has a nice look at energy differences in several governors' races, though a number of the contests are not especially competitive. Friction point: One place to watch is Texas, where oil and gas interests favor incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott (R) in his surprisingly tight race against Gina Hinojosa. Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

Investcorp, one of the Gulfâs largest asset managers, is preparing for a spree of infrastructure deals in the region as governments look for new ways to finance massive investment plans to reduce their reliance on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Gulf states will be more open to partnering with investment funds to pay for new infrastructure projects in the future as they look to preserve cash, Investcorp chief investment officer Rishi Kapoor told Semafor.
These funds have become more active in the Gulf in recent years as governments and state-owned companies seek to raise money by selling stakes in oil pipelines and other assets that for decades have been kept under state control. The scale of the buildout in new infrastructure needed in the wake of the Iran war is set to open up a bigger role for private investors.
âOne of the really attractive investment themes unfolding in the Gulf in coming years will be the renewed focus on building resiliency into essential infrastructure,â Kapoor said. Investcorp already has several deals to acquire Gulf infrastructure assets in the works and could look to raise a new infrastructure fund in the next year or two to help it boost dealmaking.

e56fffe30b8b.text: The Justice Department said Tuesday it will deploy about 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states for the first time ever to watch the polls. Why it matters: The unprecedented effort comes after courts repeatedly rejected the DOJ's efforts to force states to restrict voting for alleged noncitizens. It comes amid a long-running Trump administration push to fight voter fraud , which studies say isn't nearly as prevalent as the administration suggests. Driving the news : The department, in a statement early Tuesday, said one of its most important goals was to protect election integrity. "Today, the DOJ will further this mission by engaging in its largest monitoring effort in history—with approximately 1,000 election monitors and observers deployed, and, for the first time, in all 50 states," the department said. The department said observers would come from the DOJ, U.S. Attorney's offices, and staff from the Office of Personnel Management. What they're saying: "I am very proud we are deploying the largest monitoring effort in DOJ history, and pursuing transparency for elections in an assertive and nondiscriminatory manner," assistant attorney general Harmeet K. Dhillon said in the statement. The intrigue: Some local election officials have already expressed concerns that such a massive wave of observers could intimidate or otherwise interfere with voters. What to watch: The DOJ is still pursuing legal efforts in multiple states to have ballots segregated or otherwise impact counting.

Saudi Aramco reported a 9% rise in profit and increased dividend payments, most of which go to the Saudi state, as a jump in crude prices more than made up for lower production. Profit rose to $31.2 billion in the third quarter, driven by a 35% increase in the average selling price of its oil, even as the company tackled repeated attacks on its facilities from Yemenâs Houthis and Iranian strikes on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Despite Aramcoâs ability to export oil at higher prices, its stock has lagged the global majors that mostly operate outside the Gulf.
Although lower than prewar levels, Aramco reported higher oil production than the previous quarter as it embraced more risky ship-to-ship transfers to get crude out through Hormuz and boosted shipments through the Red Sea.
Aramco is looking to maximize production through the end of the year, âutilizing all the routes that we have,â and sees buoyant demand lasting for several years, CEO Amin Nasser said on an earnings call. It could take two years to refill depleted global oil storage reserves even if the Iran war was resolved today, Nasser said.

4c84fe5de61d.text:
Mohammedâs view
Abu Dhabiâs annual energy exhibition is buzzing, tangible proof that the UAE has absorbed the blows of the Iran war and has its eye on the future. Most conversations Iâve had at ADIPEC, one of the biggest events on the global calendar, have focused on opportunities: oil above $100 a barrel, a new unconventional oil play being unlocked in the UAE, fusion, AI, and infrastructure upgrades. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman spoke at the opening ceremony, a symbol of the close relationship between energy and technology.
Thereâs plenty to be excited about in the industry that remains the Gulfâs economic lifeblood. But this ADIPEC isnât like its predecessors, and itâs not just because of the war.
The UAEâs decision to leave OPEC has changed the gatheringâs makeup. This event previously brought together the groupâs energy ministers, with major decisions made on the sidelines. This year, Saudi Aramco doesnât even have a booth, a sign of increasingly fractured Gulf business relations.
While the biggest Saudi, Kuwaiti, Omani, and Qatari companies stayed away, the rest of the world is here, with participants from more than 170 countries. Yet the absence of top executives from ExxonMobil and Chevron, as well as US government representation, has been noticed.
Amos Hochstein, a former senior energy and national security adviser to President Joe Biden, was forceful in his critique: âI think they should be here,â he said of US officials. âThe United States and UAE are close allies, you have to be here when it counts.â
The war is transforming everything in the region, from trade flows to alliances, but the conflict itself may, in hindsight, seem temporary. The bigger shift will arguably come from AI, determining the future winners and losers. Hochstein said the UAE is a âcritical partner for the US when it comes to AI buildout,â and Sultan Al Jaber, UAE minister of industry and advanced technology and managing director and group chief executive of ADNOC, stressed the point by having Altman as the guest of honor.
ADNOC agreed to become the first energy company to deploy OpenAI Frontier, part of a partnership with OpenAI and G42 to improve operations, strengthen resilience, and increase productivity. âFrom the moment ChatGPT was born, the world has asked what energy can do for AI,â Al Jaber said. âAnd now, together, we will find out what AI can do for energy.â

Separating signal from noise on whether the US-Iran war will escalate has been difficult for months, and now itâs a cacophony. Oil prices plunged on Monday on hopes of a deal with Tehran before jumping almost 2% Tuesday after the US struck Iranâs Qeshm Island, reportedly in response to Iranian fire at an American plane. Yemenâs Houthis are still attacking Saudi Arabia and have advanced toward Aden, threatening to outflank Yemenâs Saudi-backed government forces and potentially extend Iranâs influence to Bab el-Mandeb, the Gulfâs other maritime chokepoint.
Then thereâs diplomacy. US President Donald Trump told Axios heâs in âno rushâ to resume strikes and repeated that Tehran wants a deal. US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks are also returning to Abu Dhabi next week, with Trumpâs envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner expected to attend, making an escalation during their visit seem less likely.
The US midterm elections Tuesday are perhaps the noisiest indicator. Democratic control of either chamber could complicate Trumpâs agenda in his last two years, potentially accelerating military plans before the new Congress takes office in January. But the president will still have considerable foreign policy powers.
The final signal probably matters most: Where are the bombs and planes? Three US aircraft carrier strike groups are expected to arrive near Iran within two weeks, with the USS Theodore Roosevelt the last one to make its way from Japan.

In recent weeks, weâve chronicled a rush of companies staffing up with Democrats in anticipation of a blue wave on Tuesday. But on Monday, OpenAI bucked the trend, hiring former US Army secretary Dan Driscoll for a new national security role just two months after he resigned after clashing with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
While tapping a top Republican operative close to the vice president defies conventional wisdom, itâs a good reminder that Trump remains president for another two years â an eternity in AI time â and that OpenAI sees value in advancing its priorities while it still holds executive favor. Regardless of what happens in Tuesdayâs midterm elections, OpenAI knows that Trumpâs national security apparatus remains a powerful force in deciding which new models get approved for use and who can access them.

81cb13115edb.text:
Lizâs view
Todayâs US midterm elections are a race to see who gets blamed for a host of economic problems coming down the pike. Democrats are favored to take the House, with control of the Senate still a toss-up.
Whoever wins Congress inherits a stack of problems due to detonate over the next two years â just in time to crater 2028 ambitions â and few have obvious fixes.
Inflation is running around 3.7%, rising in six of the past eight months, and the Fed has gone back to unpopular tightening. That a Trump-picked Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, is leaning hawkish into a midterm election underlines how stubborn the problem is.
The labor market is no better. Employers added just 29,000 jobs in September; July was revised into negative territory. Companies too uncertain about whatâs ahead â and unsure of exactly how AI is muddying the employment picture â are neither hiring nor firing, leaving things in what Jerome Powell earlier this year called âan uncomfortable kind of balance.â
Then there are the outside shocks. Reports that the White House is planning post-midterm strikes on Iran may push political fallout from an unpopular war outside the election window, but the economic weight of high gas and diesel prices lands on whoeverâs nominally in charge come January.
Those are the known unknowns. AI brings another set of unknown unknowns: A financial squeeze waiting to happen, as investment shows no signs of slowing down even as the returns on that investment appear even further out than we thought. A leaking AI bubble is likely to burst on the next Congressâs watch (as always, look to the jittery credit market, not the booming stock market, for signs of whatâs to come).
The second problem is political, and Congress has punted on it. Lawmakers left town in September with no movement on AI guardrails. Dozens of data-center moratoriums and AI referendums appear on the ballot today, with more than 20 in Ohio alone.
Even some of President Donald Trumpâs media allies concede that he owns the narrative on the economy no matter what happens on Capitol Hill. But a Democratic Congress would give the White House a foil it hasnât had since the back half of Trumpâs first term, and every stalled bill, shutdown, and soft jobs report could be pinned on the people holding the legislative pen â and subpoena power (more on that below in todayâs newsletter).
Either way, the winners tomorrow arenât claiming a prize so much as signing for a package.
Notable
- Who controls Congress will make little difference to the economy, analysts argue. âA lot of voters head to the polls Tuesday hoping for a fix for affordability,â The Wall Street Journalâs chief economics commentator wrote. âThey are going to be disappointed.â

The witness-prep business is about to take off for Washington law firms. As Democrats appear poised to take the gavel, at least in the hearing-happy House of Representatives, the task of helping corporate executives prepare for their turn in the chair â a DC practice known as âmurder-boardingâ â will be in high demand. Democrats have been plotting for months about how to go after corporations that have courted Trumpâs approval, Semaforâs Nicholas Wu reported earlier this year, citing missives sent to companies over things like ballroom funds, antitrust suits, and business deals involving the Trump family and one-time âfirst buddyâ Elon Musk.

Peter Donald, a former spokesman for the FBIâs New York field office and assistant NYPD commissioner who now advises companies in tight spots. âEverything will be on the table. CEOs should be ready to explain their decisions under oath.â Itâs a good time for companies to prepay any outstanding law firm bills and book some time on CEOsâ calendars for mock grilling.

Meta is prepping a big bond offering that includes its first-ever euro borrowing for up to $15 billion, people familiar with the matter tell Semafor, while Alphabet closed its second euro deal of the year.

For most companies, broadening lender bases is a test-the-pipes exercise to ensure that diverse funding is available if itâs needed. The US said it will suspend South Africa and Rwanda from its free trade pact with sub-Saharan Africa, after months of fraying ties with both nations. Washington and Pretoria have repeatedly clashed since US President Donald Trump falsely accused South Africa of carrying out a genocide of its white population. Todayâs US midterm elections will have a huge impact on the rest of US President Donald Trumpâs term, affecting his room for maneuver on personnel and policy with key implications for relations with allies.

The US has urged Venezuela to release the remaining political prisoners being held in the South American country.
More than 1,000 political prisoners have been freed since US forces seized Venezuelan leader NicolÃ¡s Maduro in a military raid on Caracas on 3 January and took him to New York, where he faces trial on drug-trafficking and torture charges.
But Venezuelan prisoners' rights group Foro Penal says 322 people remain in detention.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met his Venezuelan counterpart, Oliver Blanco, on Monday where he called for their release and discussed reforms aimed at laying the groundwork for free, fair, and credible elections, the US state department said.
The release of political prisoners has long been a demand made by Venezuelan opposition leader MarÃa Corina Machado.
Machado, who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2025, returned to Venezuela on 25 October after living in exile for almost a year. One of her first meetings was with relatives of political detainees.
Many of those in detention were arrested in the aftermath of the 2024 presidential election.
The National Electoral Council (CNE) - which is dominated by government loyalists - declared the incumbent, NicolÃ¡s Maduro, the winner of the election even though copies of the voting tallies collected by the opposition and verified by independent media suggested that the opposition candidate had won.
The Carter Center, which had sent independent observers to Venezuela, also said that the election "could not be considered democratic".
A UN fact-finding mission found, external that in the months that followed, the Venezuelan government orchestrated "a harsh repression against persons perceived as political opponents or simply because they express dissent or critical views against the authorities".
After US forces seized Maduro, his loyal vice-president, Delcy RodrÃguez, was sworn in as interim president.
While RodrÃguez has the backing of the Trump administration, opposition parties within Venezuela have been expressing impatience with the slow pace of reforms.
In Monday's statement, the US state department stressed that it remained committed to US President Donald Trump's three-phase plan, consisting of "stabilisation, economic recovery and political reconciliation, and democratic transition".
A week ago, Rubio had told journalists that Venezuela's "election infrastructure" had to be replaced in order for fresh elections to be valid.
"Not in 10 years, not in five years, not in two years; it needs to happen quickly under the timelines that we've established," he insisted.
Days later, RodrÃguez told Venezuelans in a televised address that "there will be elections" under a "renewed" electoral authority.
However, she did not give a timeline for when the election could be held.
Opposition leader Machado, on the other hand, has been pushing for elections to be held in 2027.
At one point she suggested 24 July 2027 - the anniversary of the birth of independence hero SimÃ³n Bolivar - but she has since returned to calling for a vote at some point in the next year.

An Indian tourist has died after two helicopters collided while attempting to land near the base camp of Mount Everest, two officials have confirmed to the BBC.
Verified footage of the crash showed the helicopter blades of the two aircraft clipping each other as they came into land at around 08:15 local time (02:30 GMT) in Pheriche, approximately 12km (7 miles) south of Mount Everest Base Camp.
Helicopter company Fishtail Air named the man killed in the crash as Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu.
The helicopter company said one of its vehicles was involved in the collision and that another passenger and the helicopter's captain had been injured.
The injured passengers and crew members on board were rescued and taken to Kathmandu, Fishtail Air added in a statement.
The injured passenger was a tourist from New Zealand, an official of Solukhumbu district, Bhupendra Thapa, told BBC Nepal.
The other helicopter involved was operated by Air Dynasty and had been carrying cargo, the company said.
It was operated by one crew member who sustained no injuries, it added.
A spokesman for Nepal's Civil Aviation Authority, Gyanendra Bhul, said: "It appears the accident happened when two helicopters... attempted to land at the same spot."
In the video footage of the incident, the weather conditions look clear and no strong wind effects are visible. One helicopter appears to be making a more rapid descent than the other.
Helicopters are widely used for transport in the Himalayan nation due to its challenging terrain. But its rapidly changing weather conditions and high altitude often make aviation operations hazardous.
The village of Pheriche, located on the trekking route to the summit of the world's tallest mountain, Mount Everest, is just over 4,000m (13,120ft) above sea level.
Climbing expeditions to Everest and Ama Dablam mountain are currently under way in the region, as autumn is a popular climbing season.

Apple has said it does not know when it will get more of its new foldable iPhones back in stock as the company heads towards the key Christmas trading period.
The iPhone Duo sold out just over a week after its launch, despite being Apple's most expensive smartphone at a cost of nearly $2,000.
The company warned of "constraints" in sourcing key components and admitted it was "really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance".
Meanwhile, Apple's new chief executive John Ternus said the firm was seeing an "unprecedented" price rise in memory costs, including chips, as the artificial intelligence (AI) industry continues to invest billions of dollars in building data centres.
Ternus launched the Duo after he took over from previous boss Tim Cook in September.
It is the smartphone's first major design change in almost 20 years but some buyers have reported problems with the Duo's screen.
Last week, the company said it would replace any handsets that were affected by an issue that caused a "small number" to crack along the inside fold.
As it released its latest financial figures on Monday, Apple's executives did not mention any problems with the iPhone Duo.
Ternus said he was "thrilled" by the early reaction to the foldable phone. Chief operating officer Sabih Khan said the company was working hard to get the Duo "into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible".
Apple's results for the three months to 26 September did not include sales of the Duo, which was released at the end of October.
Nevertheless, Apple said it had sold more iPhones globally over the last year than ever before.
iPhone revenue for the quarter rose 17% to $57bn (Â£42bn).
Sales of Mac computers also grew over the three months by 27% to a record $10.7bn.
Overall, Apple's sales between July and September rose from $102bn to $114bn. Pre-tax profit also increased, from $32.8bn to $36.1bn.
However, sales for both the iPad and Apple's wearable products, including its headphones and watch, fell by 10% and 7%, respectively.
Khan said that most Apple devices were still experiencing supply constraints driven in part by difficulty in getting enough microprocessors with advanced nodes.
Those components are essentially computer chip technology that allow Apple devices to operate more quickly, most of which it has manufactured through TSMC, which is based in Taiwan.
Khan said the problem was expected to continue into next year, particularly impacting iPads and Macs.
The situation has been made worse by what the company has repeatedly insisted is "unexpected demand" for its products.
Ternus noted, too, that Apple is still seeing "unprecedented" cost increases for memory, or the ability of devices to store data like apps, photos and text messages.
Much memory storage runs through data centres, which have experienced a boom in demand for space as AI chatbots and platforms - including those developed by the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic - have become popular.
Storage prices have gone up for tech companies like Apple.
Earlier this year, Cook referred to a sudden increase in data centre costs as a "thousand year flood".
Apple has lifted prices on nearly all of its hardware products by around 20%.
Sunil Krishnan from Aviva Investors told the BBC's Today programme that Apple posted "a reasonably solid set of results" with a "pretty good performance" from its iPhone business.
While there were concerns over the company's guidance on profit margins and the cost of memory chips, Krishnan added that in the broader context, "margins well north of 45% for a very well-established company, I think, are pretty impressive".
However, Apple's share price fell by 1.8% in after-hours trading.

a6f9ea1196b4.text:
Andyâs view
The prospect of steep losses for Republicans in todayâs midterms and the lame-duck presidency that ensues regardless raise a fundamental question about the outlook for a budding US-China dÃ©tente.
Can warming superpower ties outlive the Trump era?
I wouldnât count on it.
Itâs not that an election humiliation would crimp US President Donald Trumpâs diplomatic style. On the contrary, thereâs every expectation it would give him even greater incentive to build his legacy on the world stage. But the current thaw is so much an artifice of his own unabashed admiration for his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping. And a backlash is brewing.
Trump boasts of a âgreat friendshipâ with the Chinese strongman â theyâve held two summits so far this year, with plans of another meeting in Shenzhen this month, and a fourth in Miami in December â speaks of a G2 to manage global affairs, and waves away strategic concerns that might strain the bromance. (Asked about reports that Chinese satellite imagery was used by Iran to kill US troops, Trump told reporters on Air Force One: âThey basically do what we do.â)
Yet US policy on China remains very much in play, and debates will surely heat up after the midterms as the race to succeed Trump gets under way across both parties.
Although Republican hawks have largely fallen silent in Trumpâs second term, within the Beltway a bipartisan tough-on-China consensus is intact. Foreign policy elites complain that Trump is ceding the Western Pacific to Beijing (Evan Feigenbaum of the Carnegie Endowment mocks the administrationâ³â£s âreverse pivot from Asiaâ as the Pentagon diverts warships and marines to the Gulf.) Tech hawks accuse Trump of throwing away the US lead in AI by greenlighting exports of advanced Nvidia chips to China, or turning a blind eye to illicit transfers. The Taiwan lobby is outraged at his transactional approach to the island.
Moreover, such criticisms are likely to intensify if an angry Trump, smarting from midterm defeats, focuses even more of his attention on deal-making with Xi.
Ali Wyne, a US-China specialist at the International Crisis Group, sees bipartisan frustration at Trumpâs China policy winding up like a coil, ever more tightly as he gives ground to Xi, and eventually unspooling âviolently and unpredictably.â
The next president, Wyne told me, will inherit a weaker hand vis-Ã -vis China and is likely to be âfar more permissive of competitive and even confrontational actions.â
Certainly, Trumpâs successor â from either party â wonât have nearly the same latitude to manage China ties; one former American diplomat calls the president âhis own China desk officer.â (Of course, thereâs always a chance that Trump himself will flip before he steps down, as he did at the end of his first term when he blamed Xi for unleashing the pandemic on the world and wrecking his reelection chances.)
The late Henry Kissinger, the architect of Nixonâs 1972 opening to China, observed that âAmerica has no permanent friends or enemies, only interests.â In Trumpâs ardent pursuit of Xi, critics suggest the US president forgot that lesson. Once Trump goes, a return to a colder, harder, more calculating realpolitik is in the cards.
Notable
- In a recent op-ed for The New York Times, Thomas L. Friedman argues that as the worldâs leading AI superpowers, with shared interests in safeguarding against AIâs risks, the US and China may be pushed toward âmutually assured collaboration.â

After months of campaigning and billions of dollars spent on the US midterms, election day is finally here.
According to the latest public opinion surveys, Democrats appear to have the upper hand - but polls haven't always been reliable, and this year could have its own share of surprising results.
In broad strokes, however, there are three possible outcomes after Americans have their say.
Here's a look at what they could be, what the early signs might be as results come in (which you can follow later on our results page) and what it could mean for the country.
1. A big Democratic wave
If history is any guide, midterm elections tend to favour the out-of-power party.
Add in what polls suggest is a historically unpopular president, a war with Iran that has driven up consumer costs and some controversial policies - like aggressive immigration enforcement and support for data centre construction - and you have the conditions for a so-called electoral wave.
In this first scenario, a huge wave is exactly what happens.
Democrats could not only take control of the House of Representatives but far surpass the 218 seats needed for a majority. They may win not only the dozen or so races that election analysts rate as too-close-to-call, they could also flip some seats in more solidly conservative terrain.
In the Senate, this scenario would require Democrats to win all or most of the current crop of races that are toss-ups, including some in traditionally conservative states. There would be at least one eye-popping victory in a place that hasn't elected a Democrat in a generation, Texas, or in nearly a century in the case of Kansas.
If this did happen, Democrats wouldn't just take control of the Senate, they would do so with a seat or two to spare. This might avoid any drama around a potential legal challenge by Republicans in Alaska where a judge dismissed a Trump administration lawsuit over two Dan Sullivans being on the ballot.
Democrats might accomplish this by boosting turnout of their voters and winning independent voters by sizable margins. This would reverse Trump's 2024 inroads with Hispanic voters and young men. Some Republican voters might also support the Democrats or just stay home.
This kind of a result would represent a stinging rebuke for Trump and his Republican Party, setting up two years of conflict between a newly invigorated Democratic Party with its hands firmly on the lever of legislative power and a president who seldom backs away from a fight.
Early signs as the results come in:
If Democrats hold targeted House contests in Florida and win some Republican districts in North Carolina, Michigan, New York, Virginia and Kentucky. If they flip the Senate seat in South Carolina, it's going to be a good night for Democrats.
2. A Democratic trickle
Maybe the polls won't be entirely wrong, but not entirely right either.
In this scenario, it could be that while they take enough of the low-hanging fruit in the US House contests to deliver a majority, it's not a sizable one.
This would mean Democratic leaders in the chamber would regularly have to wrangle with their fringe members on the left and the centre to ensure they have enough votes to pass legislation.
On the Senate side in this hypothetical, the Democrats would just flip a seat or two - North Carolina, for instance, seems all but assured - but the contests in the conservative heartland would prove to be out of reach.
Perhaps they're unable to unseat stubbornly resilient Republican Senator Susan Collins in Maine or left-wing candidate Abdul El-Sayed can't keep Michigan in the Democratic column.
Maybe the duelling Dan Sullivans controversy is enough to sink Democratic candidate Mary Peltola in Alaska.
For this "Democratic trickle" scenario to unfold, the big Democratic turnout we've seen in early voting would be matched by a Republican surge on election day.
Trump's efforts to rally his base in Republican red states could help his party avoid the worst-case scenario. The races that were at or near the margin of error in polls might provide a mixed bag for both parties.
The result would be a divided Congress - and that's a recipe for political gridlock.
Early signs as the results come in:
If Florida stays comfortably Republican across the board. If Democrats pick up some House seats in places like Virginia and Pennsylvania, but the Republican incumbents on more secure political ground across the country avoid getting washed away in a deluge.
3. A good night for Republicans
This scenario involves Republicans resiliently holding on to both chambers of Congress.
For this to happen, the polls - which have previously underestimated Trump's support - need to be wrong and the toss-up races to mostly fall the way of Republicans.
Not only would Republican voters have to turn out in unexpectedly impressive numbers, independent and Hispanic voters who had seemingly soured on Trump's policies would have also to break his way in the end.
In this scenario, control of the House, far from being a done deal for Democrats, could end up coming down to California and its extended days-long counting process for mail-in ballots.
In the end, Republicans might eke out a slim overall majority thanks in part to efforts to draw more favourable congressional district lines in places like Texas, Florida and North Carolina.
It could also be that Republicans win all the Senate contests in the conservative states and they also flip Michigan, a seat that was held by Democrats heading into the vote.
Even if Republicans don't hold North Carolina or win in Democratic-controlled Minnesota or New Hampshire - races just on the periphery of competitiveness in this year's elections - they may at least make the Democratic candidates sweat.
If this was to happen, Trump might on Wednesday morning claim a renewed electoral mandate and push forward with his domestic and foreign policy agenda with the continued support of a Republican Congress.

3368281af41f.text: Voters are about to decide whether public backlash against the health care industry translates into meaningful policy shifts. Why it matters: Health care has never been more expensive, and it's not going to get any cheaper without significant intervention. The big picture: It's hard to see Democrats not making health care affordability a top priority in the next Congress, regardless of whether they win only a narrow majority in the House or sweep both chambers in a blowout. But the party isn't aligned on an agenda, and a strong showing by progressives could drag things leftward. Reality check: Any Democratic victory — no matter the size — will be tempered by the realities of split government, with President Trump still in office for the next two years. Larger Democratic majorities may bring greater leverage in negotiations over spending packages or raising the debt limit. And the boldest changes will probably be reserved for the campaign trail, as 2028 presidential contenders begin to vie for the party's nomination. Here's what we're watching: Medicare for All vs. moderates: What happens in Michigan's Senate race — and Maine's, to some extent — will almost certainly shape how much sway progressives have in the next two years. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has made Medicare for All central to his campaign, unabashedly supporting the idea in a race that could determine which party has control of the Senate next year. The same is true of Democrat Troy Jackson in Maine's Senate race, though Jackson has a lower national profile than El-Sayed. But Medicare for All supporters looking for a vote on the measure face an uphill battle : Despite the policy's growing popularity among the public, moderates unwilling to abolish private insurance will make up a sizable portion of any Democratic majority. The doctors-turned-politicians: Doctors are on the ballot in key races this year, and the question is how much public trust translates into votes. El-Sayed, an epidemiologist who went to medical school but isn't a practicing physician, is one example. There's also pediatrician Annie Andrews, who's mounted a strong challenge to Republican Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina, and Ohio governor candidate Amy Acton, who has focused on pediatrics and preventive medicine. "We've seen in our research over the last six-plus years that [doctors are] among the most trusted potential candidates for office, hands down," said Erik Polyak, executive director of 314 Action. MAHA on the line: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s "Make America Healthy Again" movement has focused its attention largely on the Iowa governor's race in the final weeks of the election, going all in for Republican Zach Lahn, who's pledged to take on Big Agriculture interests and the use of farm chemicals. Calling it an "existential" vote, MAHA Action founder Tony Lyons told MAGA influencer Steve Bannon that the race will be "the test of what's possible in a state, of whether we can actually take the country back from these corrupt companies, from these corrupt politicians, and really protect people." California's tax plan: Golden State voters will decide the fate of a controversial one-time wealth tax on billionaires, with most of the proceeds to be used to fund health care services. The money is intended to partly make up for Republican cuts to federal Medicaid spending but the tax is opposed by Gov. Gavin Newsom, a likely 2028 Democratic presidential contender. The measure tests voter sentiment in one of the bluest states to tax the super rich in order to fund health benefits — a potential prelude to a national debate over expanding the federal government's role in health care and how to fund it. Abortion ballot measures: Voters in four states will determine what reproductive rights in their states look like, another round of post-Roe abortion policymaking via ballot initiatives. Nevada and Virginia will consider constitutional amendments protecting the right to abortion, while Missouri will weigh a measure backed by the state legislature to repeal a 2024 pro-abortion rights amendment. Idaho voters will determine the fate of a state law guaranteeing a right to abortion until fetal viability, generally considered to begin around 23 to 24 weeks into a pregnancy, or after that in the case of a medical emergency.

87420a8af2d4.text:
Benâs view
National election days in the United States of America are biennial festivals of noise over signal.
This is the day of maximal public attention to television and online news, on par with wars and natural disasters and the World Cup finals. Hundreds of millions of people are watching TV and YouTube closely, chattering and analyzing on social media. Media companies âÂ like ours âÂ will be there to keep you company, of course, in our case with superb analysis and a thoughtful afternoon livestream.
And yet: Thereâs no other day where the volume of nonsense so outweighs the quantity of new information.
In the old days of print journalism, before websites, social media, and even cable news required that reporters broadcast nonstop, Election Day was a blast. Political reporters could sleep late, have a long lunch, even catch a movie. In the afternoon, youâd drop by a polling place for a little âB-matterâ âÂ some color and an ambiguous quote or two to bulk out a story in the early edition. âVoters lined up around the block at P.S. 87 on the Upper West Side to cast their ballots. âIt sure is crowded here,â said Bob Smith, 70.â That sort of thing.
Too Online
The modern Election Day media contains three things: anecdotes about how many people are voting; anecdotes about chicanery and hoaxes; and, long after that, results.
Early voting trends and stories about how long the lines are in reliably red or blue districts are tempting to use as data points âÂ but are notoriously misleading. You can only vote once, and it doesnât count more if it comes in early, rather than if you wait until Tuesday to stand on line.
Then there are the anecdotes. One, inevitably, will be that a voting machine somewhere in the US is on the brink. The influencers will be all over it. X, in particular, is now hyper-charged to reward engagement. A video âÂ real or manipulated âÂ of a machine in Pennsylvania or Arizona appearing to refuse to accept votes for one candidate is engagement gold. When you see these posts, remember that the US election system is wildly decentralized, secure, and largely offline, and that this story circulates every year.
There will also be hints and rumors of poll-site interference or intimidation. Both parties have a maximal incentive to play up anything like this,Â both as an early warning in case itâs real, and to motivate voters in any case. This is a global phenomenon: Recent elections in Israel and Brazil were marked by wildly viral claims of misconduct âÂ foreign funding of Arab voters in Israelâs case, polls being kept open too late in Brazilâs âÂ that evaporated the next day when they were no longer relevant.
Media companies, of course, have our own incentives to keep you engaged. There will be nonstop panels on TV and livestreams, analysts repeating analysis of days-old polls, and âÂ come afternoon âÂ figures from exit polls suggesting that Hispanics are voting in large numbers, or that the economy is a major issue. (These exit poll analyses are both largely useless and often corrected in the days after the election, but they fill the air.)
So, Election Day is a good day to sleep late, see You Can See Everything (if you havenât yet), and, of course â¦ watch our livestream.
Then when the polls start closing at 6 pm EST, the news arrives: Numbers start rolling in to replace the chatter. And, on their heels, often, litigation.
Room for Disagreement
There could be substantive news to follow if the Trump administration acts to disrupt voting on Election Day, as some suspect will happen.
A group of Democratic state officials and voting rights advocates âhave been planning how to respond if, indeed, there is real federal interference. The group has âwar-gamedâ how to react if government agents attempt to commandeer voting equipment or ballots,â ProPublica reports.

It's been a dramatic campaign, full of twists and turns. But how much have you picked up along the way? Take our quiz.

15ae37afd710.text: Data: AdImpact; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Republicans on the ballot this cycle have all but stopped mentioning President Trump in their campaign ads , according to an Axios analysis of broadcast advertising data from AdImpact. Why it matters: Trump has tried to make the 2026 midterms a referendum on his presidency. His party has run the other way. The big picture: Ads from both parties in Senate, House and gubernatorial races have shifted from a heavy focus on Trump during the primaries to a much greater emphasis on the economy in the general election. Both parties have also leaned much more heavily into health care, with a noticeable increase among House Republicans. By the numbers: The drop-off is steepest among Republicans, and especially in House races. Trump appeared in 66% of House Republicans' primary ads but shows up in just 3% of their general election ads. In Senate races, Republican ads mentioning him fell from 77% to 22%. Governor's races saw the same shift: Republican ads mentioning Trump fell 34 percentage points. Democrats have also pulled back from Trump, though less dramatically. Trump appeared in 45% of Democratic primary ads, but just 18% of their general election ads. Zoom in: Republican candidates are mentioning some of Trump's signature issues less than during the primaries. The share of Republican ads mentioning immigration has dropped 20 percentage points in Senate races and 14 points in House races. Ads referencing law enforcement fell from 11% of Republican Senate primary ads to 6% in the general election, even as their mentions of crime increased. Data: AdImpact; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Between the lines: Candidates often lean on the country's most prominent political figure in primaries, then pivot to policy issues in the general election. But this year's drop-off stands out given how hard Trump has pushed to tie himself to the midterms. He has urged voters to pretend he's on the ballot and essentially demanded ads running during the Republican midterm convention in September feature him. Of note: In this analysis, primary ads are broadcast ads that aired before a race's primary. General election ads aired between the primary and Oct. 26. The trends may be even more pronounced in ads running through Election Day. The bottom line: Most Republicans have been too scared to tell Trump how unpopular he is, Axios reported . But their ad receipts don't lie.
