The packages led to the evacuation of election offices in Louisiana and Oklahoma. Numerous states, from Idaho to Florida, said they either received letters or had them intercepted by the Postal Service. The FBI said it has video evidence of Martin's car stopping in October at mailboxes at Postal Service sites in Oklahoma City, Dallas and San Antonio. Investigators also gleaned his fingerprints from a letter addressed to FBI Director Kash Patel, whose first name was written as "Kashyap." Walmart records show Martin purchased common household goods, such as turmeric and vinegar, to create invisible ink that could be read with ultraviolet light, the FBI said. The Democratic Socialists of America apparently assisted the investigation. The FBI said it believes Martin, posing as someone using the name George Livingston, posted a message to a DSA email list in October, warning that members were traitors and eligible for arrest for treason if they vote in the Nov. 3 election. bdf10d5d2510.text: Voting is underway across the country Tuesday in a midterm election that could decide whether President Trump gets two more years of unified Republican rule — or faces a potential Democratic check on his power. Why it matters: The results will be the clearest national test of Trump's second presidency , following war abroad, economic anxiety at home and sweeping changes in Washington. Trump, facing all these challenges, has made himself the face of the Republican campaign for control. State of play: As voters head to the polls, the Trump administration is zeroing-in on the Alaska Senate race. The Department of Justice has sent more than a dozen target letters as part of its investigation into the Dan J. Sullivan campaign, which has been the subject of Trump's ire for several days. It's an escalation into the Trump administration's push for answers in the race where Democrats reportedly conducted an organized effort to recruit another "Dan Sullivan" to join Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) on the ballot. The Justice Department's move comes as the White House is circulating Election Day talking points across the administration, touting Trump's accomplishments as the GOP braces for a tough evening that could see them lose both the House and the Senate, according to some forecasters. Trump has been a massive force on the campaign trail, rallying in several states for his Republican picks. The president has claimed to voters that he is on the ballot this year, making the election about his policies and actions — despite his dismal polling ratings, plagued by the Iran war and economic anxiety. Trump spent the morning of Election Day criticizing Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) and the Daily Mail in various social media posts. Zoom in: Voting machine glitches and hiccups popped up in various spots of the country Tuesday, including in the high-profile New York House race between Rep. Mike Lawler (R) and Democratic nominee Cait Conley. Otherwise the temperature was rather low despite the power of Washington hanging in the balance. The big picture: Republicans have largely given Trump a free hand in Washington since his return to the White House. Democratic control of even one chamber of Congress would open the door to investigations, subpoenas and even more legislative gridlock. Voters are weighing the Iran war and rising energy costs , broader affordability concerns, and intensifying debate over AI's economic impact, among other issues. An unprecedented mobilization of election monitors and legal battles involving the Trump administration have raised concerns about potential disruptions and challenges to the results. Trump has said he'll respect the election results if "they're honest elections." What's at stake: Republicans enter Election Day defending narrow congressional majorities, with a number of battlegrounds and traditionally GOP districts and states shifting into toss-up territory during the campaigns' final weeks. The House: All 435 seats are on the ballot. Democrats need a net gain of three seats to reclaim the majority. Redistricting has reshaped the battlefield. The Senate: 35 seats are on the ballot. Republicans hold a 53-47 advantage, including two independents who caucus with Democrats. Democrats need a net gain of four seats. Some scenarios: Democrats flip the House: They gain greater investigative power, control of committees and leverage over spending — but Trump retains his veto and executive authority. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) could become the first Black speaker of the House, or face an opponent from his left. Democrats take Congress: Democrats' oversight power expands, while Trump's agenda faces major obstacles. A third Trump impeachment could be on the table, although being convicted in a Senate trial would require a two-thirds vote. Republicans retain Congress: Trump and GOP leaders get another two years to advance his agenda, though narrow margins could complicate plans. Between the lines: Beyond control of Congress, the results will test whether Trump's gains among young, Black and Latino voters in 2024 have endured — or if those voters are moving back toward Democrats who are trying to rebuild a winning coalition for 2028. What we're watching: Whether close races, outstanding ballots and legal challenges delay a clear verdict.

d04547405698.text: By — Joseph Wilson, Associated Press Joseph Wilson, Associated Press By — Tales Azzoni, Associated Press Tales Azzoni, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/spanish-police-investigating-after-soccer-player-dies-following-on-field-collision Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Spanish police investigating after soccer player dies following on-field collision World Nov 3, 2026 3:14 PM EST BARCELONA, Spain (AP) — Spanish police have opened an investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter after a soccer player died following an on-field collision with the opposing team's goalkeeper in a second-division match. Tenerife forward Jesús de Miguel died after he suffered cardiac arrest following the on-field collision, his club said Tuesday. He was 30. Under Spanish law, deaths from non-natural causes, including accidents, are subject to judicial investigation. Santa Cruz de Tenerife chief prosecutor José Luis Sánchez-Jáuregui told Spanish news agency EFE that criminal proceedings were unlikely, noting that the collision occurred during play. De Miguel was taken to a hospital and the match, tied 2-2, was abandoned after the incident. Tenerife's largest shareholder Rayco García told reporters that De Miguel's body would be transported to Navahermosa, in the Toledo province, at the request of his family. He said De Miguel's teammates and club officials would be present for a "final farewell." On Saturday, fans will gather at the team's stadium to honor the player, García said. "We will all join forces and get through this together," García said. Club president Felipe Miñambres said players and their families would likely need help to cope with De Miguel's death. "We will need professional help and the help of all of our fans," he said. "They will be feeling the same way that we are feeling today." The club asked for its league game at Granada on Saturday to be postponed. The heavy collision happened when Owono rushed out of his area all the way to midfield to challenge for a long ball that De Miguel was trying to reach. De Miguel initially curled on his knees, clutching his torso for a few seconds, before he fell over onto his back, with his arms falling to his sides. Owono was walking off the field after being shown the red card but turned around and joined the other players rushing to check on De Miguel. The goalkeeper's Instagram account, which had nearly 30,000 followers, had been deactivated on Tuesday. Another player with the same last name of Owono, Michel Owono, who plays for sixth-division Spanish club Can Vidalet, denounced a wave of racist insults against him by people thinking he was the Andorra goalkeeper. Fans pays tribute to CD Tenerife's Jesus de Miguel on Nov. 3, 2026, who died after suffering a cardiac arrest following a collision during a match. Photo by Borja Suarez/ Reuters De Miguel, a Madrid native, began his senior career with Leganés B in 2015 and subsequently played for a number of lower-division clubs in Spain. He joined Tenerife last year. There were no local media reports about De Miguel having a pre-existing health condition. The precise medical cause of death was not immediately disclosed. Spanish media said De Miguel is survived by his wife and their daughter. "There are no words of comfort," the club statement read. "There is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this profound sense of sorrow. We stand with his devastated family, his loved ones, and the entire Tenerife community." Andorra, which is owned by former Barcelona star Gerard Piqué, also offered its condolences, along with other clubs, the Spanish soccer federation and La Liga. "We wish to extend our deepest condolences to the family of Jesús de Miguel, to all his colleagues and friends, and to CD Tenerife. May he rest in peace," Andorra said in a statement. Piqué said on X: "I am sorry with all my soul. Rest in peace, Jesús." The players of Real Madrid held a minute of silence for De Miguel during training, while fellow topflight club Espanyol postponed the presentation of its new coach. Madrid forward Kylian Mbappé said on social media: "So much sadness. There are no words." Argentina great Lionel Messi said on Instagram: "There are no words. My condolences and lots of strength to all his family and friends." English clubs Manchester United and Liverpool joined in offering their condolences on social media. The Spanish soccer federation postponed all Copa del Rey and Copa de la Reina matches scheduled on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. UEFA said a moment of silence would be observed at all its matches this week. Life-threatening injuries from collisions in soccer are extremely rare. 133cbb4ca5c8.text: North Korea appears to have used a fake job interview as part of its months-long preparations to steal $6.3 billion from Binance, the crypto exchange said Tuesday. Why it matters : The country's hackers are weaponizing both sides of the job market , posing as recruiters and job applicants to infiltrate companies and steal billions. Driving the news : Binance said one of its software engineers was contacted in September through a "legitimate job-hunting platform" by someone posing as a project director at a fictitious company. During the first-round interview, a fake HR representative conducted a live video call with the engineer and showed off a seemingly legitimate social media profile featuring personal photos and videos. The hackers waited until the second round — after building trust with the employee — to ask them to download an infected code repository as part of an interview assignment. Separately, another software engineer also downloaded a "tampered Homebrew installation" in June to install a popular AI coding tool onto their device. Binance's security team detected the installation and replaced the device, as well as rotated all credentials, but the engineer and colleagues were all exposed to the hacker. The intrigue: The fake interview was just one of several suspected North Korean attempts to compromise Binance employees. So far in 2026, Binance said it has detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber incidents, including attempts involving fake job interviews and compromised software packages. Between the lines: North Korean hackers have spent years exploiting both sides of the hiring process. As job applicants, North Korean operatives pose as legitimate IT workers to land high-paying jobs at American companies. Those salaries are then funneled back to Pyongyang. Operatives are also increasingly posing as recruiters and prospective employees to lure in people who work at cryptocurrency firms in the hopes of tricking them into downloading malware. Data from Pindrop Security shows that IT worker fraud has been rampant in 2026: Last year, North Korean job applicants made up 1 in every 343 applications. This year, across Pindrop's customer base, those applicants now make up 1 in 47. The big picture: North Korea has found an opening in a difficult job market, where companies are eager to find qualified workers and job seekers are anxious for their next opportunity. Hiring managers have struggled to find qualified candidates , while job applicants have been anxious for years about their ability to find new roles in a tough market. Go deeper : How North Korea perfected the crypto heist

9680058e2c7f.text: Voting machines across New York's Westchester County are rejecting paper ballots on Election Day , raising concerns about potential delays in one of the nation's most competitive House races. Why it matters: Results could be delayed for one of the country's most prominent House races, between Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) and Democratic nominee Cait Conley, as officials address a problem with paper ballots. Catch up quick: The Westchester County Board of Elections said Tuesday it was aware of a problem preventing voting machines from accepting paper ballots at polling locations throughout the county. The Board of Elections said it is speaking with New York State officials and the Westchester County government "to address this issue and ensure that voting continues with as little disruption as possible." New York Attorney General Letitia James wrote on X that her office is monitoring the issue. The intrigue: Election officials initially blamed the thickness of paper ballots but later removed that explanation from their statement, per reports. The latest: On Tuesday afternoon, the New York State Board of Elections said the malfunction was linked to "an update to the county's election programming" released after initially testing Election Day equipment. Officials said the software update wasn't installed on all machines, leaving them unable to recognize and accept ballots. Officials are still working to restore the machines while voters continue casting emergency paper ballots, which will be counted once scanning resumes. What they're saying: Lawler said officials were working with vendors to resolve the problem, while Conley reassured voters that their ballots would count. Westchester County government wrote on its website: "Let us be absolutely clear: Every eligible vote will be counted." What we're hearing: Voters in the county told Fox 5 NY that they had to fill out paper ballots instead of using the machines. Voters said their ballots were placed in a security box. Other voters shared discontent with the ballots issue on social media . Katie Miller , wife of Trump adviser Stephen Miller, claimed on X: "This is how the Left steals elections. Mike Lawler's competitive district and they are turning away voters." Context: The county covers roughly 30% of New York's 17th District, which Lawler represents. The contest has emerged as a key battleground race in Democrats' push to gain control of the House. Zoom out: The ballot-scanning problems come as technology vulnerabilities have been a key issue heading into the midterms, with researchers saying some vulnerabilities remain in plain sight. Officials in Broward County, Florida, reported a computer glitch that disrupted voting at polling locations early Tuesday, CNN reports. The malfunction reportedly caused systems designed to stop voters from receiving the wrong ballots to reject all ballots. Officials said the issue was resolved. What's next: Voters at affected polling locations were urged to remain in line and cast their ballots. Editor's note: This story has been updated with information about polling glitches in Broward County, Florida.

This article was first reported by The Examination, a nonprofit newsroom that investigates global health threats.
When Rachel Curtis visited her 86-year-old grandmother in Odessa, Texas, last summer, the putrid odor of hydrogen sulfide hit her as soon as she got out of the car.
She could smell the toxic gas, which is often compared to rotten eggs and is fatal in high concentrations, inside her grandmother’s house. Her grandmother has lived about 50 yards from an oil pumpjack for decades and was used to the smell, but she was suffering from frequent headaches—a common effect of exposure to hydrogen sulfide, or H2S.
Worried about her grandmother’s health, Curtis grew even more upset when she found out who operates the pumpjack and other oil equipment nearby: Aghorn Operating. The company had recently pleaded guilty to criminal health and safety violations related to the 2019 deaths of an employee, Jacob Dean, and his wife, Natalee—who were killed by a cloud of hydrogen sulfide inside a nearby Aghorn pumphouse.
After the deaths, Curtis felt both Aghorn and authorities should be keeping better tabs on all of its facilities.
“It just really ticks me off because, I mean, she’s an 86-year-old woman who’s lived across the street from this for how many years,” said Curtis, a high school teacher who had been friendly with the Deans before she moved across the state. “I feel like something should have been done.”
Aghorn and its president, Frosty Gilliam, didn’t respond to calls, emails and detailed questions.
In a court filing last year, Aghorn stated that since the 2019 deaths, the company had hired a full-time safety manager, established written safety policies, conducted hydrogen sulfide safety training and upgraded monitors and alarms for the gas in various facilities. “Aghorn has substantially improved the safety of its facilities and instituted measures to ensure the safety of its employees and the general public,” it said.
Often called “sour gas,” hydrogen sulfide forms naturally underground in some oil-rich regions of the world and can get released into the air during oil production. It can also escape from badly sealed equipment. Low levels of the gas can irritate the eyes and respiratory system and chronic exposure has been associated with neurological problems like fatigue, impaired memory, headaches and dizziness.
As The Examination and the Houston Chronicle detailed in a 2024 investigation, tens of thousands of Texans live near hydrogen sulfide hotspots, but despite community complaints of exposure, state regulators have largely failed to hold companies accountable. When investigators find the gas seeping into the air, companies usually get what amounts to a fix-it ticket, often without any penalty. Problems can persist for years.
That pattern has continued with Aghorn, despite the deaths in the heart of the Permian Basin.
In 2019, Dean was checking on some malfunctioning equipment inside an Aghorn facility when he collapsed in a cloud of hydrogen sulfide. Natalee went looking for him and died next to him. Their kids, then 6 and 9, were sitting in the car outside.
Federal prosecutors charged Aghorn with willfully violating worker safety laws, causing the death of an employee, as well as obstruction and false statements. They added a conspiracy charge, alleging a widespread practice, continuing to 2024, of putting profits and convenience above human health and safety.
Prosecutors documented a pattern of chronic leaks and unsafe practices that continued years after the Deans’ deaths. “At Aghorn,” they wrote in a 2024 filing, “placing workers, contractors, and the public at risk was a way of doing business that was deeply ingrained in the corporate culture.”
The company pleaded guilty last year to the more limited charges of negligent endangerment and willful violation of safety laws, paying a $1 million fine. As part of the plea deal, Aghorn admitted its failure to implement workplace protections was a cause of Jacob Dean’s death and that its representatives “had neglected to control H2S emissions and provide adequate safety systems, which negligence placed Natalee Dean in imminent danger of death.” The company’s vice president, Trent Day, was sentenced to five months in prison.
Industry consultant Jim Kirksey, who reviewed the evidence for prosecutors, wrote in a report filed in the case that Aghorn mostly ignored health and safety complaints, and that the state’s oil regulator, the Texas Railroad Commission, was slow to act.
“The residents who live or work near Aghorn Operating facilities are the innocent victims of Aghorn Operating non-compliance with H2S safety regulations,” Kirksey wrote in his 2024 report, noting that complaints of headaches and nausea were commonplace. Aghorn objected to Kirksey’s qualifications in court filings.
Shortly after that report was written, Adrianna Yanez, a mother of four who lives about 11 miles west of Curtis on the outskirts of Odessa, complained to regulators about hydrogen sulfide leaks wafting toward her home that she said caused bad headaches and bouts of vomiting.
Inspectors from the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality found gas leaking from an Aghorn pumpjack just over 100 meters from her house. The company patched it, and TCEQ resolved the complaint with no penalty, records show.
The Railroad Commission then found gas leaking from storage tanks and an unlit flare about a third of a mile away and told Aghorn to fix it. Investigators came back twice and found gas still leaking. On the fourth visit, in early 2025, they didn’t see any leaks and closed the investigation.
The smell went away for a few months, Yanez said, and then it came back.
“It’s really sad because I guess they see us as the poor people who live out here on the west side of Odessa and they could care less about our health or our children,” Yanez told The Examination recently.
The Railroad Commission didn’t respond to questions about its oversight of Aghorn. Commission spok

1ac9c9efb113.text: State officials have largely taken securing the 2026 midterm elections into their own hands after nearly two years of federal program and funding cuts during the second Trump administration. Why it matters: The reduction in federal support has come as AI tools threaten to make it easier for hackers to uncover software vulnerabilities, launch cyberattacks, and spread disinformation that undermines trust in election results. Reality check: Just because a security flaw exists doesn't mean hackers can exploit it to manipulate election results. Nearly all U.S. elections maintain paper records that can be used to verify electronic tallies. Threat level: Election officials are preparing for everything from cyberattacks and AI-generated disinformation to physical threats, logistical disruptions and legal challenges. The big picture: State election officials relied on homeland security agencies, fusion centers, police, National Guard units and private cybersecurity firms to prepare for the midterms, John Milhofer, a spokesperson for the National Association of Secretaries of State, told Axios. That group and the National Association of State Election Directors are helping states exchange threat intelligence and connect with federal agencies and private sector experts. Catch up quick: State resources have become more important after the Trump administration scaled back federal election security assistance. CISA cut election security personnel and services in 2025, while federal funding for the Elections Infrastructure Information Sharing and Analysis Center, a key information-sharing network for election officials, ended that year. Election officials are receiving fewer election-specific threat briefings and less direct technical assistance, even after CISA outlined plans to restore some services in September. Zoom in: Michael Moore, chief information security officer for the Arizona secretary of state's office, told Axios that the state has been without a dedicated CISA cybersecurity adviser since March 2025. The Arizona Department of Homeland Security has helped fill the gap, providing security tools and monitoring services to smaller counties. On Election Day, Arizona is bringing together its state cybersecurity team, National Guard, the FBI and a representative from CISA's Region 9 office to coordinate responses to potential threats, Moore said. Moore's team has spent years conducting tabletop exercises covering cyberattacks, AI-generated impersonations of election officials, suspicious packages and other disruptions. Between the lines: Arizona is also getting threat intelligence from former CISA personnel who work in the space, election security nonprofits and officials in other states. Moore said his relationship with New Jersey's election security officials is particularly useful because his East Coast counterparts can warn him about threats hours before they might emerge in Arizona. What they're saying: A CISA spokesperson said in a statement that the agency will provide state and local government officials, including election officials and election vendors, "no-cost voluntary services" like vulnerability scanning and technical expertise, when they request it. "We are committed to supporting state and local elections officials to protect election infrastructure and safeguard our democracy," the spokesperson added. Yes, but: Moore said he still wants CISA to return to its 2024 staffing levels — and then double them. "If we are literally experiencing a cyberattack from a nation-state, it shouldn't be Arizona versus that nation-state," Moore said. "We're the United States of America. It should be a unified response." David Becker, executive director and founder of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, told reporters during a briefing Thursday that states have hired vendors and built their own networks to compensate for the federal retreat. "They might not be able to replace everything," Becker said. "They're not going to get the same bird's-eye national-level view of potential disinformation or potential cyber events." The bottom line: Election officials said they're prepared for disruptions, even if they can't prevent every attack. "The goal is prevent as much as we can, detect and recover," Moore said. "We're going to have some amount of disruption.... We're going to recover."

Lieb, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/voters-decide-key-ballot-measures-on-abortion-rights-congressional-redistricting-and-voter-id-laws Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Voters decide key ballot measures on abortion rights, congressional redistricting and voter ID laws Politics Nov 3, 2026 12:30 PM EST 2026 ELECTION COVERAGE: Watch Live | Poll Closing Times | All Live Results | Live Updates | Live Fact Check WASHINGTON (AP) — A battle over abortion rights is playing out in several states Tuesday as voters decide 145 proposed laws and constitutional amendments, including some that could affect voting for future elections. The ballot measures provide a political undercard for a high-profile midterm election that will determine which party controls Congress, state legislatures and gubernatorial offices in many states. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Some measures put President Donald Trump's priorities to a public test by gauging support for his attempts to reshape congressional districts, limit transgender athletes in sports and strengthen voter identification requirements. Abortion ban faces an unusual redo in Missouri Two years ago, Missouri voters became the first in the nation to pass a ballot measure undoing an existing ban on most abortions. Now voters are deciding whether to repeal the 2024 abortion rights amendment and replace it with a new prohibition — this time allowing exceptions for medical emergencies and fetal anomalies, and in cases of rape or incest up to 12 weeks of pregnancy. The proposed ban was placed on the ballot by the Republican-led Legislature. Abortion rights advocates, led by national progressive groups, have greatly outspent abortion foes in a bid to defeat the measure. READ MORE: What to look for on Election Day as questions loom over Trump In three other states, ballot measures would create a right to abortion using standards similar to what was in place nationally before the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022 and opened the door to state bans. Ballot measures in Idaho and Nevada would block bans on abortion before fetal viability, usually considered after 21 weeks. Nevada voters already approved the measure once but have to do so a second time for it to become official. In Virginia, an amendment would ensure abortion is allowed for the first two trimesters. Redistricting measures could affect 2028 elections Nine states are using new congressional districts in the midterm elections after a rare spate of mid-decade redistricting encouraged by Trump. Missouri's Republican lawmakers also had adopted new House districts designed to help the GOP win an additional seat. But courts ruled they cannot be used unless first approved by voters in a November referendum. If passed, the districts would take effect for the 2028 election. READ MORE: 13 races that will determine control of the Senate Voters in Democratic-led Maryland are deciding on a constitutional amendment that also could pave the way for new congressional districts in the 2028 election. Democratic proponents, backed by former President Barack Obama, have urged a "yes" vote as way to "stop Trump." Some Democrats also want to redistrict in Colorado. But a citizen initiative on the ballot would prohibit any potential 2028 redistricting from favoring one political party and require approval from both an independent commission and the state Supreme Court. Transgender restrictions are proposed in several states Voters in Arizona, Colorado, Missouri, Nebraska and Washington are considering measures restricting transgender athletes or medical procedures. That comes as Trump's administration has been pushing for restrictions impacting transgender people, especially youth. Most Republican-led states already bar transgender women and girls from female school sports teams. Citizen-led ballot initiatives propose similar restrictions in the Democratic-led states of Colorado and Washington. The Arizona measure would extend public school sports restrictions to private schools. And Nebraska's measure would add existing restrictions to the state constitution. A second ballot question in Colorado would ban some transgender medical treatments for minors. The Missouri abortion amendment also would add existing transgender medical restrictions to the state constitution. Five state measures seek voter ID mandates Though Trump's push for nationwide voter ID mandates remains stalled in Congress, citizen activists bypassed Democratic-led state legislatures to place new voter ID requirements on the ballot in California, Colorado and Nevada. Those measures would require government-issued identification — like driver's licenses or partial Social Security numbers — to cast ballots. The Nevada amendment already won approval in 2024 but needs a second vote to take effect. READ MORE: Election Day underway after a surge in early voting, as Trump sows doubt on results Measures referred to the ballot by Republican-led legislatures in North Carolina and Ohio would enhance existing voter ID requirements by placing them in the state constitution. Six states consider citizen voting measures Ballot measures in Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia would reinforce current election practices limiting voting to U.S. citizens. Critics argue the measures are largely symbolic and unnecessary, because voting by noncitizens is rare and already forbidden in federal elections. But noncitizens are allowed to vote in some local elections in California, Maryland, Vermont and the District of Columbia. Two years ago, similar citizen voting amendments won approval in all eight states where they appeared on ballots. A scrutiny panel has heard Jersey is in a "biodiversity crisis", amid concerns the government is not focusing on the environment enough.
Willie Peggie, government Director of Natural Environment, said the Environment Department needed time and resources for a state of nature report.
Piers Sangan, who runs Sangan Island Conversation, said a biodiversity crisis included more invasive species, fewer native species, and a decline in the ecosystem. He said the government had responsibility to ensure the environment did not "fall by the wayside" because it was a "fundamental part of our island".
The environment minister said policies were being worked on to further protect the environment.
Peggie said any state of nature report should be similar to those in the UK, external, Guernsey, external and Alderney, external.
Sangan said Jersey's biodiversity strategy had been "put on the shelf" since the early 2000s, and the island had lost animals including stoats.
He said there had been a "woeful lack of investment" in ecology.
"The environment is becoming quieter and, as someone who's been looking at this day in, day out for the last 15 years, it's becoming horribly noticeable."
He said several bird species were struggling to increase numbers.
"Even though they're still here, they're still breeding, they're not increasing in number... They are more or less extinct already and are likely to go extinct in the next few years," he said.
Environment Minister Senator Mary Le Hegarat said the countryside needed to be managed properly with a rise in invasive species.
She said: "Everybody needs to manage the countryside together, and we'll do the work and set out the policies and strategies in order to do so."
Government officials are expected to release a state of nature report in 2027, which would inform a new biodiversity strategy.
Joshua and Benjamin Voak work for the Jersey Grazing Project, which uses cows and sheep to improve and restore habitats.
Joshua Voak said it was concerning the environment had not been discussed much in the summer's election as "there are so many economic advantages to having a healthy environment".
Benjamin said biodiversity was "super important" for the island's air and water quality and the retention of habitats.
'Caution' needed over spending
Concerns around biodiversity come as questions have been raised about the government's commitment to the environment.
Deputy Hilary Jeune, who chairs the environment scrutiny panel, said ministers' draft Common Strategic Policy, external did not take the natural environment into account.
The panel worked with Le Hegarat on an amendment to address that, external.
Jeune said biodiversity needed to be "front and centre".
Professor Liz Bentley was part of the Jersey Climate Council, which suggested Jersey need to spend Â£10m per year to reach net zero by 2050, rather than the Â£4m in the Climate Emergency Fund.
She said the council recognised the financial pressure on the government, but delayed action to tackle climate change would cost more in the long-term.
"We need to consider it over decades, not over a four year budget... It's about that long-term investment."
Le Hegarat said ministers needed to be "very cautious" about spending.
She could not say how much it would cost to reach net zero by 2050, but thought investing the money in the fund was a good way forward.

Olympian Ciara Mageean has been described as a "truly remarkable, immensely talented and inspirational human being" in a tribute read out at her funeral.
Hundreds of people have paid their respects to the runner at her funeral on Tuesday.
The former European champion and two-time Olympic runner died on Sunday after she was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer.
Among those in attendance at the funeral in Portaferry, County Down, were Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill, as well as fellow Olympian Rhys McClenaghan and 1972 gold medallist Lady Mary Peters.
Mageean's funeral cortege was given a guard of honour by Portaferry GAC and her former school, Assumption Grammar in Ballynahinch.
Her death comes less than three weeks after her marriage to her long-term partner Thomas Moran.
Mourners began arriving at around midday for the 2:00 GMT requiem Mass at St Patrick's Church.
Family, friends and those wishing to pay their respects followed the funeral cortege the short distance along the Ballyphilip Road from Mageean's family home to the church.
Others in attendance included representatives for Irish President Catherine Connolly and the Irish Government, Social Democratic and Labour Party leader Claire Hanna, GAA President Jarlath Burns and former boxer Paddy Barnes.
The Mass booklet included an image of Mageean's greatest achievement on the track, the moment she crossed the line at the 2024 European Championships.
In his homily, Father Martin Kelly, who knew Mageean from her childhood, spoke of her accomplishments, her love for her husband and the joy and pride she had brought to her hometown.
Kelly recalled visiting her in hospice shortly before her death, when she suggested they go for a walk.
Despite her illness, Mageean noticed he was struggling and offered to link arms with him.
"On the way down, she knew I was struggling and she said, 'Let me link you'," he told mourners.
"One of my happiest moments and memories is that of Ciara Mageean linking my arm as we walked back to her room."
The athlete represented Ireland at the 2016 and 2020 Olympics and won gold in the 1500m at the European Athletics Championships in Rome in 2024.
She also represented Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Games, winning silver in Birmingham in 2022.
What are bowel cancer symptoms?
Noticing blood in your poo - which may appear black or dark red in the toilet bowl - can be a sign of bowel cancer.
If there is no other obvious cause for the bleeding, such as piles, the NHS recommends that you ask for an appointment with your GP, external.
The NHS also advises a check-up if you notice changes in your regular toilet habits, such as having to poo more often, or a pattern of diarrhoea or constipation.
Abdominal pain or lumps, stomach bloating and unexplained weight loss are also among symptoms which should lead to a bowel cancer test.
Bowel cancer can also cause anaemia, the features of which include extreme tiredness and shortness of breath.
The earlier bowel cancer is detected, the easier it is to treat.

67cb3704ebeb.text: By — Sophie Austin, Associated Press Sophie Austin, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/california-voters-consider-proposition-to-tax-billionaires-wealth Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter California voters consider proposition to tax billionaires' wealth Politics Nov 3, 2026 12:04 PM EST 2026 ELECTION COVERAGE: Watch Live | Poll Closing Times | All Live Results | Live Updates | Live Fact Check SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — California could become the first state in the nation to tax the net worth of billionaires Tuesday under a ballot measure that has divided liberal leaders nationally and triggered one of the most expensive ballot fights in state history as the ultra-rich scramble to figure out whether they would pay the tax or flee. Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion, with most of the revenue dedicated to replacing federal funding cuts to healthcare. Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders has framed the proposal as a monumental step toward reining in deep wealth inequality by ensuring the ultra-rich pay their fair share. But Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom warns it would prompt the state's wealthiest to move out of California and take their tax money with them. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News The "no" side has raised roughly 10 times as much as the "yes" side, thanks in large part to tech moguls and venture capitalists, who have poured millions into a political action committee fighting the measure. Billionaires are already bracing for its approval. Some of them, including Google co-founders Sergey Brin and Larry Page, started cutting ties with the state after the measure was unveiled. Mark Zuckerberg said he would stay in California for eight years and made a deal with Meta that would help him pay the tax without losing his ownership stake in the company. Backers of the proposed tax, led by the powerful labor union SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, say it's needed to help the state backfill the federal funding cuts. The union estimates the state will lose $100 billion in federal healthcare funding over five years. "It's time to collect those taxes so we can ensure that our healthcare system is still safe," said Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions. But some traditional Democratic allies, including Planned Parenthood and the California Teachers Association, are part of a coalition opposing it. They're concerned about how the tax revenue would be divvied up and about the potential impact on the state's budget if there's a mass exodus of wealthy taxpayers. California's budget relies heavily on the income tax of the state's richest residents. Californians are divided on the measure. READ MORE: What to look for on Election Day as questions loom over Trump Likely voters were slightly more likely to oppose the measure than support it in a poll conducted in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California, with 52% saying they would vote "no" and 46% saying they would vote "yes." That's an apparent shift from a PPIC survey conducted in early September, when 52% of likely voters said they'd vote for the tax and 46% said they'd vote against it. Robert Swonger, an auto glass technician living near Sacramento who's politically independent, said he planned to vote against it. "Obviously, I would like billionaires not to have as much money as they do," he said. "But I don't believe taxing them out of existence is going to work." Anthony Serrano, a Democrat living in Folsom who works for Kaiser Permanente, one of the nation's largest not-for-profit healthcare plans, said he was leaning toward voting for the tax because he tends to support "anything that is a positive for healthcare." Even if the measure wins approval from a majority of voters, it would be blocked from taking effect if at least one of two measures designed to nullify it, which are also on this year's ballot, passes and receives more "yes" votes. The proposals, which are backed by the political action committee Building a Better California, include a ban on new taxes on financial assets and other personal property, a category that excludes real estate. The committee has raised more than $333 million, about 30% of it from Brin. Progressive politicians, including Sanders and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, have long supported a federal wealth tax. Newsom says a California wealth tax would disadvantage the state, but he supports a national minimum tax on anyone with a net worth above $100 million. Days before Sanders held rallies in California cities last month urging voters to support the state measure, Newsom told reporters that the senator's focus on wealth inequality was "spot-on." But he said that "on this issue, we fundamentally disagree." Even if the proposed billionaire tax fails in California, the battle over the measure ignited a crucial dialogue on the issue, Gonzalez said. "We are taking a step forward, and we are showing other states that you can look them in the eye — you can look these billionaires in the eye — and take them on," she said. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Sophie Austin, Associated Press Sophie Austin, Associated Press

Hi, I’m Kate Waxman, and this is my first edition of Today’s Climate. I’m taking this newsletter over from my colleague Kiley Price, whom I admire for her sharp coverage. I’m a Florida native and was a fellow at Inside Climate News this summer, where I covered climate and environmental justice in my home state. That meant following fights over AI data centers, the homes least prepared for the super El Niño and water quality aid. Across all of that reporting, climate change kept showing up in power bills, insurance premiums and hurricane recovery, but rarely by name. That gap is what this week’s edition is about.
Many candidates in this year’s midterm elections have faced a dilemma heavily romanticized in literature and cinema: “Is it better to speak, or to die?” The choice between speaking up or letting silence take over has a literal, existential meaning when applied to “climate hushing.” Candidates have opted not to discuss climate change in order to protect themselves from political backlash or polarization.
The case for hushing: The logic for this is simple—talk about what voters say they care about the most. In the Environmental Voter Project’s survey of battleground voters, 66 percent ranked cost of living among their top issues, while 16 percent said the same of climate change and pollution. (You can hear more on this survey and climate hushing in the latest episode of our Inside Climate podcast.) Even a University of California, Santa Barbara, team that set out to test the hushers’ claims conceded the point on priorities: Climate ranked 12th of 15 issues. Strategists also argue the word “climate” itself is a liability. Democratic pollster Jonathan Voss told E&E News that “many Republican voters have been conditioned to feel a certain way” when they hear the word.
At a rally against a data center this summer in my home state of Florida, nobody I spoke with used the word “climate.” They talked about water, noise and their power bills. And continuing with the theme, my colleagues Claire Barber and Marianne Lavelle reported on a paper from the Searchlight Institute with a perplexing title: “The First Rule About Solving Climate Change: Don’t Say Climate Change.”
Candidates have listened. My colleague Peter Aldhous found that mentions of climate change in Democrats’ congressional press releases plummeted after 2025, giving way to energy affordability once the Iran war sent oil prices soaring. Faced with the choice to speak or hush, Syracuse University geographer Matthew Huber chose hush. For now, he wrote in The New York Times this spring, “it might be better to say nothing at all.”
The case for speaking: Despite these claims, many voters have said they want to hear more. Likely voters in eight Senate battleground states want politicians to talk more about climate and pollution, not less, by 59 percent to 17 percent, according to the Environmental Voter Project. Last week, I reported on a poll that showed that Florida likely voters chose protecting the environment over economic growth 61 percent to 26 percent. Registered Republicans agreed, 48 percent to 35 percent, and the pollster, Sean Freeder, called it “a blowout.”
Yet in the state’s Senate race, that sentiment isn’t coming through as directly as you might imagine. Rather, it’s showing up in fights over data centers, power bills and hurricane recovery. These all connect back to climate change, but people aren’t talking about that. As Sara Peach writes at Yale Climate Connections, voters take their cues from leaders. When candidates mirror the polls and stay quiet, it can create “a vicious cycle,” teaching the public the issue matters less than it does.
On one hand, it’s hard to blame the candidates for wanting to protect their political image. On the other hand, choosing silence structurally ensures the very outcome we are trying to avoid. Did candidates in your area mention climate change by name? Email me to share your observations.
The Latest on Earth
- Yerevan: The United Nations biodiversity summit, COP17, closed Saturday with the “Yerevan Pathway,” a pledge to speed up cuts to nature-harming subsidies and strengthen national plans for oceans and freshwater, but its fund for paying Indigenous and local communities left nearly empty. The Guardian’s verdict: The agreements need to be fast-tracked to make a real difference.
- Atmosphere: A new report shows that the Trump administration’s cuts to satellite weather forecasting will set the country back by a decade, according to CNN. The cuts began in spring 2025, when the administration directed NOAA to scale back its next generation of weather satellites, dropping planned instruments that would have tracked air quality, wildfire smoke and monitored water quality.
- Mediterranean: The European Union has blocked an extension of the Mediterranean deep-sea trawling ban. According to Oceanographic Magazine, this decision leaves deep-sea habitats vulnerable to the impacts of fishing.

If you want to know where climate went this election season, ask Marianne Lavelle. ICN’s Washington bureau chief has been covering national elections for over 30 years, and she reported last week that candidates and climate advocates alike have traded talk of climate risk for issues that are closer to home, like data centers and sky-high energy bills. I asked her whether climate has really gone quiet, or just changed its name.

bc2789664f14.text: Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas defeated former GOP Sen. John Sununu in the New Hampshire Senate race, AP projects. Why it matters: Pappas' victory keeps the seat in Democratic hands and could boost the party's chances of taking control of the Senate. Driving the news: Pappas led Sununu 61% to 38% with 20% of the votes counted. He'll replace retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) in January. Catch up quick: Republicans saw New Hampshire as a top pickup opportunity, with Senate Majority Leader John Thune campaigning for Sununu in the competitive race, despite polls showing Pappas ahead. Most polls compiled by the New York Times in the weeks before Election Day showed the Democratic Pappas leading Sununu by 5 to 8 percentage points. Zoom in: Although President Trump endorsed him, Sununu has shown daylight with the president, criticizing his trade war with Canada and his so-called anti-weaponization fund — and he backed Trump's primary opponents in 2016 and 2024. Still, prominent New Hampshire Republicans — including Don Bolduc , the Trump -endorsed 2022 Senate nominee — endorsed Pappas in mid-October, accusing Sununu of being too beholden to the president. Between the lines: Republicans welcomed Sununu's entry into the race because of his family's long ties to New Hampshire politics. Sununu served in the Senate from 2003 to 2009 before losing to Shaheen in 2008. His brother Chris served as governor for eight years. Senate GOP Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) posted on X in October 2025 that Sununu's decision to run catapulted New Hampshire to "a top-tier U.S. Senate race." The bottom line: Pappas' win reflects a preference New Hampshire voters expressed in pre-election polling : They wanted a check on Trump's power. Price, Associated Press By — Samy Magdy, Associated Press Samy Magdy, Associated Press By — Elena Becatoros, Associated Press Elena Becatoros, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/u-s-strikes-strait-of-hormuz-hours-before-tuesday-midterms Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter U.S. strikes Strait of Hormuz hours before Tuesday midterms World Nov 3, 2026 8:15 PM EST What appeared to be a limited strike by the United States on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz hours before Tuesday's midterm U.S. elections is raising questions about what's coming next. For weeks now, U.S. President Donald Trump has said he was considering launching a new wave of strikes on Iran after the elections. Just days ago, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pressed Trump for renewed military action, according to two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter. The Middle East and beyond have been on edge about the prospects of the U.S. resuming full-scale operations against Iran for the first time in almost two months. READ MORE: Iran says 7 oil tankers damaged in Strait of Hormuz, and other Middle East news Talks aimed at avoiding that are ongoing, and other American allies in the region are pressuring the U.S. not to resume the more than 8-month-old war that's rattled the global economy and wreaked havoc on Iran. Trump has alternated between threatening major strikes and pushing for a deal with Iran. The unpopular war and the resulting impact on U.S. gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for his Republican Party as it tries to keep control of Congress. Strikes were targeted in Strait of Hormuz Iranian state media reported explosions being heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas. A U.S. official, who wasn't authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said Monday that the strikes targeted Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against the U.S. in the strait. Iran official says US must resolve its conditions The head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council said Tuesday that the U.S. response to Tehran's demands to end the war was not convincing. Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei wrote on social media that the strait won't reopen until the U.S. addresses Iran's conditions. Iran has offered to reopen the strait, and resume talks on its nuclear program if the U.S. lifts its naval blockade on Iranian ports, waives sanctions on Iranian oil sales, and observes a ceasefire including in Lebanon. Vice President Vance buoyed hopes for a negotiated settlement Back-channel negotiations have been playing out as Israel and some Middle East allies lobby Trump. Speaking before the U.S. official confirmed strikes, U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Monday that he and Trump "both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement." The Trump administration was last known to have carried out attacks in early September. But thousands of U.S. troops remain in the waters off Iran to maintain a naval blockade aimed at preventing tankers carrying Iranian oil from reaching the global market. Another aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are also on their way to the Middle East. READ MORE: Iran war renews concerns about lasting toll of traumatic brain injuries to American troops Netanyahu pushed for another wave of strikes on Iran after the U.S. elections during a call with Trump over the weekend, according to two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter. The two officials said diplomatic efforts have made progress and that mediators are trying to advance a framework for Iran to cease its attacks in the strait in return for the U.S. lifting its blockade. The two officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified briefings they had received from American and, in one case, Israeli officials. The third person, who was briefed on the call, was not authorized to comment publicly and also spoke on the condition of anonymity. Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi has called on Iran and the U.S. to engage in dialogue and reach an agreement to resolve their ongoing conflict, warning against further military escalation in the region. Iranians keeping watch on U.S. elections Some people in Tehran were hopeful that the midterm elections would bring a shift in U.S. policies. "The American people need to make a fundamental decision and bring about real change. They need to put an end to the leadership of someone who is so extreme and who runs things through lies, someone who supports Israel, a country that is literally killing children," said 69-year-old Reza Rezaei. READ MORE: How Iran war votes in Congress became a focal point for campaign ad attacks One woman was less optimistic. "It doesn't really make much difference who comes into power," said Raheleh Movahhed, also of Tehran. "The American government and its policies have always had a problem with us. I'm not talking about the American people, mind you. I'm talking about their policies." Iran's chief negotiator says it's up to the US to prevent renewed war Iranian state television quoted the country's chief negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, as saying on Tuesday that Iran had "delivered a firm and rational response to the American side. The ball is now in America's court to prevent war." It was not immediately clear what response he was referring to. Qalibaf also warned that Iran's armed forces remained at the highest level of defensive readiness. "If Washington makes another strategic miscalculation, it should know that this time it will face a new battlefield and will find itself even more desperate than it is today," he said. cd73225ff082.text: By — Brittany Peterson, Associated Press Brittany Peterson, Associated Press By — Savannah Peters, Associated Press Savannah Peters, Associated Press By — Mead Gruver, Associated Press Mead Gruver, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/receding-floodwaters-leave-a-sea-of-mud-and-shattered-homes-in-the-u-s-southwest Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Receding floodwaters leave a sea of mud and shattered homes in the U.S. Southwest Nation Nov 3, 2026 8:06 PM EST 2026 ELECTION COVERAGE: Watch Live | Poll Closing Times | All Live Results | Live Updates | Live Fact Check PAGOSA SPRINGS, Colo. (AP) — Skies began to clear Tuesday, but while floodwaters from almost two weeks of on-and-off heavy rain still inundated parts of the U.S. Southwest, other areas left mud-caked by receding torrents presented homeowners and businessowners with the filthy work of cleanup. Jack Ellis, a retired schoolteacher, surveyed damage along the San Juan River in Pagosa Springs, Colorado, which has suffered through multiple rounds of severe flooding in recent weeks. "This is quite a disaster for everybody, especially in the low-lying areas," Ellis said. "We dig in and dig out, and that's what it's going to take." In all, more than 20 trillion gallons (76 trillion liters) of rain — 10 months of the flow over Niagara Falls — have fallen on the Four Corners states and Nevada in the past two weeks, according to former National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration chief scientist Ryan Maue. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News After rain atop rain, flood risk persists The U.S. Southwest has endured two recent major rounds of storms, with rain falling on ground already saturated from an especially wet fall. One person died in floodwaters, and police suspect a second death was weather-related. Skies were clearing after some rivers crested at levels lower than forecasted overnight, offering a measure of relief to areas that were bracing for more catastrophic flooding, including Shiprock and Farmington in northwestern New Mexico. Devin Neeley, a spokesperson for San Juan County, New Mexico, said major rivers in the area remained above flood stage. "Now it's a waiting game for the waters to recede," Neeley said, adding that the county would likely soon lift evacuation orders impacting at least 20,000 residents and begin to focus on recovery. Flooding in Florida, too, complicates voting The situation wasn't unique to the region. As downpours swamped eastern Florida, at least 20 polling places were changed in at least eight counties after Gov. Ron DeSantis issued an emergency declaration. Flooded areas included Brevard County on the east-central coast, where over 2 feet (61 centimeters) of rain has fallen since Sunday. In Palm Beach County in southeast Florida, over 20 inches (51 centimeters) fell, cutting off access to condominiums and submerging cars in parking places. Some communities in Colorado and Utah, too, had to make alternative Election Day voting plans because of the flooding. Alyssa Gallegos, a contract mail carrier for the U.S. Postal Service, spent Tuesday morning helping get mail-in ballots from mailboxes to the post office in time for a 7 p.m. deadline for counting. "Regardless if we're in a crisis and having a hard time, the world doesn't stop turning," Gallegos said. "They're not gonna wait for us, so we just gotta stay with it." In Rock Point, Arizona, in the Navajo Nation, officials were forced to relocate a polling place because of flooding impacts. Valinda Shirley, vice president of the Rock Point Chapter, the local seat of tribal government, said hundreds of voters are still unable to cast ballots in both the U.S. midterms and the Navajo Nation presidential election because a major bridge closure and washed-out dirt roads have left them stranded on election day. "I have people that are still texting me asking how I can get them out so they can vote," Shirley said Tuesday afternoon. Another blow for Colorado hot-springs tourist town An eighth-generation Pagosa Springs local, Gallegos said her ancestors went through a catastrophic flood in 1911 but no one alive in her family expected anything like it in their lifetimes. She was watching videos of the devastation on social media Monday when she spotted her stepfather's home swept off its foundation by raging floodwaters. Inside, she knew, were old photographs and other treasured possessions from her childhood. "My heart's crushed," Gallegos said. "And it's not just him, it's all the people." Cleanup and repairs could take weeks or more in Pagosa Springs, a tourist town famous for hotels with riverside hot springs. The downtown area remained closed to traffic Tuesday while workers used heavy equipment to clear mud, water and debris from roads. Walkways and bridges collapsed or were heavily damaged. Outside a resort entrance stacked with sandbags, a sign read "Love Pagosa." Basement becomes 'soup bowl' in Durango In Durango, about 60 miles (96.5 kilometers) to the west, Willow Bradner's ranch-style home was surrounded by about 2 feet (60 centimeters) of mud. Nearly 5 feet (1.5 meters) of water from an overflowing creek poured inside at one point. "Our basement became a soup bowl," she said. The basement had been a selling point when she bought the property in 2024. Bradner said she and her husband once asked if they needed flood insurance and were told they were not in a flood zone. They and their teenage daughter had been offered a place to stay through the end of the year. But the loss of their home and uncertainty about the future were overwhelming, Bradner said. "The majority of our savings is in this house," she said. "We have to dig deep, and we have to rebuild." Peters reported from Santa Fe, New Mexico, and Gruver from Fort Collins, Colorado. Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire contributed. A free press is a cornerstone of a health

Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff is projected to have won re-election in Georgia, defeating Republican challenger Mike Collins and pushing the crucial swing state deeper into Democratic control, CBS News reports.
Ossoff, a rising star in the Democratic Party, portrayed his opponent as loyal to a "failed president" and made the rising cost of living a central issue in the campaign. Georgia, a key swing state, voted for Donald Trump in 2024.
Collins had blamed rising cost of living on former President Joe Biden and defended his support for Trump's war in Iran.
With polls suggesting Ossoff held a solid lead in the race, Republicans had diverted resources from Georgia to other contests.
Brian Kemp, Georgia's term-limited Republican governor, was the favoured candidate to run against Ossoff, but he declined.
Political pundits suspected that Kemp had avoided running, wary of Ossoff's rising star power, with rumours swirling that the Democrat could be mulling a run for president in 2028.
Throughout his campaign, Ossoff downplayed such rumours, saying on multiple occasions that he has "zero interest" in a presidential bid.

The first polls have closed in the US midterm elections, which will shape the rest of Donald Trump's presidency. The outcome determines which party - Trump's Republicans or opposition Democrats - controls Congress.
It is possible the results will not be projected for several hours, days or even weeks. Here's what you need to know.
When will we know the results and who controls Congress?
Congress is made up of two parts - the lower chamber, the House of Representatives and the upper chamber, the Senate.
To win a majority in the House, a party needs 218 seats. In the Senate, a party needs 51 seats for an outright majority. But if the upper chamber is split 50-50, the vice-president has a tie-breaking vote, which gives their party control of it.
The first results to come in won't tell us much about the overall result because these races are in places considered safe bets for Republicans (Kentucky and Indiana) or Democrats (Vermont).
Throughout the night, BBC analysts will focus on the competitive races which will give an indication of how well things are going for Trump.
There are several tight Senate contests in the Eastern Time zone - like Ohio, where polls close at 19:30 EST (00:30 GMT) and Maine, where they shut at 20:00 EST (01:00 GMT). These could provide early indications of the electorate's mood.
Some key contests might start to be "called" by US media outlets. They use models to project which way a state has voted, even before the full vote count has been completed.
This happens when they believe a party or a candidate has gained a lead that cannot be beaten. But in some closely-fought states, outlets could take a long time to make their projections.
The overall timing of the result will depend on how tight the races are and which races end up being decisive.
When did we know the results in 2022?
In 2022, Republicans and Democrats were still in a tight race for control of the US Congress on 9 November, a day after the midterms.
While Republicans were favourites to win the House of Representatives, the fight for the Senate remained on a knife-edge.
The full picture took several days. CBS News projected Republicans had secured the 218 seats needed for a majority in the House on 17 November.
Counting in a crucial Senate race in Nevada took four days. The Democrats' narrow victory in the state brought them to 50 seats, allowing them to retain control of the Senate because then Vice-President Kamala Harris held a tie-breaking vote.
Georgia's Senate contest had to be settled by a run-off election because no candidate passed the 50% mark in November.
The results were not available until 7 December, when Democrats won this seat.
What are the key races to watch in 2026?
There are six Senate races deemed to be a toss-up by independent elections analyst Cook Political Report, external - Alaska, Kansas, Iowa, Maine, Ohio and Texas.
Of these, six are currently held by Republicans. The Democrats would need to win three of those seats, plus five classed as likely or leaning Democratic, to hit 51 and take control of the Senate.
Polls have suggested Democrats have a chance in Texas where former teacher James Talarico could become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988 if he defeats Ken Paxton, the current state attorney general and close Trump ally.
Democrats also need to keep hold of their seat in Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing political outsider, is up against Republican rival Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent in a closely-observed race. The state was initially classified as a "toss-up" by Cook Political Report, but was reclassified as "leans Democrat" the day before the vote.
The current Republican majority in the House, the lower chamber, is thin. They have 218 representatives, plus one independent who votes with them.
Some of the most closely-watched races in the House are in east-coast states, according to the Cook Political Report. These include New York's 17th District, Pennsylvania's 8th District and Virginia's 1st District.
When do polls close?
The results of a voter poll will be released at 17:00 EST (22:00 GMT), which will give us an indication of the issues at the forefront of voters' minds.
Then, at 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT), the first polls close in Kentucky and Indiana. After that, all eyes will be focused on the key battleground states:
- 19:30 EST (00:30 GMT) - Polls close in Ohio, where Republican Senator Jon Husted finds himself neck-and-neck with Democrat Sherrod Brown. Results from this state could give us a clue as to how the night might unfold
- 20:00 EST (01:00 GMT) - Voting ends in the tight Senate race in Maine between Republican Senator Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson and in most of Kansas and Texas
- 21:00 EST (02:00 GMT) - Polls close in Iowa, as well as in Kansas and Texas. In the hours that follow, a picture might start to emerge of whether things are going to plan for the Republicans - or the Democrats
- 01:00 EST (06:00 GMT) - Voting ends in Alaska, the last battleground state. A close Senate race between Democrat Mary Peltola and incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan has been making headlines over the inclusion of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot
How does the vote-counting work?
Each state administers its own elections and has its own rules for counting and processing votes.
Some states, like Florida, process early and mail ballots prior to election day, while others only begin tabulating on 3 November.
Local election officials verify, process and count individual votes, in a process known as canvassing.
Most states require a post-election audit that involves a manual count of ballots checked against machine totals, although rules vary across the country. Full hand counts are generally reserved for recounts.

0d249f7629f5.text: By — Martha Bellisle, Associated Press Martha Bellisle, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/authorities-release-911-call-from-the-man-who-killed-a-shooter-inside-an-oregon-elementary-school Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Authorities release 911 call from the man who killed a shooter inside an Oregon elementary school Nation Nov 3, 2026 7:32 PM EST 2026 ELECTION COVERAGE: Watch Live | Poll Closing Times | All Live Results | Live Updates | Live Fact Check A frantic 911 call from the man who fatally shot a 16-year-old shooter who killed four people at an Oregon elementary school last month was released Tuesday to The Associated Press through a public records request. In a tense call lasting a little more than a minute, Kaylub Giamanco told the 911 operator there's "someone with a gun" at the school his daughter attends. "I have a gun and I will shoot them right now," said Giamanco, who was driving home for lunch and saw the shooter at Silver Rail Elementary School. WATCH: Oregon school shooter attacked special education classroom, police say The operator implores him "don't do anything, let me get an officer there." They talk over each other and Giamanco sounds increasingly frustrated by the exchange. "I'm about to go kill this kid," he said. A few seconds later he says the shooter is entering the building. The operator asks if the shooter is firing and Giamanco says yes. The operator tries to get more information but the call ends. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News A 16-year-old had shot his way through locked doors to get into the school in Bend, Oregon, on Oct. 15, killing three children — ages 5, 8, and 11 — and a teacher in a special needs classroom. Another student was critically injured and a teacher was injured and hospitalized. A teacher tried to stop the shooter, Griffin J. John II, before Giamanco entered the school through an open window, opened the door of the classroom and fired his gun, dropping the shooter to the floor. Teacher tried to stop shooter before father arrived As Giamanco was racing toward the building, a teacher inside the school confronted the shooter in an effort to stop his progress. She threw her phone at the attacker, tackled him and wrestled with him for control of the weapon. Giamanco's arrival stopped the struggle. He said the teacher was "a real true hero" because her actions gave him an opening to shoot the attacker. The teacher, a certified learning specialist, had not been previously identified, but last week, Bend-La Pine Schools identified her as Cassidy Schutz and shared her statement. She said there were no words to describe the sadness she feels following the shooting. "This is not a story. This is a horrific and heartbreaking tragedy, and it is our real lives," Schutz wrote. "My thoughts are with those who were lost, their families, those who were hurt, and those who were there that day. My heart is with you." Schutz said her focus is on the families, the school "and my own healing." A second teacher in the classroom, Becky Drury, previously released a statement saying she never had a chance to shelter the children inside. She had tried to shut the door behind her, but the shooter was already there. "Before I could do anything more, he shot me at close range and I fell to the ground," Drury said. She was shot in her left hand and right arm. Unable to get up, she said she pretended to be dead in the hopes he would not shoot her again. Father said he was the 'last line of defense' Giamanco said in a Oregon Public Broadcasting interview that he regrets not arriving soon enough to save everyone who was killed and injured. After imploring the 911 operator to send help, Giamanco climbed into the school through a window and peeked into a nearby classroom. He saw Schutz and the shooter in profile, giving him an open shot. "I felt like I was the last line of defense between him and the rest of the children," Giamanco said. He stepped into the room and fired his gun. The teacher ran from the room and the shooter reached for his shotgun. "I looked at him and I shot him two more times to make sure that he couldn't move, because I was afraid of him shooting anybody else," he said. "If I wasn't there, I just don't know what would have happened." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. ee56edd11d38.text: By — James Brooks, Associated Press James Brooks, Associated Press By — Stefanie Dazio, Associated Press Stefanie Dazio, Associated Press By — Kostya Manenkov, Associated Press Kostya Manenkov, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/greenland-approves-trilateral-deal-with-denmark-and-u-s-following-pressure-from-trump Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Greenland approves trilateral deal with Denmark and U.S. following pressure from Trump World Nov 3, 2026 7:21 PM EST ILULISSAT, Greenland (AP) — Greenlandic lawmakers on Tuesday voted to approve an agreement between the Arctic island, Denmark and the United States to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic after months of pressure by U.S. President Donald Trump seeking to control the semiautonomous territory of a NATO ally. The trilateral deal paves the way for more U.S. bases in Greenland and eases tensions over Trump's repeated calls for the vast island to become part of the United States. The agreement's goal is to bolster the U.S. military presence on Greenland but keep the self-governing island under Danish control. It would still apply if Greenland eventually chooses independence. WATCH: What's in the Greenland agreement between U.S. and Denmark Greenlandic lawmakers voted 16-0 for the agreement, with seven abstentions, in the capital city of Nuuk. Some 570 kilometers (350 miles) north of Nuuk, Nukaaka Lund-Mathaeussen hoped that the deal's approval means the Trump administration "got what they wanted." "Hopefully after this we won't be getting underhanded threats from the American government," the 28-year-old Ilulissat resident told The Associated Press in Ilulissat after the vote. William Tukula, a 34-year-old chef in Ilulissat, said he'd seen posts on Facebook from older Greenlanders who were "a little bit scared about Trump and soldiers." The U.S. president had previously said he would not rule out the use of military force to seize control of Greenland because he declared U.S. control of it to be vital to American national security, though he also underlined his support for Greenlanders determining their own future. He later backed down from any threat. READ MORE: Why Trump wants Greenland The White House had no immediate comment on the vote, but the State Department said it "marks another major victory for American national security." "This administration is securing America's strategic interests in the Arctic, strengthening our national defense and ensuring this critical region remains free of adversarial threats," it said in a post on X. Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen signed the security agreement in September on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York. Nielsen, in a post on Facebook after Tuesday's vote, said Greenlanders stood united over the last few months despite the geopolitical tensions to show the world that the island decides its own fate. "We must be able to cooperate with other countries," he wrote, adding that the cooperation must respect "our people, our country and our rights." He added: "Greenland is our country. Greenland will always be our country." WATCH: Denmark and Greenland say sovereignty is not negotiable after Trump's meeting with Rutte Danish lawmakers are set to debate it later this month. The deal will "enter into force" once the "necessary parliamentary processes of the Kingdom of Denmark, in conjunction with Greenland, have been completed." Despite the Greenland parliament's approval, Lund-Mathaeussen said some residents on the island felt worried and powerless. "What can a regular guy like me do about the diplomatic engine?" the municipality worker said. "It's a big machine, and being a small person here in Greenland — it's hard to have any influences on those things." Nukaaraq Thomsen, a 43-year-old incineration plant worker from Ilulissat, said the trilateral deal still won't benefit Greenlanders. "My opinion is it's safe for Greenland. But not for the people — only for the land," Thomsen told the AP on Tuesday. In expanding its military presence on the island, the agreement says Washington is to award contracts for goods and services related to setting up, maintaining or dismantling such bases "to Greenlandic sources to the maximum extent possible." But Lars Erik Gabrielsen, mayor of Avannaata Municipality, is not convinced that Greenlanders will see any advantages. "It's a good deal for Denmark, NATO. Not a good deal for us," he said. "There are no benefits, no money to our society. Zero." Dazio reported from Berlin and Manenkov reported from Tallinn, Estonia. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy.
