5dc088d3b5b4.text: Republicans tried to save their House majority with a bold wave of mid-cycle redistricting. It failed in spectacular fashion on Tuesday. Why it matters: Republicans not only fell short of winning seats in several districts they redrew to favor their candidates, they put some GOP incumbents in danger of losing by spreading their support thin. Rep. Scott DesJarlais (R-Tenn.), who has mostly won landslide reelections since entering Congress in 2010, trailed his Democratic opponent by 200 votes, according to the Tennessee secretary of state's unofficial final results . Republican state legislators carved up his district in an effort to shore up neighboring Republicans, making his district nearly 20 percentage points less GOP-leaning. State of play: While Republicans succeeded in picking up a Democratic district in Tennessee to make up for that loss, they largely failed to pick up the seats they tried to make reliably Republican in other states. Florida: Republicans are set to go 0-for-4 in redistricted seats, failing to unseat Democratic Reps. Darren Soto, Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz, or capture a new seat that Democrat Pia Dandiya won. Texas: Republicans are set to narrowly win just one of the five districts they redrew heavily in their favor, with Democrats easily hanging onto several Rio Grande Valley and San Antonio-area seats. Ohio: Democratic Reps. Greg Landsman and Marcy Kaptur held on despite Republicans drawing them into more hostile territory. Alabama: Democratic Rep. Shomari Figures is also set for a comfortable win in a district Republicans had planned to fall into their hands. Louisiana: The district of retiring Democrat Rep. Cleo Fields, which Republicans made significantly more GOP-leaning will go to a December runoff between Democrat Patricia Moore and Republican Gabe Firment. One of the most stunning results of the night was Democrats' multiple apparent victories in North Carolina, where House candidates were boosted by Sen-elect Roy Cooper's strong performance at the top of the ballot. Democrats are on track to flip several seats that were rated as likely or even solidly Republican by Cook Political Report, likely unseating Republican Reps. Addison McDowell, Brad Knott and Tim Moore. They are also likely to unseat Rep. Richard Hudson, the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee. Virginia Foxx, who chairs the House Rules Committee, is behind by about 100 votes. In all, the state's House delegation could go from a 10-4 Republican majority to a 9-5 Democratic one. Between the lines: The North Carolina result is the product of a brutal 2024 gerrymander in which GOP state legislators diluted most solidly Republican districts to draw out several House Democrats. They redistricted again last year, only to put Democratic Rep. Don Davis in more hostile territory. GOP Rep. Greg Murphy — whose district was packed with more Democratic voters to make Davis' seat redder — barely hung on Tuesday night. Former Democratic Rep. Kathy Manning, who was one of the Democrats drawn out in 2024, told Axios that Tuesday's result was "absolutely" a result of GOP redistricting backfiring. The bottom line: Republicans "tried to break the laws and go against these norms in your massive authoritarian power grab," DNC vice chair Shasti Conrad told Axios. "How did that turn out?"

Delhi is once again battling worsening air pollution as the onset of winter brings a familiar deterioration in air quality to India's capital.
The city's air quality index (AQI) - which measures PM2.5, fine particulate matter that can clog lungs - has crossed 300, entering the "very poor" category and raising health concerns for millions of residents.
Breathing such polluted air over prolonged periods can cause respiratory problems and worsen existing illnesses, with children and older people particularly vulnerable.
Authorities have responded by invoking Stage II of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP), introducing measures to curb dust, vehicle emissions and other sources of pollution.
GRAP is a set of emergency measures that become progressively stricter as pollution levels rise. The latest restrictions include more intensive road cleaning, higher parking charges to discourage private vehicle use and increased public transport services. Delhi Metro has introduced 20 additional weekday train trips, while authorities have been directed to stagger government office timings to ease traffic congestion.
Officials said the measures were introduced after forecasts suggested air quality would remain very poor over the coming days.
Delhi and neighbouring parts of northern India grapple with hazardous air every winter, particularly around Diwali, one of India's biggest festivals, which is just days away.
The festival is celebrated with lights, lamps and fireworks, which often worsen the city's already poor air quality by releasing fine particles and harmful gases into the atmosphere.
The annual pollution crisis is driven by a combination of factors, including vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions, falling temperatures, low wind speeds and the burning of crop stubble in neighbouring states.
The sharp rise in pollution follows an unusually clean October, when Delhi recorded its lowest average AQI for the month in eight years.
Experts have attributed the sudden deterioration to falling temperatures, slow winds and an increase in crop-residue burning in the neighbouring states of Punjab and Haryana.
A recent storm had brought rain and stronger winds, helping clear the air. But as the weather settled, northwesterly winds returned, carrying smoke from burning fields towards the capital.
India's pollution watchdog classifies AQI readings between 301 and 400 as "very poor", while anything above 400 is considered "severe". On Wednesday morning, Delhi's AQI stood at 377.
The index takes into account eight major pollutants, including PM2.5 - tiny particles about 30 times smaller than the width of a human hair that can penetrate deep into the lungs.
With Diwali just days away, there are concerns that fireworks could push pollution levels even higher.
Last year, Delhi woke up to a toxic haze the morning after the festival, despite a court directive to use less-polluting firecrackers.
Authorities have imposed restrictions on firecrackers over the years, including outright bans on their manufacture, sale and use, but enforcing them has proved difficult.
On Monday, India's Supreme Court allowed the manufacture, sale and use of certified green firecrackers in Delhi and neighbouring areas for a limited period.
It said the crackers could be set off only between 06:00 and 07:00 local time (00:30-01:30 GMT) and between 20:00 and 22:00 (14:30-16:30 GMT) on 7 and 8 November, during the Diwali weekend.
The court also banned fireworks within 300m of hospitals, care homes, schools and other designated silence zones.
Green firecrackers use modified chemical formulations designed to produce fewer emissions than conventional fireworks. They must carry QR codes that allow buyers and authorities to verify details of their manufacturer and certification.
But ensuring that only approved firecrackers are sold remains a major challenge.
In its latest order, the Supreme Court acknowledged that conventional firecrackers had continued to be sold as green alternatives, even when a complete ban was in place.
It has directed police to patrol designated sales areas, carry out random QR-code checks and seize illegal firecrackers.
During particularly severe pollution episodes, Delhi authorities have also introduced measures such as hybrid schooling, work-from-home arrangements and restrictions on certain vehicles.
The problem is not confined to the capital. Mumbai, India's financial hub, has also recorded elevated pollution levels over the past month, despite benefiting from coastal winds that typically help disperse pollutants.
On 24 October, Mumbai's AQI had reached 322, placing it in the "very poor" category. The spike was attributed to a combination of low wind speeds, construction dust, garbage burning, firecracker emissions and pollutants carried from neighbouring regions.
The city's air quality has improved in recent days - and it recorded an AQI of 89, classified as "satisfactory", on Wednesday. Neighbouring Navi Mumbai recorded a "moderate" AQI of 118.
The improvement follows nearly two weeks of smoggy conditions, with residents sharing photos and videos of the haze on social media.

1fe4ded327c3.text: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's closely watched U.S. Senate race, the Associated Press projected. He will become the nation's first Muslim senator. Why it matters: El-Sayed's win shows how an unapologetically progressive candidate can win in a battleground state President Trump carried just two years ago. The two candidates competed for the seat vacated by retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, with Republicans hoping to flip a seat Democrats have held for decades. But the GOP failed in its endeavor — and already lost its Senate majority. The race took a stunning turn in its final days, when Democratic U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost the August primary to El-Sayed, endorsed Rogers . The move sparked furious backlash from Democrats and prompted several of Stevens' staffers, including her chief of staff, to resign. The big picture: El-Sayed, a former Detroit health director, ran on a progressive platform centered on Medicare for All, taxing billionaires and reducing corporate influence in politics. His victory comes after a contentious Democratic primary and a bitter general election campaign that featured personal attacks over his background, medical credentials and Muslim faith. Rogers, a former congressman and FBI agent who narrowly lost a 2024 Senate bid, sought to portray El-Sayed as too extreme for Michigan . El-Sayed cast Rogers as a Washington insider aligned with Trump. Trump himself escalated the attacks in the final stretch of the race, questioning El-Sayed's loyalty to the U.S. and making unsubstantiated allegations of extremist ties. El-Sayed rejected the accusations. Between the lines: El-Sayed's win offers progressives a powerful new argument in the Democratic Party's debate over how to win back voters. Zoom out: Both candidates put affordability at the center of their campaigns but offered sharply different solutions. El-Sayed called for universal health care, tackling medical debt and higher taxes on billionaire wealth. Rogers emphasized tax cuts, expanding domestic manufacturing and more transparent health care prices. He also campaigned on stronger border security and immigration enforcement. What's next: El-Sayed will arrive in Washington with an ambitious progressive agenda — but turning campaign promises into legislation will be a different challenge. His signature Medicare for All proposal faces steep political obstacles, even with Democrats winning control of the Senate. His victory also gives progressives a new national figure as Democrats begin looking toward the 2028 presidential election.

Republican South Carolina Senate candidate Darline Graham is projected to have lost her race, handing Democrats their first victory in the state for 28 years.
Democrat Annie Andrews, a former paediatrician, was on course to pull off a stunning upset in Tuesday's midterm elections, according to the BBC's US partner CBS.
Graham was appointed to fill the seat in July after the sudden death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, a move that won support from President Donald Trump.
A political newcomer, she conceded during the primary that she was "not that informed on national security".
Trump won the state by 18 points in 2024.
During her primary campaign, Graham acknowledged her lack of political experience, particularly after stumbling on a foreign policy question during a recent debate.
Asked about the US stance towards Taiwan, Graham had said: "National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military."
Her brother, Lindsey Graham, was elected to the Senate in 2002 and was one of Washington's most influential voices on foreign policy, often pushing for US military intervention overseas.

3b2fc181e3bd.text: In red states and blue, Republicans suffered losses on a scale even Democrats would never have dared to dream about 24 hours ago. Why it matters: Democrats worried that polls showing a blue wave were overestimating the party's strength. It turned out polls underestimated the size of the Democratic romp — by a lot. The margins Democrats racked up in red states were stunning: Georgia: Sen. Jon Ossoff won reelection by nearly 18 percentage points. North Carolina: Former Gov. Roy Cooper won his Senate race by roughly 19 points. Texas: State Rep. James Talarico cruised to victory by approximately 12 points. These weren't nail-biters in competitive states. They were landslides in states President Trump carried just two years ago. 1. The Texas trifecta Democrats won the Texas House, Senate and governor's mansion, giving the party unified control of state government for the first time since 1995. The sweep came alongside Talarico's double-digit victory in the U.S. Senate race. Texas, long the GOP's biggest electoral stronghold, delivered Democrats victories up and down the ballot. 2. North Carolina was a bloodbath The man in charge of steering House Republicans to victory — Rep. Richard Hudson, chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee — lost his own seat. He'll join the ranks of other defeated party leaders — Speaker Tom Foley in 1994 and Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee Chair Sean Patrick Maloney in 2022 — who spent so much time trying to build a majority that they failed to protect themselves. The carnage extended across the state. North Carolina's congressional delegation could shift from 10 Republicans and four Democrats to five Republicans and nine Democrats. 3. The ridiculously cheap wins Democrats are leading in districts that received little or no outside spending from the DCCC or House Majority PAC, the party's main House super PAC, according to AdImpact. In North Carolina's 6th, 9th and 13th districts, Missouri's 2nd and Tennessee's 4th, Democratic candidates are on track to win despite receiving little financial support from national Democratic groups. North Carolina's 6th: Democrat Cyril Jefferson didn't spend a dime on advertising, according to AdImpact. Tennessee's 4th: Democrat Victoria Broderick spent just $90,000 on her entire campaign as of Oct. 14, according to her FEC filing. AdImpact has no record of any paid TV advertising. 4. Hispanic voters swung back in South Texas Democrats are poised to control three congressional seats in the Rio Grande Valley that President Trump carried in 2024 — and the margins weren't even close. Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) was leading Republican Tano Tijerina, 66% to 30%. Democrat Bobby Pulido was leading Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz, 62% to 38%. Rep. Vicente Gonzalez (D-Texas) was leading Republican Eric Flores, 56% to 40%. The results were a dramatic reversal in a region where Republicans had made significant gains with Hispanic voters during the Trump era. 5. Democrats won deep in Trump country Democrats didn't just flip swing districts — they broke through in some of the reddest corners of the House map. In Tennessee's 4th Congressional District, which Trump carried by 24 points, Broderick was leading Rep. Scott DesJarlais by roughly 200 votes. Two years ago, Broderick received just 26.8% of the vote to DesJarlais' 70%. The bottom line: The wave didn't discriminate. It washed away good candidates and bad, senators, governors and seasoned Republicans alike.

Democrat Amy Acton has defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy to win the Ohio governorship in a bitterly contested race.
With the projected victory, Acton becomes the first Democrat and the first ever woman to win the Ohio governor's race in two decades.
Ohio, a key battleground for much of the 2000s, has voted for Republican Donald Trump in the last three presidential elections, including by 11 points in 2024.
But the gubernatorial race, where voter frustration over the economy and the cost of living was the central theme, took an unexpected turn after the Ramaswamy campaign released a deeply personal attack ad featuring Acton's estranged mother.
In the ad, Acton's mother Donna Arthur said her daughter "lied her entire life". It did not mention that Arthur's husband was charged with raping Acton when she was a child.
The controversial advert loomed over the last weeks of the race. It was criticised by former South Carolina Governor Republican Nikki Haley, while Ohio's current Republican Governor Mike DeWine called it "deeply troubling".
However, some defended it, including President Donald Trump and Vice-President JD Vance.
Trump described it as "powerful" and encouraged Ramaswamy to keep it running, while Vance, the state's former senator, said he would like fellow Republicans to stop "whining" about the ad and that he was "a little bit disgusted" by criticism from members of his own party.
Ramaswamy said his campaign would spend $4m (Â£3m) to air the ad across the state.
After the ad began airing, the editorial board of local Ohio news outlet the Columbus Dispatch endorsed Acton, describing the ad as "revolting and unsettling".
The billionaire biotech entrepreneur ran against Trump for the Republican nomination in 2024. He switched gears to the Ohio governor's race and pitched himself as a political outsider - like Trump - who wanted to develop the president's "America First" agenda.
In his concession speech, Ramaswamy said he is "rooting" for the state, as well as Acton.
Acton is a physician and public health official who talked about her experience with homelessness as a child while campaigning for affordability.
In her acceptance speech on Tuesday, she said "the healing begins today".
"My promise to Ohio, to those who voted for me and those who did not, is that I will work with anyone and everyone, and I always have to make life better for Ohioans," she said.
Acton succeeds Republican Governor Mike DeWine, who is term limited.
Ohio is a swing state that voted for Trump in the 2024 election, but now Republican candidates are facing close challenges across the country.
Democrat Sherrod Brown wins back his old Senate seat from Republican
Democrat Sherrod Brown has re-gained his Senate seat, after defeating Republican Jon Husted in one of the most expensive races this election cycle.
Husted was appointed to the role in 2025 by the state's Republican governor, after JD Vance left the position to become vice-president - but Brown took it for Democrats tonight.
He will return to Congress in January where had spent three decades before losing the seat in 2024, as President Donald Trump and Republicans swept the state.
But as Trump's approval ratings fell, and voter disatisfaction with the economy grew, Democrats placed their bets on Brown and his strong name recognition.
The win solidifies Brown, 73, as the most successful Democrat in Ohio over the last 30 years, according to NBC News.
"This victory belongs to all of us," he wrote on X. "Thank you, Ohio."

0c55d78f0327.text:
- Published
Democrat Troy Jackson has defeated longtime Republican incumbent Susan Collins in Maine, unseating the famous moderate senator in a race marked by controversy.
Jackson entered the race after replacing Graham Platner, the Democratic nominee who withdrew following a series of scandals.
First elected in 1996, Collins was the only Republican senator representing a state that has consistently voted Democratic in presidential elections since 1992.
She has cultivated a reputation as a moderate and sought to distance herself from President Donald Trump during her campaign. Jackson, a former logger, campaigned on workers' rights and accused Collins of yielding to pressure from the president.
Collins and Jackson went head to head during state debates, with Jackson making national headlines when he told the 73-year-old to "shut up".
He entered the campaign late in the season, after Planter withdrew following a series of controversies, including allegations of sexual assault. Platner has denied the allegations.
Jackson had failed to win the Democratic gubernatorial primary, but won the senate nomination in a special convention. He positioned himself as a working-class candidate and backed progressive policies like abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
His victory over Collins allows Democrats an even larger majority in the US Senate, after wins in several key states - including Texas and South Carolina - gave them control of the chamber.
Democrats also won control of the US House of Representatives, meaning they will control all of the US Congress for the last two years of Donald Trump's presidency.
Collins at times walked a tight rope with Trump. A moderate Republican, in a state that historically supported Democrats, she often criticised his policies.
She was viewed by many as a possible "swing vote" during controversial legislation, who could tip the scales either way.
She voted to convict Trump in his second impeachment trial in 2021, after the riots at the US Capitol, and also voted against Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill, which passed.
And she voted against repealing the Affordable Care Act, helping to save the health-care policy commonly referred to as Obamacare.
Yet she backed the president in many crucial votes - including voting in favour of Brett Kavanaugh's nomination for the Supreme Court and confirming Robert Kennedy Jr, a vaccine sceptic, as Health Secretary.
In debates, Jackson tied Collins to Trump's record, pointing to her voting record and arguing that she could have used her position as a key swing vote to sway the president.
Collins, though, argued she used her position leading the Senate's Appropriations Committee, which oversees writing bills that allocates federal funds to states and programmes across the US, to make a difference for Maine and its residents.

It's been an extraordinary night for the Democrats in the US midterms.
They have taken control of the Senate and the House of Representatives too.
Senate
The results in the Senate are beyond what the Democrats would have expected. North Carolina was a likely pick-up but South Carolina was a huge shock and Kansas had not returned a Democratic senator since 1932.
Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Maine have also turned blue. There is one toss-up seat to come in Alaska and even Mississippi is now on a knife edge, according to CBS News.
Polls before the election saw South Carolina as leaning Republican. It had been a deep red seat for many years, last returning a Democratic senator in 1998.
The shift from Republican to Democrat happened across the country. For example recent vote share shows Texas moved 9 points towards the Democrats when compared with the 2024 Senate race.
House
The BBC's partner CBS News projected the Democrats would win the House just after 03:00 GMT on Wednesday (22:00 EST Tuesday). The Democrats are making the gains they need to take control but have their sights set on a much bigger victory.
Two significant seats are Florida 14 and Florida 25 which the Democrats have held. This is a blow to the Republicans' attempt to redraw the boundaries in their favour.
The redistricting saw both districts move from having a majority of 2024 Kamala Harris voters to having a majority of people who voted for Donald Trump.
Florida 22, which was also redrawn to favour the Republicans, saw a victory for the Democrats too.
What turned the vote?
Hispanic voters look to be one of the key groups in the elections in Florida. The poll suggests this group backed the Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon by 55% to 44% for the Republican Ashley Moody.
This is a turnaround from the estimated 55% of Hispanic voters who backed Donald Trump in 2024.
The poll also asked what issues voters were most concerned about. It suggests that across the country the economy was the biggest issue, followed by the state of democracy.
When voters were asked if Donald Trump's policies impacted economic conditions, the poll suggests more that two-thirds believe they had made things worse.

Four oil tankers were destroyed after hitting naval sea mines, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Wednesday, a day after US officials said the US military had launched strikes on the country.
The IRGC said two of the vessels were still burning, and two additional tankers had been seized, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency. It said they were trying to travel through a prohibited southern route in the Strait of Hormuz.
The BBC has not independently verified the IRGC's claim, which came as US voters punished Republicans at the midterm elections, leading Iran's top negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, to say the results showed Americans had said no to war.
He warned Washington not to betray its public.
The IRCG also reported three tankers had been destroyed after hitting mines early on Tuesday, and that they had shot down an MQ-9 drone over the Strait.
The earlier US strikes on Qeshm were in response to the IRGC firing on a US aircraft.
Ghalibaf, who is also Iran's parliamentary speaker, posted on X, external that the midterm results showed that whether it was "conscience or the cost of living, Americans said no to war, and we endorse this message".
"If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our 'no' comes with a nightmare."
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday acknowledged the poor results for Republican congress members was partly due to the war on Iran and the consequent increased gas prices, but that he didn't regret launching it. He told the BBC's partner CBS News that the conflict would end "when I say it ends".
In an interview with the Financial Times ahead of the midterm elections on Tuesday, Trump suggested he was happy with the state of the conflict, and that he didn't consider them to be "really in a war".
Asked about comments by Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu that there would be another attack on Iran this week, Trump said they were "locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no need for it".
On Tuesday night, Trump told Fox News there were some people who would "love" to do a "heavy hit" on Iran.
"The only thing I can tell you with certainty, they will never have a nuclear weapon," Trump said.
Talks to end the conflict, which was triggered by joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February, have been stalled for months, with little sign of a breakthrough.
Ghalibaf told a parliamentary session on Tuesday that Iran "will not surrender" and the responsibility to prevent a war lay with the US.
"If Washington makes another strategic mistake, it should know that this time it will face a new battlefield and will be even more desperate than it is today as it searches for a way out," Ghalibaf said.
Meanwhile Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian maintained his government had been trying to resolve the crisis "through dialogue".
"No-one will benefit from this war" if fighting is restarted, he said on Tuesday.
Iran, which closed the Strait of Hormuz in response to the attack, has said it will only reopen it if the US agrees to demands contained in its peace plan. Foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei this week said the seven-step plan had been condensed, and could be implemented in two days if the US agreed.

Republican candidates in Florida have held off several high-profile challenges from Democrats, as results also saw the state elect its first black governor.
Republican Byron Donalds, backed by President Donald Trump, was projected to win as governor, while Republican Ashley Moody was projected to have held her seat in the senate.
She was up against Democrat Angie Nixon in the special election for Secretary of State Marco Rubio's old Senate seat.
The two wins came amid countless - and historic - gains by Democrats that gave them full control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate for the last years of Trump's presidency.
Nixon scored a surprise win in the Democratic primary to become her party's standard-bearer, although her campaign funding could not match Moody's.
Donalds had served in Congress since 2021 before running for governor, to replace long-serving Republican Governor Ron DeSantis, who was term limited and could not run again.
A big supporter of Trump, Donalds was at one point on the short list to be his running mate in 2024.
Born in Brooklyn, he moved to Florida for university and became a fixture in local politics before running for Congress.
Democrats in the state had some surprise wins, too. Republicans in Florida had helped redraw political voting maps as part of a national redistricting push to boost each political party's chances of taking seats in the House.
But in all three districts that were redrawn to help Republicans, Democrats held onto their seats.

8e3d2f14c7a6.text: Latino voters helped Democrats break Republicans' decades-long grip on Texas and reclaim both chambers of Congress on Tuesday, casting doubt on President Trump's historic 2024 gains with the fast-growing electorate. Why it matters: Republicans bet Trump's Latino breakthrough two years ago would create a lasting GOP realignment in Texas and beyond. Tuesday's results exposed how quickly those gains could unravel — and raised new questions about Republicans' coalition heading into 2028. Early results show Hispanic voters' shift aided Democrats in capturing a Senate seat and the governorship in Texas for the first time in a generation. Tuesday's results — particularly in South Texas border counties — reflected some of the anger among Hispanics over high prices and the Trump administration's immigration enforcement. "This is what happens when you mess with the Latino community. We are sending a clear message," said Hector Sanchez Barba, president and CEO of the voting group Mi Familia Vota. By the numbers: Early NBC News exit poll results showed Latino voters moving away from Republicans. Democrats' 16-point advantage in Latino party identification grew from 10 points in 2024, according to NBC's polling. Some 43% of Latino voters identified as Democrats, up from 39% in 2024. Republican identification slipped from 29% to 27%. In the early NBC exit poll, 75% of voters nationally described the economy as struggling, while 65% said Trump's policies had made economic conditions worse. State of play: Democrats reclaimed the House and Senate while ending Republicans' statewide winning streak in Texas dating to 1994. Democratic state Rep. James Talarico defeated Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton , winning a Senate seat Democrats last captured in 1988. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa ousted Republican Gov. Greg Abbott , becoming Texas' first elected Latina governor. Early returns also suggested Latino voters helped Democrats win crucial House contests in Colorado and Georgia. Comedian Cristela Alonzo attends an election night watch party for Texas Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa at Assembly Hall in Austin, Texas. Photo: Joel Angel Juarez/Getty Images What they're saying: "You know how Tim Russert would always say 'Florida, Florida, Florida?' For the last two cycles, I kept saying Texas, Texas, Texas. That's how I feel right now," Voto Latino CEO Maria Teresa Kumar told Axios. Kumar said the Democrats' historic Texas wins changes 2028 and will transform how presidential candidates talk to Latino voters and see Texas as purple. "There was this notion that we're a sleeping giant. Now, we're jumping up and down and waving our fist above the head," Janet Murguía, president and CEO of the Latino civil rights group UnidosUS told Axios. Zoom in: The clearest tests of the Latino shift came in Texas counties that Republicans had celebrated as evidence of their growing strength. Cameron County, which includes Brownsville and South Padre Island: Talarico led by 38 points in early, unofficial returns. Trump won by 6 points there in 2024. Hidalgo County, another majority-Latino border county: Talarico led by 47 points. Trump won it two years ago by 3 points. Webb County, home to Laredo: Talarico led by 49 points; it was Trump +2 in 2024. Context: Trump's 2024 success shattered longstanding assumptions about Latino voters. A Pew Research Center analysis found Trump won 48% of Latino voters in 2024, compared with 36% in 2020. An August Axios-reported poll of 17 competitive House districts foreshadowed the reversal, showing Democrats leading 58%–35% among Latino registered voters. Supporters react during a midterm election night watch party for Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico at the Long Center in Austin, Texas. Photo: Brandon Bell/Getty Image Reality check: A Democratic rebound doesn't mean Latino voters have returned to their old political loyalties. Democrats' 16-point advantage in Latino party identification remains far below their 33-point advantage in 2018, according to NBC. Republicans may have mistaken Trump's appeal for lasting GOP loyalty. Democrats risk confusing a backlash against Trump with renewed allegiance to their party. A September Axios analysis found 62% of Latino registered voters in 17 battleground districts trusted Democrats more to lower prices, compared with 36% who trusted Republicans. Economic frustration gave Democrats an opening without guaranteeing lasting support. The bottom line: Trump's Latino breakthrough reshaped politics in 2024. Two years later, those voters reminded both parties that winning their support once doesn't mean keeping it.

Democrats have torn up Donald Trump's political map on a night that will send shockwaves through American politics for years to come.
With a string of major Senate victories in states that have been reliably Republican for decades - and in Kansas's case, nearly a century - a blue tidal wave crashed across the nation, sweeping Republicans out of power.
Halfway through President Donald Trump's second term, the Democrats now have decisive control of the House of Representatives and have wrested a majority back in the Senate.
They will be able to frustrate Trump's agenda, and launch investigations into his administration. A historic third impeachment attempt could also be on the cards.
Few imagined such an outcome was possible in the months after Trump returned to the White House with unified Republican control of Congress in January 2025.
As the public mood turned against him and his party, Democrats had hopes of retaking the House.
But they contemplated a Senate map that appeared unfriendly, populated by states Trump had won comfortably just two years ago.
Instead, Democrats rewrote the political equations with victories in Texas, Maine, Kansas, Ohio, Iowa and North and South Carolina.
In comments to the BBC's US partner CBS, Trump pledged to strike deals with congressional Democrats, adding that he didn't want to have to spend his final two years in office rejecting their legislation.
He somewhat undermined that sentiment later, posting a picture to Truth Social of his trademark red baseball hat with the word "veto" emblazoned on it.
The president went on to note that his name wasn't on the ballot this year, but if it had been Republicans would have won a decisive victory.
Trump had helped elevate many of those Republican candidates, however, and had urged voters to pretend he was up for re-election.
In the Senate, Democrats flipped at least six seats, comfortably securing a majority.
Adam Hamilton won in Kansas - a state that last elected a Democrat to the Senate almost 100 years ago during the Great Depression.
James Talarico beat Republican Ken Paxton in Texas' Senate race, ending a 38-year Democratic losing streak in statewide elections there.
In South Carolina, Annie Andrews beat Darline Graham, who had been appointed to the seat after the death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham. Few analysts had that seat in play even a few months ago.
Five-term Republican Susan Collins conceded Maine's Senate election to Democrat Troy Jackson.
Paralympian Josh Turek flipped the Iowa Senate seat held by retiring Republican Senator Joni Ernst. Democrats also wrested from Republicans a Senate seat in Ohio, with Sherrod Brown's comeback victory over Jon Husted.
Meanwhile, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed looked on course to beat Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's bitterly fought Senate race.
Nor was that the end of the electoral carnage for Republicans.
Ruby-red Texas witnessed another seismic result in the governor's race.
Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa ousted the incumbent Republican Greg Abbott, who was earlier this year seen as the prohibitive favourite.
Democrats also took governors' races in Iowa, Ohio and Georgia, which made history by electing the first black woman to such a post.
Meanwhile, the party has won a House majority for the first time since 2022.
They are projected to win 245 House seats and the Republicans 166 seats.
A look at the key races offers plenty of reasons why.
Democrats flipped House seats in Texas, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Iowa, Kentucky and Colorado, among others. And they were poised to make gains in Virginia and Indiana.
Black Democrats in the southern states turned out in record number, helping to carry their party to victory. And Hispanic voters, whose support had helped secure Trump's presidential victory in 2024, swung decisively back to the Democrats.
Democrats won all three House races in the overwhelmingly Hispanic congressional districts along the Texas-Mexico border.
And Hispanic voters helped Democrats hold House seats in Florida that the state's Republicans had sought to flip by redrawing the congressional district lines.
In fact, the congressional redistricting battles that had dominated headlines for months last year ended up being a bust for the Republicans.
In Texas, they had hoped their line-drawing would net five new seats for their party. But on Tuesday they may end up losing one seat.
If there is a silver lining for conservatives, Florida as a whole still appears to tilt to the right.
Republican Senator Ashley Moody narrowly won re-election, as did congressman Byron Donalds, who was elected the Sunshine State's first black governor.
And embattled Republicans were able to hold governorships in Vermont and New Hampshire. But the bright spots were few and far between.
Just two years ago, Trump won the presidency with 48% of the vote. He claimed an electoral mandate.
He then went about governing like it, pushing sometimes unpopular policies on trade and immigration, and launching an Iran war that is opposed by most of the American public.
On Tuesday, voters gave him the kind of stinging rebuke that will not be easily forgotten.

The UK's most followed TikTok creator says he is "super excited" to be co-hosting the BBC's latest nature programme.
Naturewatch, hosted by wildlife presenters Chris Packham, Megan McCubbin and influencer Kyle Thomas, starts on Friday on BBC Two and will run all year round.
The show, which is being produced by BBC Studios' Natural History Unit, is filmed in a secret location just south of Bristol city centre, and will celebrate the best of British nature.
Thomas, who has amassed more than 33 million followers on TikTok for his videos about animals, said Naturewatch would act as a "trusted source of really brilliant factual information" as AI becomes increasingly common on social media.
He hopes his presence on the programme will attract a younger audience.
"We're going on this learning journey together," he said, adding: "I'm super, super excited. I'm learning so much already."
He explained the show would make nature accessible to everyone, with people encouraged to send videos in for the presenters to react to.
More from Bristol
McCubbin said the trio had "already been distracted" by the diverse wildlife surrounding their tiny studio in the heart of the West's countryside.
"It's really great to be in this part of the country, there's lots of brilliant wildlife here and lots of stories for us to be talking about," she added.
The programme will showcase the wildlife "people can expect to see and encounter whilst they're outside", said Packham.
It will also feature Q&A episodes, where viewers can send in seasonal questions, photos and videos to Naturewatch, external for expert analysis.
The first episode airs on BBC Two at 19:30 GMT. It will also be available on BBC Sounds and the BBC iPlayer.

Itâs been nearly four decades since Texas sent a Democrat to the US Senate, and 36 years since one occupied the governorâs mansion. That all changed Tuesday night.
While Democrats notched historic upsets nationwide â including in places like Kansas, which broke a 90-year streak â Texas carries outsized national weight given the recent corporate stampede to the state.
SpaceX, Tesla, Chevron, and Caterpillar are among the corporate giants that relocated to Texas in search of lower taxes, light-touch regulation, and a business-friendly political climate.
âIn Texas, weâre welcome,â Chevronâs Andy Walz said after announcing a move from California.
Last month, the parent company of the new Texas Stock Exchange raised $155 million in a third funding round meant to lure companies away from the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq.
Like Walz, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has cast Texas as a foil to California â a state Musk famously decried as the âstate of overregulation, overlitigation, and overtaxation,â and whose billionaire wealth tax on the ballot Tuesday has alienated business leaders.
Yet that corporate embrace has proved double-edged. Musk directed roughly $190 million of his $445 million midterm war chest into Texas, largely backing Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott. That deluge offered Democrat James Talarico an irresistible target down the stretch, allowing him to portray the race as Muskâs bid to buy a Senate seat.
Abbott, a three-term incumbent, was also called out for being on Muskâs payroll. âDoes Texas belong to the people, or is this the billionairesâ world and we just live here?â said Gina Hinojosa, who defeated Abbott to become the first Democrat elected governor since Ann Richards in 1990.
âIn less than one month, Elon Musk gave Greg Abbott $5 million to try and buy this election so that he can keep buying up Texansâ land, energy, and resources,â she added.
Hinojosa, described as âa long shotâ by the Texas Tribune and mostly ignored by Abbott for much of the year, also tapped into rising backlash over data center sprawl. She campaigned against what she termed a âBig Tech takeover of Texas land, resources, and schools.â

An Ethiopian-born American citizen has pleaded guilty to passing highly classified intelligence to Ethiopia, including information he hoped would help target and kill fighters from the Tigray region during the country's 2020-22 civil war.
Abraham Teklu Lemma, a former US contractor, admitted sharing dozens of classified documents and photographs with senior Ethiopian officials over more than two years, the US Department of Justice said.
"In doing so, he betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country, while jeopardizing our national security," said US Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Ferris Pirro.
The 54-year-old faces up to 22 years in prison under a plea agreement.
Abraham had worked as a contractor at the State Department, Justice Department and National Reconnaissance Office, the agency responsible for US intelligence satellites.
Prosecutors said Abraham worked with senior figures in Ethiopia's political, military and intelligence establishments between 2021 and his arrest in August 2023.
He secretly removed classified material from secure government facilities, sometimes copying sensitive information into handwritten notes that he carried out of the buildings. He used his position as an IT administrator to extract electronic intelligence files.
"Much of the highly classified information Lemma shared with the Ethiopian government concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia," prosecutors said.
The information included satellite imagery and details of military activities, which he passed to Ethiopian officials through encrypted messages.
The FBI said Ethiopian officials subsequently used intelligence supplied by Abraham in military operations.
Prosecutors said he hoped the information would help Ethiopia's military identify and kill paramilitary fighters.
"Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree," said John Eisenberg, the US assistant attorney general for national security.
In one message to an Ethiopian official in December 2021, he wrote: "We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia," court papers showed.
Later that day, he shared further intelligence and urged the official: "Please send Dro[nes]."
The revelations shed light on how sensitive American intelligence was passed to Ethiopian authorities during a devastating civil war that killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
It was marked by widespread allegations of atrocities, including massacres, sexual violence and attacks on civilians.
A peace agreement signed in November 2022 ended the conflict, although fighting resumed in September after both sides accused each other of not respecting the terms of that deal.
Abraham was arrested in Maryland in August 2023 following an investigation into his handling of classified intelligence.
At the time, prosecutors alleged that he had removed security markings from intelligence reports and shared information with a foreign intelligence official.
In one exchange, the official asked him to continue providing assistance, to which Lemma replied: "Roger that!"
Pirro, the US attorney, said Abraham had abused his access to some of America's most sensitive intelligence.
She accused him of betraying his colleagues and country with prosecutors saying he "will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law".
Abraham pleaded guilty to conspiring to transmit national defence information to a foreign government.
His sentencing is scheduled for 14 April 2027.

Susan Collins, taking advantage of President Donald Trump's deep unpopularity to dislodge an incumbent who had survived tough challenges in the past. LIVE RESULTS: Maine Senate midterm election "For every family doing everything they can and wondering when somebody is going to do something for them, you have gotten me into this and you're going to have someone who is fighting for you in Washington, D.C.," Jackson told the crowd at an election night party in Portland. Jackson, 58, a fifth-generation logger and former president of the state Senate, had a little more than 100 days to sell himself to Maine voters after he replaced Graham Platner as the party's nominee in July. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News He won a hastily convened nominating convention and began barnstorming the state, focusing heavily on economic issues such as the high costs of housing and healthcare. As a former campaign surrogate of independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, he was known to many progressives in the state but lacked the widespread name recognition of Collins. Collins, 73, was widely perceived as the most vulnerable Senate Republican this election year. She entered Election Day as the only Republican lawmaker in Congress from New England and was seeking her sixth term representing a state that has voted for the Democratic candidate for president since 1992. "It has been the honor of my life to serve the people of Maine in the United States Senate. I'm proud of all I have been able to accomplish for our state and for our country in the past 30 years," Collins said in a statement after calling Jackson to concede. Jackson took over the nomination during a time of crisis for Democrats Jackson hails from rural Aroostook County, among the poorest in the state, where he went to work as a lumberjack at 19. He first entered politics after leading a weeklong loggers' blockade along Maine's border with Quebec in the late 1990s protesting the hiring of Canadian loggers who were coming into Maine and driving down pay rates. The standoff ended with Jackson being escorted away by police, an unsuccessful ending that spurred him to run for elected office. He served nearly 20 years in the state House, rising up the ranks to become the Senate's top leader. Jackson initially didn't plan to run for Senate this year. Instead, he threw his hat in for the Democratic nomination for governor but lost. Platner, an oyster farmer and political newcomer, had drawn huge crowds and enthusiasm but also faced a string of controversies. After he announced in July that he would withdraw from the Senate race, Jackson won a special nominating convention later that month. It made for a rushed start to the campaign for Jackson. Since then, he has held events at churches, union halls and bars to tout issues such as workers' rights and the cost of living. At times, his campaign rhetoric is reminiscent of Sanders, who joined Jackson for rallies in October. "In the end, if you work hard, you should be able to build a decent life," Jackson said at a campaign event near Portland in September. "But that's not the reality right now." He criticized Collins as not doing enough to stop Trump. Jackson noted she voted to advance Trump's signature tax cut and budget legislation out of committee, before she was a "no" vote on its final passage. "Sen. Collins is like an arsonist who helps set the fire and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out," he said. Jackson faced blowback over his temperament during the campaign, and Collins criticized him for telling her to "shut up" during a debate. Collins attempted to woo voters on her independence Collins was first elected in 1996 and has touted her independence from Trump and her party. She has said she didn't vote for Trump in 2016, and she voted to convict the president after his 2021 impeachment over his role in the Jan. 6 Capitol riot. In January, Collins joined a handful of Republican colleagues in backing a failed effort to limit the president's ability to unilaterally use force in Venezuela. The move prompted Trump to say on social media that they "should never be elected to office again." When Vice President JD Vance made trips to Maine, Collins did not appear with him. Vance told the crowd at a May rally that he sometimes gets frustrated with the senator and wishes she were more partisan. Collins has been a top target of Democrats before. Many pollsters predicted Collins would lose to former Maine House Speaker Sara Gideon in 2020. Collins won handily during a year that Democrats won the presidential race and both U.S. House seats in Maine. During this year's race, Collins touted her longevity in the Senate and her status as a key player in powerful committees and budgeting negotiations. She said those aspects of her service remain critically important for Mainers. "It has been 92 years since a Maine senator was chair of the Senate appropriations committee, the most powerful committee in the Senate," Collins told reporters. The National Trust has vowed to "maintain the spirit" of a nature reserve while making "some small changes" after saving it from closure.
The future of Flatford Wildlife Garden, near East Bergholt in Suffolk, was thrown into doubt in October when the RSPB said it would have to sell or lease the land due to financial pressures.
It was announced in April that the site would be taken on by the National Trust and, on Tuesday, ownership of the garden officially changed hands.
RSPB Suffolk area manager Adam Rowlands said: "We are confident that their ambitions for the site align with our own ethos of how we wanted to see Flatford Wildlife Garden looked after under new ownership."
He added: "We know the National Trust will continue to maintain the garden for both wildlife and people, and we are incredibly pleased it will reopen to the public next year under their care."
Leigh Freeman, a National Trust area manager, said the purchase had been a "quite a long time in the making" for both parties and would help secure the future of the reserve, a legacy left to the RSPB by Sylvia and Margaret Richardson about 15 years ago.
"The RSPB had a look at its assets last year and I think it felt more aligned that we would look after it in the future," he said.
"It's only been open in the summer in the past, but we will be taking the winter to kind of get it ready for visitors in the spring â early March or certainly before Easter."
The gardens, which have been managed by the RSPB since 2011, boast wildlife and birds, a trail with carved wooden garden creatures and a pond.
There is also a living willow tunnel and an insect and bee "hotel" and there are activity days and talks for children and adults.
The acquisition, which also includes land next to the gardens, was made possible after the National Trust, a conservation charity that cares for historic buildings, gardens and landscapes, received support and funding from local groups.
Freeman said the first year of ownership would be spent learning more about the garden and how it "integrates with the site and people connect with it".
"There will be some small changes but we intend to maintain the spirit of the wildlife garden, that is something we are very committed to," added Freeman.
"We're also really committed to connecting it with the wider site at Flatford and providing better access."

The News
Democrats seized the House and Senate by wider margins that even party leaders had hoped in a wave election that served as a referendum on President Donald Trump.
Democratic House candidates took districts Trump won by double digits just two years ago.
They flipped Senate seats nationwide, including in Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas. Competitive races havenât been called in Michigan and Alaska, where Democrats could run up the score further.
Trump told The New York Times on Wednesday night that he âwas absolutely willingâ to accept the results of the election.
Democrats racked up stunning victories across the South. In Texas, James Talarico defeated Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988. Democrat Gina Hinojosa toppled incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, becoming the first Democrat to take the governorâs mansion since Ann Richards in 1990.
Gov. Roy Cooper of North Carolina won a Senate seat in his state, pulling off what no Democrat has there in 18 years. In South Carolina, Annie Andrews defeated Darline Graham, winning the seat formerly held by Lindsey Graham. Sen. Jon Ossoff held onto his seat in Georgia.
Democrats scored victories across the Midwest, too. Adam Hamilton defeated Republican Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas, overcoming a 94-year drought for Democrats in the state. In Iowa, Josh Turek beat Rep. Ashley Hinson to fill retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernstâs seat. In Ohio, Sherrod Brown unseated Republican Sen. Jon Husted.
Chris Pappas held retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheenâs seat for Democrats in New Hampshire.
Republican Maine Sen. Susan Collins conceded to her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson. Polls in Alaska remain open until 1 am EST.
Republicans held onto a Senate seat in Florida. Trump, reportedly watching returns from the White House, criticized Fox News coverage before most polls had closed. In a social media post Trump said Republicans would have had a better night if heâd been on the ballot.
Democratic surge
Democrats won other gubernatorial races in red states. Keisha Lance Bottoms won the gubernatorial race in Georgia, a first for a Democrat in 28 years â a positive sign for Ossoff if he decides to pursue a 2028 presidential bid, since she would appoint his successor.
Democrat Amy Acton defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, endorsed by Trump, to become the next governor of Ohio. Ramaswamy aired a late attack ad against Acton featuring her estranged mother, who backed her husband when Acton accused him of rape as a child.
Ossoff, who Republicans had hoped to unseat this year, easily blew past GOP rival Rep. Mike Collins to win re-election. Pappas prevailed over former GOP Sen. John Sununu in another race that Republicans had initially hoped to contest. In North Carolina, Cooper scored the partyâs first pickup of the night.
House Republicans are also faltering in Florida, where three seats drawn to elect Republicans have so far gone to Democrats â re-elections for Reps. Jared Moskowitz and Kathy Castor, plus a victory for Rep.-elect Pia Dandiya. The GOP initially redistricted to try to gain four new House seats.
All three of the Florida districts that Democrats have won so far on Tuesday night backed Trump in 2024. Urged to embark on mid-decade redistricting by Trump, Florida GOP Gov. Ron DeSantis has warned that his party was losing some of its advantages, driven by voter anger about the war in Iran.
Davidâs view
As the night got better and better for Democrats, I started to hear them ask: Had they built a new national majority? Had they banished MAGA for good?Then they reminded themselves: Thinking like that is what got Republicans into this mess. Two Trump victories, and a 2020 loss that kept most of his coalition intact, convinced many conservatives that they had built a new party system that combined working class voters of all races, the social conservatives who made their local parties run, and the business community that rejected Trump after Jan. 6 but came running back in 2024. Who could beat that?
Well, now we know. The Trump coalition came apart on Tuesday, with the president decisively unable to put himself âon the ballotâ and turn out his unlikely voters. Plenty of signs were there during early voting â especially in North Carolina, a killing field where Republicans lost House and state legislative seats that were gerrymandered to be impossible to lose. (On a map drawn to elect three Democrats, the party is likely to win nine seats.)
Democrats didnât pretend that they had solved all their partiesâ problems. But they did learn from Trumpâs first term, and the way they miscalculated what a fluke he was. Instead of moving to the left, betting that a more excited base could overwhelm MAGA, they nominated candidates who were willing to break with left-wing orthodoxy â Iowa Sen.-elect Josh Turek adopting a more conservative position on gender, Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico becoming a booster of the energy industry.
Their base was so furious at Trump that it was relatively easy to turn out. Persuasion was harder, but they got there; Democrats won back northeast Ohio, eastern Iowa, Texasâs Rio Grande Valley, and even parts of Florida that seemed to be racing away from their party.
And Republicans couldnât change the electorate. Trump wasnât on the ballot, obviously â but for the first time, voters did not credit Trump with good management of the economy or with keeping America out of wars. The snazziest GOP bumper sticker of the Biden years was âIâd take some mean tweets and cheap gas right now.â Without cheap gas, voters werenât willing to put up with Trumpâs AI memes, jokes about menâs asses, and obsession with building a triumphant arch in Arlington.

7e5edc5f1772.text: Senate Republicans' worst nightmare came true Tuesday night, as they watched red state after red state fall to a historic Democratic wave . Why it matters: It's hard to remember now, but Republicans started off the 2026 cycle thinking they could expand their majority. They ended the night with what one source called a "huge f**king thumping" — losing or trailing in every toss-up on the map. At the start of the cycle, top operatives saw a red wall of incumbents in Trump-friendly states, an invincible Republican Sen. Susan Collins in Maine and a vulnerable Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia, who provided a path to expanding a majority. By 9pm Tuesday night, top GOP sources were quietly accepting the reality of the return of Majority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.). "Republicans are going to wake up in a different country tomorrow and we are going to have to start from square one to reinvent a party," one senior GOP Senate aide told Axios on Tuesday evening. Between the lines: For the first time since 1972, Republicans lost a Senate seat in the home state of the chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee. The defeat of Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) came despite Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) leading the NRSC. Republicans also lost in the home state of the next expected NRSC chair, Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio). Zoom in: North Carolina and Georgia were expected to be the premiere races of the cycle not too long ago. Both were called for Democrats before 8:30pm EST. That was just the beginning of the nightmare. In Texas, Elon Musk's more than $150 million infusion wasn't enough to save Texas GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton after Paxton defeated Sen. John Cornyn in a nasty primary. In Ohio, Sen. Jon Husted's (R-Ohio) campaign had a rocky start — and wasn't bailed out by President Trump's publicity campaign about his rear end. Alaska started looking shaky even before a second Dan Sullivan joined the ballot, and Iowa wasn't a given either. In Kansas, alarm bells started ringing over an unprepared Sen. Roger Marshall. In South Carolina, Sen. Lindsey Graham died, and before Republican leaders could blink, Trump crowned Graham's sister, Darline, who had no political experience. And in Maine, Republicans held out hope that Susan Collins could pull out another miracle. A hope that quickly faded as results began to roll in. What we're hearing: "Absolutely brutal night," another senior GOP aide told us. "But also predictable. Signs were there for months. Biggest fear is that the party lacks the introspection, takes away wrong lessons, and doubles down on the policies and behavior that got us into this mess in first place." "Sometimes there are environmental challenges that even the strongest, best-resourced candidate can't overcome. We're seeing those challenges play out in real time tonight," said a third senior GOP aide. Yet another top operative conspicuously shared charts of Trump's dismal approval ratings. The bottom line: Democrats won Senate seats on Tuesday night for the first time in Texas since 1988, in Kansas since 1932 and South Carolina since 1998.

Democrat James Talarico has won a key Senate race in Texas, in what is one of the biggest upsets for Republicans in this year's elections.
Talarico's stunning victory over Republican Ken Paxton marks the first time a Democrat has won a US Senate seat in Texas since 1988 - and has helped solidify Democrats taking full control of the US Congress in a tidal wave of wins across America.
Talarico, a former schoolteacher, was a little-known figure until last year. He made the rising cost of living under Republican leadership a central theme of his run.
Paxton sought to portray Talarico's views as too progressive for the state, and campaigned alongside Trump on several occasions.
Supporters of Talarico went berserk as TVs at a watch party in Austin, the state's capital, projected him the winner.
They hugged, they kissed, and they drank to a reality that many say they dared not believe would come true.
Emerging on stage to rapturous applause at his official watch party at a nearby performing arts theatre, Talarico pronounced: "We just took back Texas."
"We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas," he continued, referring to his win over Paxton whose campaign was backed by Elon Musk, the world's richest man.
He invoked religious themes that have grown familiar to his campaign, comparing his unlikely odds to the biblical story of David and Goliath.
"This win, this win is for every Texan who's ever wondered if anyone is listening," he said. "I hear you, we hear you. And tonight the world hears you."
For decades, the idea of a Democrat winning a statewide race had felt like a pipe dream for Texas liberals.
As the nation's second most populous state, Texas has been a bastion of conservatism, routinely rolling out Republican policies that are later employed elsewhere.
But throughout the campaign, polls suggested state legislator Talarico was breaking through with voters, energising a Texas Democratic base desperate for new leadership.
Spending in the race skyrocketed, and it quickly grew to become the most expensive US Senate race in history, with more than half a billion dollars spent.
Billionaire Elon Musk poured in $158m (Â£117m) to a super PAC supporting Paxton's campaign - a point that Talarico used in attacks on Paxton's campaign.
Then two members of the Bush family, the Republican political dynasty that counts Texas as its political launchpad, backed Talarico in a stunning move foreshadowing Paxton's doom.
George Washington University political science professor Quardricos Driskell told the BBC that Paxton was a major part of Republicans' downfall, calling him an "objectively terrible candidate".
He said the win in Texas by Talarico, combined with another upset on Tuesday that ousted the state's Republican governor Greg Abbott, was "absolutely historic". Abbott's loss marked the first time a Democrat had won a race for governor in the state since the 1990s.
"This wasn't just a tsunami, not just a referendum, but this was a bloodbath," Driskell said about Democrats gains in the Lone Star State. "A clear distinction that the country wants to go in a different direction".
Talarico defeated a well-known opponent, Dallas Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett, in the Democratic primary. Then continued to maintain good polling numbers despite an onslaught of negative adverts, including attacks on past comments where he supported transgender people.
Throughout his campaign, he frequently leaned into his religious upbringing â as the grandson of a Southern Baptist preacher who spent time in a seminary â sprinkling his stump speeches with biblical references.
Paxton had been beleaguered by a number of political scandals, including his impeachment by his own party in 2023 on corruption accusations, before he was later acquitted by the state's Senate.
He was also indicted by the US Securities and Exchange Commission on federal fraud charges, but they were later dismissed.
Trump made multiple stops in Texas to beef up support for Paxton and other Republicans - including in reliably-Republican spots, signalling how concerned party leadership was about turnout.
Voters have been frustrated with high consumer costs, including the price of petrol, and largely blame Trump's tariff policies and the Iran war.
Hispanic voters and those who live along the southern US border have also taken issue with Trump's immigration policies.
Despite border crossings plummeting under Trump - something that had been popular with Texas voters - polls suggested Trump's support among Hispanics, who make up a third of the state's population, had ebbed significantly.
Surveys taken since late summer indicated a majority of Texan Hispanic voters - many of whom switched to Trump to help him win the White House in 2024 - now disapproved of the president. They also suggested that Hispanic voters were favouring Democrats over Republicans by a significant margin.
Many Texas Hispanics who spoke to the BBC before the election pointed to Trump's immigration crackdown as the reasoning behind their change of heart. They pointed to aggressive measures that led to citizens being detained and non-violent offenders being rounded up indiscriminately.

12830b547586.text:
The News
Democrats have secured control of the Senate, a shocking collapse for a Republican majority that started the midterms with what looked like an impregnable red wall of conservative states.
There were almost no blemishes for Democrats and few bright spots for Republicans. The GOP lost seats it held in Maine, Ohio, Texas, Kansas, Iowa, South Carolina, and North Carolina; failed to flip seats in New Hampshire and Georgia; and is now bracing for further losses that could hamper its effort to retake the Senate in 2028, when the map gives both parties pickup opportunities.
Other than North Carolina, the GOP-held losses are in states President Donald Trump won handily in 2024. Republicans could afford to lose up to three seats; theyâre on track to lose all of their tossup races. Senate seats in Maine and Alaska are also both at risk of flipping.
âThis is a generational wipeout,â one senior Republican strategist told Semafor. âWe are going to have a full-on GOP civil war.â
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said his party had pulled off a âgenerational remake of the Senate mapâ by winning so many tough states. After touting Democratsâ candidate qualify, he said Americans had reduced the GOPâs red wall to a âpile of bricks.â
âRepublicans made a choice and followed Trump over the cliff. Some of the time he talked about extraneous things that were ridiculous, but much of the time, he implemented things that raised their costs on electricity, on healthcare, on goods,â Schumer told reporters at a midnight press conference.
He said he heard Trumpâs remarks saying heâd work with a Democratic Congress but vowed his party is âgoing to deliver for the people of America with or without the president.â
Democrats started Tuesday night with two quick, decisive Senate victories â by Georgia incumbent Jon Ossoff and former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper â that fueled their drive deeper into red territory, to the tune of tens of millions of dollars.
Moving Money Around
The partyâs top Senate super PAC pulled down several weeksâ worth of ads in those two Southern states in recent weeks, per information shared with Semafor, saving $22 million in North Carolina and $11 million in Georgia.
The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee also scrapped some ad buys in both states down the stretch, decisions that paid off as the party won both seats early on Tuesday night. Democrats felt optimistic about taking the majority earlier in the night than some had expected after the shocking win in South Carolina.
Their decision to pull cash out of Georgia and North Carolina helped top Democratic groups approve new Senate spending in states like Mississippi, South Carolina, and Kansas. It also helped the party shore up candidates in the battleground states of Michigan and Maine as Republicansâ deep-pocketed Senate Leadership Fund super PAC poured in astounding sums.
âThe strength of the Cooper and Ossoff campaigns allowed Senate Majority PAC to re-invest our initial investments into our expanded battleground map. That is a game-changer when Republicans poured money into races,â said Lauren French, a spokesperson for Senate Majority PAC.
Senate Majority PAC spent heavily in Kansas on top of its spending in traditional battlegrounds, while the DSCC put in $500,000 in South Carolinaâs Senate race late, according to a person familiar with the buy. That spending followed $500,000 in Mississippi previously reported by Semafor.
That was only possible due to the strength of Ossoff and Cooper, who both raised gobs of money and put away their opponents weeks ago. Cooper raised more than $49 million through mid-October, and Ossoff raised more than $100 million.
Cooper and Ossoff are both notching considerable, double-digit victories over their respective opponents, Rep. Mike Collins and Michael Whatley.
Burgessâs view
In Senate races, candidate quality matters. And it can affect all of the other candidates on a partyâs slate.
Ossoff and Cooper ran such boringly effective campaigns that it allowed Democratic leaders to concentrate their efforts elsewhere. Appointed Sens. Democratic candidates flipped Republican-held seats in North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa, Texas, South Carolina and Kansas, where the president had personally chosen the GOP nominees or tried to rally voters on their behalf with campaign stops. The results were also a major reprimand from voters of Trump, who repeatedly urged voters to "pretend I'm on the ballot" as he went into primarily conservative states to shore up Republican candidates and warned of a Washington where Democrats were in power. As he tried to personalize the midterm campaign, Trump also defended his policies on tariffs and the war with Iran that drove up prices. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News A Democratic-led Senate means that the party will have more power to launch investigations into the Trump administration and can stymie his nominations to Cabinet posts and lifetime federal judgeships. The midterm results shift the center of gravity closer to Capitol Hill, where Democrats will be angling to check Trump's power after two years of acquiescence from congressional Republicans. Trump tried to shift the blame away from himself during a Fox News interview that aired early Wednesday, saying Democrats "did a good job" in their campaigns and blamed GOP candidates for losses. The results leave Trump — who watched returns at the White House with his advisers and members of his Cabinet — with dramatically diminished political capital at home and abroad. He had all but guaranteed the results will be seen as a referendum on himself by repeatedly urging voters to "pretend I'm on the ballot." But about 24 hours after Trump had uttered that, the president on Tuesday night began pointing the blame elsewhere as results came in, posting on social media: "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" Trump's choices for GOP races had their own baggage Despite urging voters to use their imagination when reading names on the ballot, Trump's hand-picked Republican candidates in Texas and South Carolina faced deep skepticism. Republican Darline Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, lost to Democrat Annie Andrews in South Carolina after a campaign in which she faced questions about her inexperience. Republican Ken Paxton, who lost to Democrat James Talarico in Texas, was impeached by his own party over corruption accusations and stained by a very public divorce. Thom Tillis in North Carolina to decide to retire after clashing with the president. Democrat Adam Hamilton defeated Republican Roger Marshall in Kansas, while Republican Ashley Hinson lost to Democrat Josh Turek. In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown regained his Senate seat that he lost two years ago, defeating appointed Republican Sen. Jon Husted in a state in which Trump and Vice President JD Vance repeatedly campaigned. With Husted, Trump had an odd fixation on his physique, frequently admiring the former football player's body during campaign rallies in Ohio and elsewhere around the country. Democrats on Tuesday also retained a key Senate seat in Georgia where another one of Trump's endorsed candidates faced controversy. In 2024, Trump won all seven states — Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina, Ohio, Georgia, Iowa and Kansas.
