The mother of a 15-year-old Ghanaian boy who was fatally shot in the United States last week has left Ghana for America after being granted an emergency visa by President Donald Trump.
"I want justice for my son," Doris Adu Gyamfi told the BBC at the airport before her departure.
She said he had dreamt of becoming a medical doctor.
Her son, Javits Frimpong, who had only been in the US for a year, was chased down and shot on Thursday morning on his way to school in the Bronx, New York.
He was taken to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead.
Police have not made any arrests and an investigation is ongoing as authorities search for three teenage boys in connection with the shooting.
His death has sparked outrage in both Ghana and the US, and reignited the debate about gun violence in America.
His mother was escorted to the airport by relatives and Dr Erieka Bennett, Head of Mission of the African Diaspora Forum.
"I'm going to America to plan my son's funeral," Gyamfi said.
She thanked the government and well-wishers for their support and prayers following her son's death.
In a social media post on Saturday, New York mayor Zohran Mamdani said Trump had agreed to grant a visa to Gyamfi so she could mourn her son in person.
Mamdani said the murder of a child was a pain no parent should endure, "let alone from thousands of miles away.â
"Javits Frimpong's mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person. I just got off the phone with President Trump, and he has agreed to grant her visa immediately," he said.
"All of New York City is mourning this tragedy," he added.
Ghana's government has condemned the killing and said it was following the case closely to ensure justice.
It has urged US authorities to conduct a thorough investigation and said it was ready to provide legal and consular support to ensure the perpetrators are brought to justice.
Police are searching for three teenage suspects who fled the scene, captured on surveillance footage.
The shooting has sparked concern among Ghanaians about the safety of children sent to study in America.

f4afcb1df036.text: Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) plans to step down as the House's top Republican after his party's epic midterm election losses wiped out their majority, according to a person familiar with his plans. Why it matters: Johnson's exit touches off a potentially contentious scramble to replace him with Republicans days away from choosing their next leaders. Johnson told staff on a Wednesday morning call that he will not run for minority leader, the person familiar with his plans said. Driving the news: House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) have been floated as potential successors, setting the stage for a bruising leadership battle. Johnson's political future remains uncertain, with questions swirling over whether he will remain in Congress or leave the House altogether after three years as speaker. The Louisiana Republican had spent months traveling across the country and raising millions of dollars in a last-ditch effort to preserve the GOP's majority. Flashback: Johnson ascended to the speakership in October 2023 as a little-known lawmaker after weeks of GOP turmoil following Kevin McCarthy's historic ousting . Johnson spent much of his speakership navigating razor-thin Republican majorities, managing persistent GOP infighting and repeated conservative rebellions that brought legislative business to a standstill. But he also emerged as a prolific fundraiser and close Trump ally, helping shepherd the president's legislative agenda through a fractious Republican conference. Yes, but: Johnson had publicly insisted he intended to remain in Republican leadership even if the GOP lost control of the House. After suggesting to Fox News that he could return to Shreveport and start a lawn care business if Republicans lost the majority, Johnson told CBS News in October that he planned to remain the top House Republican regardless of the election's outcome. His political future had become the subject of private speculation among Republicans, with many lawmakers skeptical he would run for minority leader after a GOP loss. What's next: House Republicans are scheduled to hold leadership elections Nov. 10, with candidates facing a Friday deadline to declare their intentions. The race will be decided by a secret ballot of Republican members, requiring only a majority of the conference to win. Trump could play a pivotal role in determining Johnson's successor, and Republicans are watching closely to see whether he throws his support behind a candidate.

0c3eadf7373f.text: By — Thomas Beaumont, Associated Press Thomas Beaumont, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/the-u-s-political-map-anyones-guess-after-democratic-wave Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter The U.S. political map? Anyone's guess after Democratic wave Politics Nov 4, 2026 10:14 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Voters took a wrecking ball to the traditional map of political battlegrounds, electing Democrats in states that were long considered reliably Republican. LIVE RESULTS: 2026 Midterm Election Map Kansas, South Carolina, Texas, Ohio and Iowa, all states Republican Donald Trump easily won two years ago in the presidential election, backed Democrats for the U.S. Senate and occasionally governor, too, on Tuesday. Now the question is whether the results represent a durable tectonic shift — one that could reshape the path to the presidency — or a fluke stemming from Trump's deep unpopularity and voters' unhappiness with the rising cost of living. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Either way, Republicans are reeling from losses they never expected at the start of this election year. Kansas backed a Democratic senator for the first time since 1932 as Adam Hamilton, a Methodist megachurch pastor, defeated Republican Sen. Roger Marshall. WATCH LIVE: Takeaways from the 2026 midterms and answers to your election questions South Carolina rejected Republican Sen. Darline Graham in favor of pediatrician Annie Andrews, the first Democrat to win a Senate seat there since 1998. Democratic Senate Leader Chuck Schumer of New York called it a "generational remake of the Senate map." The Democratic victories went even deeper in Texas. James Talarico beat Ken Paxton for Senate, Gina Hinojosa ousted Gov. Greg Abbott, Vikki Goodwin dislodged Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, and Nathan Johnson defeated Mayes Middleton for attorney general. Until Tuesday, no Democrat had won a statewide race in Texas since 1994. WATCH: How does The Associated Press call 2026 midterm election winners? 4 things to know "This was a wave election in Texas and across the country," Patrick acknowledged in a statement. Democrats also swept to power in states that were once battlegrounds but were more recently viewed as out of reach. Iowa chose Rob Sand for governor and Josh Turek for senator, and Ohio backed Amy Acton for governor and Sherrod Brown for senator. Brown is a former senator who lost his seat just two years ago, defeated by Republican Bernie Moreno. This time, he beat Republican Sen. Jon Husted. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has given the country's highest award for women to the US First Lady, Melania Trump.
The Order of Princess Olha, 1st Class, was awarded to Melania Trump for her "significant personal contribution to humanitarian support for Ukraine", according to the presidential decree.
It comes after the end of ceasefire in Ukraine's southern region of Kherson, which allowed for the evacuation of several hundred people from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.
Russian and Ukrainian delegations - made up of ombudsmen who were involved in the evacuation mission as well as senior officials - are due to meet at the White House on Thursday on Melania Trump's invitation.
The White House said that Melania Trump had "independently initiated engagement between the two warring nations and successfully secured a ceasefire".
"This achievement marks an unprecedented diplomatic initiative by an American First Lady", it added.
Both the Russian and Ukrainian sides repeatedly thanked Melania Trump for brokering the ceasefire, though neither elaborated on the nature or extent of her involvement.
The delegations travelling to the White House on Thursday will include Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova, as well as Ukrainian MP Davyd Arakhamia and Russian senior official Kirill Dmitriev.
Lubinets and Lantratova travelled together into Oleshky last week, in an unusual show of cooperation between Russian and Ukrainian officials.
Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads Zelensky's party in parliament, has previously been part of the Ukrainian negotiating team during peace talks with Russia.
He was responsible for informal contact between the White House and Moscow during the ceasefire, according to diplomatic sources quoted by Ukrainian media, and has confirmed he will take part in Thursday's talks.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the Russian delegation will be made up of Lantratova and Kirill Dmitriev, a Russian businessman close to the Kremlin who has frequently taken part in US-brokered ceasefire talks.
Dmitriev and Arakhamia are veteran participants in high-level peace negotiations, and it is unusual for meetings involving such senior representatives to be convened through an initiative led by a US First Lady.
No details of what the White House event will entail have been shared. "There are important meetings ahead," said Lubinets in a social media post while announcing he was on his way to the US.
On Thursday Melania Trump will also deliver remarks on the ceasefire in Oleshky at 11:00 (16:00 GMT), the White House website said.
Zelensky's decree also cited Melania Trump's wider humanitarian work, including her efforts concerning Ukrainian children affected by the war, as reasons for giving her the Princess Olga award.
Melania Trump has largely remained discreet on foreign policy matters, but in 2025 she said an "open channel of communication" had been established with Russian President Vladimir Putin, allowing for Ukrainian children displaced in the war to be reunited with families.
Earlier this year the UN said the deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia constitutes a crime against humanity and a war crime.
According to Ukraine, almost 20,000 children have been illegally sent to Russia and Belarus since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Russian, Ukrainian and American representatives are also going to meet in Abu Dhabi next week in the first trilateral meeting since February. The talks will be focused on postwar security agreements and de-escalation, US envoy Steve Witkoff said on Monday.

eddbc7b49428.text:
There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.
The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.
Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.
Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.
Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.
The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.
Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”
Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

e41f14ba2a09.text:
DR Congo ordered an investigation into suspected illegal mining, after authorities seized thousands of tons of copper and cobalt. The probe could mark the start of a tougher response to illicit operators occupying sites, following years of complaints from some of the worldâs biggest mining companies. The justice minister said police, soldiers, and mining officials confiscated more than 500 trucks and machinery at several sites in the countryâs southeast.
DR Congo, the worldâs largest cobalt producer and a major copper supplier, is courting investment in metals used in electric cars and electronics and seeking greater economic benefits from its mineral wealth. But the government faces pressure to protect investorsâ mining rights, while safeguarding nearby communities, following repeated reports of harm to residentsâ health and livelihoods.

7410a05b6a7f.text:
Nigeriaâs state oil company NNPC could float up to a 10% stake in a Lagos initial public offering and follow it up with a secondary listing in London or New York, its CEO told Reuters. The listing would be the second major energy IPO in Nigeria after that of the Dangote refinery, which sought to raise $1.6 billion.
NNPC manages Nigeriaâs joint venture agreements with oil producers such as ExxonMobil, Shell, and TotalEnergies and has subsidiaries that operate petrol stations and own the countryâs currently dormant refineries. Africaâs biggest oil producer has recorded an uptick in hydrocarbon investments in the past three years. NNPC plays a key role in the countryâs revenue generation because of its multibillion-dollar interests in oil and gas assets, but critics say it is emblematic of Nigeriaâs decades-old mismanagement of its oil earnings.

6dca3e3e8894.text:
Kenyaâs growth prospects are being undercut by corruption and other governance challenges, the World Bank said in a report. The bank warned that graft could raise Kenyaâs borrowing needs, adding pressure to an already strained debt servicing burden that swallows roughly 60% of government revenue. It estimated that the country could incur a cost of 2% of GDP a year through higher fiscal deficits.
President William Ruto, who is seeking reelection next year, is looking to assuage frustrations about his governmentâs handling of the economy and the cost of living, which have spurred street protests in recent years. Kenyaâs economy grew 5.1% in the first half of 2026, a higher rate than the same period last year. But persistent deficits and rising debt service costs still leave the economy vulnerable, the World Bank said.

a152e1968cfa.text:
Senegalâs parliament rejected a revised budget on Tuesday, complicating the heavily indebted West African countryâs efforts to restore financing from the International Monetary Fund. A long-standing row over spending policies and relations with the IMF has created instability at the top of Senegalese politics, threatening to undermine creditorsâ confidence and delay IMF approval.
The governmentâs $13 billion plan included a cut to public investment in order to cover extra costs after high oil prices made energy subsidies more expensive. But Pastef, the majority party led by parliament speaker and former Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko, argued that households and essential public services would bear too much of the burden.
The country is seeking final approval for a three-year, $2.2 billion IMF loan program intended to ease budget pressures and unlock other financing. The deal, agreed in principle in September, would replace a program frozen after billions of dollars in unreported government debt emerged in 2024.

b8023f2e70f4.text:
CVS Health confirmed Tuesday night that it would split in two, reversing the 2018 deal that brought together insurance behemoth Aetna and the 9,000-store retail pharmacy chain into a $117 billion empire.
That deal ushered in a new era of healthcare consolidation, lacing together huge swaths of a highly regulated industry into a conglomerate critics said led to less competition and higher prices for consumers. Now, these companies are facing increasing regulatory scrutiny and political pressure in Washington, which is only expected to grow after Democrats regain control of Congress in January.
âWe believe based off of where we are and how weâre performing, the businesses are best served by splitting,â CVS Chief Executive David Joyner told The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday.

7a26ad486f19.text:
American voters roundly rejected data centers nearly anywhere they were on the ballot Tuesday, a rebuke sure to rattle investors already growing skittish about the AI buildout. Residents in more than 30 localities across nine states voted for moratoriums, outright bans, and other measures, some in direct response to specific projects underway. Edgewater, Fla. overwhelmingly voted to embed a data-center ban in the cityâs charter, and voters in Perry, Ohio passed a measure placing financial and operational constraints on hyperscalers seeking tax breaks. Democrats running in more than 130 federal and gubernatorial races aired anti-tech or anti-data center ads this cycle, one analysis showed. The pressure pushed some Republican candidates including Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, an AI booster just a few months ago, into promises of tougher regulation; he lost anyway.
Banks and asset managers financing the buildout have already begun treating local opposition as a credit risk, while hyperscalers are rushing to hire community liaisons. Meanwhile, tech companies bracing for the vibe shift are trying to rebrand the data centers as âcompute campusesâ with mixed results, Semaforâs Ashley Gold reported.

ed8ea721b222.text:
Prediction markets emerged as big winners of the midterms. Kalshi and Polymarket correctly called the Democratic sweep of Congress by wider margins than most polling models, as well as key battleground races, though they missed surprises like Texas Gov. Greg Abbottâs loss and Democratic Senate victories in Iowa and South Carolina.
Trading volume on down-ballot elections grew nearly fivefold from the 2024 cycle to this yearâs midterms to $1.8 billion, according to a Semafor analysis of the sitesâ public data feeds. Sports and crypto bets still dwarf election contracts across both platforms, and the 2026 midterms attracted less trading interest than the presidential race.
Prediction markets have been racing to win over the sports-betting and gambling industriesâ customers, executing aggressive ad campaigns to expand their influence. Kalshi has struck business partnerships with media outlets including CNN and Dow Jones, and its ad campaign on Meta rivals super PAC spending; Kalshi and Polymarket have also aired a slew of star-studded ads. But itâs one thing to bring in revenue, itâs another to do what the prediction markets say they do well: predict.

b03dab954375.text:
Lizâs view
After the presidential election exactly two years ago, Elon Musk and Vivek Ramaswamy rode into Washington as protagonists of a new type of politics, running the short-lived Department of Government Efficiency. Last night, both suffered the worst defeats of their political careers.
Musk had moved many of his businesses to Texas and spent more than $200 million to hold the state for Republicans â part of a 2026 blitz that dwarfs any political spending by a single donor in a single election cycle â with returns that were diminishing, if not outright negative. Senate candidate Ken Paxtonâs numbers faded the more Musk spent. Ramaswamy lost his bid for Ohio governor, where his Republican predecessor won four years ago by 25 points, a bigger swing than can be explained by Trumpâs unpopularity and the blue wave that crested nearly everywhere.
The two seemed to embody a new type of hard-edged conservative politics that lives at the intersection of Twitter and money, driven by wealthy and successful businessmen who believed their wealth and success would translate into political victories and personal popularity.
I watched last nightâs results from Ramaswamyâs gloomy election night party at an upscale Marriott in Columbus, Ohio, where a prayer circle was going in the womenâs bathroom by 9:45 pm. The outcomes suggest that money and its purest embodiments will be forced to slip politely back behind the curtain, to support more relatable public figures. Ramaswamyâs fellow anti-woke traveler and fringe Wall Streeter, James Fishback, lost even earlier, in the primaries for Florida governor.
The biggest money in American corporate history â the huge new investments in AI â also had a hard night, as Trumpâs embrace of the technology helped doom his party. Now they have to find new ways to recast their projects as pro-worker and community-friendly to make sure the AI buildout actually happens â and to find spokespeople more appealing than the DOGE twins.
Notable
- Shares in Muskâs Tesla and SpaceX slide about 5% in pre-market trading Wednesday after Democrats won in Texas, where both companies are headquartered.

3985f505255f.text:
Yinkaâs view
Last nightâs sweeping Democratic victory in the US midterm elections heralds a shift in vibes rather than policy.
As John âJTâ Tomaszewski, the National Endowment for Democracyâs senior director for Africa, told me, African countries will âstill struggleâ to get on the agenda because of the competing domestic priorities battling for lawmakersâ attention following a chastening electoral rebuke to President Donald Trump. There will, however, be more scope for congressional scrutiny of his administrationâs policies. Democrats will likely be keen to use hearings and investigations to revisit the dismantling of USAID and the human costs of cuts to foreign assistance.
Some of that would be welcomed because there are still key questions about the administrationâs decisions that probably deserve public answers. They will certainly embarrass the White House, which is kind of the point, says Cameron Hudson, a George W. Bush-era official. But I am less convinced that the theater of hearings will translate into meaningful changes in US-Africa policy.
Veteran Democrats understand this challenge. A former US ambassador under Joe Biden told me he would like to see â but doesnât expect â a more assertive Democratic agenda setting out what the US relationship with Africa should actually look like. But, this person suggested, there isnât any political appetite left for restoring traditional development assistance: âEverybodyâs moved on from that.â
Meanwhile, African governments have more immediate concerns. One African ambassador, who asked not to be identified, noted visa bans and restrictions currently affect more than half of sub-Saharan African countries, questioning how Washington can keep promoting âcommercial diplomacyâ while making it harder for African business leaders to travel to the US. âHow can the US keep talking about moving to do commerce with Africa when its business leaders canât visit?â the ambassador asked.
There may be a new mood in Washington, but for now, African governments will have to judge Washington by what it does, not what Democrats say about what Trump has done. As the ambassador said: âWeâll welcome the changes so we can have more soberness.â
Notable
- South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said the outcome of the US midterm elections signals a shift in the geopolitical landscape that could open the way for a reset in Pretoriaâs strained ties with Washington.

- Published
Inside the Republican Party, initial shock at the stunning election results on Tuesday night quickly gave way to anger with US President Donald Trump.
After Democrats won upset after upset in deep-red states like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina, some Republicans focused their ire on Trump, arguing that his focus on his legacy and indifference to voter concerns cost the party control of Congress.
"It's on him. It's not on anybody else. It's a total, complete rejection of President Trump," Bill Miller, a top Republican lobbyist in Texas, told the BBC. "This is a disaster of the first magnitude. Nobody saw it coming like this."
Most Republicans expected to lose control of the House and were clear-eyed about the challenge of holding onto the Senate in a tough election cycle that favoured the party out of power.
But some said in interviews that Trump dragged them down with unpopular policies, a low job approval rating and obsession over construction projects in Washington.
"It was just one mistake after another," said Gregg Peppin, a Republican strategist in Minnesota. "Clearly, in state after state, people did not like the president's policies."
A White House ally said public disapproval with Trump over the Iran war, tariffs and the administration's immigration crackdown created a "perfect storm" in November.
"There's palpable frustration [within] the party about how this has all played out," the person said, and much of it is directed at Trump. Anger with Trump "is extremely high".
The BBC spoke to a dozen party operatives, campaign officials, White House allies and others, many of whom spoke on background to offer a candid assessment of Trump's approach to the midterms.
Trump and Republicans had a lot riding on the outcome on Tuesday night. A stronger showing by the president's party - as happened in 2022, when Democrats under then-President Joe Biden lost just nine seats in the House, and gained one in the Senate - would have given Republicans some momentum heading into 2028.
But Trump will instead face a motivated Democratic majority in Congress that is eager to investigate the administration, block his judicial nominees and stymie the rest of his agenda.
The midterms have ushered in an uncertain new phase in Trump's second term and may force Republicans to start grappling with their post-Trump future.
"I don't think his influence is slipping," said Steve Scheffler, the Republican National Committeeman in Iowa, speaking on the eve of the election. Still, he said, when it came to the midterms, "there were things you wish he said differently".
Trump was silent for much of the night before posting a message on Truth Social after the House and Senate were called for Democrats.
"I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter," Trump wrote.
He said in later interviews with the New York Times and Fox News that he would accept the election results. Trump told Fox he was a "little bit surprised" by the election results, but noted that the president's party typically fared poorly in midterm elections.
Since 1934, the party in the White House has only gained seats in three midterm elections. While the Democratic gains in 2026 did not set a record, the party did win dozens of House races, state governor contests and Senate seats, including in states where the party had not been competitive for decades.
Before Tuesday, Democrats had not won a Senate seat in Kansas since 1932, and had not won a statewide race in Texas in more than three decades. The party also notched surprise upsets in other reliably red states like South Carolina that were thought to be safe seats for Republicans just weeks before Election Day.
Trump and Vice-President JD Vance held dozens of campaign rallies in the run-up to the midterms. The principal Trump-aligned Super PAC, MAGA Inc., spent hundreds of millions backing Republican candidates.
Trump allies said it was unfair to hold him responsible for the party's election losses. They pointed to the history of midterm elections, and said the party was saddled with weak Republican candidates in battleground states like Georgia, Michigan and Texas.
Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee in Texas, ran "the worst Senate campaign in the country from either side of the aisle," said another Texas Republican operative, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. "If Ken's campaign knocked on 100,000 doors I'd be shocked," the source said. The person added that Paxton's victorious Democratic opponent, James Talarico, ran "a really good and smart campaign."
Others defended Trump's autumn campaign schedule, noting that he had to balance his day job of running the country with midterm travel.
"He's the president. He's not going to spend his time campaigning 24/7," said Krish Mathrani, the Michigan Republican Party's youth chair. Mathrani said Trump's campaign rallies helped drive up enthusiasm among Republican voters. "President Trump is a turnout machine," he said.
That's true in presidential elections. But Trump's vaunted turnout operation has failed to deliver in elections when he's not on the ballot, and 2026 proved no different.
Voters rejected Trump's argument that the economy was better on his watch and that he was achieving his aims in the war with Iran. The effort by Trump to portray Democrats as extreme socialists also fell flat, as voters handed victories to moderates like Roy Cooper in North Carolina.
"That just didn't work with Cooper," said a Cooper campaign official. "Trying to tag him as some socialist liberal, that wasn't going to fly."
Trump often seemed disinterested in the midterms over the summer, the period of time when Republicans in Congress shifted their focus to the election.
Trump was consumed by the war with Iran abroad and his construction overhaul of Washington at home. The projects included the under-construction ballroom and a helipad on the South Lawn of the White House, renovati

88e83951d1ca.text:
- Published
Tennis great Rafael Nadal is set to join the board of Spanish football giants Real Madrid.
Nadal won 22 Grand Slam titles, two Olympic gold medals and helped Spain claim five Davis Cups before retiring in 2024.
Real's members will be asked to approve the 40-year-old's appointment to the board at a meeting later this month.
In a statement announcing the move, external, the club said Nadal was "one of the greatest legends in the history of sport and one of the most admired and recognised Spanish athletes in the world".
"It is a great source of pride that a figure of his sporting and human stature, a benchmark of Spanish and world sport, will become part of our board of directors and contribute, from this position of responsibility, to the present and future of our club," Real added.
The tennis legend - a boyhood Real fan who holds member's number 67,778 - included a photo of himself as a child in a club kit in his response to the news.
"I want to thank president Florentino Perez and the board for proposing that I join the board of directors of Real Madrid," Nadal said in his post on X, external.
"I have accepted this proposal with great excitement, a desire to learn, and a willingness to contribute everything I can."
It is currently unclear as to what responsibilities Nadal would hold on the club's board.
Perez was re-elected to serve a new four-year term as Real president in June, having held the office since 2009.
He swiftly appointed Jose Mourinho to a second spell as head coach, hoping to improve the club's fortunes after they went a second season without a trophy in La Liga, the Champions League or the Copa del Rey.
Real are currently third in the league after 11 games - three points behind defending champions Barcelona.

74c38403bbe9.text: Democrats' big night gives them a chance to turn voter anger over high energy prices into legislative action and congressional oversight, but divisions within the party could complicate their plans. Why it matters: This was an energy election . High gasoline prices, record diesel costs, and rising power bills fueled discontent with President Trump and his party. Voters' rebukes of data centers could slow the buildout of power-hungry AI infrastructure. The latest: Stunning Senate wins in red states and House wins nationwide propelled Democrats to control of both chambers, and flipped several governor's mansions. Energy costs were prominent in key races, such as Democrats hitting GOP rivals over farmers' bills in Iowa, Kansas and Ohio. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) bashed Greg Abbott (R) over his prior embrace of data centers in the state where developers are planning big projects. The data center backlash also featured in Ohio and Pennsylvania, where Sherrod Brown defeated Sen. Jon Husted (R) and Paige Cognetti unseated Rep. Rob Bresnahan (R). Both Republicans faced criticism over their support for data centers. State of play: A detailed Democratic energy agenda hasn't emerged, but there are early clues. Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer tied Republicans to electricity costs in his first comments after returns came in. Likely Speaker-in-waiting Hakeem Jeffries has vowed to quickly push an affordability agenda, with energy as a key pillar. He tasked Reps. Nikki Budzinski (D-Ill.) and Mike Levin (D-Calif.) with leading a "Gas and Utilities Affordability Working Group" that crafted ideas, though they remain under wraps. Another potential source of ideas: Hundreds of proposals backed this year by the 100-plus member House Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition. Some could gain bipartisan backing, like support for advanced nuclear power. But other areas would be largely symbolic, like restoring some IRA tax credits. Catch up quick: In the Senate, Schumer has offered broad areas of focus around grid development, affordability and consumer protections, and clean energy. He has vowed to restore clean energy tax credits, while pledging "systematic protection for consumers from rising prices." Other ideas include more support for energy efficiency and greater transparency in utility bills. The intrigue: Democrats did not make climate change a midterm messaging focus. Watch whether progressives push to revive an explicitly climate-focused agenda. My thought bubble: Don't expect Democrats to bring back their select committee on climate change, which Republicans disbanded after winning House control in 2022. There has not been a decision announced. But the party's shift away from messaging focused on climate is reason to be doubtful, even as global warming marches on. What's next: The most immediate thing to watch is how the results may affect the politics of the bipartisan permitting deal in the lame duck. Some House progressives have argued that Dems could get a permitting deal more to their liking next year. But backers of the current bill see almost no chance of a political opening to craft a more liberal bill that Trump would sign or could even clear the Senate. The permitting fight has also opened rifts within the Democratic coalition, with multiple unions and the clean energy industry backing the bill, while many environmentalists are undecided or flatly opposed. The debate also highlights broader divisions between the "abundance movement" and progressives who want a harder line against fossil fuels Those divisions could extend well beyond the lame duck permitting fight, influencing future legislative priorities and the policy agendas of presidential hopefuls as 2028 jockeying begins in earnest. The bottom line: One thing already clear is that Democrats are lining up energy-focused oversight of Trump's diesel agreement with Moscow, offshore wind policies and much more. Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

Wild weather is a way of life for people living along the coast in the Philippines, Taiwan, China and Japan. But the last few months have been extraordinary.
A wave of intense and, at times, unpredictable storms exacerbated by the El NiÃ±o weather pattern has killed dozens, shuttered major airports and wiped out crops and infrastructure across a swathe of East Asia.
In October, nearly all of Taiwan shut down as a monster storm big enough to engulf the island of 23 million roared towards its north-eastern coast. Equivalent to a category five hurricane, Typhoon Champi's 295km/h (193mph) winds had the power to flatten homes and whip up destructive waves.
Thankfully it did not make landfall in Taiwan, skirting past the island while dousing it in rain. But it had far-reaching impacts: hundreds of flights were cancelled in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. In the Philippines' Batanes archipelago, seaside highways shut as huge waves crashed onto the shore, and in southern Japan's Okinawa islands, power was cut to 15,000 homes.
El NiÃ±o is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon in which warm waters pooling in the eastern Pacific and altered wind patterns drive extreme weather events around the world.
It happens around every two to seven years, lasting for around a year. This year's El NiÃ±o, which the UK Met Office has forecast to be the "strongest in living memory", is likely to last until February or March.
In June, Japan watched two storms - Typhoon Mekkhala and Severe Tropical Storm Higos - race towards its eastern coast simultaneously, forcing one million people to evacuate. In July, Tropical Storm Narra grazed China's southern coast along Guangxi, submerging villages and displacing tens of thousands.
August brought Super Typhoon Dolphin, which churned across the Pacific for 16 days - before slamming into eastern China, triggering heavy floods and dozens of casualties.
Later that month Typhoon Saudel made landfall in three south-eastern Chinese cities over one week, shutting transport networks and forcing thousands to evacuate.
'Burning with fever'
The Pacific Ocean, heated to record levels by El NiÃ±o, is now brimming with typhoon energy, according to the Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) metric which measures the total intensity of a season's storms. This year, the ACE reading for South East and East Asia is forecast to be nearly double the 30-year average.
El NiÃ±o also affects wind patterns and in this case, that means typhoons are tending to form further east than usual. They are also becoming stronger as they remain over warm waters for longer.
The Pacific can be likened to someone "burning with fever", says Ana Liza Solis, head of climatology at the Philippines' national weather bureau. "It can go into convulsions soon," she said at a press briefing in Manila in September.
Forecasts suggest the worst may not be over. Last month, sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific - the area monitored by the Japan Meteorological Agency for its El NiÃ±o predictions - soared to 4C above normal, the highest since records began in 1949. The previous record - 3.6C - was set in December 1997.
China's climate agency has warned of sea surface temperatures continuing to rise over the next three months because of the El NiÃ±o.
Despite typhoon season usually peaking around September to October, this is likely to raise concerns across a region that has already been battered by back-to-back storms.
'Very, very scary' simulations
In August, Typhoon Chan-Hom baffled storm watchers in Japan by crossing the country from east to west, as opposed to the usual south-to-north trajectory. Japan's well-resourced and prepared authorities were able to evacuate people swiftly, but this would be far more challenging in some neighbouring countries.
To get a better picture of how rising temperatures could amplify the risks, Manila-based climatologist Rafaela Jane Delfino and colleagues simulated the effects of warmer conditions on the Philippines' most recent monster storms, including 2013's Super Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) which killed more than 6,000 people.
They arrived at what she describes as "very, very scary findings": higher temperatures increased total accumulated rainfall by 26%. It's a devastating prospect in a country where flooding from monsoon rains and some 20 tropical storms per year has emerged as one of the main disaster risks.
In recent years, floods have paralysed entire cities for days, and tired of the annual ordeal, Filipinos have taken to the streets to protest against corruption which they say is gnawing away at millions of dollars from flood-control projects.
Delfino, in an article on the University of the Philippines website, insists leaders and officials must gain a better understanding of climate hazards if communities are to be better prepared.
Preparing for the onslaught
Countries are bracing for the immediate impact. Japan has urged citizens to stockpile food and essentials for the typhoon season, and to secure outdoor furniture that could become deadly projectiles when typhoon winds hit. China has asked local officials to identify vulnerable areas and is upgrading its warning and monitoring systems.
The Philippines and its South East Asian neighbours are preparing for disruptions to food production, especially rice, and have increased support for famers, including the provision of fertilisers.
But what happens in the long term is less clear. The window for governments to act on El NiÃ±o is "closing", the United Nations Development Programme in Asia and the Pacific said recently.
"How severely a community experiences an El NiÃ±o is decided years in advance, by where roads and settlements are built, how water is managed, who is covered by social protection and whether public budgets have room to absorb a shock.
"Every El NiÃ±o tests the resilience we have built; this one should also drive us to build more," it added.

dae6394b592a.text: By — Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/pope-leo-xiv-welcomes-bob-dylan-to-the-vatican-in-a-brief-visit Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Pope Leo XIV welcomes Bob Dylan to the Vatican in a brief visit Arts Nov 4, 2026 6:06 PM EST VATICAN CITY (AP) — Bob Dylan came knockin' on Pope Leo XIV' s door Wednesday, as the American singer-songwriter and poet visited with the American pope at the Vatican during a break between concert dates in Italy. The Vatican said the encounter was brief, with Leo giving Dylan a rosary and Dylan presenting the pope with a copy of his autobiography, "Chronicles: Volume One." READ MORE: Kennedy Center names 2026 honorees as Trump renovation battle moves show offsite Leo had quoted from an unpublished protest song Dylan penned in 1963, "Go Away You Bomb," in his 2026 book "Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift." Leo was warning against the race to rearm and the recourse to nuclear weapons and quoted the lyric, addressed to a hypothetical atomic bomb: "I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an' man-handled." Two Vatican officials accompanied Dylan: the Rev. Antonio Spadaro, a Vatican culture ministry official who also accompanied Patti Smith to a July audience with Leo; and Andrea Monda, the editor of the Vatican newspaper, L'Osservatore Romano. Spadaro said Dylan had wanted to speak with Leo, and the two met in private for a few minutes. In an essay in L'Osservatore Romano, he recalled that the former Robert Prevost, who was born in Chicago in 1955, grew up familiar with Dylan's music. He also noted that Dylan was very familiar with St. Augustine of Hippo, the inspiration of Leo's spirituality and Augustinian religious order, penning "I Dreamed I Saw St. Augustine" for the 1967 album John Wesley Harding. Dylan, who won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 2016, wore a black hoodie and a loose tie. Vatican photos of the encounter showed him with the hood over his head. It wasn't Dylan's first papal encounter: He played for Pope John Paul II, and thousands of other people, in 1997 during a concert capping a religious congress in Bologna, Italy. Dylan, who changed his name from Robert Zimmerman, was born to a Jewish family in Minnesota. He famously became a born-again Christian in 1979 and alienated some of his longtime fans with songs like "Gotta Serve Somebody" and "Saved." In more recent years, Dylan has been more circumspect about his religious beliefs. In a 2022 interview with the Wall Street Journal, Dylan said that he was a "religious person" who reads the scriptures, meditates and prays. Dylan met with Leo in between concert dates in Italy. He played in Milan on Monday and is playing Rome on Thursday. In his most recent concert before the meeting with the pope, Dylan sang his 1997 song "Tryin' to Get to Heaven" that contains the lyric, "I've been all around the world, boys/Now I'm trying to get to heaven before they close the door." AP reporter Scott Bauer contributed from Madison, Wisconsin. Democrats’ historic sweep of Texas on Tuesday raises new possibilities of environmental reform after more than 30 years of Republican rule in the home of the nation’s oil and gas industry.
That includes opportunities to cement safeguards for data center development, lower energy costs and, over time, appoint new commissioners to the state’s regulatory agencies and boost environmentally protective standards.
“We have a generational shift in leadership here,” said Adrian Shelley, state director of Public Citizen, a consumer advocacy group. “I think there’s going to be a real appetite for reform.”
Both the U.S. Senate and governor races were called before midnight Central Time, quickly crushing the longheld skepticism of the potential of a Democrat-led Texas. Democrats also took the House in the state Legislature.
The blue wave in Texas resulted, in part, from an upswell of public outrage over the state’s booming buildout of data centers for artificial intelligence that are gobbling massive amounts of electricity and failing to disclose their water use, experts said Wednesday. When the Democratic administration takes office in January, data centers will sit at the center of its political crosshairs.
“The new state leadership has a clear mandate to rein in the data center industry,” Shelley said. “I think the days of Texas being unequivocally open for business are over.”
Gina Hinojosa, a Democratic state representative who was largely unknown earlier this year, unseated three-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who was backed by some of the richest and most powerful forces across the country.
Hinojosa will be the first Hispanic politician to lead the state, where Latinos make up the largest population, and will preside over the second-largest state economy in the country, after California.
The victory of James Talarico against Attorney General Ken Paxton ends decades of Republican rule in the U.S. Senate, with the last Democratic senator elected in 1988. It was also the most expensive Senate race in history, with the richest man on earth, Elon Musk, contributing more than $160 million to secure Paxton’s victory.
Democrat Jon Rosenthal defeated a former Tarrant County GOP chair with a storied record of extremism, Bo French, for one of three seats at the state’s oil and gas regulator, the Railroad Commission.
“Pretty much everyone who won the statewide level is a champ on the environment,” said Luke Metzger, executive director of Environment Texas. “That’s really exciting.”
Midterm Shift Signals Big Risk for Data Centers in Texas
Hinojosa’s election has panicked the data center industry over its future in one of the largest markets in the U.S. While Abbott switched from issuing an enthusiastic invitation for data centers to invest and develop in Texas to a list of stringent directives, Hinojosa has campaigned on calling an immediate moratorium on new data centers.
Voters clearly want the data center industry to be held accountable, said the Lone Star Chapter of the Sierra Club’s legislative director, Cyrus Reed.
“For a long time, they’ve had not only a seat at the table, they’ve actually been creating the table with some of the laws that have been passed,” Reed said.
Hinojosa’s election signals a significant shift in Texas’ data center policies, global analysis firm Wood Mackenzie said Wednesday.
Even so, the state will remain a leading market for data center investments, given its renewable resources, natural gas infrastructure and regulatory autonomy from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, Wood Mackenzie added.
Jess Heck, the director of Texas government affairs for the Data Center Coalition, the industry’s largest trade group, said its members will continue to engage with residents and local leaders to understand community priorities and ensure the growth of digital infrastructure delivers clear benefits for Texans.
“Enhancing affordability, creating jobs, and keeping the state’s economy strong are top priorities for Texans,” Heck said in a statement to Inside Climate News. “Data centers can continue to play a crucial role in advancing those priorities by bringing investment to local communities and generating critical tax revenue to support local governments and school districts across the state.”
The Dallas-Fort Worth region has the largest concentration of data centers in the state. The most rapid expansion of the industry is in Ellis County, some 30 minutes south of downtown Dallas.
On Election Day, Lacey Hamel, 39, and Jazmin Villegas, 44, stood outside the Red Oak Municipal Center waving at voters driving in and out of the building’s lot. The two wore bright yellow shirts that said, “No More Data Centers.” They’re members of Save Our Red Oak, a group tracking and trying to slow down the expansion of data centers across seven campuses in the city.
As in other rural Texas counties with swaths of land, data centers emerged as a critical issue for the election in Red Oak.
Members of the Red Oak group had asked Abbott to call a special legislative session over the industry’s rapid growth. “That ship has sailed,” Hamel said.
Among their data center protest group, set in a staunchly Republican county where nearly two-thirds of residents voted for President Donald Trump in 2024, several people crossed party lines over frustrations on data centers, Hamel said. It informed how she voted, too.
“This is one of those issues where it’s affecting our air, it’s affecting our land, it’s affecting our water, it’s affecting our kids,” Hamel said.

An international team of lawyers on Wednesday filed a coordinated battery of lawsuits against JBS, the world’s largest meat company, and its financiers, accusing them of money laundering in connection with the destruction of the Amazon rainforest.
The 14 legal actions, filed in four European jurisdictions, accuse JBS and its affiliated banks, asset managers, accountants and lawyers of criminal complicity in connection with the meat giant’s purchase of cattle from deforested land, in violation of Brazilian law. JBS, a historically Brazilian company, is now officially headquartered in the Netherlands, though it continues to maintain major operations in Brazil and to source much of its beef from the Amazon and neighboring ecosystems.
The lawsuits are the latest attempts by advocacy groups to open up new legal avenues to challenge JBS, which recent research has found emits as much planet-warming methane as oil giants ExxonMobil and Shell combined.
The Transnational Legal Coalition, a newly formed network of advocacy groups and lawyers that prosecutes environmental crimes and filed the complaints, says the lawsuits are the first in a series of legal efforts that will target deforestation in JBS’s supply chain. Raising livestock is the biggest driver of forest loss in the world’s largest rainforest, a crucial ecosystem for stabilizing Earth’s atmosphere and a massive harbor for biodiversity.
The coalition commissioned a study to support their filings, conducted by the environmental research group AidEnvironment, which found that JBS was linked to more than 16 million deforested acres, both through direct and indirect suppliers.
The complaints focus on European Union anti-money laundering laws, which require financial institutions, attorneys and accountants to do “enhanced due diligence” on businesses that have a high risk of deforestation in their supply chains. They allege JBS makes huge profits off cattle raised on land that is likely criminally deforested, and therefore, the cattle are criminal property.
They argue these institutions, which include the banks Barclays and Rabobank, the asset manager BlackRock and accounting firms KPMG and EY, were all obligated to perform enhanced due diligence but did not. The coalition also filed a criminal complaint with public prosecutors in the Dutch criminal justice system against JBS directly, accusing the company of money laundering.
“If the European enabler complied with its enhanced due diligence obligations, it would have found out about the risk that JBS is engaged in money laundering and would either have stopped working with JBS or reported them to the criminal authorities,” said George Collecott, an attorney with the Global Legal Action Network, one of the coalition members. “As each of the financial institutions have a long-standing relationship with JBS, they haven’t done that.”
The EU’s anti-money laundering law says a failure to report suspected money laundering to authorities is an offense by both the company and company employees, including compliance officers.
“What we’re really asking is for the regulators in the U.K., Germany, Netherlands and Ireland to open an investigation into these financial institutions and investigate whether there has been a failure of these due diligence obligations,” Collecott said. “It’s really making sure the banks can’t plead ignorance.”
In a response to Inside Climate News, a Barclays spokesperson said the company had reviewed the legal complaint but could not comment. The bank said it has conducted enhanced due diligence for clients engaged in beef production since 2021.
JBS did not respond to a request for comment, nor did Rabobank, Blackrock, KPMG or EY.
As part of its long-sought effort to list on the New York Stock Exchange, which it accomplished successfully in 2025, JBS re-incorporated in the Netherlands, where many companies take advantage of Dutch tax exemptions.
Dutch law, however, requires companies to meet a “duty of care” threshold, which includes harms caused by greenhouse gases. That prompted Greenpeace Netherlands in April to file a preliminary letter with the Dutch authorities, indicating its intent to sue the company.
In this case, Greenpeace Netherlands plans to sue because of the company’s expansion into Nigeria. In its letter, the group asked for details about the company’s intended operations there, its first on the African continent. So far, Greenpeace Netherlands says, neither the Nigerian government nor JBS has provided information about its $2.5 billion investment to develop poultry, beef and pork processing facilities there.
As JBS expands its global footprint, it has also pulled back on its climate commitments. In July, the company issued its annual sustainability report, in which it said it would abandon its previous goal of reaching net-zero emissions by 2040. It also dropped any mentions of its goal to eliminate deforestation connected to its Brazilian supply chains.

Johnson, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/shorter-days-and-dark-afternoons-can-trigger-depression-heres-how-to-fight-back Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Shorter days and dark afternoons can trigger depression. Here's how to fight back Health Nov 4, 2026 5:57 PM EST As winter approaches and daylight hours grow shorter, people prone to seasonal depression can feel it in their bodies and brains. The millions of people estimated to have seasonal affective disorder, or SAD, typically have episodes of depression that begin in the fall and ease in the spring or summer. One trigger for SAD is when clocks revert to standard time, which happened Sunday across much of the U.S., bringing darker afternoons. A milder form, subsyndromal SAD, is recognized by medical experts, and there's also a summer variety of seasonal depression, though less is known about it. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. In 1984, a team led by Dr. Norman Rosenthal, then a researcher at the National Institutes of Health, first described SAD and coined the term. "I believe that because it is easy to remember, the acronym has stuck," he said. Scientists are trying to understand what causes SAD No single cause for seasonal affective disorder has been identified. The disorder affects many more women than men, according to the NIH. Symptoms can be similar to depression, and can include persistent feelings of hopelessness or pessimism and difficulty concentrating, remembering, or making decisions. In one effort to better understand what's going on, scientists are learning how specialized cells in our eyes turn the blue wavelength part of the light spectrum into neural signals affecting mood and alertness. WATCH: What to know about treating Seasonal Affective Disorder Sunlight is loaded with the blue light, so when the cells absorb it, our brains' alertness centers are activated and we feel more wakeful and possibly even happier. Researcher Kathryn Roecklein at the University of Pittsburgh tested people with and without SAD to see how their eyes reacted to blue light. As a group, people with SAD were less sensitive to blue light than others, especially during winter months. That suggests one possible cause for wintertime depression. When days get shorter, powerful light can help Many people with SAD respond to light therapy, said Dr. Paul Desan of Yale University's Winter Depression Research Clinic. The therapy can involve exposure to bright light for about a half hour in the morning, powered by devices that emit light about 20 times brighter than regular indoor light. Research supports using a light that's about 10,000 lux, a measure of brightness. You need to use it for 30 minutes every morning, according to the research. Desan said this can help not only people with SAD but also those with less-severe winter blahs. WATCH: What to know about the latest push to make daylight saving time permanent Special lights run from $50 to more than $400. Some products marketed for SAD are too dim to do much good, Desan said. Yale has tested products and offers a list of recommendations, and the nonprofit Center for Environmental Therapeutics has a consumer guide to selecting a light. If your doctor diagnosed you with SAD, check with your insurance company to see if the cost of a light might be covered. Talk therapy and medication can also help some with SAD Antidepressant medications are a first-line treatment for SAD, along with light therapy. Doctors also recommend keeping a regular sleep schedule and walking outside, even on cloudy days. Light therapy's benefits can fade when people stop using it. One type of talk therapy — cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT — has been shown in studies to have more durable effects, University of Vermont researcher Kelly Rohan said. READ MORE: Daylight saving time causes lower productivity and higher health care costs, studies say CBT involves working with a therapist to identify and modify unhelpful thoughts. Working with a therapist can help people take small steps toward having fun again, Rohan said. Try planning undemanding but enjoyable activities to break out of hibernation mode, including getting out and seeing a friend for coffee. Carla K. US regulatorsâ approval of a cheaper HIV shot has lifted hopes in some of the worldâs poorest countries, many of which are reeling from Western aid cuts.
The FDA granted tentative approval of a generic lenacapavir, a twice-a-year injection that helps prevent HIV infection. The move will make the drug available for $40 per person a year in 120 low- and middle-income countries, the Associated Press reported.
Washingtonâs funding cuts to some HIV-prevention programs in Africa left efforts there floundering, sparking fears that the continent could see hundreds of thousands of additional deaths from AIDS.
A large-scale rollout of the affordable drug could help âbring an end to the HIV epidemic,â a global health advocate said.

Another wave of cyberattacks against European supermarkets this week compromised refrigeration systems for the second time in a month, rekindling fears over the security of critical infrastructure.
While such attacks so far have been costly and inconvenient, a new era of AI-enabled cyberwarfare could portend more devastating disruptions. Franceâs national blood service, which 1,900 hospitals rely on, said Tuesday that hackers raised the temperature at cold storage units, but the attack was thwarted before any damage was done.
Experts frequently blame Russia for such incidents: Many Kremlin-aligned hacks are unsophisticated, but âthe problem is that the more they poke around, the more it is probable they can find something critical that wasnât protected well,â a cyber analyst said.

095de24ca37b.text: By — Danica Kirka, Associated Press Danica Kirka, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/ex-prince-andrew-called-to-testify-in-civil-case-1st-royal-in-156-years-to-get-witness-summons Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Ex-Prince Andrew called to testify in civil case, 1st royal in 156 years to get witness summons World Nov 4, 2026 5:44 PM EST LONDON (AP) — The former Prince Andrew has been called to testify as a witness in a civil fraud trial, marking what is believed to be the first time in more than 150 years that a member of the royal family has received a witness summons, British media reported on Wednesday. The summons comes after a judge at the High Court in London gave the green light last month for the former prince, now known as Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, to be called to testify about payments he allegedly received from the parties in the case. Mountbatten-Windsor may apply to have the summons set aside, so there is no guarantee he will testify. The lawsuit was filed by Turkish national Nebahat Evyap Isbilen, who alleges that her former adviser Selman Turk misappropriated tens of millions of pounds of her money. As part of the case, she says Turk misled her about a 750,000-pound ($1 million) payment he arranged for her to make to Mountbatten-Windsor in 2019. Mountbatten-Windsor, a younger brother of King Charles III, repaid the money in 2021 and he is not a party to the suit. Turk claims that Isbilen authorized the payment in hopes that Mountbatten-Windsor might be able to use his connections to help her husband, who has been imprisoned in Turkey since 2015. Isbilen alleges that her husband is the victim of political persecution. Isbilen's attorneys said last month that they believed this would be the first time since 1870 that a member of the royal family was subject to a witness summons. At that time, the future King Edward VII, then the Prince of Wales, was called to testify in the divorce case brought by Charles Mordaunt, a baronet and member of Parliament. The prince accepted the summons and denied having improper relations with Mordaunt's wife, Harriet Mordaunt. Mountbatten-Windsor is facing his own legal troubles as several British police forces investigate his links to the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. British authorities began their inquiries after the U.S. Department of Justice released millions of pages of documents from its investigation of Epstein earlier this year. Charles stripped Mountbatten-Windsor of his princely title in late 2025 as he tried to shield the royal family from the scandal surrounding his brother's relationship with Epstein. Georgia voters have broken the Republican grip on the state’s energy regulator, giving Democrats control of the Public Service Commission for the first time in 30 years.
Their victories come amid growing frustration over rising electricity bills, a data center buildout and calls for greater accountability from Georgia Power.
On Tuesday, Democrat Peter Hubbard was reelected after winning a seat in a special election last year. Democrat Sheila Edwards, a community activist and business owner, also won a seat.
“Thank you, Georgia!” Hubbard said in a Facebook post early Wednesday. “You have spoken, and Shelia Edwards and I are ready to keep fighting for a future that puts Georgians at the center of our energy policy.”
“Throughout this campaign, I’ve talked about putting People Before Profits, addressing rising utility bills, bringing transparency and accountability to the Public Service Commission, and making sure large data centers pay their fair share,” Edwards said in a Facebook post. “Those commitments don’t end with an election.”
The result is a major shift for the PSC, which regulates public utilities, including the state’s largest energy utility, Georgia Power. Commissioners are tasked with regulating utility rates, overseeing utility service and reliability and approving utility resource plans and major infrastructure investments.
Republicans held a 5-0 majority on the commission from 2006 until 2025, when Hubbard and fellow Democrat Alicia Johnson won seats.
During those nearly two decades, Georgia Power customers saw major rate increases in 2007, 2010, 2013, 2019 and 2022. Since 2023, six more have raised monthly bills by about $44.
Much of the increases were driven by costs tied to the troubled expansion of nuclear Plant Vogtle, in Burke County. Construction began in 2009 after commission approval, with the project expected to finish in 2017 before a series of setbacks. In the end, it took 15 years to complete and went more than $17 billion over budget. While customers continue to pay for the project, the costs of building out gas plants to power data centers have been tacked onto their bills.
“The results show that people are very angry about data centers and climate emissions,” said Patty Durand, founder of Georgians for Affordable Energy. She pointed to a series of protests demanding clean energy in 2024 and 2025. “I won’t pretend it’s not about high bills too, but those are tied to gas and data centers as well.”
The election of Hubbard and Johnson in 2025 was the first signal Georgia voters wanted change in the way utilities, and especially rate increases, are regulated. “It was shocking,” said Charles Bullock, a political science professor at the University of Georgia. “It may have been a straw in the wind of the state’s political realignment.”
Johnson won a five-year term, while Hubbard was elected for just one year, due to a special election schedule. His reelection means he will be in office until 2032, with an early stamp of approval from voters. 
Edwards beat first-time candidate Josh Tolbert by 10.6 points and Hubbard beat former Republican Commissioner Fitz Johnson by 12.8 points, the largest margin of any statewide candidate this cycle in Georgia other than U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff, who beat his Republican opponent, U.S. Rep. Mike Collins, by about 17 points.
The Democrats’ victories came despite being outspent by Republican candidates and outside groups. The Republican campaigns raised more than $1 million combined, largely driven by Fitz Johnson’s fundraising, compared with less than $600,000 for the Democratic candidates. Democratic fundraising relied more heavily on individual donations, while Republican candidates received substantially more money from corporate donors.

According to an analysis by the Energy and Policy Institute, the two Republican candidates received a combined $214,100 in contributions of $500 or more from donors associated with entities regulated by the PSC, compared with just $6,500 for the Democratic candidates.
Outside spending in the races topped $5 million, much of it going toward television, digital and other campaign advertising. More than $3 million went toward supporting Tolbert, nearly all of it through a group called Powering Georgia’s Future, which is backed by a separate entity, Competence Matters. Competence Matters is not required to disclose donors. Both Powering Georgia’s Future and Competence Matters websites went dark following the election.
Another $1.5 million was spent through Georgia Conservation Voters in support of Hubbard and Edwards. That money came from the group’s national affiliate, the League of Conservation Voters, as well as from entities including the Jane Fonda Climate PAC and Green Advocacy Project.
Grassroots efforts by volunteers, watchdog groups and activists also helped support the Democratic campaigns. A coalition of more than 30 groups, including Georgians for Affordable Energy, Georgia WAND and Young Democrats of Georgia, organized social media outreach and distributed flyers, yard signs and bumper stickers to compete with the better-funded Republican campaigns.
The results reflect growing political attention to energy costs and utility policy. Nationally, Democrats flipped Senate and House seats in deep red states where Americans have been hit hardest by energy prices and data center buildouts. 
The Democratic majority on the PSC will have an opportunity to follow through on campaign promises to increase scrutiny of Georgia Power and strengthen consumer protections. After their election last year, Alicia Johnson and Hubbard opposed a $16 billion grid expansion dominated by natural gas, which ultimately passed 3-2. 3eb9fe28310b.text: By — Josh Funk, Associated Press Josh Funk, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/whats-next-in-the-investigation-of-the-learjet-crash-in-florida-that-killed-9 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What's next in the investigation of the Learjet crash in Florida that killed 9? Nation Nov 4, 2026 5:37 PM EST Investigators are just beginning the lengthy process of determining why a business jet plummeted from the sky in Florida after encountering a thunderstorm and slammed into the ground with such force that it created a crater and shattered the plane. The National Transportation Safety Board is leading the investigation into the crash that killed all nine people aboard the Bahamas-bound Learjet, and it will likely take more than a year to determine the cause. READ MORE: All 9 people aboard a jet that crashed in Florida have died, transportation secretary says Dramatic bystander videos combined with the the disturbing final radio transmissions as the pilots realize their fate will give investigators important clues. The cockpit voice recorder would also help if investigators can find it intact. "Our mission is to understand not just what happened, but why it happened, and to recommend changes to prevent it from happening again," NTSB member Tom Chapman said. Here's what investigators are doing now and what comes next: Investigators are gathering critical evidence The NTSB team will spend days collecting every piece of the plane they can find. Investigators said Tuesday that pieces of a key part of the tail called the elevator, which controls the plane's pitch, were found more than a mile away from the main crater. That confirms the plane started to break apart before impact. Chapman said investigators are searching for the Learjet's cockpit voice recorder because it could provide crucial details about what the pilots said to each other as they encountered turbulence, ice formed on the wings and they lost control of the aircraft. "That will be very important data," Chapman said. But being unable to find that recorder won't doom the investigation. "Without it, our folks are very, very good. We're still able to do some incredible detective work and determine how things transpired." READ MORE: Palm Beach plane crash footage isn't AI-generated, despite social media claims The co-pilot told air traffic controllers that the plane was being thrown up and down more than 700 feet (213 meters) and she asked them for a better route through the area. It's not clear why the pilots didn't fly around the storms. Torrential rains in Florida over the past week have hindered the investigators' work. The crater filled with rainwater, possibly concealing parts of the wreckage under water, and a utility pole had to be removed. The NTSB asked anyone who finds part of the plane to report that to investigators to collect. The initial NTSB report will take about a month The agency's findings so far are limited, but its experts will publish a preliminary report describing the facts of what happened about 30 days after the crash. It won't include analysis or cause, which will come in a later more detailed report. The force of the crash and the fire destroyed much of the plane. Any evidence investigators are able to gather will be taken to a secure hangar where they can test or try to reassemble smashed components to better understand what happened. READ MORE: Parts of jet's tail found more than a mile from plane crash site in South Florida, official says Retired airline pilot and aviation safety expert John Cox said he doesn't understand why the plane descended from its cruising altitude of 41,000 feet (12,500 meters) as it approached the storms. The pilots steered around a larger storm cell but appeared to head directly into a rapidly developing smaller one, Cox said. "If I'm looking at thunderstorms, I'd rather be at 41 than at 35. You've got a better view, you're more likely to be on top of it, or at least, in the very wispy tops of it," Cox said. "I don't understand why they came down." Investigators will try to determine whether they knew that storm cell was there, what the plane's weather radar showed and whether the pilots checked any other weather services. Investigators will dig deeper Weather will be a key early focus of the investigation. NTSB experts will work with the National Weather Service and the Federal Aviation Administration to get a better idea of what the plane encountered at around 35,000 feet (11,000 meters). Images that overlay the flight path atop weather radar maps show the Learjet flew directly into a small red storm cell that quickly worsened. But the agency will consider a myriad of factors that may have contributed to the crash. Investigators will review maintenance records and any history of problems with the plane. They will also interview officials at Upper Jets, the company that operated the flight, as well as air traffic controllers and people who work at the airport in Austin, Texas, from where the plane departed. Videos and photos shot by bystanders can also provide crucial clues about what happened. The NTSB will also collect surveillance footage that might show the crash. In certain high-profile crashes, the NTSB can hold investigative hearings during which investigators question people, as it did after last year's UPS plane crash. The final report could take more than a year Generally, it takes 12 to 18 months for the NTSB to complete a crash investigation, but complicated cases can take longer. NTSB's roughly 400 workers are pursuing more than 1,200 active investigations. Final reports include extensive details about what happened and identify the probable causes. The NTSB recommends changes to prevent similar crashes and improve safety, but it doesn't have the power to require those changes to be installed or enforced. The responsibility for adopting those falls to the FAA, the industry and Congress

9081f3b8fd97.text: By — Russ Bynum, Associated Press Russ Bynum, Associated Press By — Chris O'Meara, Associated Press Chris O'Meara, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/florida-sheriff-says-2-dead-including-suspect-as-witnesses-report-shooting-at-tampa-office-complex Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Florida sheriff says 2 dead, including suspect, as witnesses report shooting at Tampa office complex Nation Nov 4, 2026 5:14 PM EST TAMPA, Fla. (AP) — Florida authorities said two people were dead, including a suspect, after witnesses reported a shooting Wednesday at Citibank's sprawling business complex that employs thousands in the Tampa area. More than 360 deputies swarmed the campus, the Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office said. TV video showed long lines of workers streaming out of the office buildings. The sheriff's office said in a social media post that it had "responded to an active threat and is currently clearing the building." The sheriff's office said a suspect and one other person were dead. It was not immediately known whether anyone else was injured. "We believe this is a targeted incident," Sheriff Chad Chronister posted on the social platform X. The Citibank campus in suburban Tampa includes four three-story office buildings that house thousands of the banking giant's employees. Radio traffic on Broadcastify.com from officers who responded to the Citibank complex described an exhaustive floor-by-floor search of the complex's buildings. Officers found people sheltering in locked rooms and closets, and carefully escorted them from the buildings and parking garage. Citigroup said in a statement that it was "aware of an incident" at the complex and was cooperating with authorities. Doug Merritt said he was startled when his son called him from the Citibank campus, saying he had fled after hearing gunshots. "He was very close to it," Merritt told The Associated Press. "He left all this stuff where he was at and he was able to get out of there." For around an hour, Merritt said, he didn't know whether his son was safe as he struggled to get in touch over a bad internet connection. "I wanted him to get to safety," he said. "I was upset." Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia. AP journalists Cybele Mayes-Osterman in Chicago, R.J. Rico in Atlanta and Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed to this story.
