Dem lawmakers vow inquest into CISA cuts, intel policy
House Democrats will investigate the administration's cyberdefense cuts, while Senate Dems will control confirmation hearings for the officials who lead the nation’s security agencies.
House Democrats plan to investigate how the Trump administration’s cuts to the nation’s cyberdefense agency affected its ability to protect federal networks and help states secure elections, while their Senate counterparts vow to scrutinize whether intelligence agencies can deliver findings that contradict the president without putting analysts’ jobs at risk.
Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., who is in line to chair the House Homeland Security Committee when Democrats take both houses of Congress in January, said he and his colleagues would examine the department’s use of its powers against Americans, its immigration enforcement practices, and its dealings with contractors.
The party’s wins in both chambers mean Democrats will decide which officials to call before Congress and what records to seek, under subpoena authorities given to whichever party has the majority in a given chamber.
If a permanent director for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency is nominated again, Senate Democrats will also have a say in who leads the agency. The same can be said for a nominee to lead the National Counterterrorism Center, whose previous leader resigned earlier this year.
“We will investigate the administration weaponizing DHS against Americans, its out of control immigration policies, and its blatantly corrupt self-dealing,” Thompson told Nextgov/FCW. “The American people expect nothing less, and we will deliver.”
The panel also plans to examine the department’s surveillance of Americans engaged in protected speech, its handling of whistleblowers and whether federal officials steered contracts to political allies. On cybersecurity, they want to know how DHS is preparing for attacks aided by artificial intelligence and what became of services the department scaled back.
What CISA lost in the cuts
Thompson and Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., who is positioned to chair the Homeland Security cyber subcommittee, have already asked Congress’ watchdog to assess the impact of staffing cuts at CISA, which helps defend civilian federal networks and other frequent hacker targets like water systems and telecom networks.
CISA lost roughly a third of its workforce after Trump retook office, though the agency has made efforts to refill its roster. By September, about 250 prospective hires had tentative offers and were waiting for clearances, acting Director Nick Andersen said, as part of an effort under DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin to recant some of the cuts made to the cyberdefense agency over the last two years.
Ramirez, in a June interview with Nextgov/FCW, said she was planning a significant DHS overhaul bill for next year. She also gave positive feedback on CISA’s rehiring plans, though she added it may not be enough.
In a post on X after the election, she had a message for Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, White House aide Stephen Miller and others involved in immigration enforcement: “Clear your schedule.”
In the Senate, the retirement of Michigan Democrat Gary Peters puts Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., next in seniority among Democrats on the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. Hassan and Peters have already asked DHS to preserve records belonging to former Secretary Kristi Noem and her adviser Corey Lewandowski.
Hassan has also pressed CISA on its own security practices after reports that a contractor left agency account information and passwords in a public database.
One issue facing both homeland security panels could come due before Democrats take over. A law protecting companies from lawsuits when they share information about cyber threats is operating under a temporary extension through Dec. 11. Without a longer renewal planted this year, the incoming chairs could inherit a fight over the legal protections companies rely on when communicating with the government about cyberattacks.
When intelligence findings conflict with the White House
Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., and Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., are in line to chair the intelligence committees in their respective chambers after two years of disputes over whether spy agencies can deliver findings that contradict the president without putting analysts’ jobs at risk.
One major dispute centered on Tren de Aragua, the Venezuelan gang Trump said was carrying out an invasion at the direction of Nicolás Maduro’s government.
Most U.S. intelligence agencies assessed that Maduro was not directing the gang’s operations in the United States. Then-Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard subsequently fired the two leaders of the National Intelligence Council, which produced the assessment.
Warner also challenged Gabbard directly over Iran. At a Senate hearing in March, weeks after the U.S. and Israel went to war, he pressed her on a passage in her written testimony that she skipped in her opening remarks. It said Iran had made no effort to rebuild its uranium enrichment capability after U.S. strikes the previous June, a finding that bore on President Donald Trump’s claim that Iran posed an imminent threat.
A day earlier, Joe Kent, Trump’s director of the National Counterterrorism Center, had resigned over the war, saying he did not believe Iran posed such a threat.
Last June, after Trump said U.S. strikes had “obliterated” three Iranian nuclear sites, a preliminary Defense Intelligence Agency assessment suggested the attacks could have set the program back only a few months.
When Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired DIA Director Lt. Gen. Jeffrey Kruse that August without explanation, Warner pointed to the dispute in accusing the administration of “treating intelligence as a loyalty test.”

0f87c4499652.text: By — Scott Bauer, Associated Press Scott Bauer, Associated Press By — Geoff Mulvihill, Associated Press Geoff Mulvihill, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/democrats-win-full-control-of-more-state-governments-and-the-texas-house Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Democrats win full control of more state governments and the Texas House Politics Nov 4, 2026 4:50 PM EST MADISON, Wis. (AP) — Democrats in Texas took control of the state House after historic wins for governor and U.S. Senate, part of a series of sweeping gains nationwide in Tuesday's elections that shifted the balance of power across several battleground and Republican-leaning states. It will be the first time Democrats control the House in Texas since Republicans took over after the 2002 election. Republicans are keeping control of the Senate in the state — which also elected Gina Hinojosa its first Democratic governor since George W. Bush ousted Ann Richards in 1994. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. In this year's midterm elections, the party took full control — both statehouse chambers and governors' offices — in at least five states where they previously shared power. The wins put pressure on the party to answer to an electorate angry over the rising cost of living, high gas prices, inflation and the lack of affordable housing. State governments shape a wide array of policies affecting everyday lives, including tax rates and abortion rights, school choice and education funding, data center development, and the use of artificial intelligence and law enforcement surveillance cameras. WATCH: Takeaways from the 2026 midterms and answers to your election questions "Now it's time to deliver," said Devin Remiker, chairman of Wisconsin's Democratic Party, which retained the governor's office and successfully flipped both chambers of the state Legislature, breaking a 16-year Republican majority. Democrats prevail in battleground states Democrats also won or retained full control of both chambers of the legislatures in Michigan, Minnesota and Pennsylvania and kept the governor's office for trifectas in all three. In Nevada, they gained control by winning the governor's seat and retaining the legislature. There will be pressure on Democrats in Wisconsin and other battleground states to redraw congressional maps, just as President Donald Trump successfully urged eight Republican-led states to do ahead of this election. But that backfired, with Republicans losing most of the Democratic-held seats they had targeted to flip and others they had banked on winning. The Republican congressional redistricting in Texas may have mobilized additional Democratic voters in some parts of the state who helped drive gains in the statehouse, said Mark Jones, a political science professor at Rice University in Houston. But "when we're trying to think about why Democrats won, it's one man in the White House and his policies — Donald Trump," Jones said. Even under maps that favored Republicans in Wisconsin, Democrats picked up two congressional seats in Tuesday's races. That means the state will have an evenly divided congressional delegation in 2027. Democrats also break up Republican trifectas and supermajorities Democrats will also hold at least 28 governorships in 2027, with pickups in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and Texas — states long held by Republicans. And the party broke or prevented Republican supermajorities in nine legislative chambers in eight states: Florida, South Carolina, Indiana, Missouri, Iowa, Ohio, Kansas and North Carolina. That means Republicans would need help from Democratic lawmakers to override a Democratic governor's veto in Iowa, Ohio and North Carolina. The Associated Press has not called the governor's race in Kansas. The wins come after Democrats lost nearly 1,000 state legislative seats during President Barack Obama's tenure, a slide they've been trying to reverse for several cycles. READ MORE: Democrats win governorships in Texas and other GOP-controlled states in rebuke to Republicans It's the biggest single-election change of partisan power in state governments since 2010, said Katie Owens Hubler, director of elections and redistricting at the National Conference of State Legislatures. Lawmakers who will soon be in the majority say the change brings expectations. "We know that people will be counting on us to deliver, and we take that incredibly seriously," said Wisconsin state Rep. Greta Neubauer, currently the minority leader of state Assembly Democrats. Heather Williams, president of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, said the party won "historic levels of power in statehouses." She said they hadn't flipped this many seats nationwide since the 1980s. This time, she said, Democrats will have to focus on issues that matter to middle-class voters such as improving educational opportunities and increasing access to healthcare, particularly in rural areas. "This election is about kitchen-table issues; it's about economic opportunities," she said Wednesday. "That is what the mandate is about." Wins put spotlight on Democratic priorities in 2027 The cost of groceries, housing, healthcare, gas and utility bills were campaign talking points after legislative sessions packed with bills aiming to make life more affordable for Americans, while also providing tax relief and reining in data center development and the use of artificial intelligence. The coming legislative session could see major efforts to lighten the tax burden on the middle class, relax housing regulations, expand access to healthcare, and force utilities and data center developers to do more to stop electricity bills from rising. 1c4fccfb4d83.text: Democrats' midterm tsunami obscured a major polling miss: Surveys correctly anticipated a blue wave, but failed to capture its full force. Why it matters: Pollsters appear to have underestimated Democrats by a wider margin than they underestimated Republicans in 2016 or 2024 — even if they got the headline outcome right this time. By the numbers: Democrats are on track to win the national House popular vote by roughly 13 points, compared with a final Silver Bulletin polling average of 8.9 points, according to an initial analysis by The Argument's Lakshya Jain . That roughly 4-point gap is similar to the 2020 polling miss that underestimated Republicans and larger than the average partisan errors in 2016 and 2024, though comparisons to presidential years are imperfect. The big picture: Pollsters entered the 2026 midterms having underrated Trump's support in three consecutive presidential elections. Their central challenge was accounting for Republican voters who might be missing from their surveys. Many polling organizations have sought to compensate by weighting results based on party affiliation or how respondents voted in previous elections. A Pew analysis found that nearly 70% of national polls used such political weighting in 2024. In an October analysis , The Washington Post warned that a collapse in turnout among Trump voters could cause polls calibrated to the 2024 electorate to underestimate Democrats. Tuesday's results raise questions about whether the industry's efforts to correct past polling misses contributed to a new one. Reality check: Some of the pollsters that projected the largest Democratic margins appear to have come closest to the final result. AtlasIntel placed itself first in a ranking of final national House polls based on its projection of the popular-vote margin. It's the second straight election where the pollster stood out for its accuracy. AtlasIntel's final poll showed Democrats leading by 14.1 points, just 0.3 points from the firm's projected final margin of 13.8. Tufts University, New York Times/Siena, Change Research and RMG Research rounded out the top five in AtlasIntel's rankings.

Cancellations, investigations, and even impeachment could be ahead under Democratic Congress
Efforts like Autonomous Warfare Command, the Golden Fleet, and more could crumble without funding.
The Defense Department was already in Congress’s bipartisan bad graces before the midterm elections. In the wake of the Democrats’ overwhelming victory, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the Trump administration are likely to face even more pushback for their handling of the Iran war and their plans for pricey initiatives like Golden Dome, Golden Fleet and Autonomous Warfare Command.
And that’s if Hegseth sticks around. Some lawmakers have voiced an intention to impeach him, while rumors swirl that he is angling to be appointed to Tennessee Governor-Elect Marsha Blackburn’s vacated Senate seat.
“My read is that nearly all Democrats and an increasing number of Republicans still want to remove Hegseth,” Todd Harrison, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, told Defense One. “He has done nothing to improve his position with members of Congress since the House adjourned over this issue back in September, and it will be at the top of the docket when they get back next week.”
In the meantime, it doesn’t appear that Donald Trump intends to fire him. On Wednesday, the president told reporters that he thinks Hegseth is “doing a very good job.” Trump said he hadn’t heard that Hegseth was being considered for the Senate job, but said he’d be “very popular” in the office.
If Trump does change his mind, Harrison said, now would be the time to push him out and still have time to get a replacement nominated and confirmed.
Once the new Congress is seated in the new year, he added, “they will have a hard time getting anyone confirmed.”
Lawmakers will likely face pressure to investigate Hegseth and his administration for their handling of the Iran war, Harrison said, as well as “potentially improper access and contract awards for Trump’s political allies” like Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey.
Whether Hegseth stays or goes, much of his work reshaping the Defense Department is unlikely to stick, Harrison said. Anything that requires new funding is likely to hit a brick wall, and even initiatives that don’t cost anything may be undone by law.
“I think AUTOWARCOM is something they can do without Congress, but I would not expect it to receive any significant funding of its own,” he said. “The Golden Fleet definitely requires Congress for funding, so that is a dead idea—the battleship in particular.”
Democrats will also have the chance to roll back Hegseth’s culture-war pet projects, by passing laws allowing transgender troops to serve openly, re-renaming Army bases to follow the determinations of a congressionally mandated commission and perhaps even enshrining women’s right to serve in combat roles.
“In general, if it is a Hegseth initiative that requires congressional authorization or funding, it is likely not going to happen,” Harrison said. “If it is something the administration can do on its own, they will probably still try and then the new Congress may try to pass statutes that undo these changes.”
There may also be roadblocks for anything that the administration aimed to fund via a proposed 2027 reconciliation bill, such as billions for autonomous capabilities and critical munitions procurement.
“Assuming the huge increase in munitions funding requested through reconciliation does not pass in the lame duck, that is something the next Congress will have to deal with,” Harrison said.
The jettisoning of a reconciliation bill would also shrink the Trump administration’s $1.5 trillion defense proposal down to a “still substantial” $1.1 trillion, Mark Cancian, a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Defense One.
“Many of the major defense initiatives have bipartisan support — drones, munitions, shipbuilding, and missile defense,” Cancian said. “There will be some drone organization, though it may not be a combatant command.”
A rebranding of Trump’s Golden Dome and the Boeing F-47, the Air Force’s six-generation fighter named for Trump’s position in the line of U.S. presidents, could also be expected, he said.
The Defense Department could also face pressure from some familiar faces, including Representative-elect Elaine Luria, D-Va., a retired Navy commander who won back her former House of Representatives seat, and who previously held a seat on the House Armed Services Committee.
In South Carolina, Nancy Lacore, a former Navy admiral that Hegseth forced to retire last year, flipped former Rep. Nancy Mace’s House seat, leaving open another HASC position.
“At this point, I don’t think they have the votes for removal in the Senate,” Harrison said of a Hegseth impeachment. “But it could be enough of an embarrassment to the administration if a decent number of Republicans in the House vote to impeach that they push Hegseth out.”

4d0135a8d527.text: By — Josef Federman, Associated Press Josef Federman, Associated Press By — Natalie Melzer, Associated Press Natalie Melzer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/israels-president-takes-first-steps-on-building-new-government-after-accepting-election-results Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Israel's president takes first steps on building new government after accepting election results World Nov 4, 2026 4:16 PM EST JERUSALEM (AP) — Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday accepted the certified results of last week's parliamentary elections as legally binding and began consultations with party representatives on forming a new government. The move dealt a blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's efforts to discredit the vote, in which he and his allies lost their majority in parliament, known as the Knesset, while Arab-led parties made historic gains. WATCH: What's next for Israel after election produces political gridlock "The elections are over. Now is the time to face reality," Herzog said. Netanyahu and his supporters have repeatedly made unsubstantiated claims that Arab-led parties had "stolen" the election, possibly with foreign assistance. Herzog began consultations with party leaders on Wednesday night to determine whom to designate to form a government — a process that could bring Netanyahu's opponents to power. Commission finds no fraud in Israel's election Israel's elections commission said earlier on Wednesday that after a thorough investigation of all parties' claims of fraud, it had found "no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results." Netanyahu's Likud party did not respond to a request for comment. A separate investigation by the Shin Bet intelligence service, which is headed by David Zini, a Netanyahu appointee and loyalist, into allegations of foreign interference in the election is still ongoing. In a private meeting Wednesday of the elections committee's members, its head, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, read out an intelligence assessment from the Shin Bet saying the agency believed there had been a "widespread phenomenon involving the influx of substantial funds into Israel from foreign states," including from countries hostile toward Israel. READ MORE: Israeli officials say elections will stand after Netanyahu claimed Arabs stole vote The Shin Bet provided no evidence to explain its assertion. The Associated Press obtained a transcript of the assessment from a person who attended the meeting and requested anonymity to discuss a closed-door meeting. The committee has previously said that while claims about foreign actors seeking to influence the election are serious and under investigation, it does not believe that any such interference affected the results — even if it had happened. Sohlberg reiterated that stance on Wednesday. "At this stage, these are merely suspicions, and even if they are substantiated, the scope of their potential impact is limited," he said during a ceremony to present the certified election results to Herzog. Sohlberg added that it was dangerous to cast doubt on the results and said they are legally binding. Public trust in the electoral process is "easy to destroy, yet very difficult to repair," he warned. Consultations kick off coalition-building process In the Oct. 27 vote, neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the bloc of allies of his chief rival, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, secured a parliamentary majority needed to form a new government, raising the possibility of an alliance between the two rivals or an alliance between Eisenkot and some of the Arab-led parties. Herzog began a series of sit-downs with political parties on Wednesday. Three factions — all aligned with Netanyahu's religious-nationalist base — recommended Netanyahu be given a chance to form a coalition government, while a fourth — led by a former Netanyahu ally turned rival — recommended Eisenkot. Eight more parties, including the two Arab-led factions, are scheduled to meet Herzog on Thursday, with Eisenkot's Yashar and Netanyahu's Likud speaking last. WATCH: Projections show no clear winner in Israel's election After the consultations, Herzog will choose the candidate — most likely Netanyahu or Eisenkot — who he believes is most likely to be able to form a coalition government. He has several days to announce his decision, which will then set the stage for weeks of negotiations. If neither man can put together a government, the country would hold a new election early next year. Intelligence agency's request to interrogate senior Arab lawmakers is rejected The Shin Bet sought approval from Israel's attorney general on Tuesday to interrogate several elected officials as part of its separate investigation, including Ra'am party leader Mansour Abbas and other senior Arab lawmakers, Israeli media reported. In a statement rejecting the request, Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara said: "It is not permissible to interrogate citizens or elected officials without evidence to justify such action." WATCH: Retired Israeli general on what the election results tell us The Joint List of Arab parties condemned the request, calling it a "campaign of incitement" by Netanyahu and his allies designed to delegitimize the Arab vote. National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, a far-right ally of Netanyahu, called on the Shin Bet, over which he has no authority, to "arrest all the leaders of the Arab political parties" and interrogate them in "basement interrogation cells until these suspicions are fully clarified." Herzog said Wednesday that the Shin Bet's investigation into possible foreign interference should proceed, but cautioned that Arab Israeli voters "must not be smeared." "I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently," Herzog said. Melzer reported from Nahariya, Israel. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy

1fc13100a110.text: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) formally launched his bid for speaker of the House on Wednesday in a letter to colleagues obtained by Axios. Why it matters: Jeffries is widely expected to secure the speaker's gavel after House Democrats' landslide midterm win. He would make history as the first African American to serve in the role. Jeffries, who was first elected to Congress in 2012, has led the House Democratic caucus since former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) stepped down in 2022. What he's saying: "I write to humbly request your support in connection with my candidacy to serve as the next Speaker of the House of Representatives," Jeffries wrote. "We must now deliver the dramatic change the American people are demanding in the majority," he continued. Jeffries wrote that "every single member of our majority will play a meaningful role" and that his goal is to empower House Democrats to "act decisively in three key areas: (1) Affordability (2) Accountability and (3) American Values." Between the lines: While some incoming progressive and red-district Democrats have declined to commit to supporting Jeffries for speaker, he is not expected to face any serious opposition for the role. The big majority House Democrats won on Tuesday will further help to insulate him from any would-be rebels in his caucus. Zoom out: Jeffries' senior leadership team is similarly expected to run uncontested: Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) for majority leader. Democratic Caucus chair Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.) for majority whip. Democratic Caucus vice chair Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) for Democratic caucus chair. Assistant Leader Joe Neguse (D-Colo.) for assistant speaker. Read the letter in full, via DocumentCloud : Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

917d978e0699.text: Republicans barely had time to absorb their sweeping midterm losses before President Trump returned to a familiar comfort zone: D.C. construction projects. Why it matters: Voters just delivered an overwhelming rebuke of the administration, demanding that politicians focus on the cost of living, yet the president remains fixed on remaking the nation's capital in his image. Driving the news: Trump hosted reporters at the White House on Wednesday for a previously unscheduled event to update them on the East Wing ballroom's construction, marking his first remarks to the White House press pool since the election. He spent the majority of his remarks discussing planned architectural changes around D.C., including a proposed Triumphal Arch, the National Garden of American Heroes and a planned expansion of a publicly owned golf course that would likely eliminate popular running and biking paths. His remarks came after a pre-election appearance Monday, during which he praised the new pipes installed at the Reflecting Pool and a proposed promenade from the Lincoln Memorial to the Potomac River. What they're saying: Trump addressed criticism he sometimes receives for working on his construction projects, saying he was "doing it because the White House is the ultimate symbol of America, and it's got to be pristine." "It's got to be perfect. And if you take a look at it, that's what it is right now. You have no idea how much work we had to do." He also noted that he spends "very little time" working on the White House, but said he does it because "it's relaxing …I love construction." Catch up quick: Democrats outperformed expectations in Tuesday's midterms, flipping the Senate before the night was over and then the House a few hours later, according to the AP. Democrats have gained complete control of at least five previously divided state governments while ending Republican trifectas in several other states. In ruby-red Texas, the white whale of potential pickups, Democrats flipped the governor's mansion, a Senate seat and now control the state House. Zoom in: "President Trump's commitment to restoring our Nation's treasured landmarks should be celebrated and does not distract from his work to lower costs, strengthen our economy, and improve the lives of American families," a White House spokesperson told Axios in an emailed statement. "While making our Nation's capital safe and beautiful again as he promised to do, President Trump remains focused on lowering costs, driving down inflation, creating good-paying jobs, reshoring our manufacturing industry, unleashing American energy dominance, securing new investment, securing our borders, deporting dangerous illegal criminals from our communities, and enforcing tough-on-crime policies." Zoom out: Trump also briefly discussed his immigration policies and efforts to lower crime around D.C. during his Wednesday speech. He later took questions from reporters, during which he reiterated that Republicans would have won had he been on the ballot. 9a835dea6b08.text: By — Stan Choe, Associated Press Stan Choe, Associated Press By — David McHugh, Associated Press David McHugh, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/u-s-stocks-surge-and-the-dow-soars-1500-points-as-brent-oils-price-drops-below-95-per-barrel Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter U.S. stocks surge, and the Dow soars 1,500 points as Brent oil's price drops below $95 per barrel Economy Nov 4, 2026 3:47 PM EST NEW YORK (AP) — U.S. stocks are soaring Wednesday after President Donald Trump's party lost its sole control of Washington in the midterm elections. Stocks generally do well in the months following any midterm U.S. election, regardless of who wins, and the S&P 500 jumped 1.8%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 1,519 points, or 2.9%, as of 2:06 p.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 1.9% higher. Stocks of solar-power companies, dollar stores and hospital owners helped lead the way as Wall Street tried to sort the winners from losers following the widespread losses for Republicans. Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Trump's social-media company, the artificial-intelligence industry and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil fell below $100 for the first time in nearly a month. Vice President JD Vance blamed the war with Iran, which caused a spike in oil prices, for Republicans' midterm losses. Strategists along Wall Street had been urging investors not to get swept up in the election because it may not matter much for the broad market in the long term. Prices for stocks depend more on where profits for companies and interest rates are heading than on who controls what in Washington. "Earnings trump elections," according to Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management. Still, Wall Street may have gotten a preferred political scenario as Democrats are set to take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. Wall Street generally prefers split control of Washington because it lessens the risk of transformative changes to the economy. WATCH: Takeaways from the 2026 midterms and answers to your election questions Much remains impossible to predict, of course, and Trump retains executive authority over key areas such as defense, foreign policy and in some instances trade. A downbeat forecast could be that "Trump is not now a lame duck, but an angry duck" who might restart tensions over tariffs and NATO allies' levels of military spending, said Carsten Brzeski, global chief of macro at ING Bank. An optimistic view, Brzeski said, is that Trump becomes "a tame duck ... that he will slow down any disruptive efforts and that he will put more focus on trying to win the Nobel Peace Prize by ending the two big wars without big disruption, and on trade, nothing happens but a few words." Here's a look at some of the moves rippling through financial markets: Trump Media and Tesla are down Trump's social-media company, Trump Media & Technology Group, was one of the market's bigger losers, down 16.6%. READ MORE: Trump Media replaces Nunes as Truth Social CEO after stock plunge that wiped out billions Since briefly touching a peak of $175 five years ago, it's dropped toward $5. Its main business is Truth Social, which is most well known for Trump's postings on the platform. Elon Musk's businesses also struggled. Tesla fell 2.4%, and SpaceX sank 4.8%. Musk, a former top Trump adviser, is among the possible targets for investigations by a Democratic-controlled Congress. AI companies in general are under pressure Trump has been a big backer of the AI industry, and Democratic victories across the country could mean more regulation or restrictions. Concerns have grown across political parties about AI in general. Investors see Democratic wins in Texas in particular as possibly slowing the build out of further AI data centers. AI-related stocks came into Election Day already under pressure because of worries their prices had shot too high. WATCH: News Wrap: AI giant Anthropic preparing for initial public offering Nvidia, the chip company that quickly became the poster child of the frenzy around AI-related stocks, sank 1.8% and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. As the dust was still settling on the Democratic midterm wave that crashed across America, the official White House account posted a photograph on X of a stern-looking Donald Trump standing behind his desk in the Oval Office.
"Trump is still your president," the caption read.
It's the kind of message Trump surely wants to project â of a president firmly in charge and unbowed despite a dramatic electoral setback.
Left unsaid was that even without control of Congress, American presidents still have broad powers that they can exercise. And Trump has already shown that he is more than willing to push the boundaries of his executive authority.
But also unacknowledged was that the clock is ticking on Trump's presidency â and it will get increasingly more difficult for him to use the powers at his disposal.
Many of his most significant moves have been through presidential orders rather than laws passed by the Republican-controlled Congress.
That includes tariffs imposed on allies and adversaries alike as well as the military operations launched in Venezuela and Iran.
At home, he unilaterally slashed congressionally approved federal spending across government.
Even with the Democrats' majority in the House and Senate, Trump can continue to pursue actions like these â and more â in the final two years of his term. And if the Democrats try to curtail it through legislation, the Constitution provides Trump with a uniquely formidable response â the presidential veto, which can only be overridden by congressional majorities larger than the ones that Democrats will hold.
However, just because some of these powers are still at Trump's fingertips does not mean he retains the political will to do so. There are legions of new Democrats heading to Washington promising to oppose his every move. And the biggest obstacles may come from within Trump's own ranks.
For two years the president has displayed a vice-like grip on the Republican Party, keeping his partisan rank and file in Congress and across the US in line through a combination of political rewards and bare-knuckle threats.
Now, however, there are signs that his hold may be loosening.
Some Republicans have begun showing a willingness to criticise his decisions in a way few would dare even a few months ago. His own vice-president, JD Vance, penned a lengthy post on social media blaming the war in Iran that Trump launched with Israel for Tuesday's sweeping Republican defeat.
"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, then do so," Vance wrote. "But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."
Already rumours are circulating that members of Trump's presidential team could be on the chopping block. According to BBC US media partner CBS News, the president is asking close advisers whether he should replace Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, one of the architects of the war. The president denied it.
Such a move would echo George W Bush's move to replace Donald Rumsfeld, a driving force behind the Iraq war, in response to his 2006 "thumping" â the last time Democrats won congressional majorities of Tuesday's scope in a midterm election.
"Republicans who think that they need to pivot away from Trumpism and from the [Make America Great Again] movement are going to either try to emphasise different policy issues, or they're going to try to frame themselves in ways that show some daylight between themselves and Donald Trump," said David Miller, an assistant professor of government at American University.
On Tuesday night, Trump posted on social media and spoke to a series of media outlets, saying in realtime how he would deal with the Democrats â pledging co-operation one moment, and threatening vetoes of liberal legislation in the next.
Then on Wednesday, as construction workers raised the final beam for the White House ballroom he is building despite a lawsuit attempting to halt its progress, he responded to a few questions about the political future.
"I'll get along probably with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive," he said. "But I have the power of the veto."
In 1995, months after Republicans took control of Congress in a wave election that left Democrats similarly reeling, an isolated and defensive President Bill Clinton insisted that he still mattered and that he had powers left to wield.
"The president is still relevant here," he said, plaintively.
Clinton, still in his first term, had time to rebound politically â and he won re-election the following year.
Time, however, is not on Trump's side.
With Republicans licking their wounds, he may try to make a similar argument to the powers in Washington and the American public.
But with each passing day, the man who loves to dominate the spotlight in US politics may find his powers â and, more importantly, his authority to wield them â slipping through his fingers.

Democrats’ Election Rout Is Poised To Dramatically Reorder Federal Health Policy
Democrats’ decisive sweep of the U.S. House and Senate in Tuesday’s elections will reshape the direction of federal health policy — setting the stage for oversight investigations, a legislative push to reverse cuts to the Affordable Care Act and Medicaid, and a focus on lowering costs such as insurance premiums and drug prices.
The conclusive string of victories sets up Democrats to argue that voters — who said in preelection surveys that healthcare affordability was a top concern — have given them a clear mandate to overturn historic cuts President Donald Trump and Republicans made to public healthcare programs.
The breadth of success, including wins by Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and other progressives, is likely to embolden some Democrats to forge ahead with ambitious policy proposals such as expanding Medicare, the federal insurance program for people age 65 and older, to cover all Americans. Their plan is to be positioned as the party that prioritizes lowering healthcare costs for the 2028 presidential election.
Party leaders, though, will need buy-in from Trump to advance any healthcare agenda. While he has veto power, he may be interested in brokering legislative deals as he seeks to cement his legacy and deflect fallout from investigations into his administration’s handling of the war against Iran, mass deportations, contracting scandals, and other controversies.
Democrats were projected to win at least 237 of 435 seats in the House and at least 54 Senate seats as of Wednesday afternoon, according to The Associated Press. Several key races remained unresolved, including Senate contests in Alaska and Mississippi.
As election results continued coming out into early-morning Wednesday, Trump said in a phone interview with Politico that he had spoken with Democratic Party leaders and that voters had sent a message he must work with them “to make sure things go well for our country.”
“I don’t want to just be sitting there for two years vetoing everything,” Trump said. “They want to see things happen, too.”
But how Trump’s new conciliatory position plays out in undoing GOP-led changes, such as new work requirements for many adults enrolled in Medicaid, the state-federal program for low-income and disabled people, remains to be seen. Republicans touted their overhaul of Medicaid and other changes to health programs wrought by their One Big Beautiful Bill Act as signature achievements in midterm campaigns.
Democrats, however, will have to carefully balance their policy moves against their desire to investigate a host of concerns surrounding the nation’s top health official, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has dismantled U.S. vaccine recommendations, gutted the staff of federal health agencies, and cut public health funding.
“Democrats will put forward an expansive healthcare agenda, including reversal of cuts to Medicaid and the ACA, but achieving all of that will be impossible with President Trump still in the White House,” said Larry Levitt, an executive vice president at KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News.
New Year, New Congress, New Majority
An early order of business for Democrats in 2027 will likely be a legislative push to restore enhanced subsidies that reduced the price millions of people paid for Obamacare health plans. The larger subsidies were created during the covid-19 pandemic, as part of economic relief programs, but ended last year after Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress declined to extend them.
Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the current Democratic House leader widely expected to become speaker of the House, told CNN on Wednesday that the party should bring back the subsidies to help struggling families.
“My guess is it would be rolled into a broader budget negotiation or package that may or may not involve other healthcare priorities, like restoring Medicaid cuts or other things that are priorities for Democrats,” said Sabrina Corlette, a co-director of the Center on Health Insurance Reforms at Georgetown University.
If they act decisively, said Leslie Dach, who chairs the Democratic-aligned advocacy group Protect Our Care, Democrats could both renew the ACA’s expired subsidies and extend the enrollment period for 2027 coverage, which ends in most states on Jan. 15, shortly after the new Congress is scheduled to be sworn in.
They would need to act within days of assuming control, Dach said.
“Congress will be sworn in during open enrollment, at a time when people will be having to make difficult and horrific choices about their healthcare, given the further increases in premiums due to the Republicans,” he said.
Premiums for Affordable Care Act benchmark plans are set to increase by an average of 13% for 2027, according to KFF researchers.
With Congress likely to pass another short-term government funding bill in December, the stage will be set for incoming lawmakers to also fight a battle over Medicaid spending cuts in the spring, said Rodney Whitlock, a healthcare consultant who previously worked for Republicans in Congress.
Democrats — many of whom put healthcare affordability at the center of their election campaigns — are now well positioned to place that issue at the center of negotiations with Trump over federal spending.
“If you’ve got the opportunity for a battle in March over fiscal year funding — and Democrats picking and choosing what they want to make this first battle about with a unified, controlled Congress with the president — damn, doesn’t it scream healthcare?” Whitlock said. “Doesn’t it scream repeal or delay all the Medicaid cuts?”

This story was produced in partnership by Inside Climate News and the Texas Newsroom, the state’s network of public radio stations.
Amid a spate of historic political upsets across Texas, voters in the industrial port city of Corpus Christi on Tuesday overwhelmingly approved a citizen-led petition to impose steep fees for water use on the region’s refineries and chemical plants during future droughts.
The measure passed by a two-to-one margin despite heavy spending by industry groups in opposition—a dramatic rebuke of industrial interests in a port city that leads the nation in crude oil exports.
“The people have woken up,” said Sylvia Campos, a member of the Corpus Christi City Council and the Democratic Socialists of America who supported the measure. “We overcame all that money.”
The city’s referendum was part of an earth-shattering election across Texas, a fortress of conservative politics and the seat of the nation’s energy sector, which saw Democratic challengers wipe incumbent Republicans out of every statewide office on the ballot.
The new governor-elect of Texas, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, has described her politics as “economic populism.”
“In the past we evaluated politics as right versus left, I just don’t think those labels apply at this moment,” Hinojosa told the New York Times in October. “Things are so stacked against working people in this country.”
In Corpus Christi, a Gulf Coast city of 300,000, partisan lines didn’t mark the political divisions that emerged over the referendum on industrial water fees, according to Paul Gottemoller, a professor of political science at Del Mar College in Corpus Christi.
“It’s kind of a country club, business, chamber of commerce thing versus a populism thing,” Gottemoller said. “You do have populist and business sentiments on both sides of the political aisle.”
The measure, proposed as an amendment to the city’s charter, would levy millions of dollars in surcharges on the region’s largest water users—industrial titans like ExxonMobil, Valero and OxyChem—the next time its main reservoirs drop below 30 percent full.
Refineries, chemical plants and other industrial facilities account for more than half of all water consumption in the Corpus Christi region, where reservoirs almost dried up entirely this year.
“There’s clearly some anger and resentment about the water issue,” Gottemoller said.
For now, the referendum remains a mostly symbolic win for the voters that supported it. The amendment would take effect after a five-year grace period, during which time it will likely face a litany of legal challenges from industry groups, according to Corpus Christi City Manager Peter Zanoni.
“It has significant legal implications that the city will have to address,” Zanoni said.
The city will face big challenges defending the policy in court and before the state’s Public Utility Commission, Zanoni said.
Industry groups spent hundreds of thousands of dollars supporting candidates and policies in city elections that revolved largely around water, Zanoni said.
A Message to Businesses
The charter amendment “raises broader concerns about the message Corpus Christi sends to businesses considering whether to invest, expand, or create jobs here,” wrote Dolly Trolley, a local industry promoter and school board member, in the Corpus Christi Caller-Times this week. “These companies make long-term investments requiring dependable infrastructure and predictable operating conditions.”
Groups including the Coastal Bend Coalition and Coastal Bend Industries Association did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
This story is funded by readers like you.
Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.
Donate Now
Texas Campaign for the Environment, which helped lead and finance the petition drive, said in a press release after the amendment’s approval on Tuesday, “Its victory is proof that the community is tired of being plundered.”
“Industry will try to block its implementation through legal channels,” the press release said. “TCE stands ready to defend the sovereignty of Corpus Christi voters.”
Early this year, as an unprecedented water crisis loomed, groups including TCE, the Democratic Socialists of America and For the Greater Good gathered almost 13,000 verified signatures of registered voters on a petition for the charter amendment.
Epic rainfall in July refilled local reservoirs above critical levels. In August, the Corpus Christi City Council approved the petition for November’s ballot, against the advice of city staff.
“This victory is bigger than one water policy,” said Armon Alex, director of the petition campaign for TCE. “It is proof that residents can use the democratic tools available to us to take greater control over the resources and decisions that shape our lives.”
Most of the region’s largest water users currently pay about $4.50 per 1,000 gallons of water supplied by the city of Corpus Christi. The charter amendment would increase the price by $3 when reservoirs fall below 30 percent, by $6 when they fall below 20 percent and by $12 if the city declares a “water emergency.”
For companies that use millions of gallons of water per day, that would mean millions of dollars added to monthly water bills. The region’s largest water user, a plastics plant owned jointly by ExxonMobil and Saudi Basic Industries Corp, used 13.5 million gallons per day in 2025, almost as much as all residents of Corpus Christi combined.
Under the charter amendment, that facility would face about $810,000 in additional water costs every day while reservoirs remain below 20 percent, like they recently did for 19 months between December 2024 and July of this year.

The Trump redistricting plan "was systematically dismantled," former Attorney General Eric Holder, chair of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, said in an election night statement. "And given the opportunity, voters instead chose to elect a new Democratic majority." New districts presumed continuing support for Trump Congressional voting districts typically are redrawn after a census at the start of each decade to account for population changes. But the presumed Republican districts got undercut by shifting viewpoints of Trump. The AP Voter Poll found about 6 in 10 disapprove of how Trump is handling the presidency. Views of Trump's priorities also were mostly negative. "It's foolish to presume that the electorate in one year is going to look like the electorate in another in a time of radical swings in public opinion," Levitt said. "I think it is likely that some line-drawers got cocky." Redistricting fell flat in the Rio Grande Valley In Texas, Republicans reconfigured three heavily Latino districts in the Rio Grande Valley, which had shifted toward Trump in 2024, to try to boost their chances of unseating Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez. But both won reelection Tuesday. And Democrats instead unseated Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz, whose district is sandwiched between theirs. Though De La Cruz's new district retained the same percentage of Trump-inclined voters as the 2024 version, about 3 in 5 voting-age residents were new — making it harder for her to compete against Democratic challenger Bobby Pulido, a well-known Latin Grammy award winner. President Donald Trump is known to occasionally seek collaboration with â even offer praise to â his opponents. Newly ascendant Democrats, however, arenât in much of a dealmaking mood.
As Democrats prepare to take control of the House and Senate next year, they are already plotting out ways to investigate the president, his administration, and its allies. Democratsâ ravenous appetite for investigations â and the White Houseâs hostility towards them â raises serious questions about whether the two parties will be able to work together to any extent, even as administration officials begin floating opportunities for bipartisan cooperation.
âTheyâre going to be out for blood,â one Trump administration official told Semafor.
Democrats have spent Trumpâs second term on the sidelines, trying to learn from the aftermath of the first Trump administration. Even before voters delivered Republicans a generational rebuke, leaders had been methodically mapping out a multi-pronged oversight approach.
Incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia, D-Calif., told Semafor his committee will be âlaser focused on four major lanesâ â the Trump family, immigration, corporations, and convicted sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein.
âWeâve been laying the groundwork,â said Garcia, who released a statement after the midterms advising Republicans to âlawyer up.â He predicted that every Democratic committee chair would get in on the action: âThereâs more than enough corruption to go around.â
Prior to the election, returning and incoming House Democrats had expressed âan incredible amount of interestâ in joining the Oversight panel, Garcia said. Now, leaders in both chambers believe voters have given them free rein to take their efforts to the next level.
âAmericans are calling for accountability, not accomodation,â Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Wednesday. âWhenever Trump defies the will of the American people or the law, we will launch investigations, take him to court, and entangle him in legislative razor wire.â
The administration is already warning them to back off.
âAs the President has said, heâs willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people,â White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Semafor.
Its resistance is no surprise to Democrats, who had already begun strategizing how to circumvent Trump by probing the private sector instead. Government officials can invoke executive privilege to avoid providing documents, as they have in the Kennedy Center case; corporate leaders cannot.
âWe are cognizant of lessons learned from Trump 1.0 of how much they use the courts to string out the process,â said Dan Goshorn, Senate Finance Committee Democratsâ chief investigation counsel, said.
âSo from our perspective, private companies have more of a reputational risk and are going to be more willing to cooperate,â Goshorn added. âWeâre going to go wherever the information is.â
a modicum of legislative optimism
After the bruising results, Trump on Tuesday suggested heâs open to collaborating with Democrats on legislation, telling The New York Times that âweâll probably work something out.â
Some administration officials predicted Trump and Democrats could find common ground on changing immigration enforcement and addressing pharmaceutical costs â though one Trump adviser expressed skepticism at the idea of an immigration deal, pointing to exit polls showing that the issue remained one of the few Republican strengths.
That adviser suggested the president and Democrats could also work together on AI â particularly rules around data centers â and other cost-of-living issues. Specific bipartisan ideas could include enacting manufacturing and clean energy tax credits or reauthorizing federal transportation programs.
Trump âat his core does like dealmaking,â one person close to the White House told Semafor.
But itâs unclear how long that goodwill can last amid a torrent of congressional oversight. Trumpâs aides are bracing for impact, with the administration official predicting Democrats would try to tear down Trumpâs new ballroom.
âThereâs going to be a lot more war than peace,â a former Trump administration official said. âThe Democrats feel they have a mandate to torture the administration with subpoenas and lawfare.â
Spending legislation will pose an early first test. Government funding is slated to lapse next month, which Garcia said Democrats will use to finalize their plans for next year.
âItâs going to be very hard for Democrats to look at what happened [Tuesday] and â¦ pass a clean continuing resolution that locks in Medicaid cuts and SNAP cuts and ICE funding and Pentagon funding after youâve just seen the biggest mandate in the history of midterm elections against the Republican agenda,â Groundwork Collaborativeâs Alex Jacquez told Semafor.
Working with Democrats would also inevitably expose Trump to criticism from his own party. The person close to the White House warned a bipartisan immigration deal could âdamage the GOP even further.â

396a57ec2a1e.text: Data: The Downballot , Ballotpedia , AP ; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Republican mapmakers thought they were drawing at least a dozen comfortably red districts to protect their House majority. Why it matters: They weren't red enough . In the seven states where Republicans redrew congressional boundaries, the GOP is on track to lose as many as eight seats — rather than gain the 15 it had hoped to pick up. With two exceptions — TX-32 and TN-09 — the pickups Republicans penciled in never materialized. Then there was a bloodbath in North Carolina. Zoom in: At the heart of the GOP's miscalculation was a bet that the 2026 electorate would look like 2024's. Instead, voters behaved more like they had in 2020 — or even 2018. TX-34: Republicans made an already Trump-leaning district significantly redder, shifting it from Trump +4 to Trump +10. Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez still won by nearly 16 percentage points. TX-23: Republicans made an already red district slightly less Republican, shifting it from Trump +16 to Trump +15. Democrat Katy Padilla Stout won by eight points. TX-15: Rep. Monica De La Cruz's district remained essentially unchanged at Trump +18. She lost by 25 points. Between the lines: The GOP's heaviest losses came in Ohio and North Carolina districts that Republican mapmakers barely touched. Rather than shore up districts Trump had won by double digits, Republicans concentrated on making two Democratic-held seats in Ohio and one in North Carolina redder, betting they would flip in a normal election year. But 2026 was anything but normal. The bottom line: Perhaps the clearest example of a dummymander — when mapmakers spread their own voters too thin in pursuit of additional seats — came in Tennessee's 4th District . Republicans redrew TN-04 from Trump +44 to Trump +24, sacrificing much of its enormous GOP cushion. Democrat Victoria Broderick appears to have won by just 280 votes.

Why it matters: Elections have consequences. Wednesday's price drop — around $8 per barrel — deepened after Vance posted on X that "everyone knows" the war is why Republicans got pummeled and "any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there." Sen. Chuck Schumer (D), the likely Senate majority leader in the next Congress, vowed that Democrats will push to end the war. JD Vance's statement amplified that sentiment," Ben Cahill, a nonresident senior fellow with the Atlantic Council, told Axios via email. What they're saying: Pavel Molchanov, an analyst with Raymond James, said in remarks circulated to reporters that Vance's post was a "key catalyst" for today's oil price plunge. "The market is saying that Congress and members of his own administration are likely to start acting as a constraint on President Trump's war in Iran," Seb Barker, a strategist with the hedge fund, Marshall Wace, tells the Financial Times. Catch up quick: Oil prices were already falling to start the week on signs of new U.S.-Iran diplomacy. What we're watching: "[I]t remains unclear whether Vance's comments signal a more dovish stance toward Iran," Molchanov said. "For oil prices to sustainably move lower, a durable off-ramp is needed," he added.

828d02a4fedb.text: By — Will Weissert, Associated Press Will Weissert, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-trump-previews-ballroom-construction-the-day-after-voters-rejected-gop-rule Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Trump previews ballroom construction the day after voters rejected GOP rule Politics Nov 4, 2026 2:27 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump gave extended comments Wednesday, not about the Republican Party's midterm election wipeout but instead justifying his building a sprawling White House ballroom. Watch Trump's remarks in the video player above. Trump invited reporters into a cavernous construction site and talked about the building project for nearly 20 minutes without mention sweeping Republican defeats around the country the night before. READ MORE: How Trump and Republicans lost the 2026 midterm elections, according to AP Voter Poll "This has been a structure the likes of which has never been seen anywhere," Trump said before watching crews erect what he said would be the project's last beam and even signing what was being built. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The president had no public events on his schedule originally, but called reporters together at the last minute. He also briefly took questions, insisting, "If I were on the ballot I would have won." He said a series of rallies he held leading up the election featured a lot of love from his supporters that "we weren't able to transfer love to the candidates." Trump's continued heavy focus on the building project comes as midterm voters said they thought he was concentrating on the wrong issues during this year's campaign. About two-thirds of voters said Trump does not have the right priorities, according to The AP Voter Poll survey — and the overwhelming majority of these voters supported Democratic House candidates. Roughly one-third of voters said Trump has the right priorities. Even as Trump evaded blame for the election fallout, he had used a flurry of late campaign rallies to implore supporters to pretend that he was on the ballot. READ MORE: Trump says Democrats 'did a good job,' blames Republican candidates for midterm losses Now he may work just as tirelessly to insist it wasn't his fault. Republican losses swept Democrats into control of Congress with a wave of Senate victories that once seemed far-fetched in GOP strongholds. There were wins in South Carolina and Kansas, which had not elected a Democratic senator since 1932. In Texas, Democrats had been shut out of every statewide race for more than three decades, until Tuesday. Trump was already backpedaling even before the full extent of his party's defeat was known. On election night, he sounded more humble than usual, pledging to work with Democrats and to accept the election results. But he was still seeking to deflect responsibility. "I don't like to consider it a defeat for me. I wasn't on the ballot," he told Fox News. Voters, he said, just "didn't like the candidates" on the ballot. In fact, The Voter Poll suggests that Trump was a drag on GOP candidates. Only 4 in 10 voters nationwide approved of how Trump was handling the presidency. In losing Ohio, Iowa, Maine and North Carolina, majorities said the Republican Senate candidates were "too supportive" of the unpopular president. Going further, on his social media site, the president nonetheless insisted that if he had been running, "We would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" Trump usually blames anyone and everyone but himself Trump has a long history of passing the buck, on issues large and small, but especially when there are ballot-box failures. After Republicans lost the House in the 2018 midterms during Trump's first term, he blamed defeated members of his own party. Utah Rep. Mia Love, who had tried to distance herself from him, "gave me no love, but then she lost. Too bad," the president said. He mocked other losing lawmakers for not embracing him — Florida's Carlos Curbelo, Colorado's Mike Coffman, Virginia's Barbara Comstock, and Illinois' Peter Roskam — with the same words he would use eight years later: "My name wasn't on the ballot." Now he's trying to deflect blame once more, despite having urged voters to "pretend I'm on the ballot." An Associated Press analysis of the 39 Trump speeches and rallies Trump staged since Sept. 1 showed the president used a version of the phrase in 30 of them. In some addresses he returned to the subject more than once, though, meaning there were at least 40 instances where he appealed to voters to engage in that bit of make-believe. Presidents usually acknowledge responsibility for midterm losses After their parties take hits in midterm elections, most White Houses engage in some soul-searching, with the president publicly shouldering at least part of the responsibility. A day after big Republican congressional gains in 2010, Democrat Barack Obama said he took "a shellacking." Republican George W. Bush described Democratic victories in the 2006 midterms as "a thumping." But Trump, known for defying all kinds of presidential norms, began laying the groundwork for avoiding blame this cycle well before balloting began. He told Punchbowl News in August that voters were angry at Republicans "but they're not angry at me." Trump posted on his social media site last month that should Texas Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton lose — and he did — "it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove." That's despite Trump's risky endorsement of scandal-marred Paxton in the primary over incumbent Cornyn, who first got to the Senate in 2002 and was considered the safer bet. 1aac0dedf55c.text: Tuesday's election was great for Democrats. It was bad for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and some of the White House's most ambitious national security projects. Why it matters: Surprise wins across the map for Democrats — including in the Deep South — complicate a lot for the Trump administration. Republicans have relied on a simple-majority funding mechanism known as reconciliation to pay for marquee projects like Golden Dome . That option is now a long shot over the next few months, and impossible after that. Outrage over the Iran war, well beyond the half-year mark, is sure to turbocharge a long list of congressional inquiries. And lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, including Reps. Pat Ryan (D-N.Y.) and Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), have suggested impeaching Hegseth. Follow the money: Defense analysts agree prospects for the administration's full $1.5 trillion defense budget look grim. A Wednesday note from TD Cowen's Washington Research Group warned "Trump 'branded' projects are dead." Golden Dome, Golden Fleet and "other signature efforts," it added, "will be curbed." Meanwhile, Todd Harrison, an American Enterprise Institute defense budget expert, said it's unlikely the lame-duck congressional session will pass reconciliation and instead will keep the defense budget operating under a continuing resolution into next year. "They're all at risk," Harrison said of reconciliation-backed programs. "My base expectation is nothing happens on the defense budget." The other side: The Pentagon did not respond to a request for comment. Between the lines: Some of the most powerful Republican lawmakers on defense matters were defeated or are on pace to lose. Sen. Susan Collins, the appropriations chairwoman, lost to Troy Jackson in Maine . Sen. Darline Graham, also on appropriations, lost to Annie Andrews in South Carolina . Rep. Jen Kiggans, a member of the armed services and veterans affairs committees, lost to Elaine Luria in Virginia . And as of Wednesday afternoon, Reps. Rob Wittman of Virginia, Mike Turner of Ohio, Scott DesJarlais of Tennessee and Jeff Crank of Colorado all trailed their Democratic challengers. What they're saying: Hegseth himself may be on the hot seat. "Secretary Hegseth's chaotic and incompetent leadership has made America weaker and less safe, and now he will be forced to answer for it," Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), a member of the appropriations, armed services and intelligence committees, told Axios. "We owe it to our service members, our military families and the American people to make sure that" Hegseth and the broader Trump administration "are held fully accountable," she added. Yes, but: President Trump told reporters he's not considering replacing Hegseth. "No, I think he's doing a very good job," he said. The bottom line: "People do expect there will be investigations and there will be oversight and all that, and certainly that will have an impact," VJ Sahi, a partner at strategic advisory firm Clark Street Associates, told Axios. 383286176d57.text: By — Jill Lawless, Associated Press Jill Lawless, Associated Press By — Rob Gillies, Associated Press Rob Gillies, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/world-leaders-who-sparred-with-trump-express-mix-of-relief-caution-at-gop-election-rout Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter World leaders who sparred with Trump express mix of relief, caution at GOP election rout World Nov 4, 2026 1:53 PM EST LONDON (AP) — World leaders who have sparred with the "America first" President Donald Trump greeted the rout of his Republican Party in the U.S. midterm elections with a measure of relief on Wednesday, allowing themselves to hope for a less combative U.S. foreign policy. READ MORE: Democrats usher in a new era with their resounding sweep of the House and the Senate But that hope was seasoned with expectation that American voters' rebuke would not necessarily end the U.S. conflict with Iran or change Trump's policies on tariffs or his lukewarm-at-best support for Ukraine and America's European allies. READ MORE: Iranian leaders say midterm results show U.S. voters have rejected Trump's war That and "the conflict in Ukraine started by Russia. These are the things we have to focus on now." But others in Europe cautioned that, with Trump in power for two more years, there would be no quick change to American foreign policy, which has strained defense, economic and diplomatic alliances. The president has berated European leaders over everything from immigration to wind farms, roiled their economies with tariffs, threatened to pull the U.S. out of NATO and expressed a desire to take over Greenland, a semiautonomous territory of NATO ally Denmark. Austrian Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger said that "independently of the election outcome, our security and prosperity in Austria and Europe must not depend on how people in Kansas or Iowa vote. That's why we are strengthening our own defense capability and our own competitiveness." Laurel Rapp, director of the U.S. and North America program at the Chatham House think tank, said there won't be "a 'we're back' moment in the U.S. relationship with Europe." "I don't expect this will significantly change the administration's approach to Europe," she said. "It's been a very transactional one, one that has deep skepticism about the value Europe can offer the U.S. in terms of a defense relationship." "I guess we'll see in a few weeks," when the new Congress takes over in January, he said. But Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province has been battered by Trump's tariffs on automobiles and steel, said the Democrats' sweeping victory would give Canada "a little more leverage" and declared it a win for the country and the world. Russia hopes Trump will stick to his current approach The Trump administration also has tried to pressure Ukraine to end a war that Russia started with its full-scale invasion in 2022. Ukraine accused Washington of delaying the delivery of vital interceptor missiles and reported that a temporary disruption to the Starlink and Starshield satellite internet service impeded its ability to defend against Russian attacks. Last month, even as he fired insults at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Trump waived sanctions on Russia even though Congress had overwhelmingly approved the measures as part of legislation aimed at supporting Ukraine. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday that Russia hoped Trump "will continue his peacemaking efforts" regardless of the election outcome. fde8e92013d8.text: Democrats' sweeping statehouse gains Tuesday have opened a path to effectively replacing the Electoral College with a national popular vote in time for the 2028 presidential election — without needing to amend the Constitution. Why it matters: The results could give Democrats the legislative power to fundamentally change how America picks its president, potentially ending the possibility of winning the White House while losing the national popular vote. Driving the news: Democrats have won control of the governorship and both legislative chambers in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Arizona, Wisconsin and Nevada, enough to push an agreement called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact beyond the 270-vote threshold required to take effect. The compact has been enacted by 18 states and Washington, D.C. since launching in 2006, representing 222 electoral votes so far. The agreement only kicks in when participating states collectively control at least 270 electoral votes. The five new Democratic trifectas could bring the total to 283. How it works: Americans don't directly elect the president. Instead, they actually cast ballots to choose electors, whose votes determine the winner every four years. Nearly every state awards all its electoral votes to the statewide winner. Maine and Nebraska also award electors based on congressional district results. But the Constitution explicitly gives states power to appoint electors "in such Manner as the Legislature thereof may direct." Under the compact, participating states would instead award their electoral votes to the national popular-vote winner once the agreement reaches 270 electoral votes. Yes, but: The five states would still need to enact the compact, and it's not clear if it will be a priority for the new Democratic states. The Electoral College would formally remain in place, and the compact could face constitutional challenges, including over whether congressional approval is required. Michigan failed to enact it during its previous Democratic trifecta from 2023 to 2024, and Nevada's then-Democratic governor vetoed the compact in 2019, warning it could diminish his state's influence over presidential elections. Notre Dame law professor Derek Muller has argued that the compact would be unconstitutional without congressional approval, which he contends is required under the Constitution's Compact Clause. What to watch: Whether and how legislators in the new trifecta states move forward. Lawmakers in all five states have previously introduced legislation to join the compact.
