The war on Iran is stripping the western Pacific of US naval forces
“It’s really a big problem. It’s a problem for credibility. It’s a problem for our allies in the Far East,” one expert said.
Half of the U.S. Navy’s Japan-based destroyers are currently supporting the war on Iran, belying Trump-administration strategy documents that called the Pacific theater a top priority and undermining relations with Western Pacific allies.
Five of the 10 destroyers homeported in Yokosuka, along with the Yokosuka-based aircraft carrier George Washington, are deployed to U.S. Central Command’s area of responsibility to help fight a war of choice. Navy officials have told the crews of at least some of those destroyers they won’t return home until 2027.
“It’s really a big problem. It’s a problem for credibility. It’s a problem for our allies in the Far East…who, in a lot of cases, have been planning months in advance for carrier visits and for carrier battle group visits,” said Ralph Cossa, chairman and WSD-Handa chair in peace studies for the Honolulu-based Pacific Forum. And aircraft carriers deploy with several other types of ships, he pointed out.
“That’s all assets that normally would be in the Pacific, that normally would be showing the flag, that normally would be reminding our allies of our commitment. And they’re nowhere to be found.”
This is not what is prescribed by the National Security Strategy, which was released less than a year ago. “Preventing conflict requires a vigilant posture in the Indo-Pacific,” the NSS says. “The days in which the Middle East dominated American foreign policy in both long-term planning and day-to-day execution are thankfully over.” This was echoed in January by the National Defense Strategy, which declared that its top priorities were the U.S. homeland and deterring China.
But five weeks later, President Trump launched a war against Iran. And although Operation Epic Fury officially concluded in June, the Pentagon is keeping a large force in the region, making occasional attacks, and waiting to see whether Trump will order more.
U.S. Pacific Command officials pushed back on the suggestion that they are scaling back the China-deterrence mission.
“Our commitment to the security of the Indo-Pacific and to our allies and partners remains steadfast,” a PACOM spokesperson said, adding that the command “remains focused on deterring aggression and maintaining the readiness required to execute our assigned missions. We continually assess operational requirements and coordinate with the Department of War to ensure our forces have the capabilities and support necessary to meet them.”
Highlighting the recent Keen Sword military exercise, which included participation from the California-based Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group, the spokesperson said “continuous training and exercises across the Indo-Pacific strengthen readiness and interoperability, while demonstrating our ability to respond to regional contingencies.”
Last week, at the TechNet Indo-Pacific conference in Honolulu, PACOM’s deputy commander, Lt. Gen. George Rowell, underscored that message in a keynote speech.
“Our mandate at U.S. Pacific Command is very clear: deterrence is our highest duty, and our guiding framework is to establish denial defense in the first island chain. We aim to prove that military aggressions will be infeasible, escalation will be catastrophic, and the costs of conflict far outweigh any gains.”
But, said Katherine Kuzminski, vice president of studies at the Center for a New American Security, sending so many of the U.S. Navy warships that are earmarked for patrolling the Pacific to the Middle East—and keeping them there for much longer than traditional Navy deployments—indicates “that our operations currently are not aligning with the administration’s stated national security strategy and national defense strategy, and that makes it really difficult at the service level or at the combatant command level to determine what the requirements are going to be.”
The military must be ready to respond, Kuzminski said, so “if there was some sort of incident that happens in the Indo-Pacific, we would want to be able to shift all of our resources there. But right now we’re kind of treating the [U.S. Central Command area of responsibility] in that way when we’ve committed to not be bogged down in the CENTCOM AOR.”
It’s not the first time the U.S. pivoted on the Pacific.
In 2012, under President Barack Obama, the Pentagon called for a “rebalance to the Indo-Pacific region,” including moving more troops and ships to the area. In 2016, then-Defense Secretary Ash Carter said the rebalance was not transient, but “enduring.” One year later, during the first Trump administration, a State Department official declared the rebalance officially dead.
Chinese president Xi Jinping has reportedly told his military to be prepared to take Taiwan by 2027. Cossa, like other experts, said he doesn’t believe “for a minute” that the Chinese will actually attack Taiwan next year, “but certainly, part of deterrence is convincing Xi that the U.S. has a commitment in this area and that we are going to respond. And when we have a third of our operational fleet out in the Middle East, that just sends the wrong signal.”
Keeping 7th Fleet sailors in the U.S. Navy Central region “for a year is going to be really poor for morale aboard ship and at home,” a Navy officer and expert on Pacific security told Defense One. “Trying to hide the cost by pulling [7th Fleet] away from home is just accounting fraud, and is hurting the fleet’s ability to show up for exercises in the Pacific, which will create its own hangover of damaged credibility, and contributes to the perception that the U.S. isn’t living up to its commitments on security in the region. I’ve heard that the fleet has been told to expect a 17 DDG requirement [in the Middle East] until 2029, which is insane. In terms of deterrent capability, most people I know think this

7fb59ef0aedb.text: Democratic socialist Nithya Raman toppled embattled Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass in a stunning upset, putting South Asian immigrants on course to lead America's two largest cities. Why it matters: With New York's Zohran Mamdani already in office, Raman's win puts democratic socialists on track to run two of America's most powerful city halls — testing whether their promises on affordable housing and better government can survive the pressures of governing. The big picture: Raman's victory marks a historic shift in urban American politics as voters embrace a new generation of immigrant leaders challenging the Democratic establishment. Raman, 45, immigrated from India as a child. Mamdani, New York's mayor, also has South Asian roots and immigrated to the U.S. Both built their political careers around affordability and inequality, giving democratic socialism a powerful foothold in America's largest cities. State of play: The Associated Press called the race for Raman Thursday, making Bass the first Los Angeles mayor in two decades to lose reelection. Raman led Bass 52.1% to 47.9% in unofficial results released Thursday. Ballot counting continues. Bass, who won in 2022, conceded and pledged a smooth transition. Raman takes office Dec. 14. Raman defeated a political heavyweight backed by California Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and much of the City Council. Zoom in: Raman capitalized on growing frustration over homelessness, housing costs and Bass' handling of the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire. A September Berkeley IGS/L.A. Times poll showed Raman leading Bass 66%-4% among likely voters under 30 and 45%-21% among Latino likely voters. Bass narrowed the gap. The final Berkeley poll showed the candidates tied at 40%, with 19% undecided. Among Latino likely voters, Raman's lead shrank to 43%-40%. Raman launched her challenge in February after previously endorsing Bass, turning former allies into political rivals. Zoom out: Democratic socialism's reach now extends beyond New York and Los Angeles. Washington, D.C., voters also elected democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George Tuesday, delivering another major victory for the movement. The wins raise questions about the Democratic Party's future as younger progressives challenge established leaders. Yes, but: Raman has carved out an independent path that sometimes puts her at odds with fellow socialists. She has repeatedly clashed with the Democratic Socialists of America over Israel, policing and housing. National DSA leaders voted 14-13 Monday against withdrawing her endorsement after a dispute over how the Los Angeles chapter vetted her stance on the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement targeting Israel. The group's Los Angeles chapter previously censured Raman for accepting an endorsement from Democrats for Israel-Los Angeles. She has stressed her political independence. Between the lines: Raman's winning pitch focused less on socialist ideology and more on making City Hall work. She told Axios and Noticias Telemundo at Visionarios that her approach amounts to "sewer socialism" or "pothole politics." "I just want government to work for the people," Raman said. That message could offer progressive candidates a model for building coalitions beyond traditional socialist activists. The bottom line: Winning City Hall may prove easier than running it. Raman faces a homelessness crisis, a housing shortage and the 2028 Olympics — with the nation watching whether democratic socialism can deliver on its promises.

b3bd8c70d856.text: By — Matthew Daly, Associated Press Matthew Daly, Associated Press By — Gary Fields, Associated Press Gary Fields, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/key-federal-panel-expected-to-approve-trumps-arch-amid-court-challenge Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Key federal panel expected to approve Trump's arch amid court challenge Politics Nov 5, 2026 4:34 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal panel was expected Thursday to approve President Donald Trump's proposed memorial arch in Washington at the end of a meeting that drew dozens of opponents to a key part of the president's push to leave his imprint on the nation's capital. The approval would clear a hurdle on the road to breaking ground on the project, and the administration has said it could launch construction within a day of the vote. But the proposed 250-foot (76-meter) tall gilded arch still faced legal challenges. READ MORE: Virginia and D.C. sue over Trump's arch, adding to legal challenges as government wants work to begin The remote, call-in hearing — which crashed repeatedly and was accompanied by a nearly universally negative comment section — drew witnesses who gave impassioned, three-minute comments opposing an arch they said will destroy the solemnity of the nearby Arlington National Cemetery. The Trump-appointed chairman of the commission, however, launched into a gushing appraisal of the towering monument and lauded Trump for wanting to build it. "President Trump understands as president and a superb builder that it's important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments," said Mark Paoletta, the commission's chairman. As Trump has often remarked, "the great cities around the world have arches: Paris, Rome, London," said Paoletta, who also serves as general counsel for the White House Office of Management and Budget. In addition to Paoletta, the arch received support during the hearing from Republican lawmakers and a veteran who praised the administration's efforts to build the monument. The commission oversees construction on federal land in the city and began reviewing the arch plan in June. Trump is working to remake Washington The arch is one of several projects around Washington that the Republican president has undertaken as he alters the capital to his tastes — from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Those projects could soon face intense scrutiny after Democrats gained control of Congress in the midterm elections this week. Many of the plans are being challenged in the courts, and three lawsuits have been filed opposing the arch. A judge has been asked to block the construction so long as lawsuits are still being litigated, and she could rule as early as Thursday. Rep. Jared Huffman, a California Democrat who is set to chair the House Natural Resources Committee, called the project ill-advised and illegal. "This arch would dishonor America," Huffman told the commission. He called the proposed arch "a tribute to Donald Trump," not veterans as Trump administration officials claim. The monument is similar to those built for emperors or kings, Huffman said, adding that Trump was using veterans as a pretext to build a memorial to himself. Opponents argue the arch is too big for the skyline and would disrupt carefully designed sight lines between landmarks in and around the capital — most prominently the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery — that were meant to symbolize the reunification of the North and the South after the Civil War. But the opposition has done little to influence the members of the commission, which is led by some of Trump's closest allies. Trump appointed Paoletta to chair the 12-member panel. Two other commissioners are also White House aides. Trump wants an arch, but it faces legal challenges Still, a federal judge on Monday complicated Trump's efforts to move quickly on the project. U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan, who is overseeing a lawsuit challenging the Trump administration's plans, said she must be told of any decision by the planning commission within an hour. The order set the same time limits for any decision by the National Park Service and the Department of the Interior. Before Thursday's hearing began, attorneys with the Justice Department filed a notice with Chutkan informing her that a contractor had already done site prep work on Oct. 31, with what she said appeared to be no authorization from the National Park Service. The plaintiffs in the three lawsuits are calling for a halt to work on a monument that is set to be built on a patch of grass off a bridge that spans the Potomac River and connects Washington with Arlington National Cemetery, in Arlington, Virginia. When complete, the monument would be 100 feet (30 meters) taller than the Statue of Liberty without its pedestal. Critics, including the plaintiffs, argue that the Trump administration must seek congressional approval. The administration maintains that Congress cleared the way for a monument at Memorial Circle decades ago. Paoletta said it was a "national disgrace" that a memorial arch had not been placed there, despite a 1925 law that designated such a memorial, he said. California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead to life in prison.
"We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honour the victims," he said in a letter.
The decision to spare death row inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed an inmate since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs each year. Only 13 inmates have been executed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978.
The decision comes as Newsom, the Democratic leader of the most populous US state, has been discussed as a possible 2028 contender for president.
Newsom, who is term limited, is winding down his final months in office. Fellow Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to take over after the midterm elections on Tuesday.
Newsom explained in his letter that he is exercising his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences to life without the possibility of parole.
"After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom said. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us".
California has historically had the largest population of death row inmates. Newsom had previously ordered a halt to the death penalty in the state in 2019.
Newsom, describing his decision as a difficult but "righteous action", said that although many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die, he has concluded that "the state cannot morally kill them".
He said that by every measure, California's system for administering the death penalty "is a failure", and that it has not and cannot be fairly applied, resulting in the conviction of innocent people.
Life without the possibility of parole is the most severe punishment he can lawfully impose and that the state can ethically enforce, he said.
He acknowledged that his clemency action will anger and hurt some Californians and said that it will "always weigh heavily on me".
"As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," he wrote.
"For this reason, I am compelled to follow my conscience and, as authorised by our Constitution, take this action for the welfare of the State of California."
Because individual states have the power to prosecute crimes and order executions, much of the power lies with state governors.
The decision comes after the high-profile botched execution of a woman in Tennessee in late September and while executions have been on the rise in the US. There are three executions scheduled for Thursday in Indiana, Florida and Alabama.
Most of Newsom's action on Thursday will need court approval, CalMatters reported. For the commutations of the nearly 400 prisoners convicted of multiple felonies, at least four of seven judges on the California Supreme Court have to sign off.
Anthony D Romero, the executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union, applauded Newsom's action.
"These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long," Romero said.
"By taking this step, Gov. Newsom has affirmed that the death penalty has no place in California and he showed real courage by confronting racialised injustice head-on."
On the federal level, President Donald Trump, a long-time supporter of the death penalty, has described capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".
In 2020, during his first term, he ended a nearly two-decade moratorium on the federal death penalty, by ordering 13 executions over a six-month period.
While the moratorium returned under President Biden, on the first day of Trump's second term in 2025, he signed an executive order that re-instated the death penalty.
No federal executions have been carried out since he signed it, however. In the US, both the federal government and local states authorities can order executions.
The death penalty is legal in 27 states, but has been abolished in 23 states and Washington DC, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a national non-profit.
California, which primarily uses lethal injection for executions, used to house male death row prisoners in San Quentin State Prison north of San Francisco, and female inmates in the Central California Women's Facility in the Central Valley.
But a 2016 ballot measure allowed for their transfer to other facilities that provide a necessary level of security, according to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation.

b66453d13d67.text:
Octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from New Zealand’s national aquarium?
The cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game plan, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.
Octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”
Sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, says Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.
Kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.
One, two, three — free!
Octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.
Common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.
When the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.
Out the door on four
When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.
Mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba says. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.
The team hopes these escape artists will inspire new soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, says Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”
Studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook says. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.
Currently, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.

1accc759c7af.text: California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced Thursday he plans to commute all 548 of the state's death sentences to life without parole, a sweeping decision that could empty the nation's largest death row. Why it matters: If Newsom follows through, it will be the largest mass commutation of death sentences in U.S. history , reducing the national death-row population by more than a quarter. The move comes during Newsom's final months as governor and ahead of a potential 2028 bid for president. What he's saying: "I know we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency," Newsom wrote in a letter to Californians. "Many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die. But as Governor, I have concluded the state cannot morally kill them." "We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honor their victims." "This decision is among the most difficult of my career," he wrote. Context: Newsom can commute some sentences on his own, but prisoners with multiple felony convictions need approval from the California Supreme Court before their sentences can be reduced, per the California Constitution . Yes, but: This won't end the death penalty in California. It remains legal even though the state hasn't performed one since 2006 . In fact, California voters rejected ballot measures in 2012 and 2016 to end capital punishment. Flashback: Shortly after taking office, Newsom instituted a moratorium on executions , reprieving 737 prisoners from death row. The ACLU has been pushing Newsom to commute death row sentences since former President Biden did so in 2024 for 37 federal prisoners. Other Democratic governors have similarly commuted death sentences, including North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper , who commuted 15 in 2024. Zoom out: The death penalty faces heavy scrutiny nationwide after Tennessee's failed execution attempt of Christa Pike and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth 's call for a public execution.

e398c4df672f.text: One of the biggest nail-biters of the 2026 election isn't playing out in a purple state, but crimson Mississippi, where Democrat Scott Colom is trying to pull off a Magnolia State upset. The big picture: It's one of the most remarkable currents of Tuesday's blue wave. The race pitted Colom, a Democratic district attorney powered by grassroots clout, against incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith in a state Trump won by some 23 points in 2024. The big picture: The coalition Colom built with his viral ads and the historic tenor of his candidacy faces the ultimate Deep South test. The race remains too close to call. "The flag has already been planted in Mississippi that a new day has arrived, and whether these final votes carry Scott Colom into that victory column, we will find out," says Nadine Smith, president and CEO of Color Of Change. "But … change has arrived." Follow the money: Colom's was one of the red-state races that drew the attention of Florida attorney Steve Pajcic, whose family-run super PAC New Deal for All sought to boost Dems in under-the-radar races. Mississippi, where they invested around $1.1 million, was ideal "in size and in potential," he tells Axios. That money went far on Mississippi's less-expensive airwaves. The most-aired ad in the closing week featured an Epstein survivor condemning Hyde-Smith, Axios' Donica Phifer reported. New Deal for All paid for the ad, which inundated Mississippi's TV markets. Catch up quick: In October, Axios reported that Senate Republicans were weighing a cash infusion into the race. The GOP Senate Leadership Fund eventually made an investment. Democrats ' Senate Majority PAC announced a $1.2 million ad campaign, and Colom also drew party heavy-hitters like former Vice President Kamala Harris and former President Clinton for appearances. Former President Obama also cut an ad. Zoom out: The race's seismic nature is also fueled by history. Colom would be Mississippi's first Black senator elected since Reconstruction, and its first Democrat elected to the Senate since the 1980s. Colom's campaign leaned into the fight for Black Americans' right to vote, producing an ad about civil rights leader Medgar Evers and how his efforts ultimately cost the NAACP's first Mississippi field officer his life. "You can't talk about the struggle for Black freedom without talking about Mississippi, and that is why the symbolism of this moment is so powerful," Smith says. Flashback: Hyde-Smith set the stage for her dragged-out drama with Colom in 2023: She blocked former President Joe Biden's nomination of Colom to be a U.S. District Court Judge for the Northern District of Mississippi — despite fellow Republican Sen. Roger Wicker backing him. Black Mississippians favored Colom 91% to Hyde-Smith's 7% per New York Times voter trend estimates , something political analysts have said was key for a Democrat to win: strong Black turnout, combined with a quarter of white Mississippians' support. The Supreme Court's ruling limiting the Voting Rights Act , empowering Republican redistricting and diluting Black votes, also pushed Black voters to the polls, Smith said. The SCOTUS ruling awoke "a giant," Smith said. "People were not going to be discouraged; they were going to be galvanized." What we're watching: Pajcic tells Axios that the 2026 vote is a door to historic moments. "It's a new Mississippi, and it goes with a new South Carolina, a new Georgia, a new North Carolina, new Texas," Pajcic says. "We've got a new South." Go deeper: Democrats poised to break GOP's 16-year grip on statehouses

PHOENIX—Two years after President Donald Trump won Arizona with 52 percent of the vote, Democrats are poised to win a trifecta in the state House, Senate and governor’s office, and could potentially win every statewide elected position. The battleground state’s blue wave could fundamentally alter how it responds to increasingly deadly heat and persistent drought brought on by climate change.
Central to the Democrats’ wins, party members and candidates said, was their focus on addressing the state’s growing energy demand and declining water resources, which are increasingly top issues for Arizonans.
Attorney General Kris Mayes, who has made protecting the state’s water resources and fighting rising energy costs her top two priorities, won her bid for reelection. Democrats Clara Pratte and Jonathon Hill took two seats on the state’s currently all-Republican commission that regulates utilities. And, for the first time since 1966, Democrats are almost guaranteed to have a trifecta with incumbent Gov. Katie Hobbs winning her reelection bid against Republican-candidate Rep. Andy Biggs. Even the party’s candidate for state mine inspector, Brian Matlock, leads in the polls, with his potential win marking the first time that seat has gone to a Democrat since 1976.
Taken together, the Democrats’ wins present an opportunity for major changes to how the state approaches climate change and energy policy, potentially paving the way for new renewable energy development and groundwater regulations. The latter has proven to be one of the state’s stickiest policy debates over the last decade, and an issue where Hobbs has attempted to make strides but been stopped from enacting reform by the Republican-controlled legislature.
“What we’ve seen is data centers have brought [energy and water] issues to the forefront,” Priya Sundareshan, Democratic leader in the state Senate, told Inside Climate News at the Arizona Democrats watch party Tuesday night. “The bipartisan response to data centers that we know voters have is around their energy use and their water use, and those are fundamentally questions that we have failed to address at the state level, and we continue to fail to address because of Republican control of the legislature.”
Arizona knows extreme weather well, she said, from record-hot summers to flooding that left communities evacuated over the last week to dwindling water supplies.
“All of that is directly tied to the changing climate, and that’s something where we can tie that picture together and be able to show voters that we can see the big picture,” Sundareshan said. “We can work toward a future that makes sure that we can all live here.”
In an interview with Inside Climate News, Mayes, the attorney general, said focusing her office and campaign on energy and water issues “were pivotal” to her victory. During her first four years, Mayes sued Fondomonte Arizona, a subsidiary of a Saudi Arabian company, which was pumping an unlimited amount of water from a groundwater basin on state trust land to irrigate alfalfa that was eventually fed to cattle in Saudi Arabia. She also challenged the Arizona Corporation Commission—of which she was once an elected member—over its decisions to roll back renewable energy and energy efficiency programs. And she has called for a statewide moratorium on new data center development until a plan for them can be developed.

“I did 70 town halls all over Arizona, many of them about water and data centers,” she said. “I think that resonated with Arizonans. People are worried about our water supplies, and they didn’t think that they had politicians working hard enough on those issues, and they saw in me somebody that was willing to stick my neck out against powerful entities and I will continue to do that.”
Many of the state’s races are far from a done deal, with only a fraction of the votes counted so far. But Democrats hold overwhelming leads for many seats that put them out of reach for Republicans. The final count for the state Senate and House remain undecided, though it is clear Democrats will have a majority in both.
Democrats flipped Scottsdale’s Congressional District 1 in one of the country’s most contested races, with Dr. Amish Shah winning the seat he failed to take in 2024. They also beat incumbent Republican Juan Ciscomani in southern Arizona’s Congressional District 6, with Democrat JoAnna Mendoza flipping the seat.
But it’s too early to call some of the state’s other races for the U.S. House of Representatives. Democrats are maintaining close races in three other Republican-held districts. Only one Arizona Republican, Paul Gosar, has won his reelection for his House seat so far.
Polling has consistently shown energy and water issues were top of mind for voters. The Center for the Future of Arizona found 69 percent of voters don’t have confidence that the state will have enough water in the long-term, and that water was the top issue for its voters. Recent polling from The Nature Conservancy in Arizona and the Arizona PIRG Education Fund found about 80 percent of Arizonans said their electricity bills rose in the last two years. More than 60 percent said their summer power bills are difficult to afford.
“The people of Arizona deserve leaders who are looking out for us and ensuring that we can afford to fill our gas tank and keep our lights on, and that’s why they re-elected Governor Hobbs,” said Climate Power’s Arizona State Director Diali Avila in a statement. “Andy Biggs and his fellow Republicans rubber-stamped Trump’s agenda at every turn, and now they’re paying the price. Arizonans need relief from skyrocketing costs, and Governor Hobbs will work to bring down costs for Arizonans—not enrich oil and gas billionai

More than 1,000 tonnes of "sewage sludge" have been seen at a landfill site near Doncaster, according to an MP for the town.
Lee Pitcher said in a Facebook post he had been told the waste was being stored in "an uncovered stockpile" at the site in Finningley.
The Labour MP said he had been in contact with the Environment Agency (EA), which confirmed on Thursday that it had "set out a series of actions" for the site's operator following an inspection.
The landfill, located in a former quarry, is operated by Tetron Finningley Ltd, which has not previously responded when contacted for comment by the BBC.
Pitcher, who is the MP for Doncaster East and the Isle of Axholme, said EA officers visited the landfill on 9 October and, after he "chased" them for their findings, they responded on Tuesday.
He said the EA had told him that during the visit "approximately 1,000 tonnes of sewage sludge were observed being stored externally in an uncovered stockpile" and had "identified concerns regarding whether site activities were being undertaken in accordance with the operating techniques and management arrangements described within the approved documents".
Pitcher said the EA had given the landfill operator until 10 November to resolve the issue.
The MP said he had subsequently contacted the EA again about "potential asbestos disposal at the site, along with the air quality and environmental ramifications this could bring".
Last month, Ed Bradley, a director of the neighbouring Doncaster Moto Parc, said he had been forced to close the venue after people attending the motocross track were suffering from "headaches, nausea and generally feeling unwell" from the smells.
He said he was concerned that the business may no longer be viable if it continues to remain closed.
In a statement on Facebook, he said: "For months, we have raised concerns about the terrible odours coming from the neighbouring site, the effects on our staff and customers, and our inability to operate safely.
"Despite those reports, the situation has continued.
"Unfortunately, while the authorities have been investigating, the financial consequences for Doncaster Moto Parc have been devastating.
"We are now facing the very real possibility of losing the business altogether."
An Environment Agency spokesperson said: "We expect site operators to manage odour effectively and have identified issues around odour management at this site.
"Following an inspection, we have set out a series of actions that we expect the operator to comply with and will not hesitate to take further enforcement action should that be required."

The warnings came in thick and fast, targeting one airline or airport after another.
In nearly all cases - London's Heathrow airport being a notable exception - they were taken to be credible enough to divert the aircraft in question, or even in Italy's case, to scramble fighter jets to escort it.
They all turned out to be false, which does not, of course, mean that the next ones will not be real.
It is hardly surprising that the simultaneous, co-ordinated nature of these airline hoaxes, coupled with other malicious actions across Europe, are causing some people to point the finger of suspicion at Russia.
Following a series of cyber-attacks and mysterious drone sightings over sensitive sites earlier this year, in the past few days we have seen the remote hacking of supermarket freezers, as well as a blood bank, a suspicious incident on Poland's border with Russia, and in August a drone attack Germany's Leipzig Halle airport which its interior minister publicly blamed on Moscow.
So is Russia behind this?
There are many who argue, based purely on circumstantial evidence, that this must surely be yet another example of "hybrid", "grey zone" or "sub-threshold" warfare - actions that damage a nation's infrastructure or society but which tend to be anonymous, deniable and which fall short of triggering Nato's Article 5 and thereby mobilising a response by the West.
Moscow is certainly furious with Nato for supporting Ukraine and, in doing so, frustrating the Kremlin's plans to swallow up that country and effectively terminate its independence.
Russian bloggers have also suggested that, if Ukraine's drones are currently making Russia's airports unsafe, and Western sanctions are blocking Russian airlines from European airspace, then why shouldn't Western nations feel the same pain?
But as of Thursday evening no hard evidence had emerged linking the airline hoaxes to Russia, Iran or any proxy groups controlled by them.
There is the email threat sent on Thursday morning to airport authorities in Rome, purporting to be from "Fighters of the Male State".
That name likely refers to the Russian group Muzhskoi Legion or "Male Legion", an ultra-right group with such extreme views it was banned by a Moscow court in 2021.
Yet, it retained tens of thousands of online followers on Telegram as it cheered on the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in the following year.
But the email sent to Rome, even if genuine - and who is to say it is not another group hiding behind that name? - is unlikely to provide the leads that police and airport authorities need to pin down who is generating these hoaxes and why.
For national police forces, airport authorities and transport ministries trying to work out who is behind these hoaxes and how best to mitigate their effect when they happen again, the task is not to go with who they think might be the most likely culprits but instead to follow the cold, hard leads - if they can find them.

Eight people have been killed and one seriously injured in a series of shootings in western Turkey.
The attacks took place in the Afyonkarahisar province on Thursday, with victims found in several locations in three separate vehicles, according to local reports.
The suspect fled, triggering a manhunt, and authorities later said he had been arrested in EskiÅehir province.
CCTV footage published in Turkish media showed a man in a black jacket, white trousers and glasses clutching a long weapon as he stood by a red minivan.
Turkey's state-run Anadolu Agency reported that three people were killed near Ayazini village and three others near Kiyir village. In Yukaritandir, two women were found injured and later died in hospital.
Two teachers were reportedly among the dead.
Local media said roads leading to the affected villages were closed by police, while officers launched a large-scale operation to find the suspect.
The newspaper Milliyet reported that a vehicle allegedly taken by the attacker had been later found stuck in mud - the suspect having abandoned it before fleeing on foot.
In a statement posted on social media, the Afyonkarahisar Governorate said "all relevant institutions of our state have been working in coordination since the very first moment and are meticulously carrying out the necessary work".

US First Lady Melania Trump called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine as she welcomed Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House following last week's truce in the southern region of Kherson.
Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire, which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering.
"The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.
The unusual White House event saw senior Ukrainian and Russian officials meet away from the setting of official US-brokered peace talks they have been holding without success since last year.
The delegations were made up of Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova, as well as Ukrainian MP Davyd Arakhamia and Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev.
Melania Trump was credited by all for playing a key though unspecified role in the ceasefire, and all parties conveyed to her the gratitude of the Russian and Ukrainian presidents.
The US first lady said she had "reviewed demining plans, aerial images, assessed roadways, and discussed evacuation routes, hospital access, vehicles, and medical resources" during the truce.
"Last week in Oleshky and neighbouring areas of Kherson, people experienced the simple joys of life for the first time since 2022," Trump said. "They walked down familiar streets without fear of explosions."
She thanked both Volodymyr Zelensky and Vladimir Putin, making no reference to the origins of the war, which began when the Russian president launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and which has caused thousands of civilian casualties and the displacement of millions.
Dmitriev, a businessman and Kremlin special envoy who has previously represented Moscow during peace talks with Ukraine, thanked Trump for "saving and touching so many lives".
"Let us continue making a humanitarian contribution together; this is within our power," Dmitriev said, before gifting Melania Trump a framed drawing by an 11-year-old Oleshky evacuee.
He also praised Trump for her work on reuniting children separated from their families by the war. These include children allegedly abducted by Russia.
Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads Zelensky's party in parliament who has also been part of the Ukrainian negotiating team, said the Oleshky ceasefire had constituted the "biggest de-escalation since 2022".
"We are creating a momentum where both sides are learning theâ¦ mechanics of how to actually keep the peace when the peace comes," he added.
He acknowledged that the "political track" of negotiations to end the conflict was "complex" but said Ukrainians were asking Melania Trump "to keep going and find new missions and de-escalate more."
At the end of the event, Trump handed Dmitriev and Arakhamia two letters to be hand-delivered to their respective presidents.
The White House later said Melania Trump had invited her guests to view two historic artifacts which she had "personally selected as powerful symbols of peace".
One was an 18th Century medicine chest which was removed from the White House when the British set it on fire in 1812. "Once adversaries, the United States and Great Britain ultimately established a strong alliance," the White House said.
The second artifact was a cup gifted in 1899 to the French ambassador in recognition of his efforts to bring the Spanish-American war to an end.
Melania Trump has generally remained discreet on foreign policy matters, and neither Moscow nor Kyiv have elaborated on the nature or extent of her involvement in coordinating the delicate ceasefire - the most enduring and widespread of the war so far.
A source who works in the local government of the Kherson region told the BBC that work on the Oleshky evacuation had been ongoing for almost a year.
However, the source said, "at a certain point other individuals became involved, seemingly after most of the groundwork had already been laid and subsequently began taking credit for the progress that had been made."
It was difficult to determine exactly who had played what role and at which stage of the process, the source acknowledged, adding that "those who had been directly involved in the negotiations for nearly a year were eventually prohibited from communicating publicly about the matter."
Speaking after the meeting in the White House had taken place, President Zelensky said the success of the Oleshky ceasefire "had proved a very simple thing: when Putin wants the fighting to stop, it stops."
"The same applies to our people who are held in Russian captivity. When Putin wants, they go home."
A source close to American officials shared a similar assessment, implying to the BBC that despite the outward praise, "the person who made [the ceasefire] possible, whether we like it or not, is essentially Putin."
"And this was done in order to pass the ball to [Donald] Trump... so that it would have some positive effect for his midterm elections."
There has been no change whatsoever in Russia's position, Ukrainian political analyst Dmytro Levus told the BBC.
Moscow "agreed to it because there was pressure from the American side... In doing so, the Russians confirmed Zelenskyy's words that, when necessary, it turns out Russia can quickly stop firing and even maintain that ceasefire."
As the frontline region of Kherson experienced its first six days of peace in several years, the rest of Ukraine continued to come under Russian attack.
This week, several drone and missile attacks killed and injured civilians across the country. On Monday alone, more than 40 people were killed in a single Russian strike on an aid distribution centre in the region of Zaporizhzhia. More are thought to still be buried under the rubble.
Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko in Kyiv

7fc6c5f05d35.text: By — Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press By — Rebecca Santana, Associated Press Rebecca Santana, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/trump-administration-held-talks-with-iran-on-deporting-iranians-during-the-war-court-documents-show Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump administration held talks with Iran on deporting Iranians during the war, court documents show World Nov 5, 2026 2:04 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's administration held secret talks with Iran on deporting Iranians even as the war there dragged on, court documents show. The court documents unsealed Thursday show the Republican administration as recently as mid-October said it had plans to deport the Iranians through an unnamed third country, although it was unclear when it intended to do so. The judge in the case ordered the government to give the court 24-hour notice of any finalized plans to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country and five days' written notice before any such deportation is carried out. READ MORE: ICE and Iran worked together to deport Iranians from U.S., newly released emails show The documents show that the administration maintained contacts with Iranian officials during the war over the removals, specifically for submitting travel documents and figuring out "possible avenues for removal." Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News "We are at war with a country where the President of the United States has said, as recently as two or three days ago, if not yesterday, that it is essentially lawless ... A country that is an enemy of the United States, according to the current president. A country that, according to our president, murdered tens of thousands of protestors," Judge Ana Reyes said according to the Oct. 15 transcript. READ MORE: Vance blames Iran war for GOP midterm losses "And what you're telling me is that the United States of America is going to send individuals back to that region, facing what you and I and everyone who would ever look at this would know would be, at a minimum, a serious threat of certain death." "Yes, your honor," Justice Department attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel said. "The government is executing lawful orders of removal." The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The development emerged from an ongoing lawsuit that alleges the Trump administration's immigration agencies have been sharing confidential information about Iranian asylum seekers with the Iranian government, violating national immigration regulations and endangering countless Iranians, court filings argue. The new court documents show the coordination continued during the war. READ MORE: Iranian leaders say midterm results show U.S. voters have rejected Trump's war The lawsuit depicts a coordinated campaign between the U.S. and Iranian governments to identify Iranians in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody and pressure them to return to Iran — a marked departure from decades of diplomatic hostility between the two governments and an ongoing war. DHS has denied that it is sharing asylum application records with the Iranian government. Hundreds of emails exchanged between U.S. immigration officials exposed how the two countries worked together to arrange for more than 100 Iranians to be flown back to Iran on three immigration flights in September and December 2025 and January 2026. Deportations of Iranians back to their home country are historically rare, owing to the lack of diplomatic relations between the U.S. and Iran and the possible persecution they could face if they were sent to Iran. But under the Trump administration, ICE has aggressively pushed to deport people even from countries that have typically been reluctant to take people back or with whom the U.S. has had icy or no diplomatic relations. Sometimes that has meant sending people back to their home country but it has also meant deporting people to other countries that they have no connection with. The Trump administration has deported people, including Iranians, to countries other than their own in an attempt to circumvent diplomatic hurdles with governments that won't take their people back. During Trump's second term, countries including El Salvador, Costa Rica and Panama have accepted noncitizens from the U.S. In June, an Iranian woman was among the two dozen migrants the U.S. deported to the Central African Republic. Activists abroad have expressed concern about deportees returning to Iran, whose theocracy has been cracking down on intellectuals and where the government vociferously cracks down on any dissent. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Democrats have been celebrating their sweeping midterm victories, including flipping control of both chambers of Congress - but several critical races were still too close to be called on Thursday.
Votes are still being counted in two surprisingly tight Senate races in historically red states, Alaska and Mississippi, which could decide the true scale of Democrats' majority.
Several US House races are also too close to call, including that of Lauren Boebert, a prominent ally of President Donald Trump, who is facing a tight re-election contest in Colorado against Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher.
Here are the races Americans are watching closely.
1. US Senate race in Mississippi
What and who are on the ballot: The race for Mississippi's Senate seat remains dramatically close with Democrat Scott Colom leading Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by a little over 1,100 votes. The state has until 10 November to count provisional and late-arriving mail ballots.
On the campaign trail, Colom focused his message on plans to address economic concerns, while Hyde-Smith, the first woman to represent Mississippi in the US Congress, was endorsed by Trump and campaigned with him.
Why it matters: If Colom wins, he would be the first black US senator elected in Mississippi since 1875 - and the first Democrat since 1982. Mississippi is a state home to the largest percentage of African Americans in the US, a group that overwhelmingly votes Democratic and showed up in large numbers this election.
2. US Senate race in Alaska
What and who are on the ballot: It's another extremely tight race being watched nationally with Democrat Mary Peltola leading Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan by just over 600 votes with more ballots to be counted.
Peltola, a former congresswoman and Native American, campaigned for "fish, family and freedom", while two-term Republican Senator Sullivan focused on his efforts to get Americans tax cuts and "unleash Alaska's energy potential".
Why it matters: The race has been marred with controversy because of the appearance of another candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
Last week, The New York Times reported allegations that Peltola and Alaska Democrats sought to confuse voters by recruiting the independent Dan Sullivan in order to siphon votes from the Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. Peltola has denied any knowledge of such a scheme.
3. A number of House races in purple and red states
What and who are on the ballot: Trump ally Lauren Boebert is trailing Democrat Eileen Laubacher by a narrow margin in Colorado's Fourth District with 7% of votes left to be counted. In Tennessee's reliably Republican Fourth District, Representative Scott DesJarlais is trailing Democrat Victoria Broderick. In Arizona's Second District, incumbent Republican Eli Crane is leading Democrat Jonathan Nez by fewer than 4,000 votes with still many to be counted.
Why it matters: A loss for Boebert, DesJarlais and other Republicans in House races in Nevada and Ohio would mean an even larger majority for Democrats in the chamber - and a bigger rejection of Trump and his Make America Great Again movement.
4. California billionaire wealth tax
What and who are on the ballot: California Proposition 40 would require a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state's roughly 200 billionaires to raise tens of billions of dollars in revenue. As of Wednesday, a million more people had voted against the measure than in favour, though only 61% of votes have been counted.
Why it matters: The measure would mark the first-ever wealth tax on billionaires in the US, which proponents say would raise $100bn for health care and education. But the proposition divided Democrats, with Governor Gavin Newsom opposing it.
5. Kansas governor race
What and who are on the ballot: For Kansas's next governor, Democrat Cindy Holscher is leading Republican Ty Masterson by a few thousand votes.
Holscher campaigned over escalating prices, while Masterson touted his pro-business, pro-agriculture, and pro-oil and gas credentials.
Why it matters: For more than 50 years, Kansas has elected governors from the opposite party of their predecessors. If Masterson wins, that trend would continue. Holscher's victory would break it by putting another Democrat in office after two-term Governor Laura Kelly.

Science has reached a new low. Temperature, that is.
Scientists cooled a collection of atoms to about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin. That’s barely a smidge above absolute zero (−273.15° Celsius). The atoms formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a quantum state of matter, colder than any before, researchers report November 5 in Science.
To achieve that record-low chill, scientists took their work to space. The atoms orbited Earth aboard China’s Tiangong space station. There, researchers used laser-based traps to contain 20,000 rubidium atoms and reduce their motion, thereby cooling them. At an atomic level, temperature is tied to motion: Atoms and molecules in the air around us move more slowly when it’s colder. Similarly, in systems of cold atoms, scientists can define an effective temperature based on how slowly the atoms spread apart when they are allowed to expand.
On Earth, gravitational forces cause clouds of atoms to sag, reducing the effectiveness of cooling. But on the space station, the atoms experienced microgravity, the apparent weightlessness of an object in free fall.
To make a Bose-Einstein condensate, a disorderly gaggle of atoms is cooled until the atoms all take on the same quantum state, acting as one entity. By experimenting with ultracold atoms, researchers can study exotic states of matter and other mysterious physics. And they can test fundamental concepts, such as the equivalence principle — the idea that explains why objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.
Spacefaring Bose-Einstein condensates were previously made on the International Space Station, at effective temperatures as low as 52 picokelvins. And an experiment on Earth, in which atoms were dropped down a tower to induce weightlessness, reached 38 picokelvins. But drop tower experiments are limited by the time their free fall lasts. That’s not an issue for experiments in Earth’s orbit. So cold atoms in space are really taking off.

Hackers are targeting refrigerators worldwide, US agencies warn
The warning follows Nextgov/FCW reporting that officials suspect Iran-linked hackers were behind freezer failures at military commissaries.
Federal agencies warned Thursday that hackers are targeting refrigeration systems worldwide, urging operators to secure equipment whose recent failures have spoiled food and created fire hazards.
CISA, the FBI, and the departments of Health and Human Services, Agriculture, and Transportation issued joint warnings that attackers are targeting electronic temperature controls at grocery stores and cold storage facilities.
The warning follows Nextgov/FCW’s report last week that U.S. officials suspect Iran-linked hackers were behind freezer malfunctions at military bases across the country. Those incidents began around late August and have affected roughly six commissaries, the on-base grocery stores that serve military personnel. Reuters initially reported that the Pentagon was treating the freezer incidents as possible cyberattacks.
In France, hackers targeted refrigeration systems at three regional blood banks overnight Sunday into Monday. And this week, a new wave of supermarket attacks raised fridge temperatures at stores in Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg and elsewhere, forcing retailers to discard food. The incidents followed attacks at hundreds of French establishments in October.
The U.S. notice does not name who is responsible for the cyber sabotage.
Hackers could force refrigerators and freezers into continuous heating or defrost cycles, the agencies said. They could also prevent operators from seeing current temperatures, making it harder to monitor conditions inside the units. Beyond spoiled inventory and damaged equipment, the agencies warned of fire hazards and potential harm to consumers who use products kept at unsafe temperatures.
Such hacks are possible because various digital vulnerabilities tied to refrigeration controls can expose their underlying equipment to hacking and sabotage, including devices connected to the internet that are used to remotely monitor or control temperatures.
“Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target,” said Chris Butera, CISA’s acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity.
Hospitals, pharmaceutical suppliers, chemical companies and transportation providers also depend on these systems.
“We are seeing these systems targeted across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk,” said Brett Leatherman, the FBI’s cyber branch operations director.
The agencies urged operators to remove control systems from the public internet and secure any remote access they still need. They also recommended separating refrigeration controls from business networks, replacing default passwords, installing security updates and retiring equipment that manufacturers no longer support.
The hacks follow a pattern closely aligned with Iranian hackers, said Nahman Khayet, the co-founder and CEO at Alt Security.
“They’ve been playing this game for many years,” he said in an interview. “Think about how hard it is to replace those refrigerators, right? They’re huge things. It’s very costly. And also you don’t want to do any disruption to those because they probably hold a lot of items which are important, like food.”
That dynamic means that it’s unlikely the devices are getting the latest security updates, which Iranian cyber operators have often leveraged to get inside systems, including various types of critical infrastructure, he added.
European authorities issued their own joint warning Wednesday, calling for immediate action to secure exposed equipment. The European Commission, cybersecurity agency ENISA, Europol and national authorities are coordinating their response and sharing information about the incidents.

68140da1ca34.text: By — Colleen Barry, Associated Press Colleen Barry, Associated Press By — Angela Charlton, Associated Press Angela Charlton, Associated Press By — David Biller, Associated Press David Biller, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/more-than-a-dozen-flights-in-europe-receive-bomb-threats-that-an-official-calls-malicious-hoaxes Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter More than a dozen flights in Europe receive bomb threats that an official calls 'malicious' hoaxes World Nov 5, 2026 1:47 PM EST MILAN (AP) — Bomb threats targeted more than a dozen flights in Europe on Thursday, leading to a slew of emergency landings and military escorts in some cases, authorities said. No hazardous or suspicious materials have been found in what a British official called "malicious" hoaxes. Several similar threats targeted planes earlier this week, prompting searches and diversions. Europe has experienced a slew of other disruptions recently, such as attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems, drone incursions and mysterious triggers to alert apps. READ MORE: Flights across Europe face disruption after false bomb threats While fake bomb threats are relatively common, it is unusual to see so many in a single day. They come at a time of increased geopolitical tensions and warnings from authorities that Russia may be ramping up so-called hybrid threats in Europe. It was not known whether this week's threats were linked, who sent them or what their aims were. An email containing the threat to Rome-bound planes was sent on behalf of a group that describes itself as anti-feminist, according to a copy provided by an airport official and reviewed by The Associated Press. An official from another European airport said the threat they received also came from a group calling itself anti-feminist, and used some of the same language. It wasn't clear if the two threats were sent by the same group. Both officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to share the information. 'Stress-testing' governments and driving up costs Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, senior fellow at the Bruegel think tank in Brussels, said the threats were "stress-testing" how European governments and airport officials respond, and whether their responses were coordinated. The idea behind the threats "appears to be to sow chaos, uncertainty, about the reliability of air traffic across Europe" and could have "cascading effects" — like economic damage and costs related to inspection, investigation and cleaning aircraft. Joji Waites, who heads flight safety at the British Airline Pilots' Association, said the industry has put in place "proved mechanisms" for dealing with such threats, including a team of assessors to grade the level of threat in a red-amber-green color-coding system, quick notification of flight crews, and the evacuation of planes on the ground. Each flight disruption could cost airlines as much as $250,000, on a par with the possible costs of dealing with an unruly passenger, said Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England. "And that's because you might end up with the crew going out of hours. You might need replacement crew. You have got passengers that miss their flight connections," Baum said. "It knocks everything out of sync for the rest of the day for the airline in question." Military escorts incur expenses, too, which would be borne by governments rather than airlines, he added. Officials decry the hoaxes Britain's transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, told British broadcasters that flights across Europe have been hit by "malicious hoax threats." European Union Transport Commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas told reporters in Dublin that it was "too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked." "National investigations remain ongoing," he said, adding that an EU information-sharing mechanism on aviation security had been activated. A French air base is on high security An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a military air base in France after receiving a threat, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu's office said. The flight landed safely at the base in Evreux, which was under high alert, and military bomb disposal teams were examining the plane, the office said. Lecornu ordered warplanes to intercept the plane because the pilot "didn't cooperate as expected with the authorities," his office said. It declined to comment further. Hours after the flight landed, the plane was sitting on the tarmac with a Red Cross vehicle nearby while explosive experts with dogs examined it. An investigation was opened by French aviation security authorities. The regional prosecutor, Remi Coutin, said in a statement that the pilot and co-pilot were being questioned about what happened. Italian air force jets escort a Finnair flight Italian air force fighter jets escorted a Finnair flight that departed Helsinki bound for Rome after an email threat was received, the air force said in a statement. A Croatian fighter jet first intercepted it in Croatian airspace before handing it off to the Italians, the Croatian defense ministry said. Finnair said that two of its flights, including the one that received the military escort and landed safely in Rome, "faced unfounded hoax bomb scares." The other flight, operated by Jettime from Helsinki to Vienna, landed safely at its destination, and was expected to return to service after an inspection, Finnair said. Three Ryanair flights bound for Sofia, Bulgaria, meanwhile, also received military escorts and made emergency landings after bomb threats, officials said. Two of the flights — one from Copenhagen, Denmark, and the other from Madrid — landed safely in Sofia, airport officials told reporters. The third, from London, was diverted and landed safely in Plovdiv, Bulgaria's second-largest city, Plovdiv Airport CEO Krassimir Peshe

Navy, Marines: it’s easier to buy new amphibious ships than fix old ones faster
With the average amphib sidelined more than half the time, the services have drawn up a plan to add 9 more instead.
The Marine Corps thinks it will need 40 amphibious ships—up from the Navy’s current 31—to achieve its long-sought goal of keeping three Amphibious Ready Groups with embarked Marine Expeditionary Units deployed at all times.
It's a shift in strategy that reflects the Navy’s struggle to reduce the amount of time its ships and submarines spend under repair. Few U.S. warships meet the service’s goal of being ready to go 80 percent of the time, and, on average, amphibious ships are out of service more often than not.
“If I'm sitting at 31 today, the only way for me to realistically increase that inventory is for me to build new ships and do a service-life extension on some of the ships that I currently have in the inventory, so that I am able to keep to maintain an inventory while I'm building new ships,” Shon Brodie, the Marine Corps’s deputy director of Maritime Expeditionary Warfare, told reporters Wednesday.
Brodie said the vice chief of naval operations and the assistant commandant of the Marine Corps have drawn up a plan that would increase the number of amphibious ships by about 25 percent, which would theoretically fill the gap while readiness levels are below 80 percent.
This larger amphib fleet would include 13 big-deck amphibious assault ships and 27 smaller dock ships, up from today’s nine and 22, he said.
The Navy and Marine Corps are to sit down with lawmakers this month to discuss how to fund the project, Brodie said.
That may not be realistic, said Bryan Clark, senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, just because of the massive expense it would require to operate and maintain 40 amphibs.
“And because maintenance costs grow, the Navy can't do all the work it needs to do on a ship, some of which is also deferred to a future availability,” Clark said. “The result is a readiness spiral where ships decline in material condition.”
A new Hudson Institute fleet design study suggests 35 amphibs, taking into consideration that those ships are vulnerable to a near-peer adversary and probably not a self-contained solution once the shooting starts.
“Larger surface combatants need to devote nearly all their weapons capacity to defense once the shooting starts, which necessitates them defending carriers that can conduct offensive operations at range and scale,” he said.
At the same time, the Navy isn’t giving up on doing a better job maintaining the ships it has.
“We're marginally better than we were before, and the expectation is that we can increase beyond marginally better here over the next couple of maintenance cycles,” Brodie said.
But the kicker is that not everything is within their control. If ARG deployments get extended, as they have been quite frequently recently, that increases wear-and-tear on the ships and loads down already delayed maintenance periods.
“So you've got to bring the ship back on time, get it in maintenance on time,” to make the plan work, Brodie said.
The aim is to enable the services to keep deployed three Amphibious Ready Groups-Marine Expeditionary Units, the three-ship formations that carry more than 2,000 Marines and their aircraft and weapons.
Commandant Gen. Eric Smith laid out his case for a 3.0 MEU-ARG presence in a 2025 oped in Defense One. Smith argued that national security required “one from the East Coast, one from the West, and one patrolling from Okinawa, Japan. (If you ask our combatant commanders what they need, the answer isn’t a total of three ARG/MEUs; it’s closer to five or six.) 3.0 is the minimum required to provide our nation and the Joint Force with a capability that can serve as both a warfighting formation and a cross-service integrator.
“It’s what keeps pressure on our adversaries, supports the maritime fight, and gives combatant commanders and national decision makers scalable options they can employ without delay to buy time, create decision-space, and if required to do so, be first to fight.“

Timâs view
One of the many ironies of Tuesdayâs Democratic sweep of Congress was that for Big Oil, the same bull energy market that delivered one of its most profitable years ever also returned power to the party thatâs often bent on bringing the industry to heel.
Still, Mike Sommers, who as president of the American Petroleum Institute is the countryâs top oil lobbyist, told me heâs not particularly worried about a green backlash. Thatâs in part because the blue wave carried many more affordability-minded moderates than climate-focused progressives: âI think we just elected a lot of Joe Manchins and Mary Landrieus,â he said, referring to a pair of well-known former Democratic senators who advocated for the industry.
Sommers said itâs possible that the Trump administrationâs oil deal with Venezuela becomes a target for oversight hearings. Democrats, while not able to directly control US national security strategy, can also flex their powers over the budget and personnel confirmations to pressure US President Donald Trump on a deal with Iran, which would push oil prices down.
But apart from that, in practice thereâs not a whole lot that Congress can do to hurt the oil industry; the more tangible actions tend to come from the executive branch, like former US President Joe Bidenâs freeze on LNG terminals. Between an ongoing refinery crunch and the AI power rush, any legislative or budget proposal that appears to take molecules off the market isnât likely to go far, and industry leaders appear ready to swallow their pride: âWeâre here to serve,â Hunter Hunt, CEO of Texas driller Hunt Energy, told me in Abu Dhabi. âWeâll adjust as best we can.â
Sommers is anxious to see the permitting reform bill currently awaiting approval in the Senate, which would give a major boost to energy projects of all stripes, passed before Democrats take their majority seats in January. The Senate is due to vote on Monday about whether to bring it to the floor for passage, a vote that some progressives may try to undermine, targeting a more renewables-friendly deal. But the toxic relationship between Democratic leaders and the White House, as my colleagues reported, means the more likely outcome is no deal at all.
Meanwhile, executives from âLittle Oilâ companies on the tradeshow floor at ADIPEC this week werenât thrilled by the election outcome, but not really sweating it either. âOil will survive,â said Tom Inman, whose Houston company Dragon Products makes pumps and other fracking gear. âDemocrats have tried to shut us down before. But itâs still very easy to sell oil.â

None of the injuries were believed to be life-threatening, police said. "They're all at the hospital. They are being cared for right now," Des Moines police Sgt. Paul Parizek said of the victims. Parizek said officers responded within three minutes and quickly captured the suspect, who was found just east of the post office. The shooting happened on the second floor of the facility, and reports started coming in around 9:10 a.m. The post office is just north of downtown Des Moines and across the street from one of the city's main hospitals. The building is a four-story regional sorting facility with a walk-in service counter accessible to the public. It was not immediately clear whether the victims were employees or members of the public. Gov. Kim Reynolds said she's in contact with the Department of Public Safety regarding the shooting. "We are monitoring the situation and our prayers are with everyone involved," she posted online. "Grateful for the immediate response by law enforcement." Des Moines Public Schools said the district's nearby elementary school, welcome center and nutrition center went into a secure status after police notified the district of the shooting at 9:20 a.m., meaning no one was allowed in or out of the buildings.
