Pope Leo XIV is beginning a lengthy trip to Latin America just three weeks after surgery for lung cancer - a tour that includes a much-anticipated "homecoming" to Peru where he was a priest for many years.
The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".
It was Leo himself who revealed last month that doctors had discovered a tumour during a routine scan. The growth was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung and his medical team then confirmed the cancer had not spread.
At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes".
Back on track
"The Vatican's message with this trip is, 'that was a short episode and now we're back on track'," Professor Massimo Faggioli of Villanova University told the BBC, pointing out that the Pope has had a busy return to work since his surgery.
"We have seen him in these last few days making speeches, audiences and so on. He seems in great shape. That was important."
The 12-day tour would be demanding for anyone, though. It incorporates multiple long-haul and local flights and covers thousands of miles from the Amazon to the Andes.
The starting point will be Uruguay, where the number of Catholics has fallen away steeply in recent years and which is getting its first Papal visit in four decades.
Leo then heads for Argentina, homeland of Pope Francis, his predecessor.
"This visit is also a homage to Francis, who didn't make it to Argentina [as pope]," says Father Fernando Laguna, the rector of Santa Maria Addolorata, Argentina's national church in Rome.
"When this visit by Pope Leo was announced, it filled all of our hearts with joy," he told the BBC. "I always thought he would go, despite his illness. I don't think he ever thought of calling it off!"
The priest is installing a big screen inside the church in Rome to allow parishioners to follow all the key moments of the trip from afar. The building is already decked out with posters declaring Pope Leo is welcome in Argentina. "We're waiting for you!", one proclaims.
This leg of the Pope's journey - which includes meetings with heads of state as well as religious events - could be the most politically sensitive. President Javier Milei once called Pope Francis "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor. In turn, Argentina's bishops have criticised Milei's harsh austerity measures, making sweeping cuts to social spending.
But Milei has already welcomed Pope Leo, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy". Millions are expected to turn out to greet him.
'Homecoming' to Peru
The highlight of the trip is undoubtedly saved for last, when Pope Leo reaches Peru - described by the Vatican as a return to his roots.
"He knows these streets," is how a spokeswoman put it.
Born in the US, the then Robert Prevost spent almost 20 years in Peru, on and off, and even has Peruvian citizenship. That time is seen as fundamental to shaping his papacy.
His schedule includes a return to the diocese of Chiclayo where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until Francis moved him to the Vatican almost a decade later.
He will also travel to Cusco, former capital of the Inca Empire, to say Mass more than 3,000m above sea level before heading to Pucallpa in the Amazon.
In all three countries, the Vatican says the Pope will have meetings with survivors of clerical sexual abuse - an issue which clouded a 2018 visit to Chile and Peru by his predecessor.
"This is how the papacy reconnects with Latin America after Francis, whose visits to the region were not always seamless," is how Professor Faggioli sees it.
He believes Pope Leo has a strong sense of the unity of the Americas as one continent. "Democracies are in trouble there, so there are so many things he can address," he suggests.
"The big question then is the United States. There's no question he wants to go. So will he travel when [President Donald] Trump is still in office? I'm sure they're thinking about this."

d5ce8d81a94d.text: As Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and Republicans grapple with stunning losses, every remaining race matters. Some races are still too close to call, including Senate battles in both Alaska and Mississippi. Congressional correspondent Lisa Desjardins reports. Amna Nawaz: As Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and Republicans grapple with stunning losses, every remaining race matters. And some races are still too close to call. That includes tight Senate contests in both Alaska and Mississippi. Our congressional correspondent, Lisa Desjardins, starts us off tonight. Lisa Desjardins: In a diner in Mississippi, Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom displayed the energy that got him here, saying hello to all and joining a morning prayer. He and his Republican opponent, Cindy Hyde-Smith, are in a razor-thin race, but Colom gained several hundred votes overnight. Both parties are carefully watching the counting of provisional ballots now. Hyde-Smith did not appear today, but Mississippi's Republican Party chairman held a news conference. Mike Hurst: Any time you have an election that's this close and any time we want to make sure that our laws are being followed, we want to make sure that there's nothing untoward done. Lisa Desjardins: But Colom was confident of a win and a message from it. Scott Colom: We're going to show the country that Mississippi matters, right? We have great people that are full of great values, and we have a vision for our country that really people could learn something from. Lisa Desjardins: Alaska is the other state where a key Senate race still hangs by a razor's edge. A sizable amount of votes are yet to be counted, some from such remote areas, they must be flown in by plane. Mike Zoske, Alaska Voter: Now, there's a lot of votes that still have to come in from the bush, a lot of votes out there. And they typically vote Democratic, but I don't know how they're going to vote. Lisa Desjardins: Amidst the blue tsunami, there has been one Republican flip of a current blue House seat in Maine. Democrat Matt Dunlap conceded to the state's former Governor Paul LePage in a race that almost went to a ranked-choice count. And in a stunning upset in Los Angeles, Democratic Socialist Nithya Raman will be the city's new mayor after young voters surged for her and incumbent Karen Bass conceded. Raman will be L.A.'s first Asian American mayor. The margin is to be determined, but control of Congress is set for Democrats. And every part of the country is digesting the results, from an Iowa bar, where some drowned out their shock. Man: I woke up to my daughter saying: "The liberals are taking over." I turned it on, and I saw it as, like, surely not. Lisa Desjardins: And others chewed on understanding. Kelia Rice, Iowa Voter: With prices going up and the war and things just building on everybody, they finally decided that maybe we'll give it a chance to the Democratic Party and we'll switch our views for a moment and maybe they will help us. Lisa Desjardins: To a farmers market near Austin, where voters reckoned with the state's new blue tone. Carol Belk, Texas Voter: Disillusionment with what Trump has been doing or not doing. So we voted for Trump the last three times. So that really surprised me, the switch. the complete switch-over. Lisa Desjardins: That swing toward a new team of Democrats in Texas came largely from a new coalition of young voters and Latinos, like this college student. Sophia Flores, Texas Voter: It's the party that votes for the underdog, I like to say. Like, they vote for the little man. They try for the little man. They fight for us, rather than big corporations, big money, stuff like that. Lisa Desjardins: The range of Democratic voters was sweeping, including this cattle rancher in Kansas, who had a more watchful message for the party. Tom Holmquist, Kansas Voter: I was telling my wife this morning, I said, OK, they won. The Democrats won. They have taken 54 seats and 250 House seats. Don't blow it. Don't fall into that same trap, and actually do the things that for us. Amna Nawaz: As ballots are still being counted, Lisa Desjardins is back at the Super Screen to break down the numbers. So, Lisa, two days out post-election, what are the numbers when it comes to control of Congress? Lisa Desjardins: It really is hour by hour. Let's start with the Senate and those two big races a lot of folks are watching. What's going on in Alaska? It is exactly where it was when I talked to you one night ago. We are still waiting for ballots potentially to fly in by mail. This could be at least 10 days, maybe more, depending on how things go, with a possible look at ranked-choice. But since I have this magical screen, let's fly 3,000 miles away and go to Mississippi. Where is that race? Also where it was last night. We have Scott Colom ahead just by about 1,800 votes. We are waiting for Hinds County still, which looks like it still has 10 percent of its votes out. So this will be a waiting game, but we will keep you updated. Let's fly to the top of the country and look at the House of Representatives, where we have -- actually had quite a lot of news in the last day. Democrats now are up 40 seats. That is the net number of seats they have flipped. They only needed to flip three in order to get the House into their control. And as the races I'm watching start closing, there are still seven seats that Democrats right now are poised to flip. So that would be, right, a tremendous gain for them, potentially 47 seats. Republicans are having a couple of flips. There are two in particular. One is here just outside of Dallas in Texas 32, and also in Tennessee's Ninth District right there. But, Amna, both of these were redistricted specifically to give Republicans an advantage. Amna Nawaz: Tell us more about that, Lisa, that unprecedented mid-decade redistricting effort led by Republicans. You have been tracking the results. What do we know? Lisa Desjardins

c7dd1e9c5b75.text: In our news wrap Thursday, Harmeet Dhillon is stepping down as head of the Justice Department's civil rights division, Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian officials to mark a localized ceasefire and European authorities are investigating a series of bomb threats that targeted more than a dozen flights. Amna Nawaz: We start the day's other headlines with a high-level departure at the Justice Department. Harmeet Dhillon is stepping down as head of the agency's Civil Rights Division. The conservative attorney oversaw a massive overhaul of the office, shifting its focus from protecting the rights of minorities to pursuing President Trump's agenda. That included lawsuits against elite universities, scrapping police reform efforts, and pushing dozens of states for their voter registration lists. In a statement, Dhillon said the job has been -- quote -- "the honor of a lifetime." Her departure comes just two days after massive Republican losses in the midterm elections. First lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian officials at the White House today to mark a localized cease-fire she helped broker last month. Mrs. Trump said she hopes the deal in Oleshky, the Ukrainian city captured by Russia early on in the war -- quote -- "inspires greater peace." First Lady Melania Trump: We have chosen humanity over war. Undeniably, the lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. Amna Nawaz: Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, also spoke at the event and presented the first lady with an award. And in a sight rarely seen in the White House, an aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin took to the podium. Kirill Dmitriev, a U.S.-sanctioned Russian financier, thanked Mrs. Trump and Putin for the peace deal. Kirill Dmitriev, Russian Special Envoy: President Putin personally gave all of the necessary instructions to ensure the successful implementation of the local cease-fire in Oleshky. Ukrainian side abided by cease-fire. And this humanitarian mission shows what can be achieved when compassion, determination and cooperation come together. Amna Nawaz: Speaking later in the Oval Office, President Trump said he met with Dmitriev, but not with the visiting Ukrainian officials. And he told reporters that a -- quote -- "big agreement" is in the works aimed at ending the war. Meanwhile, on the ground, both countries carried out strikes today. Authorities in Ukraine's Kyiv region say a Russian attack sparked a fire that injured at least one person. And in a Russian-controlled area of Eastern Ukraine, officials say a Ukrainian attack on a bus killed at least five people and wounded 13 others. In Europe, authorities are investigating a series of bomb threats that targeted more than a dozen flights, prompting emergency landings and even military escorts. From Spain to Poland, planes were forced to land, disrupting travel across the region. No suspicious materials were found, and one British official described these as malicious hoaxes. The threats follow similar incidents earlier this week. No explosives were found in those instances either. Passengers on affected flights today described their experience. Elena Pala, Threatened Flight Passenger (through interpreter): When we landed, I commented on how good the flight had been. But the moment I stepped off the plane, I saw fire trucks. The aircraft was surrounded. Woman (through interpreter): They inspected the luggage, had us get off, lined three of us up, told us to step aside and checked the luggage with dogs. Amna Nawaz: Authorities haven't determined who issued the threats, but they come as European officials have warned about a rise in Russian sabotage and so-called hybrid attacks. In France, officials say more than 600,000 people took to the streets nationwide today, demanding higher wages and more funding for education. There were some clashes between protesters and police, though most of the demonstrations were peaceful. Today's included both public and private sector workers and were part of a general strike that disrupted some public transportation and other services. It follows weeks of student-led protests that have sometimes turned violent. The unrest has pressured the nation's government ahead of presidential elections next year. British comedian Russell Brand was found guilty today of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others. Photographers swarmed a police van carrying Brand as it left a London court. He was also found not guilty of three other charges. The case stems from the late 1990s and 2000s, when Brand became known for his suggestive humor and promiscuity. Prosecutors say he was a manipulative predator, though Brand has denied the charges. The 51-year-old was denied bail and will be sentenced on Monday, with the judge saying he faces significant time in prison. Turning now to sports news, Cristiano Ronaldo is retiring from international football after more than two decades playing for Portugal. He shared the news today on social media. Cristiano Ronaldo, (through interpreter): It was not an easy decision, because some decisions are not made with the mind alone. They are also made with the heart. Amna Nawaz: The striker's career spans six World Cups, and he holds the men's international scoring record with 146 goals. The decision follows a series of public disputes with Portugal's new manager. In a statement, the Portuguese Football Federation expressed its deep gratitude, calling him -- quote -- "the greatest player of all time." The 41-year-old will continue to play at the club level in Saudi Arabia, where he's aiming for his 1,000th career goal. And the biggest night in fashion has a new theme for 2027. The Metropolitan Museum of Art announced today that it will showcase ordinary items and materials like jeans or plastic and how designers transform them into fashion. The show is called "extraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday." And it replaces a planned exhibit focused on th

fae1702af4ac.text: By — Aamer Madhani, Associated Press Aamer Madhani, Associated Press By — Linley Sanders, Associated Press Linley Sanders, Associated Press By — Samy Magdy, Associated Press Samy Magdy, Associated Press By — Matthew Lee, Associated Press Matthew Lee, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/after-midterms-trump-is-left-to-weigh-his-next-move-in-iran-war-that-contributed-to-gop-loss Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter After midterms, Trump is left to weigh his next move in Iran war that contributed to GOP loss Politics Nov 5, 2026 6:46 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — As he takes stock of his Republican Party's midterm drubbing, President Donald Trump now faces the difficult question of what to do about his unpopular 8-month-old war against Iran. For weeks, Trump has threatened to return to a full-scale bombardment of Iran once the U.S. elections were in the rearview mirror if Tehran did not come to a settlement under terms acceptable to him. READ MORE: Iranian leaders say midterm results show U.S. voters have rejected Trump's war In his first comments on Wednesday after Democrats' resounding election victory — a wave powered in part by the American electorate's dissatisfaction with the war — Trump largely agreed with Vice President JD Vance, who publicly ruminated on the war being a catastrophe for Republicans. And in an Oval Office exchange with reporters Thursday, Trump suggested that the election losses aren't weighing on his calculations. "If we have to do the rest of the Iran thing, we're very much locked in," Trump said. The strikes, and counterstrikes, have caused tens of billions of dollars of damage in the region. And the conflict has reached into the pocketbook of families around the globe with elevated gas prices and rising costs in just about every sector. Now, as Trump ponders his next move, the stakes couldn't be higher for Iran, the Middle East and the global economy writ large. Trump may be less restrained, but the conflict is now more complicated While oil is flowing again from the Strait of Hormuz with the help of U.S. Navy escorts for international tankers, the conflict has spread to the Red Sea with Iran-backed Houthi rebels and a Saudi Arabia -led coalition fighting it out. The situation in the Red Sea remains particularly volatile. The Houthis are attacking Yemeni civilians and Saudi infrastructure, and are looking to bolster ties with militant groups across the Horn of Africa. The attacks by the Yemen-based Houthis on areas controlled by the internationally recognized Yemeni government have also worsened a growing humanitarian crisis. The threat that the region faces from Iran and its proxy groups, noted a senior Yemeni government official, "did not change overnight" with the U.S. elections, urging Washington to avoid hasty decisions. The official was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the basis of anonymity. "There's reason to suspect that Trump may feel less restrained given that the political damage is done," said Brian Haggerty, a former senior analyst at the Central Intelligence Agency who focused on Middle East security issues. "At the same time, the strategic calculus or the strategic logic of what you hope to achieve through an escalation of strikes against Iran is no different today than it was a week ago or a month ago." Trump has at least a few options, analysts say Haggerty, who now works with Defense Priorities, a Washington think tank, said Trump could choose to maintain something close to the current posture, with the U.S. military carrying out what it calls "defensive strikes" while continuing its naval blockade to restrict the flow of Iranian oil to the global market. Another option is striking Iran's Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to its nuclear program that is buried deep underground in central Iran, said David Schenker, who served as assistant secretary of state for Near Eastern affairs in Trump's first term. Trump has repeatedly suggested he was considering targeting the site. Schenker said Trump could then walk away and contend he had done sufficient damage to Iran's nuclear program — and perhaps try to pursue a "fig leaf agreement" that restores freedom of navigation to the Strait of Hormuz, offers Iran some degree of sanctions relief, and punts additional nuclear talks to the future. Yet another option would be to follow up on threats Trump made earlier in the war to launch massive attacks on Iranian infrastructure. "The Iranians may believe the president is wounded and constrained by Congress, but the opposite can also be true," Schenker said. But such escalation would likely exacerbate the oil and energy price problem that many voters cited as a reason for supporting Democrats on Tuesday, Schenker said. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil tumbled below $95 on Wednesday after the election, touching its lowest level in two months, a signal that markets do not expect major strikes. Iran, of course, also has a say, analysts note. "Once you start a fistfight, you can stop throwing punches. That doesn't mean the other combatant will stop throwing punches," said Bradley Bowman, an analyst at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. "We can try to end the war, but what do we do if the Islamic Republic of Iran continues to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz?" Regional officials are on high alert for what Trump does next Middle East officials had been hanging on Trump's every word in the weeks leading up to the U.S. elections, looking for clues on how the Republican leader was weighing his next steps. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pressed for renewed strikes on Iran during a call over the weekend with Trump, who would not commit to taking military action, according to a person who was briefed on it. Three Middle Eastern government officials said on Wednesday that Trump and his administration had seemed to be signaling to Iran that its leve

d48a36390bf5.text: Tuesday's election results were not just closely watched in the U.S. American elections, in many ways, have become global events and the Democratic wave led to an extraordinary outpouring. Nick Schifrin gauges that reaction. Amna Nawaz: Well, Tuesday's election results weren't just closely watched here at home. American elections in many ways become global events. And this Democratic wave has led to an extraordinary outpouring. Nick Schifrin gauges that reaction, beginning with Iran. Nick Schifrin: On the darkened streets of Iran overnight, the regime put President Donald Trump in jail. This fake lockup followed Democrats locking down Election Day victories. Iranian leaders resisted a preelection agreement and believe they helped hand President Trump electoral defeat. Iran's chief negotiator relished the rebuke and said it should end the war. But Iran's supreme leader, warned divided American government will not lead to American concessions, a sentiment echoed on the streets of Tehran. Ali Akbar Mashayekhi, Iranian Demonstrator (through interpreter): It's always the same cycle, negotiations, then war, then back to negotiations, then war again. We're not afraid of war. If they want to fight, we will fight back. Nick Schifrin: Trump agreed with his vice president that the war in Iran, now entering its ninth month, triggered a blue tsunami. President Donald Trump: It's largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term. Nick Schifrin: But the war has only brought Iran closer to its allies, including Russia. Today, Russian President Vladimir Putin welcomed Iran's National Security Council Chief Mohsen Rezaei. Iranian weapon designs have helped Russia target Ukraine. And so it was again today when Russian drones and missiles hit Kyiv. Ukrainian officials tell "PBS News Hour" they are skeptical the new Congress can shift U.S. policy. But some European leaders hope a new Democratic Congress can make a difference. Kaja Kallas, Foreign Affairs High Representative, European Commission: I hope that the new Congress and the new Senate will continue supporting Ukraine and also putting more pressure on Russia. Man: Today, democracy won in America. Nick Schifrin: Across Europe, some officials publicly breathe a sigh of relief and described Democrats as kindred spirits. And in the Global South, some leaders said the midterms could result in a reset. Cyril Ramaphosa, South African President: I do think that this is going to introduce a new era in world relations, really. Nick Schifrin: But one country's current leaders do not welcome that new era. President Donald Trump: We have already agreed that, by the end of this year, we won't be paying Israel. Nick Schifrin: On FOX News earlier this week, President Trump announced the U.S. would stop giving Israel grants to buy American jets and weapons. Israel will now have to use its own money. Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan Senator-Elect: I think the fact that we're fighting the war in Iran is a function of what the prime minister of Israel wanted. Nick Schifrin: And this election produced what may prove the most hostile U.S. Congress to Israel in history. Democrats now face a choice, whether to go further and try to block weapons sales to Israel and whether to end funding for the war in Iran. Amna Nawaz: And Nick is here with me now. Nick, let's begin with that war in Iran. Where are negotiations to end it? Nick Schifrin: A senior regional and senior American official both tell me that, before the elections, the two sides were close to a deal that would have returned them to the memorandum of understanding earlier this year. One official, in fact, Amna, told me it was 80 percent there. And that deal would have included an agreement for Iran to downblend its highly enriched uranium. Now, before the June 2025 strikes, the U.N.'s nuclear agency reported Iran had nearly 1,000 pounds of 60 percent enriched uranium, a small step away from weapons-grade. Iran's agreeing to downblend its stockpile would be a significant concession on their part. It would also mean the U.S. would accept some Iranian-enriched uranium, at least for now, Amna. The agreement would also include the U.S. is lifting sanctions and unfreezing some Iranian assets, and it would have reopened the strait without any kind of tolls, according to these officials. 9344591304b2.text: California Gov. Gavin Newsom commuted the state’s entire death row population to life in prison without parole. The decision could grant clemency to 548 people. Newsom had previously put a moratorium on executions in the state in 2019, but left hundreds on death row. Amna Nawaz discussed more with Robin Maher of the Death Penalty Information Center. Amna Nawaz: California Governor Gavin Newsom announced the largest mass commutation in the country's history, changing the state's entire death row population sentences to life in prison without parole. The decision could grant clemency to 548 people. Newsom, who is considering a run for the presidency, wrote in a letter to constituents that -- quote -- "State-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us." Newsom had previously put a moratorium on executions in the state in 2019, but left hundreds on death row. For more on all of this, I'm joined by Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center. Welcome back, and thanks for joining us. So, the largest such commutation in the nation's history. We should point out, though, California has not executed anyone since 2006. Does this decision have a real impact or is it more about sending a message? Robin Maher: Oh, I think it does. I mean, both historically and symbolically, this decision carries real significance. I mean, this mass commutation will remove more than 500 people from death row. That's 30 percent of the total number of people on death rows throughout the United States. And Governor Newsom very publicly wrestled with this decision, taking the time to first consult with victims' family members and corrections officials, judges, lawyers, and many others. He also looked to the research and the evidence that revealed that the death penalty in California was a very costly, deeply flawed policy choice. And I think all of that careful work and consultation led to today's decision. Amna Nawaz: And yet it's not a decision being supported by all. Some families who lost loved ones in these crimes are not backing it, Marc Klaas among them, as I'm sure you know, the father of Polly Klaas, who was 12 years old when she was kidnapped from her home and murdered in 1993. He told The New York Times today, "We're talking about serial killers, spree killers, cop killers, baby killers, talking about the absolute worst people in our society without a doubt. And he's putting his energy into commuting these characters?"" The head of Crime Victims United said: "Families were asked to trust the justice system through trials, appeals, and decades of anguish. Their loved ones deserve more than a blanket decision that sweeps aside individual judgments." What do you say to that, Robin? Robin Maher: Right. Well, I'm not surprised. I am sure that some victims' family members are disappointed, just as others feel a sense of relief that these sentences are now final, and the sense of uncertainty and retraumatization that so many family members feel during these lengthy appeals is now over. I mean, one important thing to consider is that the money, the tremendous amount of money that has been necessary to prop up the death penalty in California can now be reinvested in meaningful solutions to prevent violent crime from occurring and also to support family members who are still grieving from these terrible losses. Amna Nawaz: There are some groups already talking about potentially suing Newsom to stop that. Could this move be stalled? Robin Maher: I don't think so. The California Constitution is very clear that Governor Newsom's authority to make these decisions is absolute and final. There are a number of people on the row whose sentences the commutation will need to be reviewed by the California Supreme Court. Anyone who has two felony convictions will need the court to first approve of this recommendation to commute their sentences. But his decision regarding the other commutations is final. Amna Nawaz: Robin, in the minute or so I have left, we should point out both Indiana and Florida carried out executions in their states today. Alabama plans to do one later this evening. And, of course, we have seen this national debate after the botched execution of Christa Pike. When it comes to that debate, where are most Americans on this issue? Robin Maher: Well, public support for the death penalty has been declining, pretty steadily declining over the last several years. Now barely a majority of people support use of the death penalty, and the largest number ever have very serious concerns about its reliability and its fairness. So things have certainly changed quite a bit in the last few years. We're expecting a new poll to be released later this month. Amna Nawaz: All right, that is Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center. Robin, thank you for your time. Robin Maher: My pleasure.

Where is that information? So those are serious questions that deserve answers. Liz Landers: Leader Jeffries has said that Democrats are focused on affordability and accountability. Let's be really clear. Donald Trump's been impeached twice. He commits probably an impeachable offense every week. The Senate has not convicted him. And so there's not enough votes in the Senate to impeach him now. And so what I think is important is that we focus on what we can do, which is stopping and slowing the Trump agenda. And that's going to be our focus. Liz Landers: What about impeaching Cabinet members like the defense secretary, Hegseth? Rep. Robert Garcia: Look, I think we will see if Hegse

a86099ab2928.text: There are few places where the consequences of the Trump administration's cuts to global aid programs are more apparent than South Sudan. With a raging civil war in Sudan to its north, South Sudan is contending not just with its own underserved people, but with more than a million Sudanese refugees. Special correspondent Anna Conkling of Noosphere, a new journalism app, reports. Amna Nawaz: There are few places where the consequences of the Trump administration's cuts to global aid programs are more apparent than South Sudan. With a raging civil war in Sudan to its north, South Sudan, also still racked by conflict, is contending with its own underserved population and more than a million Sudanese refugees. Special correspondent Anna Conkling of Noosphere, a new journalism app, reports from Renk in South Sudan. Anna Conkling: Those raspy, labored breaths are Kalia's. She spent 15 days in the pediatric ward of this hospital in Renk just south of the Sudan border. She is just 11 months old. And like so many of the babies here, she is starving. Woman: So we are giving for bed two, which is 90. Anna Conkling: Nurse Shadiya is preparing formula for them all. In addition to the breathing trouble, Kalia has severe fever and she's lost too much weight. Doctors are trying to formulate treatment for her. Kout Kout, Clinical Officer, Renk Civil Hospital: of recent weight loss, we suspect T.B. And we are treating it now. Anna Conkling: T.B. is... Kout Kout: Yes. Anna Conkling: ... tuberculosis. Kout Kout: Yes, tuberculosis. And it is meningitis. Meningitis T.B. is in the brain. But the good thing for this girl is not coughing. There's no cough. Yes, that's the good thing of it. Anna Conkling: Is she expected to survive? Kout Kout: Actually, we are monitoring it over 24 hours. Now we will see. Anna Conkling: A few beds down is Azma, a 1.5-year-old Sudanese refugee who has been sick for five months. Doctors told me that her hair fell out from malnutrition. And she's now being treated for pneumonia and sepsis, likely resulting from the malnutrition. Her mother, Fatima, says she was referred here from another hospital. Kalia and Azma are just two of the more than 500 patients that arrive here needing help every day. But as international aid cuts decimate South Sudan's health care system, hospitals like this one are struggling to carry on. Much of that is because of the war to the north in Sudan, from which South Sudan gained independence 15 years ago. It is the world's worst humanitarian crisis. Millions have been displaced internally. Millions more are now refugees, and the war has no end in sight. In Renk, the refugee influx has strained the hospital beyond a breaking point. They try to treat local cases like Kalia's, while helping some of the up to 3,000 refugees that flee Sudan each week. The hospital's pharmacy plays a vital role in its ability to continue to operate. But it's running low on medication and has no way to refill them. Dr. Suhier told us she faces the challenges of devastating aid cuts every day. The pharmacy is completely funded by international partners. And one of the medication that they're running critically low on are malaria tablets. And it's the rainy season here in Renk, which means that there's a lot more mosquitoes out and a lot more infections. Suhier watches her supply of medication diminish with little hope that they will be replaced. Cuts to foreign programs like USAID are not only causing shortages. They're also costing lives. Relief International, a global human rights organization based in Washington, D.C., is one of the main partners here. But the hospital said the agency reduced its presence at the end of September. I asked Dr. Suhier what their absence will mean for the hospital. Suhier Ahmed Deng, Pharmacist, Renk Civil Hospital: Until now, even today, if you look to my eyes, they are so red because of thinking. We think a lot to have the solution, but we cannot tell anyone that to come and to walk in a state that we don't have money. Here, if there is not any support, they will die without medicine, without food, so better for them to go again to work to Sudan, to die there. Man: So this is the OPD site. Anna Conkling: Throughout the hospital, evidence of the gutting of foreign assistance is everywhere. We learned that doctors are forced to decide each day which ward most needs generator power. So, over here is another part of the ward. And you can see that there's not really any electricity, there's no lights on, and when we were here on Saturday, the staff told us that this ward doesn't really have a lot of electricity because the generator isn't being used as a priority here. The intensive care unit had no power at all the day we were there. It was also running low on most of the medication it needed to help its 12 patients. Despite the shortages, the hospital still hopes to serve as a stabilization point for the refugees who stream into Renk each week. For those who need it, surgery is still being scheduled on Tuesdays and Wednesdays. The patients recover in urine-soaked rooms filled with flies and an inescapable heat. But this is the desperate state of health care today in South Sudan. Back in the pediatric ward, one bed is now completely empty. We are told that Kalia, the 11-month-old girl who was having trouble breathing, died eight hours after our visit. The official cause was malnutrition. The nurse said that Kalia's death deeply saddened the parents of other patients here. Once hopeful for their child's recovery, they now fear death. But, as we were leaving, we found baby Azma sitting up and playing with her mom. Doctors say she's recovering from her illness and is expected to make a full recovery. "Alhamdulillah," says Fatima, "Praise be to God." For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Anna Conkling with Noosphere in Renk, South Sudan.

0400bccd5222.text: By — Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/hegseth-allows-national-guard-to-boost-dc-patrols-with-military-vehicles-boats-and-patrol-cars Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Hegseth allows National Guard to boost DC patrols with military vehicles, boats and patrol cars Politics Nov 5, 2026 6:31 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has signed off on the National Guard ramping up its presence in the nation's capital in military vehicles and boats as troops deepen their integration with local law enforcement. WATCH: The effectiveness and cost of the National Guard deployment in D.C. In two memos signed Oct. 29 and obtained by The Associated Press, Hegseth approved the National Guard to use 60 military police cars as well as tactical vehicles, patrol boats and portable light towers during increased patrols around Washington. Troops will also be able to carry rifles during some operations but not in Metro rail stations. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The sight of vehicles that look more at home on a battlefield than a city street will harken back to when President Donald Trump first deployed the National Guard in August 2025 for what he called a crime-fighting mission. Tactical vehicles and troops carrying guns initially were seen at some Washington landmarks. National Guard members have supported law enforcement operations, patrolled neighborhoods, dispersed homeless camps and helped with citywide cleanup efforts. READ MORE: Trump wants to clear homeless encampments. Here's what usually happens, according to experts A boost in troop presence comes amid increased issues involving Guard members assigned to the city, including the arrest of a Georgia serviceman for pulling a gun on a fellow Guard member, the arrest of a Guard member for carrying an unauthorized firearm, and the shooting of a Guardsman while trying to break up a fight. The memos say "visibility patrols," a mainstay of the Guard's mission in Washington, are going to be expanded and 20 light towers will be employed to "enhance force protection in patrol zones." But Hegseth says the maximum number of deployed Guard members would stay at 3,500, lower than a summertime peak of about 5,000 during America's 250th anniversary celebrations. Hegseth signed off on the National Guard using patrol cars and tactical vehicles to support law enforcement operations, though the memos stressed that the patrol cars need to be marked as "National Guard" and troops need to be in uniform. Two National Guard patrol boats will also be used "to provide operational maritime support." The memos forbid troops from conducting high-speed chases. The memos suggest that troops will play a greater role in taking on "gangs and drug traffickers." Hegseth is continuing to provide six analysts "to address organized drug distribution within D.C.," and troops who are supporting anti-gang and drug operations will now be able to carry rifles in addition to their traditional pistols. One of the memos grants the U.S. Marshals Service the use of the D.C. National Guard's 260th Special Purpose Brigade — a unit that functioned as a "quick reaction force" — to help protect "key federal leaders" and help secure and defend "key federal facilities." A Marshals Service request for National Guard helicopters or the use of troops "to clean up abandoned tires in specific areas of D.C." was denied in a Nov. 4 memo, however. When asked about the memos, the Pentagon confirmed that Hegseth "authorized the continued use of National Guard personnel and capabilities in support of the Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful mission." The District of Columbia, which sued in September 2025 over the National Guard deployment, has argued that the mobilization is an illegal use of the military for domestic law enforcement. A federal appeals court panel heard arguments Oct. 14 after a lower court sided with the city. Nearly 3,100 Guard members from various states are in Washington, including more than 500 from Georgia, the largest contingent behind the District of Columbia, which had 514 members involved as of Monday. 6477aa142612.text: President Trump said after meeting with his national security advisers Thursday that he'll soon decide whether to resume all-out war in Iran now that the midterms are over. Why it matters: The election was seen as an inflection point for Trump on whether to unleash a new wave of bombing to try to bring the war to an end. The president, at least for now, is considering three options: launch new strikes, continue to strangle Iran's regime economically, or cut a deal that includes significant concessions to the Iranians. On Thursday, Trump and his top national security advisers met on Iran for the first time since the election, as part of his weekly intelligence briefing, two U.S. officials said. What he's saying: "Now we will make a decision," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. "Do we want to go further" with strikes to ensure Iran's nuclear program is dead and that "it will never happen again?" he added. "I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible, but maybe I will have to. You'll know soon enough." State of play: As Trump was weighing his next move, there was a flurry of diplomatic activity Thursday, including multiple phone calls between Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and regional mediators from Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Oman and Egypt. The Qatari mediators continued discussions with the Iranians and the White House about a draft proposal calling for the two sides to take a series of steps over two days to build mutual confidence toward a broader deal. On the first day, the U.S. would lift its naval blockade and release some of Iran's frozen funds. In return, Iran would issue an official invitation to the International Atomic Energy Agency to send inspectors to bombed nuclear sites, based on an agreement reached in Cairo a year ago, regional sources said. On the second day, the Strait of Hormuz would reopen, after which nuclear talks would resume, focusing on Iran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium. The big picture: The secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei — a key player in indirect negotiations with the U.S. — met with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin on Thursday. The meeting took place several days after a call between Putin and Rezaei and proposals by the Russian president to mediate between the U.S. and Iran. Rezaei said he delivered a message to Putin from Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. He added that Putin stressed he is ready to try to help end the war. "We told Mr. Putin that we announced seven conditions to the Americans regarding diplomacy, and that until the Americans fulfill our seven conditions, neither the Strait of Hormuz will be opened nor will there be any negotiations," Rezaei said after the meeting. What to watch: U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) is finalizing preparations to potentially resume major combat operations in Iran, though it hasn't received a new directive from Washington, a U.S. official said. One signal that the U.S. plans renewed strikes could be the arrival of a third U.S. Navy aircraft carrier strike group in the Middle East. A U.S. official said the USS Theodore Roosevelt and its strike group will spend a few days in Singapore starting Friday for a port call. It won't reach CENTCOM's area of responsibility before mid-November.

400b83e99386.text: D.L. Hughley is one of comedy’s most enduring stars. His new memoir, “Charlie’s Boy,” offers a candid look at fatherhood, family trauma, and the path he took from South Central LA to some of the biggest stages on the planet. Geoff Bennett spoke with Hughley about all that and more, including his heated confrontation with Bill Cosby, on this week’s episode of "Settle In." Amna Nawaz: D.L. Hughley is one of comedy's most enduring stars. His new memoir, "Charlie's Boy," is a candid look at fatherhood, family trauma, and the path he took from South Central L.A. to some of the biggest stages on the planet. For our podcast "Settle In," Geoff Bennett spoke with him about all of that and more, including his heated confrontation with Bill Cosby years ago. Geoff Bennett: You described this extraordinary confrontation with Bill Cosby on your radio show. D.L. Hughley, Author, "Charlie's Boy": Right. Geoff Bennett: And this was before the Hannibal Buress situation that unearthed all the accusations and then basically saw the spiral of Bill Cosby, the public spiral of him. D.L. Hughley: Right. Right. Geoff Bennett: And he was criticizing your comedy and criticizing your use of the N-word. D.L. Hughley: Right. Geoff Bennett: And you fired back by bringing up the allegations against him. Take me back to that moment. D.L. Hughley: So he -- I had worked at a station in New York, and Bill had come in because he was doing a show in Pennsylvania. And so he was coming on to do press for it. And I was -- my co-stars were Jacque Reid and Steve Wilson. And when Bill -- I was like, I'm not going doing this interview because it's going to go left if I get on. But he was being so dismissive to them that I finally got on and go: "Mr. Cosby, what is it you would like for us to know?" And he said: "Who is this?" And I said, "D.L. Hughley." "D.L. Hughley, Well, you say (EXPLETIVE DELETED) all the time, and you go back where you say this." I said: "No offense, Mr. Cosby, I say (EXPLETIVE DELETED) but I never had a coed wake up with their panties on backwards." (LAUGHTER) D.L. There are two cardboard boxes in Meenu Rana's living room in Delhi. One is filled with Diwali decorations and twinkling lights. The other holds air purifiers.
"The mornings have already started feeling stuffy. It will get worse in the coming days, so it's better to be prepared," says the 43-year-old teacher.
She is not alone. Every year, as winter and the festive season approach, residents of India's capital begin preparing for something far less celebratory: months of breathing polluted air.
Delhi and its satellite cities record some of the world's highest pollution levels through the year. But as winter sets in, the air often becomes unbearable.
Falling temperatures and slower winds trap pollutants close to the ground instead of allowing them to disperse. Smoke from crop residue burning in neighbouring states adds to emissions from vehicles and factories, as well as construction dust. Firecrackers used during festivals often worsen air quality.
The result is noxious air and a familiar question: why does pollution return year after year, and why hasn't more been done to tackle it?
This year, however, the Delhi government announced its Winter Action Plan months before the worst of the smog arrived. The plan is in place from 1 November to 28 February, covering the months when pollution usually spikes.
Experts have called this a step in the right direction, noting that in previous years measures were often rolled out only after the air quality got too bad to ignore. However, they say this by itself won't be enough, calling for more holistic, long-lasting measures.
Just days after the plan came into effect, the city is slipping back into a depressingly familiar pattern.
This week, a grey haze hangs over Delhi, along with a distinct smoky smell that residents unwillingly recognise. People complain of irritation in their eyes and difficulty breathing, and coughs and sneezes are heard everywhere.
For those who can afford them, air purifiers have become a household necessity. Outdoors, people wear masks or cover their faces with cloth, trying to protect themselves from the worst of the pollution.
Tackling pollution was among the promises made by the governing Bharatiya Janata Party during its election campaign last year. Its winter action plan is now a major test of that pledge.
The plan restricts the entry of older, more polluting vehicles registered outside Delhi and denies fuel to vehicles without a certificate which shows they meet emission standards. Demolitions and outdoor construction work that generate dust have been temporarily banned.
Private vehicle use is being discouraged - the government has asked offices to allow half of their employees to work from home, introduced staggered office timings for its staff and doubled parking charges. It says it will also strengthen pollution monitoring and enforcement and promote public transport and electric vehicles.
These measures are separate from the Graded Response Action Plan (Grap), which is overseen by the federal Commission for Air Quality Management.
Grap introduces restrictions in stages, with stricter measures kicking in as pollution levels rise. This week, its second stage is in force, restricting the use of diesel generators and burning of coal and firewood.
Expert say on paper, these actions collectively provide a roadmap for responding to rising pollution levels but their success ultimately depends on enforcement.
"There are a lot of positive changes as far as planning is concerned, but when it comes to execution, we probably still stand at the same level," says Parthaa Bosu, strategic adviser at the Environmental Defense Fund, a non-profit group focused on delivering climate solutions.
Others argue that the problem goes much deeper.
"If we want to reduce pollution, we need to set targets for every sector - including power generation, industry and transport - not just vehicle entry, construction and stubble burning," says Manoj Kumar, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
"We know how much each sector and each state contributes to pollution. We can set targets to reduce emissions from each of them over the next five years."
Bosu points out that an issue which does not get enough attention is secondary pollutants - when gases in the air react with sunlight, water vapour and other substances to form harmful particles that contribute to pollution.
"Pollution is not just caused by biomass burning or vehicles," he says. "Dust being stirred up from the ground, coal and fly ash, materials burned at brick kilns and the large-scale burning of urban waste are also contributing to the problem. And much of this is still not being stopped."
Delhi's pollution problem is also affected by what happens outside the city. Pollutants travel into Delhi from neighbouring states and other parts of northern India, worsening the situation, Bosu explains.
This means that measures taken by Delhi can achieve only so much. Tackling the problem requires neighbouring states and the wider northern region to work together, he adds.
In the meantime, pollution is harming people's health every day.
During winter, government monitoring stations in Delhi frequently record Air Quality Index (AQI) readings above 300, classified as "very poor".
On particularly bad days, readings can reach 500, the highest point on India's scale. That does not mean pollution cannot rise further, only that domestic trackers do not record it. International trackers such as Swiss-based IQAir have recorded readings close to 1,000 on some days.
The World Health Organization recommends average PM2.5 levels over 24 hours should not exceed 15 micrograms per cubic metre. In Delhi, levels are often at more than 25 times that limit during pollution season.

The crisis at Ueno Bank turned Peña's long-ruling Colorado Party against him, a stunning reversal for the former International Monetary Fund economist who had enjoyed the backing of the country's most powerful politicians and was welcomed in Washington just weeks ago as a key ally of the Trump administration. READ MORE: How the digital era helped speed up bank runs Minutes after Peña's announcement, the lower house voted 78-0 to impeach him, sending the charges to the Senate. Congressional leaders will continue voting Friday on whether to accept Peña's resignation, which would clear the way for Vice President Pedro Alliana to be sworn in without waiting for a Senate trial. Opposition senators are continuing to demand that Peña be removed from office, arguing that allowing him to resign would preserve his eligibility to become a senator for life, with legal protections that could prevent his prosecution, should Paraguay's Attorney General Emiliano Rolón Fernández opt to file charges. Rolón has ordered three criminal investigations into the Ueno Bank crisis, including allegations involving Peña and other current and former government officials, the prosecutor's office said Thursday. The investigations will examine authorities' oversight of the bank, their handling of its failure and the placement of public funds in the lender. Peña said he would cooperate with investigators. "Whatever the outcome of this process, I will act with responsibility and respect for the Constitution," he said on X. Earlier Thursday, Peña said in a video posted to X that he was stepping down in the interest of "the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions." Even Peña's mentor, Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, backed impeachment, saying the party would not side with "the plundering of public and private funds and pensioners' money." The United States Treasury sanctioned Cartes in 2023 over bribery allegations, but the Trump administration lifted the sanctions last year. Peña, who until last year held a stake in a company linked to Ueno, expressed contrition. But he stopped short of accepting responsibility for the turmoil, which has left millions of depositors, retirees and workers scrambling to recoup their frozen savings and unpaid wages. "I want to apologize to the people if I have failed them at any point," he said. "It was never my intention to betray the trust they placed in me." From star lender to seized bank Ueno Bank, which exploded from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, claimed more than 60% of Paraguay's adults as customers. Many Paraguayans are left asking how a bank linked to the president could grow so rapidly in size and importance despite repeated warnings about its lending practices. The answer lies in the uncomfortable proximity of Peña's Colorado Party to the country's regulators and business elite, a weakness that has endured even as steady economic management and rapid growth recently earned Paraguay coveted investment-grade credit ratings. "Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings," said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. "We are fed up with 70 years of plunder." Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries as it grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium. Government money poured into Ueno's coffers under Peña. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender. As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams. But worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad. As recently as last month, Peña defended Ueno and the central bank's oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public. Long lines outside branches but customers are locked out But on Monday, it all came crashing down. Regulators investigating Ueno's loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending, the central bank said, as well as expenses the bank had wrongly counted as assets. Once the books were corrected, Ueno's capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, fell to less than half the legal minimum. The central bank announced the lender's seizure Tuesday, beginning a process to transfer deposits and recoverable assets to other banks before liquidating what remained. Prime Minister Mark Carney has taken advantage of an oil revenue windfall to include tens of billions of dollars in new spending in his second federal budget, which focuses on building national sovereignty and addressing the high cost of living.
"That's what this budget does: it's the next big step in our action plan to make this country more independent, more sovereign," Carney said on Thursday.
"It focuses on growth, on people and that sovereignty, so we can live our lives as we wish."
The budget - titled Masters of Our Destiny - lays the groundwork for a Canada that is less reliant on the US for trade. It also aims to tackle the stubborn affordability crisis by promising billions to end homelessness and build new housing.
The C$142bn in new spending over the next five years is thanks to better than expected revenues from oil prices bolstered by the Iran War.
Canada's deficit is over C$50bn ($36bn; Â£27bn), with no path to balance.
Despite new spending, the budget shows that Carney has kept his previous fiscal goals intact.
The country still expects its GDP to grow modestly in the next year, outpacing all G7 countries except the US. Its unemployment rate, while unsteady month-to-month, is overall lower than last year.
But as people continue to feel squeezed by inflation and unaffordable housing, pressure has been building on Carney to translate his major investments into relief for the average Canadian.
And some sectors of the economy are feeling deep pain due to US President Donald Trump's tariffs on key Canadian industries, leading to thousands of job losses and uncertainty that has slowed business investment.
Here is a breakdown of some of the key takeaways for the 2026 federal budget.
A plan to end homelessness within a decade
One of the largest line items in Carney's second budget is an C$11.2bn commitment over the next four years to combat homelessness.
This includes funding for supportive housing, mental health and addictions treatment.
Statistics Canada reported last year that one in eight Canadian households have experienced a form of homelessness in their lifetime.
The government will also boost a grocery benefit that is available to low-and-modest income Canadians, which is estimated to provide C$2,570 for a family of four within one year.
Canada's opposition Conservatives have been pressing the Liberal government on cost of living, and have routinely accused the prime minister of spending too much time on foreign trade missions and not enough addressing kitchen table issues.
There are signs that Canadians are struggling to make ends meet. Average hourly wages have not kept up with inflation, according to Statistics Canada. Food bank usage has hit record highs.
The average price of a home in Canada has dropped around 22% in recent years, mostly due to a clamp down on immigration. But houses are still too expensive for many in Canada's major cities - namely Toronto and Vancouver.
And like the rest of the world, the rising price of fuel has made everything - from gas to groceries - more expensive.
No boost to immigration levels any time soon
After hitting record population growth in 2023, which was fuelled largely by immigration, Canada has scaled back its newcomer targets significantly.
This includes a cap on international students and temporary foreign workers, which have been relied on by companies to ease labour shortages.
The Carney government has previously said it will keep its permanent resident admission target to 380,000 people annually until 2028.
Meanwhile, it will gradually reduce its temporary resident arrivals to 370,000.
There has been pressure on Carney to increase some of those numbers. A report from the Royal Bank of Canada in September, external warned that "without immigration, the country's population would shrink to half its size by the turn of the century".
On the other hand, the Conservative opposition has called on the government to further lower its targets.
In the new budget, Carney has opted to keep immigration levels flat.
Helping businesses through US tariff dispute
A big focus of the Carney government has been reducing Canada's reliance on the US as a trade partner, while also helping cushion the blow from Trump's tariffs on its key sectors.
Last year, it promised millions in backing for businesses working to develop new export markets. It also lowered Canada's marginal effective tax rate in a bid to stop businesses from moving to the US to escape tariff pains.
This budget builds on that, including plans to support specific sectors hit by US tariffs like steel and forestry.
The new funding was welcome by Canada's forestry sector, with the BC Council of Forest Industries saying in a statement that the support "comes at a critical time for workers".
Since March 2025, the Carney government has set aside nearly C$44bn in support for workers and businesses hit by US tariffs, the budget notes.
The budget states that "diversification will take time, given the scale and depth of Canada's economic relationship with the United States. But the shift is underway".
Sovereignty through arts - and rockets
Sovereignty is a big theme in Carney's second budget, which proposes funding different measures to strengthen Canadian identity - whether it be through the arts or in space.
Canada is the only G7 country that does not have the capability to launch its own rockets. A line item in the budget looks to change that, with C$2.7bn earmarked to developing Canadian space technology and launch infrastructure.
On arts and culture, Carney is promising a tax exemption on income that is made through "original and creative artistic works".
The budget also sets aside C$32.2m over four years to establish a free national digital library for Canadians. It will launch with at least 200 titles with plans to expand in coming years.
Carney had previously pledged to significantly boost defence spending to meet the Nato target of 5% of annual GDP by 2035.

World Nov 5, 2026 5:31 PM EST LONDON (AP) — Hundreds of airline passengers in Europe had their flights diverted or given military escorts this week after a series of bomb threats that officials have said were malicious hoaxes. READ MORE: Flights across Europe face disruption after false bomb threats It was not immediately known who was behind the threats, which came at a time of rising tensions with Russia and warnings that it may be ramping up so-called hybrid attacks in Europe. Here's what happens when airlines receive bomb threats. Threats are assessed and then relayed to pilots Assessors determine whether a threat is credible, partially credible or not credible, according to Joji Waites, director of flight safety, policy and regulation for the British Airline Pilots' Association. If deemed credible, the flight crew is informed right away and the captain makes all the decisions, guided by a safety checklist, said Waites. If the aircraft is on the ground, that would mean evacuation. If already in flight, the priority would be to land as soon and as safely as possible. "Pilots are highly trained and skilled professionals. Their expertise is invaluable in ensuring passenger safety and keeping aviation one of the safest forms of transport there is," Waites said. Airlines, airport operators and law enforcement generally follow guidelines developed by the European Union Aviation Safety Agency and the International Civil Aviation Organization, which conducts audits to ensure compliance. Flight crew training includes live situational exercises covering various threats, including how to search for explosives that may have been smuggled on board. Diverting and inspecting flights is costly When threats are called in, airline employees are instructed to keep the caller on the line and to gather as much information as possible, according to aviation security expert Philip Baum. Many of the threats received this week were sent by email, with enough information for authorities to determine that aircraft needed inspection. That can be costly for airlines. Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England, said diverting a flight because of an unruly passenger or a bomb threat can cost up to $250,000. The costs may be lower in this case because most of the disrupted flights were short-haul, where there is less likelihood of overnight delays, he said. Empty threats could test defenses The intent with these threats "appears to be to sow chaos, uncertainty, about the reliability of air traffic across Europe," said Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, senior fellow at the Bruegel think tank in Brussels. The threats could also be testing the relative response time and level of coordination among authorities in different countries, with the aim of identifying weaknesses for future attacks. "Do the authorities in Poland respond at the same speed and with the same urgency, et cetera, as the authorities of Italy, for instance?" Kirkegaard said, comparing such threats to a "stress test" of the system. Carlson reported from Brussels and Hadjicostis from Nicosia, Cyprus. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Trump met with Putin's envoy Politics Nov 5, 2026 5:04 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said he met with Vladimir Putin's envoy at the White House on Thursday but did not meet with Ukrainian officials who were also visiting. Watch the event in the video player above. Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office, Trump said he had a meeting with Kirill Dmitriev. "I can't tell you what I discussed," Trump said. READ MORE: Russian strikes on Ukrainian aid site kill at least 31 people, with dozens still missing Asked if he had met with Ukrainian representatives, Trump said he had not. Representatives from both countries were at the White House for an event honoring Melania Trump's work brokering a ceasefire in Oleshky. After declining to elaborate on his meeting with Dmitriev, Trump suggested some sort of deal is in the works. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News "Its going to be an agreement, it's going to be a big agreement and it's going to involve more than Ukraine," Trump said, adding that it might include all of Europe. Melania Trump on Thursday brought together Russian and Ukrainian officials to mark the localized ceasefire she brokered between their nations in a besieged Ukrainian village. WATCH: Zelenskyy confirms Ukraine hacked back after Russia's cyberattack of its emergency alert system Speaking at her invitation, Dmitriev thanked the first lady for her "distinguished humanitarian role" in securing the six-day truce. Dmitriev added that Putin personally gave instructions as part of the operation and sent his thanks to Melania Trump. The head of the parliamentary faction of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's party, Davyd Arakhamia, and Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, also spoke at the event. Arakhamia told the first lady she did an "amazing job" and encouraged her to keep helping the Ukrainian people, who have endured more than four years of war after Putin sent his troops across the border and invaded the country in 2022. "Definitely we would like to ask you to keep going and to find new missions and to de-escalate more as much as possible," Arakhamia said. The first lady has worked with both countries since last year to reunite families separated by the war. So far, she has helped nearly three dozen children return to their relatives. She said Thursday that she hoped the Oleshky ceasefire could become more enduring and more widespread. "Let Oleshky be the modest spark that grows into a lasting flame of peace," she said. Zelenskyy, in a speech in Spain on Friday, said the operation in Oleshky proved "something very simple. When Putin wants the fighting to stop, it stops. And there was real silence, no attacks some days, and we saved hundreds of lives." First lady tackles foreign policy challenge The ceasefire is the latest example of how Melania Trump has become more involved in foreign affairs than some of her recent predecessors, who typically travel abroad to spread U.S. goodwill and avoid involvement with warring countries. In 2022, months after Russia invaded Ukraine, first lady Jill Biden traveled to western Ukraine to visit with Zelenskyy's wife in a town far away from the front lines. Under tight security, first lady Laura Bush made several visits to war-torn Afghanistan. In an announcement that came as a surprise, the White House said on Oct. 23 that the first lady had brokered the ceasefire to help with the delivery of much-needed humanitarian aid and to allow civilians to evacuate from a place she described as being "on the brink of disaster." Ukrainian, Russian and U.S. negotiators earlier that day had reached an agreement to deliver relief to Oleshky in the war-divided region of Kherson in southern Ukraine. The local ceasefire was in effect from Oct. 27 to Nov. 1 and amounted to the most significant truce since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. An estimated 2,000 people remained in Oleshky when the temporary truce took hold. They were offered the choice of evacuating to territory controlled by Ukraine or Russia, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies. Supplies were delivered during the six-day window while hundreds of Oleshky residents crossed into Ukrainian-held territory in a major evacuation operation. Melania Trump said Thursday that nearly 800 people had evacuated Oleshky, and she described how she initiated talks with officials in both countries after learning about the situation at an event she held on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly session in September. She said she and her top adviser, Marc Beckman, worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the ceasefire. Situation in Oleshky was dire Food and medical supplies had been scarce for months in Oleshky, once a city of about 24,000 residents that sits on the Dnipro River separating Ukrainian forces from the city's Russian occupiers. There is no electricity, heat or running water. Oleshky was captured by Moscow's forces on the first day of Russia's full-scale invasion. Its buildings were shelled and burned, and its infrastructure damaged. In June 2023, floodwaters inundated the city after the Kakhovka Dam collapsed from an explosion that an Associated Press investigation found was likely caused by the Russian military. Hundreds of residents were killed. Those left in the city along Ukraine's southeastern front face death from hunger or disease as another harsh winter looms. Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, has been found guilty of incitement and sentenced to four years in jail, in a case that has raised concerns about political freedom in the East African country.
A panel of three judges at the High Court in Dar es Salaam acquitted him of the more serious offence of treason, saying prosecutors had failed to prove a key element of that charge.
The 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, was charged over remarks he made while campaigning for electoral reforms ahead of the disputed 2025 general election.
Lissu, who leads the opposition Chadema party, has denied the charges, describing the prosecution as politically motivated.
The court said the incitement case stemmed from his campaign over his campaign slogan "No Reforms, No Election."
"By uttering those words with the intention of disseminating them to the public, the accused incited the public to disrupt the 2025 elections," the court ruled.
Lissu has been on trial on charges of treason and says this is the first time he has heard of the separate charge of incitement.
"The offense of incitement is one that you, honourable judges, have manufactured. You have created an offense that did not exist, and you have done so on political directives," said Lissu, when he was given a chance to address the judges.
He added that he would like to apply for bail as this was possible for incitement, unlike treason.
He has leave to appeal at the Court of Appeal - the country's highest court.
Treason is among Tanzania's most serious offences and can carry the death penalty.
President Samia Suluhu Hassan won the October 2025 election with 98% of the vote - a result the opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as her two main challengers, including Lissu, were excluded.
Her government has repeatedly denied targeting its opponents.
The Chadema leader was arrested six months before the poll, shortly after launching a campaign demanding changes to the electoral system under the slogan "No Reforms, No Election".
Prosecutors accused him of making statements intended to incite the public to disrupt the election and threaten the government.
They argued that his remarks, which were also circulated online, amounted to treason.
But Lissu, a lawyer who represented himself during the trial, maintained that his comments were part of a legitimate political campaign for constitutional and electoral reform.
He argued that prosecutors had taken his statements out of context and failed to prove that he had committed any crime.
Some of the demands raised by Chadema were:
- Electoral commissioners should be independently appointed (not by the president)
- Police should allow all parties to campaign free of intimidation
- Government-appointed district chiefs should no longer act as returning officers
- Party agents should be able to observe counting without harassment
- It should be possible to challenge presidential election results in court.
During his time in remand custody at Dar es Salaam's Ukonga Prison, Lissu went on hunger strike twice for brief periods when he said he was not allowed access to his lawyers or relatives. He also complained that guards listened to what should have been private consultations his lawyers.
These allegations have been denied by the prison authorities.
His case has attracted international attention, with rights groups expressing concern about the treatment of opposition politicians and the shrinking space for political dissent in Tanzania.
Last year's election was followed by widespread protests and a violent security crackdown that left at least 500 people dead, according to an official inquiry.
Opposition groups have said the death toll was much higher and demanded an independent investigation.
The government has defended its handling of the unrest and rejected accusations of widespread political repression.
Samia, 66, has insisted the election was fair and transparent and blamed foreigners for the unrest, saying it was part of a plot to overthrow her. She has set up another commission to inquiry to identify those behind the violence.
Lissu has long been one of Tanzania's most outspoken critics of the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party, which, along with its predecessor Tanu, has dominated the country's politics since independence.
He first became an MP in 2010, representing a constituency near his birth place in Singida, 320km (200 miles) north-west of the capital, Dodoma.
In September 2017, the Chadema politician narrowly survived an assassination attempt when gunmen sprayed his vehicle with bullets outside his home in Dodoma.
He was shot multiple times and underwent extensive medical treatment abroad.
The attack, whose perpetrators have never been brought to justice, forced him to spend years outside Tanzania.
He returned to contest the 2020 presidential election against the late President John Magufuli, but lost in a vote that the opposition alleged was marred by widespread irregularities.
Lissu subsequently returned to exile before coming back to Tanzania in 2023, following President Samia's decision to lift a ban on opposition political rallies.
His return was initially seen as a sign of renewed political openness after years of restrictions under Magufuli, who died in office in 2021.
But relations between the government and the opposition deteriorated as the country approached the 2025 election.
Lissu became Chadema's national chairman in January 2025 and intensified his demands for electoral reforms.
His conviction is likely to deepen concerns about the state of democracy in Tanzania.
Last week, rights group Amnesty International accused the government of continuing its crackdown following the election and "weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear".
The authorities did not respond to a request for comment.
