52f6d6104e5e.text: Voters were unambiguous on Tuesday: Don't B.S. us. Don't say you'll lower prices and end wars and corruption, then do the opposite. It's really that simple. This isn't so different from when Americans told Democrats not to B.S. them about Joe Biden's health, or about the words they should use, or social behaviors they should adopt. Why it matters: Most Americans agree broadly on most things, most of the time. They want competent politicians to focus on issues that meaningfully impact their lives. Like clockwork, every two years, Americans feel the party in power fails to deliver this — so they punish the incumbents at the polls. Politicians and some journalists tend to treat the American people as dopes and dupes who don't get what's happening in front of their faces. Tuesday's midterms, which will live in history as a Watergate-level reset for democracy, show that voters were paying attention and hit a boiling point. They didn't hide it. Polls consistently showed that all they really care about is rising inflation, job insecurity, ending the war, and stopping the rampant corruption. This was a repudiation of overreach, incompetence and corruption. People will tolerate it in small doses, but eventually reject it. In an age when people trust institutions less all the time , our institutions held. Courts restrained executive-branch excess. The press kept doing its job. Voters did theirs. But for all the hand-wringing that America is crumbling, that democracy is fading, or elections are eroding, the system worked. Remember: most Americans are normal and resilient. We should celebrate that. Despite it all, America works. For years, we've been reminding you about the power of Normal America : The vast majority of people — including our siblings, who are scattered from Oshkosh to Oregon — don't marinate in cable news, obsess about X or wake up thinking about Washington. They volunteer, they give to good causes, they'll help you in a pinch. They're good, they're fair ... and they're smart. Between the lines: That's Normal America. Sometimes when we're making a tough call about journalism or business, we ask ourselves: "What would the person at the bar think?" It's a useful, clarifying proxy for: What would seem on the level through the lens of common sense and plain fairness? The person at the bar, and the voter in the booth, didn't want their soccer coach deported, didn't want their business to crumble because of a war of choice that's dragging on and on, didn't want the president's family and friends to enrich themselves while Normal America was wheezing. What we're watching: Democrats will be tempted and pressured to overreach. If they overinterpret their mandate the way Republicans did, they'll be punished, like clockwork. Here's what Republicans and Democrats will do if they're smart: Watch Texas. A seemingly impenetrable red state turned all blue, from the U.S. Senate to the governor's office to the state legislature. If Democrats can keep Texas, Republicans have no path to the presidency. Look at what happened in those southern border counties in Texas. These were the people who demanded tighter borders and punished Democrats when they wouldn't listen. But they're the same people who are saying stop with the thuggery and targeting of nonviolent people. Republicans were obliterated in those areas for not listening. Then look to the Texas suburbs, where you have many more traditional Republicans and moderate Democrats. They looked at Ken Paxton and said he's simply not on the level, even if they might agree with him on a lot of ideas. Corruption is never a good look. Enabling it and elevating it is even worse. The bottom line: This remains a 50-50 nation — a simple fact that every party and power instantly, constantly ignores. Once again, Normal Americans spoke: Ignore or B.S. them at your peril.

One child and one young adult have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.
The bus was travelling between Lyon and Bourg-en-Bresse when it crashed at around 07:00 local time on Friday in the town of Lent, around 34 miles (55km) from the border with Switzerland.
The town's mayor Yves Cristin told French media the bus "left the road and hit a tree in the ditch".
The bus was carrying 43 passengers, including 15 children, the Bourg-en-Bresse prosecutor's office said. Three people are in a critical condition and a further 13 have sustained minor injuries.
The driver is reported to have been taken to hospital after sustaining injuries and has not yet been questioned by police, the prosecutor's office added.
Earlier, French education minister Ãdouard Geffray said the crash involved students.
He told reporters it was "always difficult when our children are victims of accidents of this nature".
Photos circulating in French media show a blue and white bus tilted in what appears to be a ditch on the roadside. Trees line the side of the road. The front of the bus appears to be heavily damaged.
Emergency services were at the scene and medical helicopters were deployed to take victims with serious injuries to a specialised hospital.
French Transport minister Philippe Tabarot, who was on his way to the area, said more than 100 firefighters had also been sent.
The local town hall has been opened to provide shelter and coordinate with emergency services, the local mayor said.

The News
Republicansâ stunning midterm defeat is forcing them to confront a question that will shape their 2028 primary: Can their next standard-bearer come from inside the Trump administration?
Vice President JD Vance remains the most prominent potential successor to President Donald Trump, but his blunt X post pinning the partyâs Tuesday collapse on the Iran war showed heâs aware that itâs a political liability for all Republicans heading into 2028. And concerns about Vanceâs viability are brewing in some corners of the GOP.
âThe biggest loser Tuesday night, heading into 2028, was JD Vance,â one Republican strategist argued. â2028 shifted from a conversation about who could carry the torch of Trumpism, to who can rebuild the movement from shambles.â
Vance isnât the only prospective candidate tied to Trump with new problems after the midterms. While former Speaker Newt Gingrich suggested that Tuesday night might have opened a 2028 lane for Secretary of State Marco Rubio â whoâs indicated that he has no plans to run â anyone in Trumpâs circle could face similar headwinds.
That includes administration officials who are occasionally whispered about as harboring presidential ambitions, like Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Semafor spoke with more than a half-dozen Republicans, inside and close to the administration, who are starting to doubt that voters will embrace Trumpâs chosen successor.
âItâs an open race, no question about it,â one person close to the White House said of the looming 2028 debate.
Others in the party are focused on an even touchier topic: Are Republicans doomed for 2028, particularly if the war drags on and voters continue feeling the economic effects?
âThere are a lot of Republicans who desperately do not want Donald Trump to be the conversation in 2028. But theyâre living in a fantasy world â and the reality is, Donald Trump will always be a big part of the Republican conversation,â said a second person close to the White House. âThe actual question is: Can any Republican win?â
Outsiders See An Opening
Democratsâ huge margin of victory in Tuesdayâs popular vote for the House, estimated at 13 points, stemmed in large part from fury over Trumpâs handling of the economy. Exit polls showed nearly nine out of 10 voters considered the cost of living as a big factor in their vote, while the majority of voters expressed dissatisfaction with the direction of the country.
As one Trump ally put it, the night was a âdisasterâ for the GOP.
Thatâs creating opportunities for Republicans who have kept separate political identities during Trumpâs second term. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who lost to Trump in the 2024 primary, acknowledged that the midterms were a ârebukeâ of the president. He also amplified Floridaâs GOP successes, a rare bright spot for the party on Tuesday.
Some Republicans who were critical of DeSantis during his 2024 run suggested to Semafor this week that they and other doubters would be quieter in 2028 if he chose to run.
Others are more skeptical that Trump defenders (and Trump himself) could resist the temptation to attack DeSantis, particularly if he campaigns with more direct criticism of the president.
Walking a more middle road when it comes to anti-Trump sentiment is Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, who has long previewed a potential run. Cruz described the midterm results as âa Watergate-level repudiation,â blaming Trumpâs tariffs and the dragging war â both of which he voted to affirm â as well as a disconnect between extreme wealth and everyday Americans.
Vanceâs Theory of the Case
The vice presidentâs social media postmortem showcased his balancing act: supporting Trump while looking toward his own political future.
âThe reason we lost is the war,â Vance wrote on X. âThe president himself said so last night.â
Vanceâs allies argue that, if he decides to run, he might be the only candidate close enough to Trump to break from the president without paying harsh consequences. One of those allies described it as creating space to be âhis own man without criticizing or alienating the president.â
Trump seemed unbothered by the vice presidentâs assessment of the midterms, telling reporters âitâs largely trueâ while standing by his decision to go to war.
Yet Vance has declined to clearly oppose the conflict since it began; his views have emerged in subtle gestures, like taking the lead on negotiations with Tehran. As Gingrich put it, âa good bit of the luster has come off the bloomâ for Vance 2028, thanks to the âgo-slow strategy blowing up in Iran.â
The View From Trump
Trump is in no rush to focus on 2028, or issue any sort of endorsement. Asked about the topic earlier this week, he told reporters that he speaks with Vance âabout a lot of thingsâ and emphasized that anyone could ultimately jump into the race.
âYou donât know whoâs talking about running,â Trump said. âYouâre going to have people running â¦ maybe a lot of people running. Maybe nobodyâs going to run. Maybe [Vance] wonât run. I donât know whoâs going to run.â
Shelbyâs view
Electoral catastrophes, like the ones Republicans just experienced, are bound to prompt panic and hand-wringing about the future. But the midterms have surfaced a question that I hear a lot: Can anyone successfully lead this party for the years after Trump leaves the stage?
The GOPâs 2028 hopefuls are damned if they do, damned if they donât. Running as an anti-Trump figure will carry risks; running on loyalty to him will pose separate problems.
The biggest unknown is Trump himself. If he can find a way to wind down the war and refocus on earning back Americansâ trust over the next two years, he could leave his successor with a clearer path.
Notable
- Democratic Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, seen as a potential 2028 candidate as well, is already trying to tie Vance closely to Trump: He told CNN this week Vance âis out promotingâ the policies that have turned off voters.
- Rubio dismissed the idea that he is planning to leave the Trump administrati

db55ea156274.text: Talk of subpoenas and warnings to "lawyer up" hint at the extent of the health care investigations and oversight hearings that Democrats are expected to launch once they take control of Congress. Why it matters: Democrats have been building a paper trail for months to probe instances of political interference in vaccine policies, whether Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. benefited financially from vaccine litigation and more. But the early efforts will more likely be directed at making a case for changes to federal Medicaid cuts, showcasing health affordability problems and examining whether federal health agencies are sufficiently funded and staffed. "You don't just do oversight to raise hell," said Tim Stretton, director of the Congressional Oversight Initiative at the Project On Government Oversight. "Trying to create some systematic change is arguably more important." What we're hearing: The House Oversight, Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees will be focal points of early activity, along with the Senate health and Finance committees. Some law firms already are advising their corporate clients to cooperate with committee staffs and minimize their exposure to possible negative headlines from hearings. One prominent player will be the likely new House Oversight chair, Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) — the one who publicly warned Republicans to "lawyer up" on Tuesday after Democrats flipped control of the House. The former Long Beach mayor lost his mother, a frontline health worker, and stepfather to COVID and has publicly assailed Kennedy for undermining public health and preventing or delaying needed cures. Bernie Sanders' expected return to chair the Senate health committee will give the Vermont independent another chance to harness public outrage on drug prices and spar with Kennedy over his tenure as health secretary. Zoom in: The power shift in Congress gives Democrats the ability to subpoena witnesses, demand records and hold officials and individuals in contempt if they don't comply. Hearings and investigations into problems with Affordable Care Act markets, drug pricing or hospital billing will likely be bipartisan in nature and feature ordinary citizens, to put a face on the problem. But Democrats will surely blame Trump administration policies and the conduct of officials for making Americans worse off. Garcia has said corruption within the administration is responsible for affordability woes. Along similar lines, likely Senate Finance Chair Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) has suggested that President Trump's drug pricing agreements amount to "sweetheart deals" with the pharmaceutical industry that won't help the vast majority of Americans. What we're watching: Kennedy's tenure as secretary may constitute its own category of oversight and consume committees in both houses. Sanders is expected to bring up internal communications that the health committee's Democrats obtained from former Centers for Disease Control and Prevention chief medical officer Debra Houry. Democrats say they show Kennedy changed vaccine recommendations without expert review and directed a federal vaccine advisory panel's actions to undermine access to vaccines. Some of the activity took place around the time former CDC director Susan Monarez was ousted over vaccine recommendations and could shed light on whether officials misrepresented the rationale for revising recommendations. Another group of senators, including Wyden and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), has questioned whether Kennedy personally benefited from a $50 million settlement around Merck's Gardasil human papillomavirus vaccine. Kennedy, a prominent vaccine critic, said during his confirmation process that he divested a contingency-fee interest in certain Gardasil lawsuits, but the senators want to know whether his ethics agreement correctly described the arrangement or whether there were conflicts of interest. On the House side, Energy and Commerce Committee Democrats have focused on activities like the Food and Drug Administration blocking the publication of studies showing COVID and shingles vaccines were safe and what they contend is a trend of suppressing data that doesn't sync with his views. The other side: "Secretary Kennedy has delivered the most sweeping public health reforms in modern history. Oversight hearings will not distract him from serving the American people. He will continue to put prevention at the center of health care to end the chronic disease epidemic and Make America Healthy Again," said Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson Emily Hilliard. David Mansdoerfer, a senior health official in the first Trump administration, said he expects DOGE cuts to be a key focus of Democrats' oversight, followed by decision-making around vaccines, research grants and health agency budgets. "Outside of some minor procedural issues, I don't see a ton of substantive areas that are anything more than just an oversight hearing YouTube highlight clip," Mansdoerfer wrote on X. The bottom line: For all the confrontational rhetoric, the administration and Democrats will pick and choose their battles, per a client alert from law firm Morrison Foerster. It notes the White House has added legal staff to prepare for oversight, and that the administration may assert executive privilege over certain presidential communications with private parties.

abed5b7e7bce.text: President Trump has told advisers that he plans to keep raising money for his political operation — a move aimed at salvaging his clout after the GOP's midterm debacle. Why it matters: Maintaining a political organization — either his existing MAGA Inc. super PAC or one to be created — would give Trump a vehicle to try to influence elections in 2028 and beyond, including the next presidential contest. It also would give Trump a way to pressure GOP lawmakers who consider breaking with him as the unpopular president enters his lame-duck era and Democrats prepare congressional investigations into his administration. Trump's MAGA Inc. enforced party discipline during the 2026 primary campaigns when it helped defeat Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie (R), an outspoken Trump critic. Zoom in: MAGA Inc. has been the centerpiece of Trump's political operation during his second term, raising nearly $450 million since the beginning of 2025. The group received massive checks from cryptocurrency and AI industry donors, along with Republican megadonors such as Elon Musk and Miriam Adelson. Trump has hosted high-dollar fundraising dinners at Mar-a-Lago and his golf club in Sterling, Va., drawing business leaders eager to curry favor with the president. Some donors subsequently benefited from administration decisions. The New York Times reported that a medical products company whose executives and affiliates gave $5 million to MAGA Inc. benefited from an administration decision to delay Medicare reimbursement restrictions, for example. By the numbers: MAGA Inc. spent more than $400 million on the midterms, making it one of the election's biggest spending forces, according to a source familiar with the totals. The massive investment failed to prevent Republicans from losing control of Congress amid voter anger over Trump's war on Iran, high prices and corruption concerns. As of Oct. 14, MAGA Inc. had more than $164 million in the bank, though it spent tens of millions more on TV and digital advertising in the campaign's final weeks so it's unclear how much remains. The group invested aggressively in traditionally safe GOP seats that had become competitive, helping some Republicans survive, according to party operatives. Yes, but: Raising money could become much harder with Democrats controlling Congress and major donors beginning to look turning their attention toward 2028. Republicans say Trump's diminished political clout will make it harder to attract the enormous checks that have flowed into MAGA Inc. The prospect of congressional investigations into alleged pay-for-play arrangements involving donors to Trump's political operation could further discourage contributions. Technology executives who contributed heavily to the group may increasingly turn to Democrats, while major Republican donors shift their attention to prospective 2028 presidential candidates. What they're saying: A MAGA Inc. spokesperson declined to comment. White House spokespeople didn't respond to a request for comment.

737babbd2885.text: Democrats have made climate change a centerpiece of their campaigns for years — but this year they barely mentioned it. Why it matters: The midterms showed just how far the topic has fallen down the political priority list, even within the party most committed to addressing it — and suggest affordability will shape how Democrats govern next year. Driving the news: Democrats up and down the ballot campaigned overwhelmingly on affordability, including fuel prices surging amid President Trump's Iran war and rising electricity bills, accentuated by the AI boom. The big picture: The relative absence of climate change is striking considering that Democrats of all political stripes won big. Zoom in: Even some of the party's most prominent climate advocates emphasized affordability over climate change — or reconsidered ambitious climate policies in response to rising costs. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, who previously championed the state's ambitious climate agenda, pushed to weaken parts of its landmark climate law this year, citing affordability concerns. Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.), who co-authored the Green New Deal, played down the proposal during his reelection campaign, emphasizing affordability and other priorities instead. Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico, who has previously warned about fossil fuels' impact on the planet, campaigned on protecting oil and gas jobs alongside expanding renewable energy and lowering electricity bills. Flashback: The political shift has been underway since the 2024 presidential election, when even climate-focused groups began de-emphasizing climate change in their political advertising, a trend that persisted through the midterms. State of play: On a call with reporters the day after the election, leading environmental groups celebrated Democrats' victories as a rejection of Trump's energy policies, arguing that his attacks on clean energy contributed to higher electricity bills. "Trump's energy agenda was an economic disaster for families and a political disaster for Republicans, and voters sent a very loud message," said Lori Lodes, president of Climate Power, an advocacy group that spent heavily on the election. Yes, but: While the Green New Deal-era approach of campaigning explicitly on climate change is mostly gone, Democrats are repositioning clean energy as one part of a broader focus on affordability and the economy. "There's no question that climate change is going to be a more vocal part of the agenda under Democrat leadership," said Jason Grumet, head of the American Clean Power Association, this week. "And I think that people recognize that the solution flows more from an abundance premise than a restrictive premise." Zoom out: The affordability-first approach reflects a broader reckoning within the climate movement. "We have to find the limited spaces for progress in a world where climate is even more deprioritized than it was a couple years ago," Armond Cohen, executive director of Clean Air Task Force, told Axios in an interview before the election. Cohen's organization recently unveiled a revised strategy focused on climate solutions that governments can more realistically afford and that can attract support across political lines. What we're watching: The election of Democrats in traditionally Republican, fossil-fuel-producing states like Texas could reinforce the party's emphasis on affordable energy and economic development rather than an explicit transition away from fossil fuels. Reality check: Even though climate change has faded as a top political priority, its physical impacts — and mounting economic costs — aren't going away. The intrigue: As Axios' Ben Geman pointed out earlier this week, Democrats are unlikely to revive the House Select Committee on the Climate Crisis , though no decision has been announced. A current-day version could instead focus on energy affordability, building on efforts like the existing Gas and Utilities Affordability Working Group . What's next: Next week will offer a split-screen reality. The Senate is poised to begin debate on a wonky but important bill aimed at expediting energy projects of all kinds, whose impact on climate change could be significant — or not. Meanwhile, some Democratic lawmakers plan to attend the annual United Nations climate conference beginning Monday in Antalya, Turkey.

The News
READING, Pa. â A few days before he won re-election by 22 points, Gov. Josh Shapiro was barely mentioning his Republican opponent anymore. Heâd share his stages with local Democratic candidates, ask for a Democratic majority in the state Senate, and explain what it could do.
âIâm going to the good people of Pennsylvania, saying: I want to raise your minimum wage,â Shapiro told Semafor. âI want to have a big housing and critical infrastructure fund. Thatâs the stuff they can expect to see from us, and Iâm going to stay true to that.â
Tuesdayâs Democratic landslides gave the party full control of multiple swing states â not just Shapiroâs Pennsylvania, but Wisconsin, Arizona, Michigan, Nevada, and Minnesota. Democrats won legislative trifectas big enough to pass progressive bills that had gathered dust and lint under Republican control.
Instead, swing-state governors plan to focus on popular economic proposals that won over voters ââ lowering living costs, taxes, and healthcare â and not the left-wing agenda items demonized in billions of dollars in GOP ads.
After their biggest wins in decades, Democratic state leaders are coalescing around moderation, rather than the progressive politics that shaped the party in Trumpâs first term and during Joe Bidenâs presidency.
âIâm committed to moving our state forward,â Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., told reporters at her first press conference as governor-elect. âNot to the left, not to the right, but forward.â
In Wisconsin, where Democrats won their first governing trifecta since 2008, Gov.-elect David Crowley ran on expanding Medicaid, which Republicans in Madison refused to do for eight years under retiring Gov. Tony Evers.
âWeâre going to expand access to quality affordable healthcare that offers real options for families, our children, our seniors, and people with disabilities,â Crowley said after beating GOP Rep. Tom Tiffany.
Medicaid expansion was also top of mind for Democratic winners in Georgia and Texas, where the party elected governors and won control of the lower house of their state legislatures. In DC, Democrats plan to fight next year to restore Medicaid funding that was cut or restricted by Republicans in 2025; in states, Democrats are confident that Republicans, chastened by their losses, might be willing to expand health care coverage.
âI truly believe that this is an issue we can get bipartisan support with,â Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms said on Wednesday.
Not on the agenda: progressive bills focused on crime and social issues.
In New York state, the passage of cash bail reform during Trumpâs presidency became a target for Republicans who over-performed in 2022 and 2024, blaming Democrats for a temporary rise in crime.
In Minnesota, Gov. Tim Walzâs 2022 sweep helped Democrats pass a pile of bills that were halted by Republicans. That made him a surprising star among left-leaning Democrats â and gave Republicans a number of attack points against his party in 2024, such as when they mocked âTampon Timâ for making sanitary products available in boysâ restrooms in public schools.
Democrats are talking more cautiously now, and the party is rooting them on from DC. At a Thursday post-election conference organized by the Center for American Progress, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said that the people whoâd beaten invincible-looking Republicans needed space to vote and govern their way. That, he said, could help the whole party.
âInstead of letting Fox News define what a Democrat is, our Democrats in these states will define what a Democrat is,â said Schumer.
Even some Democrats who had endorsed more progressive policies in the past were urging the party to focus on economic needs first, and convince the voters who broke from the GOP this year that the party deserved a long-term mandate.
In a memo shared with supporters of the Democracy Alliance, a progressive donor collective, the group urged Democrats with trifectas to âpass structural reforms that make it easier for everyone to participate in our democracy, and to improve the lives of working families â setting a model for whatâs possible nationwide.â
It would be a mistake, it said, for the party to âtake any of this cycleâs demographic swings for granted.â
Davidâs view
The slow-moving Democratic story of the last two years has been the end of the old ârising American electorateâ theory. After their 2018 wins, many influential Democrats and their donors suggested that a new, more progressive majority was forming as a reaction to Donald Trump. That confidence decreased after their 2020 victory, which was narrower than they expected, and it was shredded in 2024.
This time, Democrats generally agree that âeconomic populismâ won everywhere, that voters gave them a chance because prices were too high, and that they had defused the power of some cultural issues by telling voters they would not act on them. That is going to be tested next year, but itâs the plan right now.
Room for Disagreement
Kelley Robinson, the president of the LGBTQ+ advocacy group the Human Rights Campaign, told Semafor that the âfirst thing that weâre going to ask [Democrats] to deliver on is showing how they can make life more affordable for all Americans, including the LGBTQ+ community.â
If Democrats believed that they could pass economic bills and not pass the Equality Act, which would enshrine civil rights protections based on sexual orientation and gender identity, they were mistaken, she said.
âI would just remind folks that advocating for the LGBTQ+ community is an affordability issue,â said Robinson. âLook, if I can get fired at work because of my sexual orientation or gender identity, that is an economic issue. If Iâm not allowed to shop in certain stores because of my sexual orientation or gender identity, that is an economic issue. If my kids cannot go to a school because they are the children of LGBTQ+ parents, please believe that is an economic issue thatâs going to be hitting

The News
House Democrats are debating the future of the chamberâs select panel on US-China competition.
One option for overhauling the committee, according to people familiar with the situation, is broadening its focus beyond China to explore issues related to other bad foreign actors.
But the decisions on the select panel are ultimately up to Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, whoâs said the caucus will discuss future steps.
A Jeffries spokesperson said oversight of China-related matters will be an important priority next Congress regardless of committee structure.
One complication for the future of the panel: Its current top Democrat, Rep. Ro Khanna of California, likely plans to run for president. If he runs, that would mean Democrats might have to switch chairs midway through Congress.
The last Democrat to serve as its ranking member, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill., stepped down when he launched his unsuccessful Senate bid.
The bipartisan panel, established in 2023 under GOP House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, examines US competition with China, including issues involving technology transfers and export controls.

Healthcare affordability. Abortion access. “Medicare for All.” Healthcare was a major force behind the big wins for Democrats in this week’s midterm elections. But the debate over what the Democratic Party will do next is just getting started.
KFF Health News chief Washington correspondent Julie Rovner appeared on WAMU’s Health Hub on Nov. 4 to explore what Democrats might do with their newfound power. However, with President Donald Trump still in office, this blue wave is likely to crash into legislative limits.

Midterm Wave Sets a Course for ‘Medicare for All’ Fight
LANSING, Mich. — Fifteen years working as an emergency room nurse has convinced Kim Bogan that the only way to fix the American healthcare system is to tear it down and start over.
Her patients arriving for triage are sicker than ever. They can’t afford many of the prescriptions they get in the ER. And sometimes when patients die, she wonders if she could have saved them had she not been caring for five or six other people at once.
That’s why she spent the past year shuttling between 12-hour shifts at this city’s Sparrow Hospital and campaigning for Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat who made “Medicare for All” a signature issue in his congressional campaign and is now a senator-elect.
But she realizes that just because progressive candidates successfully campaigned on some form of the policy in states such as Texas, Iowa, Maine, and Michigan, it doesn’t mean Medicare for All will be an easy sell. “Nobody expected that,” Bogan said.
Medicare for All typically refers to a government health program that would guarantee Americans coverage by replacing most or all private insurance. Critics are already pointing out that, even in a blue wave as massive as the 2026 midterms, the most vocal Medicare for All champions generally won by smaller margins than more moderate Democrats.
“Whatever else people voted for in this midterm election — anger about inflation, anger about corruption, anger about the Iran war — they by and large didn’t vote to have the government take over health insurance,” said Jonathan Oberlander, a professor and healthcare reform expert at the University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill.
Still, supporters of universal healthcare see this moment as a once-in-a-generation opportunity because Americans are buckling under the weight of healthcare costs and are hungry for change. Several states, including Oregon, are already exploring what it would take to set up single-payer systems.
The affordability crisis “dominated this election, and Medicare for All speaks to that,” Oberlander said. Medicare for All supporters expect the policy agenda will gain major momentum heading into the 2028 Democratic presidential primaries, he said.
But more moderate Democrats may see the idea’s growing popularity as a threat to gains they made in states such as Iowa, Kansas, and South Carolina. “If Democrats want to hold those seats, which were very difficult to win, they’re probably not interested in passing Medicare for All,” Oberlander said. “That’s a huge political risk in red-leaning states. So just because Democrats have a majority doesn’t mean it’s a majority for Medicare for All.”
Previous Medicare for All proposals would have required getting millions of people to willingly give up their existing coverage, fueling unprecedented opposition from the healthcare industry, said Michael Cannon, a healthcare economist at the libertarian Cato Institute and a Medicare for All opponent.
“If Medicare for All actually had the price levels that Bernie Sanders and Abdul El-Sayed envision, the industry would tear it to shreds,” he said.
And even as voters say they support Medicare for All in greater numbers than in nearly a decade, support falters when they’re presented with common arguments against it — like it could lead to higher taxes or delays in treatment — according to a recent KFF poll.
Jaime Bardenhagen said she feels a little guilty about the idea of getting her healthcare coverage from the government. A former nurse in rural Leelanau County in northern Michigan, Bardenhagen has Parkinson’s and sialidosis, a rare genetic disease that can cause seizures.
Yet she “feels bad” about qualifying for disability benefits next year. Such programs were something she “didn’t believe in” while growing up on a farm, she said. You were supposed to work for what you needed, she said, not rely on government support. “And I did work as hard as I could, for as long as I could.”
But like millions of Americans, Bardenhagen and her husband saw their health insurance costs skyrocket this year, after enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies expired.
Their monthly premiums went from $700 to $1,300, with a deductible of $7,500. They started putting off medical tests her doctor wanted, she said. “We couldn’t afford that,” she said.
Her husband voted for Donald Trump in 2016, Bardenhagen said. This time, he stayed home. Bardenhagen, a Democrat, also considered sitting out the midterms. “I just don’t trust either party anymore,” she said.
Despite those misgivings, she says she supports Medicare for All. Her years as a nurse left her disillusioned with the current healthcare system, she said.
She felt the insurance companies, not doctors, were calling the shots, determining which prescriptions and procedures patients could receive. Wouldn’t it be fairer, she figured, if “good people” in government were making those calls? “So, absolutely, the government should take it over.”
That takeover is Cannon’s worst-case scenario. The libertarian economist said giving the federal government greater control over the healthcare system would only backfire. Patients would be left “in even more vulnerable positions, because they would be relying for their access to healthcare on government spending that is just not sustainable.”
Medicare for All supporters are naive to think the government could negotiate lower drug and healthcare prices by replacing private plans with a public one, he said. “Everyone knows that the industry is going to end up running the show, and that has been the case since they passed Medicare,” Cannon said.
For Bardenhagen, the message she wants Democrats to take from the midterms is simple: “Do something,” the former nurse said.

Democrats’ electoral sweep has shaken the ground beneath a permitting reform bill in Congress, raising doubts about whether the measure has enough support to advance in an initial Senate vote scheduled for Monday.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said on Thursday in a statement to POLITICO that he opposed the bipartisan bill in its current form, joining some fellow Democrats and environmental groups in raising concerns that the legislation would revise federal laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act.
Even before Jeffries’ statement, mounting evidence showed support for the bill was wavering.
The legislation, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, has support from business groups tied to renewable energy and fossil fuels. They tout its potential to reduce consumer energy costs by bringing new supplies online. The measure would ease regulatory barriers to build energy projects of just about every type—clean and dirty—and it would weaken the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act.
And a new report by Kevin Kircher, a mechanical engineering professor at Purdue University, attempts to quantify the proposal’s broader emissions consequences, identifying potential harms that previous analyses may have missed by examining only parts of the bill.
The Senate is scheduled to vote Monday on whether to begin debate on the bill. Its co-sponsors are Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.V.), Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Mike Lee (R-Utah) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.)
Lobbyist Chris Moyer, founder of Echo Communications Advisors, said Democrats’ overwhelming wins in the midterm elections have changed the landscape for the bill. He previously hoped Congress would pass it in the lame-duck session, which begins next week, but has since changed his mind.
“The numbers we’re looking at in the House and Senate are just massive and Democrats will have a ton of leverage,” Moyer said in an interview. He previously worked on Capitol Hill as an aide to the late Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid.
Republicans will control the House and Senate in the lame-duck session, but Democrats will have comfortable majorities when the 120th Congress begins in January. Democrats will soon have more clout to address crucial clean energy roadblocks, like long queues for interconnection to the electric grid, without the trade-offs currently in the legislation that could speed the building of fossil fuel infrastructure in sensitive areas, Moyer said.
“If there’s a way to address some of the concerns that are being raised from the environmental and public lands standpoint and from the Tribal standpoint, and also preserve a lot of the good things that have been negotiated already, that’s something it seems there should be interest in this Congress in working on,” Moyer said. “It can be part of the affordability agenda that the incoming majorities are going to focus on.”
Scott Segal, a longtime environmental policy expert with the Washington, D.C., law and lobbying firm Bracewell, which represents both fossil fuel and renewable energy interests, sees little chance that the legislation will pass by the end of the year.
“In a situation where one side has won a tremendous landslide, they are usually not set to do a lot of lame-duck production,” he said in a post-election webinar. “With something like permitting reform, the Democrats might rightly say that they’d like to negotiate their own version of it.”
Although it might be difficult to imagine Democrats finding common ground with Trump on the issues, Segal noted that some of the most significant U.S. environmental and energy laws have been enacted during periods of divided government in Washington: for example, the National Environmental Policy Act and the original Clean Air Act in 1970, the big Clean Air Act amendments in 1990, and the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007.
“When there’s a distribution of leverage, you can create the conditions for advancing legislation, provided that people on both sides of the aisle don’t let the perfect be the enemy of the good,” Segal said. “Almost every major environmental statute occurred under exactly these circumstances, with Dems controlling both houses of Congress and a strong Republican in the White House.”
Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.) said Wednesday that he is waiting to see an amendment drafted by the bill’s Senate co-sponsors before deciding whether he supports the legislation. The amendment, whose text has not been disclosed, responds to some of the objections, including that the bill may tie the hands of a future president’s ability to oppose projects.
“There were some pretty significant structural problems with the first version that came out,” Casten said in a conference call that primarily focused on election results.
Costs and Benefits
Kircher, the Purdue mechanical engineering professor, published his report on the bill this week, aiming to provide a more comprehensive assessment than previous analyses, which focused largely on the power sector provisions and overlooked other parts of the legislation with potential emissions implications.
Kircher built a model that calculates the bill’s potential effects, comparing a baseline of 2025 data with a hypothetical 2025 in which the measure was law. He found the bill would increase revenue and jobs in both fossil fuel and clean energy industries, with larger increases for fossil fuels. The bill also would likely increase energy-related greenhouse gas emissions and deaths attributable to air pollution from fossil fuels.
He weighed the trade-offs between negative effects, such as air pollution deaths, and positive ones, such as accelerating renewable energy construction. Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says.
He did not spell out whether it plans to stop making them entirely or shift production elsewhere, but did say the decision was to "make room" for building more of its self-driving Cybercab cars.
But the project's lead engineer, Wes Morrill, appeared to suggest the vehicle was being discontinued, writing on X: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab."
With its distinctive angular looks, the Cybertruck attracted diehard fans, but was beset by delays before being launched in 2023 and has had disappointing sales numbers since.
Tesla fans have been mourning the news online, with one person calling it "the best vehicle Tesla has ever made, external" as he lamented it being "discontinued next year".
Musk responded to the user, external with the word "true", adding: "But the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time."
The vehicle has always been a passion project for Musk. He said it was "way more awesome than people realise, external" in March, and called it the "best product Tesla has ever made to date, external" in April.
But there have always been big questions about whether consumers shared that view and whether the Cybertruck could cut through and earn a spot in the US' lucrative truck market.
It was not helped by inauspicious introduction to the public in 2019 when Musk attempted to show off the Cybertruck's apparently unbreakable glass, only for it to shatter during a live demonstration.
Despite the gaffe, the Cybertruck ended up receiving a 146,000 orders, Musk said in 2019, while it was still in development.
In the end, the vehicle launched in 2023, keeping its novel design - an angular shape with a body made of stainless steel.
Tesla fans praised its retro-futuristic look, which some said looked like something "straight out of Blade Runner, external".
But critics were far less kind, joking about its appearance and labelling it "ugly as sin, external".
Several recalls - including in 2025 affecting more than 46,000 Cybertrucks over concerns part of its trim could fall off - would not have helped.
And then there's the price.
"We need to make it at a price that people can afford," Musk told Wall Street analysts that year - which ended up being $61,000 (then Â£48,000) for all the "bells and whistles".
In 2026, the so-called "Cyberbeast" model comes in at $102,000.

FAIRFAX, Iowa—Nearly 50 people gathered at the American Legion Post on a July evening to learn about a proposed natural gas plant less than three miles from town. Seated in folding chairs, they pulled out their phones and typed responses to a simple question: How are you feeling?
The words “angry,” “disgusted” and “scared” flashed across a TV screen at the front of the room.
For many, the meeting drudged up a familiar feeling of frustration.
Nine months earlier, Interstate Power and Light, an Iowa-based subsidiary of Alliant Energy, had abandoned plans to build a natural gas-fired power plant in Fairfax after fierce opposition from residents and leaders at the nearby Eastern Iowa Airport.
But the reprieve was short-lived. In March, Alliant announced plans to instead purchase land just outside of town for a new plant.
The proposed 160-acre site is in unincorporated Linn County territory, right over the border from neighboring Benton County. The cities of Fairfax, Atkins and Cedar Rapids, home to a combined 140,000 residents, all fall within three miles of the proposed plant. The facilities’ 150-foot-tall exhaust towers would emit carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, particulate matter and volatile organic compounds.
From the podium at the American Legion, Jon Lee, a spokesperson for the grassroots group Save Morgan Valley, urged his neighbors to remain engaged with plans for the plant. “Big decisions like this deserve real answers,” Lee said. “Stay informed, and keep showing up.”
All summer long, the group mobilized opposition. Members invited neighbors to town halls, filed testimony with the Iowa Utilities Commission and presented a united front in matching orange shirts at county zoning commission and board of supervisor meetings.
Their persistence is paying off.
In October, the three-person Linn County Board of Supervisors voted unanimously to reject Alliant’s rezoning request for the proposed site, after nearly four hours of comments from residents and Alliant representatives.
Concerns raised by residents at the hearing spanned land use, water use and utility rates. But comments repeatedly returned to the projected emissions of the proposed plant.
“We’re living in an era of extraordinary technological advancement, and yet when it comes to powering that advancement we’re being told that building another fossil fuel power plant is the answer,” Jenny Kellison, of Fairfax, told the supervisors. “I find that incredibly disappointing.”
Supervisor Sami Scheetz voted against the rezoning request, arguing that Alliant’s proposal failed to meet county requirements for water and wastewater infrastructure. Still, he told Inside Climate News, the board’s decision reflected “overwhelming,” bipartisan community opposition to the plant being built.
“What was really important for me was a constituent just asking me, ‘Do you think this is good for the community?’ And I really didn’t feel comfortable saying yes to that,” Scheetz said.
According to Alliant’s filings with the Iowa Utilities Commission, the Morgan Valley Energy Center would consist of three single-cycle combustion turbines, designed to start up quickly during periods of high load demand. The application notes possible plans to expand to a combined-cycle facility in the future.
“We are disappointed with the Linn County Board of Supervisors’ decision not to approve the Morgan Valley Energy Center application,” Alliant wrote in a statement to Inside Climate News.
“We’re living in an era of extraordinary technological advancement, and yet when it comes to powering that advancement we’re being told that building another fossil fuel power plant is the answer.”
— Jenny Kellison, Fairfax resident
The proposed power plant “is critical to meeting growing energy demand and supporting the reliable electric service that customers and communities depend on,” the utility added. “Alliant Energy has decades of experience safely operating energy infrastructure under rigorous regulatory and environmental oversight.”
Single-cycle gas “peaker” plants are significantly less fuel-efficient than combined-cycle plants, resulting in higher carbon dioxide emissions per unit of power generated. The Morgan Valley Energy Center would produce roughly one and a half million tons of carbon dioxide equivalents each year, according to Alliant’s air construction permit application with the state Department of Natural Resources.
While Alliant has not directly linked the additional generation to multiple hyper-scale data centers under development in and around Cedar Rapids, several company representatives acknowledged during the October hearing that the data centers have driven load growth across their service area.
“Alliant Energy does not build generation to serve a single customer or industry,” said Ben Rogers, a senior community and public affairs specialist for Alliant and a former Linn County supervisor. “Data centers are an important source of new demand, but they are not the only reason the electric system must continue to evolve.”

22dd14344fab.text: Religious "nones" outnumbered white evangelicals by a stunning ten percentage points in the 2026 midterms electorate, up from just one point in 2024. Why it matters: The era of conservative white evangelicals dominating America's religious-political narrative faces a mathematical collapse. By the numbers: White evangelical or born-again Christians accounted for 17% of voters Tuesday, down from 23% in 2024 and 24% in 2022 , according to preliminary 2026 voter polling and earlier exit polls. Their Republican loyalty barely budged: 82% backed GOP House candidates, compared with 84% in 2024 and 83% in 2022. Religiously unaffiliated voters, known as "nones," accounted for 27% of the electorate Tuesday, compared with 24% in 2024. Their Democratic support climbed from 70% to 78%. What they're saying: "In most of those midwestern states, the white evangelicals are outnumbered in the population by the white mainline Protestants," Robert P. Jones, president and founder of the nonpartisan Public Religion Research Institute (PRRI), told Axios. Jones said their decline over roughly two decades extends beyond election results, with evangelical denominations losing millions of members. The big picture: White evangelical Protestants account for just 13% of American adults, down from 23% in 2006, according to PRRI's 2025 Census of American Religion . Yet they accounted for 17% of voters Tuesday, a larger share than their population footprint, though the surveys define the group differently. Religious "nones" now account for 28% of adults, up from 16% in 2006. Zoom in: Even Trump's most loyal religious supporters have cooled on his second term. His approval among white evangelical Protestants fell from 78% in early 2025 to 58% before the midterms, according to Pew Research Center . They remain the only major religious group Pew analyzed in which a majority approves of his performance. Between the lines: So far, the religious right's shrinking demographic footprint hasn't weakened its influence in Washington. Trump established a White House Faith Office and created a Justice Department task force to investigate anti-Christian bias.

cb8eb6265c35.text:
The Signal Interview
An 11-item menu board from the 1950s still hangs in McDonaldâs Chicago headquarters, recalling the era when Ray Kroc struck his franchise agreement with the McDonald brothers and began building the worldâs best known fast-food chain. The 10-cent root beers are long gone, but Chris Kempczinski, who marked his seventh anniversary as CEO this week, is having to pay new attention to its value proposition.
The business is facing a âchallengingâ US consumer environment, he told investors this week, with comparable sales falling 0.2% in the three months to September. Kempczinskiâs assurance that the company had started to turn things around in the last month of the quarter helped revive a stock that had fallen a jarring 32% between February and October. But to reverse the drop in customer visits, he has had to put more marketing dollars behind potentially slimmer-margin deals, like a $2 breakfast sandwich with free fries for loyalty program members.
âOur goal is straightforward,â Kempczinski told Wall Street: âCustomers should see a clear and compelling value proposition every time they consider McDonaldâs.â
Few companies see as many consumers each week as McDonaldâs does, and it has seen growing numbers of lower-income Americans staying home for breakfast or skipping it altogether, Kempczinski says in an interview for The CEO Signal.
âHousing, medical care, childcare, utilities, transport â all of those things are putting, I think, a lot of pressure on peopleâs disposable income,â he says.
McDonaldâs sometimes benefits in tough economic times, as higher-earning households trade down from pricier restaurants. But the US economyâs current âK-shapedâ nature means that wealthier households are still eating out in pricier restaurants, rather than trading down to eat burgers and fries.
Reserving the right to get smarter in a franchised system
Kempczinskiâs $8.5 billion game plan, announced in June and dubbed âMcDonaldâs > NEXT,â is the second strategic overhaul of his tenure. Designed to update the groupâs menu and modernize restaurants, he expects it to lift sales and margins by making McDonaldâs âmore customersâ first choice more often.â
The complication is that about 95% of the worldâs 46,000 McDonaldâs restaurants are owned and operated by franchisees â and some have pushed back against a proposal that could require $650,000 to $800,000 of investment per store.
There is tension in any business where customers want better value, franchisees want healthier returns, and shareholders want faster growth. McDonaldâs relies on its 5,000 independent partners to execute its strategy, Kempczinski notes, which means he must operate âthrough influence, not through direct control.â
A clear focus on growth can unite his disparate stakeholders, he believes. âIf you have growth and the pie is expanding, itâs amazing how harmonious everything is,â he says. âWhen the pie isnât growing, then everybody starts to think about their share â¦ and then a system can turn on itself.â
Restaurant upgrades are essential for driving that growth, he says, because âyou canât sell a $5 burger in a $1 lobby.â But he knows he canât influence franchisees who think heâs not listening to them, and he says the headline number McDonaldâs put on its proposals âfor sure is going to get knocked downâ in response to their feedback.
He wonât be so âdogmaticâ about the details of his strategy that he wonât learn from their feedback, he says. âWe have a saying here at McDonaldâs: We reserve the right to get smarter.â
This week, he told analysts he feels âoverall, goodâ about franchiseesâ willingness to roll out the upgrades his strategic plan requires.
Changing a risk-averse culture through âpositive shamingâ
Kempczinski, who grew up in a Catholic household in Cincinnati and would visit McDonaldâs after Friday night football games, admits to some Midwestern conservatism. When he was invited to pick art for his office from the McDonaldâs archive, he chose an all-American Norman Rockwell painting.
But the former Procter & Gamble brand executive says he balances those instincts with a restlessness that he is trying to bring to McDonaldâs. âThe company is never going to go faster than the pace that the CEO sets,â he says, and he is pushing people to take more risks and make faster decisions.
McDonaldâs is âawesomeâ at testing new offerings and ideas, Kempczinski says, by way of example. With thousands of restaurants, âwe can do A/B testing forever â¦ but you can also test for too long.â The danger in a collaborative culture like at McDonaldâs is that âeverybody owns it and nobody owns it,â he observes. âYes, we all need to work together, but at the end of the day, there needs to be a person or a group whoâs actually held accountable for the results.â
A CEO can do that by appointing people to senior positions who model the behavior they want others to adopt, he says. And, instead of shaming people for their mistakes, he believes âpositive shamingâ â praising top performers who set the right example â gets better results.
The lessons of a Big Arch and a little bite
McDonaldâs menu now ranges from Cookie Butter Iced Coffee to the Red Bull Dragonberry Energizer drink, and includes far more chicken than it once did. Demand for chicken has been surging for several years, and the home of the Big Mac already sells more of it than KFC or Chick-fil-A.
But Kempczinski sees âa lot of headroomâ to sell more still, he says, with a push to add KFC-style breaded chicken to the menu. McDonaldâs already commands more than 40% of the beef business in its 10 biggest markets, amounting to about $50 billion, he explains â but it has only 20% of the $130 billion chicken market. His strategy is about more than building on the power of McNuggets and McCrispy Strips, he says. âItâs just simple math.â

Somalia's Supreme Court has ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud unlawfully extended his term, escalating a political crisis and a standoff between the presidency and judiciary.
Thursday's ruling came a day after Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed - a move which the court said the president lacked the authority to take.
The court also ordered political leaders to agree on an electoral plan within 30 days and hold elections within 90 days, potentially disrupting government plans for nationwide polls next year.
Mohamud's four-year mandate expired in May, but his administration extended it by a year through law changes approved by parliament in March.
Opposition groups accuse him of using the constitutional changes to prolong his rule.
But the president insists the reforms are necessary to move Somalia towards fully democratic elections, replacing the clan-based system in which elders pick their representatives.
Somalia last held nationwide direct elections in 1969 and has been wracked by civil war for more than 30 years, with Islamist militant group al-Shabaab controlling many rural areas.
On Thursday, the Supreme Court ruled that the constitutional changes could not be applied retrospectively to the president's current term.
In a separate decision, the court declared the chief justice's dismissal "null and void", accusing the presidency of interfering with judicial independence.
The president appointed Ibrahim Idle Suleiman, who previously held the position, to replace Ahmed.
The presidency said the dismissal followed complaints about the administration of justice and was intended to achieve a just and transparent judiciary.
But the court rejected that explanation, insisting that the chief justice could only be removed through established constitutional procedures.
Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed welcomed the court ruling, saying "the country is facing a grave political crisis", calling on Mohamud to embrace a consensus-based approach.
The confrontation escalated on Thursday when former Prime Minister Hassan Ali Khaire accused the president of deploying security forces to the Supreme Court and attempting to arrest its chief justice.
Khaire accused the president of launching an "assault on the Supreme Court", according to the AFP news agency.
"Somalia stands at a dangerous juncture. The dismantling of our judiciary is a direct threat to the rule of law," he said.
AFP said it could not independently verify the reported security deployment, although photographs circulating in Somali media appeared to show armed personnel inside the court compound.
The rulings have thrown Somalia's electoral timetable into uncertainty.
The electoral commission has scheduled parliamentary elections for 15 April 2027 and a presidential vote a month later, but opposition groups and the regional administrations of Puntland and Jubaland reject the timetable.
Mohamud has called for national talks from 14 to 18 November to resolve the deadlock, but opposition leaders have questioned his legitimacy to convene the discussions.
The political turmoil comes as Somalia continues to battle al-Shabaab, which controls large parts of the countryside despite years of military operations.
Uganda, the largest contributor of troops to the African Union mission fighting the militants, announced this week that it planned to withdraw its forces by the end of the year, adding to concerns about Somalia's security.

Newer defense companies should prepare for potential Congressional anti-corruption probes and examine ties to the Trump administration before the new Democrat-led Congress goes into session next year, said Kristina Moore, a partner with Womble Bond Dickinson law firm in Washington, D.C.
Companies should take stock of their board and think about “preparedness,” which means “understanding what oversight is and is not,” Moore, who was previously a Congressional investigator and has advised clients undergoing such probes, told Defense One. “There is a lot of uniqueness to this space.”
How Congress handles privileged communications can be a common surprise, she said.
“Congress's position is that common law privileges, attorney-client privilege, work product privilege—they recognize that at their discretion. And so that's going to be surprising, where a lot of general counsels might be under the operating assumption that ‘that's a privileged conversation [because] I was in the room, outside counsel was in the room. That's privileged, right?’ That might not be the case,” Moore said, adding that it’s important for companies to understand how Congress works, what they’re looking for, and the tools they use.
“If you get a letter from Congress, generally there's a two week timeline—and that's actually if Congress is being generous. That's a very short clock to respond to before pressure goes up in terms of threatening the compulsory process or actually implementing the compulsory process.”
Moore said the hot topics ripe for Congressional investigation are Iran, Venezuela—including boat strikes to curb alleged drug imports to the U.S.—and AI policy and use.
“That is in the zone of great interest. And then the question is: Are you in that zone? Do you have any interesting information? Were there any talks with the president?” she said. “Definitely now is a time to take and assess what your risk is and how do you organize the business around that risk in order to navigate what may come.”
Welcome
You’ve reached the Defense Business Brief, where we dig into what the Pentagon buys, who they’re buying from, and why. Send along your tips, feedback, and song recommendations to lwilliams@defenseone.com. Check out the Defense Business Brief archive here, and tell your friends to subscribe!
Zooming in on foreign military sales. The Trump administration has pushed for more foreign military sales, and ushered in reforms last year. That could lead to more scrutiny in 2027 with Democrats leading Congress, said Shaun McDougall, lead defense analyst for Forecast International, a sister brand of Defense One.
- “The administration has been very open with trying to push or get sales as high as possible. And so you have maybe more controversial deals with places like Saudi Arabia or Turkey, where Democrats might try to put up some roadblocks,” he said.
- “Those are things that could also impact U.S. companies…from high-end stuff like the F-35, to munitions, to smaller components.”
Could demand for some military equipment stay relatively level? It’s possible, McDougall said: “Things like the Iran war, aid to Ukraine—there's some overlapping requirements with both of those that could impact acquisition and contractors.”
- “Demand for missile defense, [counterdrone] capabilities, low-cost interceptors, low-cost munitions. There's demand for that type of stuff…but depending on how those conflicts proceed and how the U.S. approaches it could impact near-term demand.”
One company’s ‘blue wave’ outlook: Bipartisan work on the Hill should prevail.
- “The push to modernize and equip the military has support on both sides of the aisle. The next Congress can continue making headway to find new defense technology,” Ben Kesling, Chariot Defense’s government relations head, told Defense One via email.
- “A unit operating at the edge still needs weaponry, comms, sensors, [command and control], and power, whoever chairs the committee in January. The next Congress will have hard debates over budgets and policy, but getting affordable, durable capabilities into the hands of American troops has already drawn support from both parties…That work should carry forward.”
In Hawaii last week, the Defense Information Systems Agency completed its Olympus Fires exercise alongside foreign partners and military components in the Pacific, with the goal of everyone using the same digital environment to share the data needed to find and precisely shoot a target.
- “To bring those teams together in a common environment with common data to deliver those capabilities—that was the demonstration we were able to deliver. No swivel chair,” said Col. Michael Hlad, commander of DISA’s Pacific regional field command.
- For example, a Marine Corps Air Naval Gunfire Liaison Company, or ANGLICO, team was able to locate and pinpoint a target that could then be “executed by a Canadian shooter,” Hlad told Defense One following his TechNet Indo-Pacific session.
- Being able to take data, share it to locate and track and fire on a target “all in the same environment, is something we haven't been able to demonstrate before,” he said.
- A full analysis is pending, but one early takeaway was “a clear understanding of what's capable from a coalition environment” and a plan to expand the series to evaluate other areas, including logistics and maneuver, Hlad said.
- Related: GDIT’s Vion Edge was also tested during the exercise to demonstrate “a tactical kit that provides all of your core [mission partner environment] services…when a network may go down temporarily,” Jason Myers, vice president of defense agencies for GDIT, told Defense One. For example: “We had one military service [where] their network had gone down. They moved all their logs onto our platform and used our AI capability to diagnose and identify what needed to be fixed…to be able to get it back up within a matter of hours.”

Iran appears to be undertaking significant new construction near at least two of its major missile sites and repairing bases damaged by months of US and Israeli air strikes, analysis of satellite images suggests.
Evidence of digging and new buildings are visible in satellite imagery taken in November at the Garmdareh military base in Karaj near the capital Tehran and the Shahroud base in the north, analysts at British intelligence company MAIAR, who reviewed the photos, told BBC Verify.
At least 12 other military sites, including missile complexes and air bases, appear to show signs of repairs. New roofs have been built on destroyed buildings at the Kermanshah missile base in western Iran, near the border with Iraq, while damaged buildings and debris have been cleared at the Parchin military complex - which has been repeatedly repaired despite a succession of air strikes - east of the capital.
The excavations near Shahroud could potentially be related to the production of missiles, said Jim Lamson, a former CIA analyst who focused on Iran. He said that because the nearby air base at Shahroud has been targeted multiple times in recent years, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) is probably trying to find ways to move its production facilities underground.
A MAIAR analyst said that Iran has "a pattern of moving infrastructure underground to protect them from further strikes". Mark Mellett, a defence analyst and former head of the Irish military, said the construction of underground facilities had the added benefit of making it "harder for outside observers to assess the extent and operational status".
Speculation has mounted in recent weeks that the US could resume attacks on Iran after the midterm elections held earlier this week. But on Wednesday Vice-President JD Vance cited the war's unpopularity with voters for the Republicans' poor performance in this week's poll, saying that it may have cost his party control of the Senate "for the next 6 years".
At multiple bases across the country, Iranian forces have focused on carrying-out small-scale repairs to complexes which have been heavily damaged by air strikes since the start of the US-Israeli war.
Analysts said that satellite images appear to show that significant construction has been completed at the Taleghan 2 facility at the Parchin military complex, with damaged buildings levelled and the aftermath of attacks on an underground bunker repaired and reinforced with concrete.
At Karaj and Shahroud, satellite images appear to show significant excavation. At Karaj, multiple vehicles were visible in satellite images, while improvements appear to have been carried out to the nearby airbase.
The images from Karaj appear to show "a new portal for an underground facility", said Sam Lair, research analyst at the Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI), which has looked extensively into recent developments at Iranian sites.
Analysis from Janes also indicates there appears to be a new facility under construction at Karaj, including tunnel entrances and structures which could indicate an expansion of nearby damaged or destroyed missile bases - or could also be for storage or other purposes.
The construction work is unlikely to be part of an effort to deceive foreign intelligence agencies, said Janes analyst Sean O'Connor. He said such a project "would be costly and may achieve little".
The developments come after repeated assurances from the White House that US-Israeli attacks have depleted the Iranian armed forces, which US President Donald Trump dismissed as a "complete and total mess".
A Pentagon spokesperson previously said that the US had "destroyed up to 90% of Iran's drone, ballistic missile, and naval industrial base" and "significantly degraded" the country's ability to launch drone and missile attacks.
But Iran claims it retains large stockpiles of missiles, and footage broadcast on state TV this week claimed to show dozens of missiles at the entrance to an underground facility in southern Iran. Back in August, state TV footage also claimed to show Khordad surface-to-air missiles emerging out of a tunnel near the southern city of Bandar Abbas.
A MAIAR analyst also identified new construction and excavations outside tunnel entrances near the city of Qom, close to the Fordo underground uranium enrichment complex, which has been bombed by both the US and Israel multiple times.
Activity related to military assets would show that Tehran is bracing itself for further attacks by the US and Israel, said Mark Cancian, a military analyst with International Security Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).
"The purpose is to better defend itself against future attacks," he said. "It also indicates a priority on rebuilding military capability rather than rehabilitating the economy."
Additional reporting by Barbara Metzler.

Macau has sentenced an ex-lawmaker and pro-democracy campaigner to 12 years and six months' jail in the city's first national security case.
Following a closed-door trial, Au Kam San, 69, was convicted on Friday of "subversion against the political power of the state", among other offences.
His wife Virginia Cheang condemned the ruling, calling the case a "groundless persecution designed to humiliate Au".
Macau was handed back to China in 1999, ending over 400 years of Portuguese administration. Its national security law came into effect in 2009, criminalising acts of treason, secession, and subversion against the Chinese Communist Party.
The law was revised in 2023, broadening its scope to include non-violent acts of secession, and again this year, to allow for trials to be held behind closed doors.
Prosecutors had accused Au of assisting and collaborating with "external hostile organisations" by collecting, preparing and disseminating information that was "manifestly filled with political claims of a subversive nature against the state".
These took place "over a long period of time", the prosecutors claim.
Au was arrested in July 2025 and later charged with three counts of subverting the state's power, three counts of endangering national security by establishing contact with foreign organisations, and one count of breach of confidentiality.
He was found guilty of four of the seven charges following a three-day trial which ended in September. A judge had ordered that the trial be held behind closed doors "to ensure that no prejudice is caused to the interests of national security".
Macau's authorities never publicly disclosed the details of the case. Au's family had earlier told the media Au was not allowed to seek his own legal representation and had instead been assigned a lawyer by the court.
Au's wife Cheang said she hoped authorities would grant her and her family permission to regularly write to and visit Au in prison.
"I dare not hope for more as I believe that will only lead to greater disappointment," she said in an open letter on Friday.
Au, who was formerly a primary school teacher, was elected to the Legislative Assembly in September 2001. For 20 years, he served as one of only a handful of pro-democracy lawmakers in the legislature, largely made up of pro-Beijing loyalists.
Au had co-organised annual vigils in Macau to commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing.
These vigils were previously tolerated in places like Macau and Hong Kong, but have effectively been banned in both cities since China imposed a sweeping national security law on Hong Kong in 2020.
Au's jailing comes a day after Hong Kong sentenced Joshua Wong, the face of its now-quashed democracy movement, to 10 years in jail. Wong, 30, whose activism started when he was just a teen, has been in custody for the last six years.

One of the UK's smallest accredited zoos is celebrating after "extra special" pied tamarin twins were born at the site.
Shaldon Wildlife Trust, in Devon, said the critically endangered twins were born on 29 September to mum Bobby and dad Pedra. Its director, Zak Showell, said it was a "challenge" to breed the species.
The trust said the animals were among the most endangered primates in South America. Bosses said the infants were "thriving" and had started to hitch rides on their parents' backs as they explored their habitat.
Showell said: "For a zoo of our size to achieve this and to be one of just two European zoos to manage it this year is an unbelievable proud moment for our small team."
"It has been an incredible year for births here at Shaldon, but these twins are extra special," he said.
"Pied tamarins are exceptionally delicate animals, and breeding them successfully is a challenge."
The trust said the primates required "stress-free environments and specialist care".
It said zoo keepers intentionally kept the news of the arrivals under wraps for a few weeks to give the "delicate family complete peace and quiet".
The species is listed as critically endangered on the International Union of Conservation and Nature's (IUCN) Red List.
The zoo said, in the wild, they were restricted to "a shrinking pocket of rainforest" around Manaus, Brazil.
